summary: The yoke walk is a strongman event where you carry a heavy, free-standing frame loaded with weight across your shoulders and back, walking it forward for a set distance. Because the load sits across your whole back instead of in your hands, it demands total-body stability on top of raw leg strength. It suits lifters who already squat and carry weight confidently and want a test of strength, balance, and grit under a heavy, awkward load.
whyItWorks: The yoke frame sits across your upper back similar to a loaded squat bar, so your quads drive each step the same way they'd drive a squat, but you're doing it while moving instead of standing in one spot. Because the frame is a rigid, free-standing structure rather than a barbell you control with your hands, any shift in the weight transfers straight into your torso, which is why your abdominals, lower back, and hip muscles (your abductors and adductors) have to brace hard with every step to keep the frame from tipping. Your calves, hamstrings, and glutes work through each stride the same way they would in a loaded walk, just under a heavier, less forgiving load than a normal carry.
setup: Load the yoke frame with a weight you can lift off the rack and walk with confidently.
Position yourself under the frame so the crossbar sits across your upper back and shoulders, the same spot as a loaded squat bar.
Stand up fully to lift the frame off the rack before taking your first step.
Brace your core hard before you start walking, not after you've already taken a step.
execution: Take short, quick steps rather than long strides once the frame is lifted.
Keep your torso upright and your eyes forward, not down at your feet.
Walk the full marked distance without setting the frame down.
Keep your steps even and controlled, especially if the frame starts to sway.
Set the frame down under control at the finish line rather than dropping it.
Reset and brace again before any additional attempts.
formCues: Short, quick steps beat long strides under this load.
Brace your core before you lift, not mid-stride.
Keep your eyes up and forward the whole walk.
Let your hips and knees absorb each step, don't lock them out.
breathing: Take a big brace and breath right before you lift the frame, then breathe in short bursts between steps rather than holding your breath for the whole distance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking long strides that let the heavy frame sway side to side.
commonMistakes.correction: Shorten your steps so each one is quick and controlled, which keeps the frame's momentum from building up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking down at your feet instead of straight ahead.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your eyes on a point ahead of you; looking down shifts your weight forward and makes the frame harder to control.

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading more weight than you can lift off the rack and walk confidently with on your first attempt.
commonMistakes.correction: Test a lift-off with the loaded frame before committing to a full walk; if you can't stand up with it cleanly, reduce the weight.

programmingNotes: This is a maximally demanding full-body carry under a heavy, unstable load, so one yoke session every one to two weeks is enough; it's closer to a max-effort lift than a conditioning drill.
Two to four short, heavy walks of 15 to 20 meters, with full rest between each one, covers a complete session.
Treat it as the main event of a strongman-style training day rather than something you tack onto the end of a regular squat or deadlift session.
Build up distance and weight separately: master a shorter distance with a given load before extending the walk, rather than increasing both at once.
safetyNotes: Confirm you can lift the loaded frame off the rack cleanly before attempting a full walk; struggling with the initial lift under an unstable load is a common way to get hurt.
Have a clear, obstacle-free path for the full walking distance before you start.
Set the frame down under control the moment it starts to sway beyond what you can manage, rather than trying to fight it back to center.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for a yoke walk?
faq.answer: Start with a weight you can lift off the rack and walk 10 to 15 meters with confidently before you try anything heavier. The unstable, shifting load makes this feel much heavier than the same weight on a squat bar.

faq.question: Can I do a yoke walk without strongman equipment?
faq.answer: A farmer's walk with heavy dumbbells or a loaded trap bar trains a similar carry-and-stabilize pattern if a yoke frame isn't available, though the load sits in your hands instead of across your back.

faq.question: Yoke walk vs farmer's walk, what's the difference?
faq.answer: A farmer's walk holds weight in your hands at your sides, which challenges your grip along with your legs and core. The yoke walk puts the load across your back like a squat, so it leans harder on your legs and your ability to keep a heavy, shifting frame balanced over your base.

faq.question: Why does the yoke feel so much heavier than the same weight squatted?
faq.answer: A free-standing frame isn't fixed in place the way a barbell in a rack is, so every step you take lets the weight shift slightly, and your core and hips have to correct for that shift constantly. That constant stabilizing work is what makes a given weight feel heavier to walk with than to squat.

alternatives.name: Sled Push
alternatives.reason: Trains similar full-body leg drive and bracing under heavy resistance using a sled instead of a loaded frame, useful when yoke equipment isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Farmer's Walk
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the loaded-walking pattern but holds the weight in your hands instead of across an unstable frame on your back, a far less technical entry into carries.

summary: The Bradford press, also called a rocky press, is a barbell shoulder exercise where you press the bar just above your head and alternate tapping it near the back of your neck and near your forehead, without ever locking your elbows out. It builds shoulder strength under continuous tension and suits lifters looking for a change of pace from a standard overhead press, particularly ones who want to avoid a hard, straight-arm lockout.
whyItWorks: A normal overhead press gives your shoulders a brief rest at lockout, where your elbows and the bar's weight line up and the muscles can relax for a beat. The Bradford press removes that rest point entirely by keeping the bar moving between two positions just above your head, so your front and rear deltoids and your triceps stay under load for the whole set. Alternating the direction the bar travels also works both the front and back portions of the deltoid across a single rep instead of just the front, which is where most of the load lands on a standard press.
setup: Set a barbell in a rack at upper-chest height, or have a spotter hand it to you.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it to your upper chest.
Stand or sit tall with your core braced before the first rep.
execution: Press the bar up and slightly back until it clears the top of your head near your neck, without touching it.
Without pausing at the top, reverse direction and lower the bar forward.
Press it back up in front until it clears your forehead, again without touching it.
Keep alternating between the two positions in a smooth, continuous rhythm for the set.
formCues: Never let the bar touch your head, clear it by a couple of inches.
Move at a controlled pace, this isn't a fast lift.
Keep your core braced so your ribs don't flare as you press.
Let your elbows travel a natural path instead of forcing them out wide.
breathing: Take a breath and brace before you start the set, then breathe in short exhales at each direction change rather than holding your breath through the whole rep sequence.

commonMistakes.mistake: Locking the elbows out fully at either end of the movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop just short of lockout in both directions so the shoulders never get a break, that continuous tension is the entire point of the exercise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar drift too far forward or back and losing balance.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the range of motion tight, just enough to clear your head, and use a lighter weight than you would on a straight overhead press until you've got the path dialed in.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using leg drive or a backward lean to move the bar.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hips and knees still and let the shoulders and triceps do the pressing, save leg drive for a push press instead.

programmingNotes: This is best treated as an accessory shoulder movement rather than your main press for the week, since the constant tension makes even light loads feel demanding fast.
Use lighter weight than your usual overhead press and moderate reps of eight to twelve, placed after a heavier pressing exercise in the session.
Once a week is plenty if you're already doing a heavier press earlier in the same workout, since both movements load the same shoulder muscles.
safetyNotes: This asks for decent shoulder mobility, so stop and switch to a standard press if you feel pinching at the front of the shoulder.
Use a weight noticeably lighter than your regular overhead press until the back-and-forth path feels controlled.
Have a spotter or a rack nearby the first few times you try it, since the moving bar path is less forgiving than a straight press if you lose control.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for Bradford presses?
faq.answer: Less than your regular overhead press. The moving bar path and the lack of a lockout rest make even a modest weight feel heavier than the number on the bar suggests.

faq.question: Are Bradford presses safe for people with shoulder issues?
faq.answer: Some lifters use them specifically because they avoid a hard lockout, but they still ask for good shoulder mobility. Stop and switch to a different press if you feel any pinching at the front of the shoulder.

faq.question: What's the difference between a Bradford press and a regular overhead press?
faq.answer: A regular press moves the bar in one direction to a full lockout overhead. A Bradford press moves the bar back and forth just above your head between two positions, with your elbows never fully locking out.

faq.question: Can I do this without a barbell?
faq.answer: The back-and-forth path is built around a straight bar. A standard dumbbell shoulder press is a better substitute if you don't have a barbell available.

faq.question: Is the Bradford press a good exercise for beginners?
faq.answer: It's manageable once you're already comfortable pressing overhead, since the real challenge is controlling the bar path rather than moving heavy weight. If you're brand new to overhead pressing, build up on a standard press first and add this in as a lighter accessory once your shoulders are used to the pattern.

alternatives.name: Standing Bradford Press
alternatives.reason: Same alternating press pattern done strictly standing, useful if you don't have a rack set up for the seated version.

alternatives.name: Barbell Shoulder Press
alternatives.reason: A standard barbell press with a full lockout, a good substitute when you want overhead loading without the back-and-forth bar path.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
easierVariations.reason: Drops the alternating front-and-back bar path for a straight overhead press, so you can build pressing strength and shoulder control before adding the trickier positioning.

harderVariations.name: Push Press
harderVariations.reason: Adds leg drive to the overhead push once your shoulders handle continuous tension well, letting you move heavier loads overhead.

summary: The hang clean starts with the barbell held at thigh or knee height instead of on the floor, then drives it up in one explosive pull before catching it across your front shoulders. Starting from the hang removes the first pull off the floor, letting you focus entirely on hip extension and the catch, which makes it a common way to build clean technique and explosive power for lifters who already have a floor clean or deadlift under them.
whyItWorks: Beginning the movement from the hang isolates the second pull, the explosive hip extension that generates most of the bar speed in a full clean, without the technical demands of pulling from the floor first. That makes it easier to groove a fast, aggressive hip extension and a clean catch position, both of which carry directly over to the full clean. The shortened range also means less total fatigue per rep than a floor clean, so you can train the explosive pull pattern more often without accumulating as much wear.
setup: Set the bar at thigh height, either from a rack or by deadlifting it up to that position.
Grip the bar just outside your legs, using a hook grip if you have one.
Stand tall with your shoulders slightly over the bar and a soft bend in your knees.
Brace your core before you start the downward hinge into the hang.
execution: Push your hips back to lower the bar to just above or below your knees.
Reverse direction and extend your hips explosively, driving the bar upward.
Finish the pull with a hard shrug and a rise onto your toes.
Pull yourself down and under the bar, rotating your elbows around and forward.
Catch the bar across your front shoulders, dropping into a quarter or full squat depending on the weight.
Stand fully upright to complete the rep.
formCues: Bar stays close to your legs on the way down and up.
Hips finish the pull, not your arms.
Elbows whip around fast into the catch.
Land the catch with your chest up and heels down.
breathing: Brace and hold your breath through the drop into the hang and the pull, then exhale once you're standing tall with the bar racked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping into the hang too low, past the knees, before starting the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the hang position at or just above the knees unless you're specifically training the below-the-knees variation; a lower hang changes the pull mechanics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms before the hips have fully extended.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your arms straight until your hips and knees lock out; let the bar's upward speed come from your legs and hips first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the bar too low, letting it rest on the wrists instead of the shoulders.
commonMistakes.correction: Whip your elbows around and up quickly as you drop under the bar so it settles across your front shoulders, not your forearms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting the pull from the hang too slowly, treating it like a deadlift instead of an explosive movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the initial hinge into the hang controlled, but commit to maximum speed the moment you reverse direction and start the pull; a slow start here just means less bar speed by the top.

programmingNotes: This is a technical, explosive barbell movement, so once a week as your main pulling exercise is a sound default unless you're deliberately spreading lighter technique volume across more sessions.
Program it early in a session while you're fresh; bar speed and catch timing both degrade quickly once you're fatigued.
Sets of 2 to 4 reps at a weight you can catch cleanly every time keep the movement sharp, since this isn't an exercise that benefits from grinding out high reps.

Reset your hang position for every rep rather than bouncing straight into the next pull from the catch; resetting keeps the movement pattern honest instead of letting momentum cover for a sloppy start.
safetyNotes: If you can't consistently catch the bar in a stable front-rack position, drop the weight and rebuild the catch before adding load back.

Learn the movement with an empty bar or light weight and, ideally, a coach's eyes on your technique before loading it heavily; the fast bar path makes bad habits harder to self-correct than in a slow lift.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for hang cleans?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of 2 to 4 reps at a weight you can catch cleanly every time is a common starting structure. Quality of each rep matters more than pushing for higher reps.

faq.question: What's the difference between a hang clean and a regular clean?
faq.answer: A regular clean starts from the floor and includes the first pull off the ground. A hang clean starts with the bar already at thigh or knee height, skipping that first pull and focusing entirely on the explosive second pull and catch.

faq.question: Can I do hang cleans without a barbell?
faq.answer: A kettlebell hang clean trains the same pull-and-catch pattern one arm at a time, and a dumbbell clean works as a lower-technical-demand option while you learn the timing.

faq.question: Why do my wrists hurt when I catch a hang clean?
faq.answer: That usually means the bar is landing on your wrists instead of resting across your shoulders. Focus on whipping your elbows up and forward faster during the catch so your shoulders, not your wrists, take the weight.

alternatives.name: Kettlebell Hang Clean
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hang-to-catch pattern one arm at a time with a kettlebell, useful if a barbell or platform isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Clean Pull
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same explosive hip extension and shrug without the catch, useful for building the pull before adding the timing demands of racking the bar.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Clean
easierVariations.reason: Teaches the same hang-position pull-and-catch pattern with dumbbells, lower technical demand while you build the timing.

harderVariations.name: Clean
harderVariations.reason: Starts the pull from the floor instead of the hang, adding the first-pull phase and a longer range once the hang position feels automatic.

summary: The one-arm flat bench dumbbell flye lies you on a flat bench and sweeps a single dumbbell out and back in a wide arc, isolating one pec at a time instead of pressing with both arms together. It's a chest isolation move that lets you feel and fix a strength gap between sides, since one arm can't borrow help from the other.
whyItWorks: A flye keeps your elbow at a fairly fixed bend and moves the weight through an arc rather than a straight push, which puts more of the load directly on the chest fibers stretching across your ribcage instead of splitting it with the triceps the way a press does. Doing it one arm at a time also forces your torso to stay still against the slight rotational pull of the dumbbell, so your core gets some quiet extra work while the chest handles the main movement.
setup: Lie flat on a bench with your feet planted on the floor.
Hold a single dumbbell above your chest with your arm slightly bent, palm facing in.
Rest your free hand on your stomach or on the bench for a stable base.
Keep your shoulder blades pulled back and down against the bench before the first rep.
execution: Lower the dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc, keeping the slight bend in your elbow constant.
Stop when you feel a stretch across your chest, roughly level with the bench.
Reverse the arc, sweeping the dumbbell back up and in toward the center of your chest.
Keep your torso still throughout; don't let the working arm pull your shoulder off the bench.
Squeeze your chest briefly at the top before starting the next rep.
Finish your reps on one side before switching arms.
formCues: Arc, don't press.
Keep the elbow bend fixed the whole way.
Stop the stretch at shoulder level, not lower.
Torso stays flat on the bench.
breathing: Inhale as the dumbbell lowers out to the side, exhale as you sweep it back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending and straightening the elbow during the rep, turning the flye into a one-arm press.
commonMistakes.correction: Lock in a slight elbow bend at the start and keep it constant through the whole arc.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lowering the dumbbell too far past shoulder level.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent once you feel a solid chest stretch; going lower strains the shoulder joint without adding benefit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the working shoulder lift off the bench to reach further.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep both shoulder blades pinned to the bench and shorten the range if you need to lift to complete it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a dumbbell too heavy to control through the full arc.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can move smoothly through the whole range without jerking at the bottom.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps per arm suit this well, since it's a single-joint isolation move rather than a heavy compound lift.
Because it's isolation work with light to moderate loads, most people can fit it in two or three times a week without extra soreness carrying over.
Place it after your main pressing work in a session; the shoulder stretch it demands is easier to control once you're already warmed up.
Increase reps toward 15 before adding weight; the stretch position is where fatigue shows up first.
safetyNotes: Choose a lighter dumbbell than you'd press; the stretched-out shoulder position carries more strain than pressing does.
Stop the descent well before you feel any pinching at the front of the shoulder.

faq.question: How many reps of the one-arm dumbbell flye should I do?
faq.answer: Ten to 15 reps per arm for two or three sets works well, since it's an isolation move meant for lighter, controlled loads.

faq.question: Can I do this flye without a bench?
faq.answer: You can perform it lying on the floor, though the range at the bottom will be shorter since the floor stops your arm sooner than a bench does.

faq.question: One-arm flye vs regular two-arm dumbbell flye, which should I pick?
faq.answer: The two-arm version is the standard choice for most chest days. The one-arm version is worth adding when you want to isolate a side that feels weaker or less engaged.

faq.question: Why does my shoulder hurt during dumbbell flyes?
faq.answer: It's usually the dumbbell dropping too low or too heavy a weight pulling the shoulder past a safe stretch. Shorten the range and lighten the load until the discomfort clears.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Flyes
alternatives.reason: Trains both sides of the chest at once with the same arcing motion, useful if balancing the effort side to side isn't a priority today.

easierVariations.name: Machine Pec Fly
easierVariations.reason: The machine fixes the path for you, which is a gentler way to learn the arcing motion before you control it freehand with a dumbbell.

summary: The lower back curl is a small, controlled movement where you tilt your pelvis to lift your lower back slightly off the floor, using your lower abdominals rather than momentum. It's less a stretch than a way to feel and switch on the deep abdominal contraction that a lot of people never notice during bigger core exercises. Because the range is tiny and the load is only your own bodyweight, it works well as a warm-up or as a way to reconnect with your core before harder ab work.
whyItWorks: Tilting your pelvis backward, so your lower back flattens and then curls slightly off the floor, is driven by your lower abdominal fibers rather than your hip flexors, which is why this movement stays gentle even though it looks similar to exercises that can strain the neck or hips. Keeping the motion small and slow means your abs have to hold the contraction rather than swing through it, which builds the kind of core control that shows up in bigger lifts later.
setup: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Rest your arms by your sides, palms down.
Let your lower back settle into its natural, slightly arched position before you begin.
execution: Tighten your lower abs to tilt your pelvis backward, flattening your lower back against the floor.
Continue the tilt until your tailbone curls slightly up off the floor.
Hold the curled position for a second or two, keeping your hips and shoulders still.
Release slowly, letting your lower back and tailbone return to the floor.
Repeat the tilt and release for the set without rushing between reps.
formCues: Move from the pelvis, not the legs.
Keep the lift small and slow.
Feel it low in your abs, not in your neck.
Breathe normally through the hold.
breathing: Exhale as you curl your lower back up, inhale as you release back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pushing through the feet to force the hips up, turning the curl into a small bridge.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your feet relaxed on the floor and let the lift come from tightening your lower abs alone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps so the movement becomes a bounce instead of a controlled curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down and hold the curled position for a beat before releasing, so your abs actually do the holding.

programmingNotes: This is gentle enough to do daily, either as part of a warm-up or as a short core activation drill before other ab work.
Two or three sets of 10 to 15 slow reps is plenty; more reps done fast won't add much once the movement stops feeling controlled.
It pairs well right before a bigger ab exercise like a reverse crunch, so your lower abs are already switched on.
safetyNotes: Keep the range small; this isn't meant to lift your hips high off the floor, and forcing more height usually just recruits your legs instead of your abs.
Stop if you feel any strain in your lower back rather than a light contraction in your abdominals.

faq.question: How many reps of the lower back curl should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 slow, controlled reps is plenty, since this is meant to be a gentle activation drill rather than a max-effort ab exercise.

faq.question: Can I do this without any equipment?
faq.answer: Yes, it only needs your bodyweight and a floor or mat, which makes it easy to fit in at home or as part of a warm-up anywhere.

faq.question: Why can't I feel my lower back lifting off the floor?
faq.answer: The lift is meant to be very small, often just a light unweighting of your tailbone rather than a visible rise. Focus on the feeling of your lower abs tightening rather than watching for a big movement.

alternatives.name: Pelvic Tilt Into Bridge
alternatives.reason: Uses the same starting tilt but continues into a bridge, a good option if you want to add glute and lower-back work to the same setup.

easierVariations.name: Standing Pelvic Tilt
easierVariations.reason: Practices the same pelvic tilt standing up, where gravity isn't pulling on your lower back and the movement is easier to feel and control.

harderVariations.name: Reverse Crunch
harderVariations.reason: Takes the same posterior pelvic tilt further, lifting the hips fully off the floor for a bigger range and more abdominal work.

summary: The landmine 180 has you gripping the free end of a barbell anchored in a landmine sleeve, arms extended in front of your chest, then rotating your hips and torso to swing the bar down toward one hip and back up across to the other. Your feet pivot with the movement instead of staying planted, so the rotation comes from your hips and core rather than just your arms. It trains your abdominals to control rotational force, the quality that separates a strong, stable torso from one that just looks strong standing still.
whyItWorks: Most core training asks your abs to resist a straight-line force, like bracing against a heavy squat. The landmine 180 asks something different: your abdominals, obliques included, have to control torque as the bar's weight tries to keep swinging past where you want it to stop. Your glutes and lower back work isometrically to keep your hips stable as your feet pivot, and your shoulders stay engaged to keep the bar's arc smooth rather than letting it flop from side to side. That combination, rotational control on top of a stable base, is what carries over to throwing, swinging a bat or racket, or turning to grab something heavy without tweaking your back.
setup: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a sturdy corner.
Stand facing the anchor point with feet roughly shoulder-width apart, gripping the free end of the bar with both hands, arms extended in front of your chest.
Brace your core before the bar moves at all.
execution: Rotate your hips and torso together, letting your back foot pivot, to swing the bar down toward one hip.
Let the bar tap near hip height, then reverse the rotation.
Drive back through center and continue the rotation to the opposite hip, pivoting the other foot this time.
Keep your arms relatively fixed relative to your chest; the movement should come from your hips and trunk, not your shoulders swinging the bar on their own.
Control the speed on both sides rather than letting momentum carry the bar.
formCues: Rotation starts at the hips, not the arms.
Back foot pivots with the turn instead of staying glued down.
Arms stay locked relative to your chest throughout.
Control both ends of the swing; don't let the bar's weight pull you past center.
breathing: Exhale as you rotate toward each side, inhale briefly as you pass back through center.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the bar with the arms and shoulders while the hips stay locked in place.
commonMistakes.correction: Feel your back foot pivot on every rep; if it isn't moving, the rotation isn't coming from your hips.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting momentum carry the bar past a controlled range at the bottom of each swing.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and stop the bar at hip height instead of letting it drop further.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding or arching the lower back to chase more rotation.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the rotation happening through the hips and thoracic spine, and shorten the range if your lower back is taking over.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting with too much weight on the bar.
commonMistakes.correction: Landmine 180s reward control far more than load; start with just the empty bar until the pattern feels smooth on both sides.

programmingNotes: Two to three sets of 8 to 10 rotations per side is a solid starting dose, since the movement is more about control than fatigue.
This one earns a spot early in a core or warm-up block rather than at the end of a session, because clean hip rotation gets harder to feel once you're tired.
Add weight only after both sides look and feel identical; a heavier bar on an already-uneven rotation just bakes the imbalance in deeper.
It pairs naturally with a static anti-rotation hold like the pallof press, one for dynamic control and one for resisting rotation altogether.
safetyNotes: Keep the range short enough that your lower back stays neutral through the whole rotation; this is a hip and core movement, not a lower-back one.
Make sure the landmine sleeve or corner anchor is genuinely stable before loading the bar; a bar that slips mid-rotation is the real risk here, not the exercise itself.

faq.question: What muscles does the landmine 180 work?
faq.answer: It's primarily an abdominal and oblique exercise, with your glutes and lower back stabilizing your hips through the rotation and your shoulders holding the bar steady.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for landmine 180s?
faq.answer: Start with just the empty bar. This exercise is about controlling rotation, not moving maximum load, so add weight gradually and only once both sides feel even.

faq.question: What can I do instead of landmine 180s if I don't have a landmine attachment?
faq.answer: A pallof press with a cable or band trains the same anti-rotation core control without needing a barbell setup at all.

faq.question: Are landmine 180s bad for your lower back?
faq.answer: Done with a short, controlled range and a neutral spine, they're not. Rounding your back to force a bigger swing is what turns a hip rotation exercise into a lower-back one.

alternatives.name: Pallof Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same anti-rotation core control using a cable or band, no barbell or landmine setup required.

easierVariations.name: Russian Twist
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same rotational core control with just bodyweight, no barbell or landmine anchor needed.

harderVariations.name: Medicine Ball Full Twist
harderVariations.reason: Adds an explosive, full release of the same rotation instead of a controlled back-and-forth swing.

summary: The one-arm incline lateral raise has you lie on your side against an inclined bench and lift a dumbbell out to the side, targeting the middle deltoid without any help from your legs or torso to swing the weight up. Lying against the bench removes momentum almost entirely, which makes it one of the stricter ways to isolate that muscle and build rounder-looking shoulders.
whyItWorks: A standing lateral raise gives your body room to lean back or dip your knees to help launch the dumbbell, which takes real work away from the side delt without you noticing. Bracing against an incline bench pins your torso in place, so the shoulder has to lift the weight on its own with no assistance from body English, which is exactly what you want when the goal is isolating that one muscle rather than just moving the weight from A to B.
setup: Set a bench to roughly a 30 to 45 degree incline.
Lie on your side against it, chest supported, with your top arm holding a light dumbbell hanging down.
Keep a slight bend in your elbow, and let your bottom arm rest wherever it's comfortable for balance.
Keep your torso pinned against the bench before the first rep.
execution: Raise the dumbbell out to the side, leading with your elbow rather than your hand.
Lift until your arm is roughly in line with your shoulder, no higher.
Pause for a beat at the top, feeling the tension in the middle of your shoulder.
Lower the dumbbell back down slowly, resisting gravity rather than letting it drop.
Keep your torso flat against the bench the entire time, without twisting to help the lift.
Complete your reps on one side, then switch to the other arm.
formCues: Elbow leads the raise.
Stop at shoulder height.
Torso pinned to the bench, no swinging.
Slow on the way down.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the dumbbell out to the side, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Raising the dumbbell above shoulder height.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the lift once your arm is level with your shoulder; going higher shifts the work to your traps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbow straighten completely during the raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a slight, steady bend in the elbow throughout, which keeps the load on the shoulder rather than the joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a dumbbell heavy enough that the torso lifts off the bench to help.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until your chest stays pinned to the bench for every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the dumbbell drop quickly on the way down.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower it over two or three seconds; the controlled descent is where a lot of the growth stimulus comes from.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 12 to 15 reps per arm suits this well, since the side delt is a small muscle worked in isolation.
With light loads and strict form, most people can train it two or three times a week without much soreness carryover.
Do it after any heavier overhead pressing in your session, since fatigued delts make the strict form harder to hold.
Add reps before adding weight; this exercise loses its point the moment momentum starts doing the lifting.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light enough that your form doesn't break down before the set ends.
Stop if you feel pinching at the top of the shoulder rather than pushing through it.

faq.question: How many reps of the one-arm incline lateral raise should I do?
faq.answer: Twelve to 15 reps per arm for two or three sets is a good range, since this is isolation work best done with lighter weight and strict form.

faq.question: Can I do a lateral raise without an incline bench?
faq.answer: Yes, a standing side lateral raise trains the same muscle, though it allows a bit more momentum than the incline version does.

faq.question: One-arm incline lateral raise vs standing lateral raise, which is better?
faq.answer: The incline version is stricter and isolates the side delt more completely because your torso can't help swing the weight. The standing version is easier to set up and fine for most training days.

faq.question: Why do I feel lateral raises in my traps instead of my shoulders?
faq.answer: That usually happens when the dumbbell goes above shoulder height or shrugging creeps in. Keep the raise capped at shoulder level and relax your traps as you lift.

alternatives.name: Seated Side Lateral Raise
alternatives.reason: Trains the same strict lateral raise pattern from a seated position if an incline bench isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Side Lateral Raise
easierVariations.reason: Standing removes the incline bench setup and lets a little momentum help, an easier entry point before you isolate the strict lying version.

harderVariations.name: Cable Lateral Raise
harderVariations.reason: Keeps constant tension on the shoulder through the whole arc instead of the lighter load at the top a dumbbell gives you.

summary: The machine shoulder (military) press seats you upright and lets you push a set of handles overhead along a fixed track, training your shoulders and triceps in a supported compound push. Because the machine controls the bar path for you, it's a common way to build overhead pressing strength without needing to balance a barbell or a pair of dumbbells at the same time. The backrest also keeps your torso upright, which takes the guesswork out of staying stable under the load.
whyItWorks: Pressing something overhead means your shoulders and triceps have to extend your arms against gravity along a vertical line, and a compound press like this recruits both at once instead of isolating either. Because the machine sets the handle path, your shoulders and triceps supply the actual force while the machine's frame handles the balancing work a free-weight press would ask of your core and stabilizing muscles. That trade-off is exactly why a beginner can typically press more weight, and press it more consistently, on this machine than with a barbell overhead.
setup: Adjust the seat height so the handles start level with the top of your shoulders.
Sit with your back flat against the backrest and your feet planted on the floor.
Grip the handles with your palms facing forward or slightly angled, whichever the machine's handle position offers.
execution: Press the handles straight up until your arms are extended but not locked out hard.
Pause briefly at the top without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears.
Lower the handles back down with control until your elbows are level with your shoulders.
Keep your back flat against the pad through the entire rep.
Repeat for the set without arching your lower back off the backrest.
formCues: Back stays flat against the pad the whole rep.
Press straight up, not forward.
Stop just short of locking the elbows out hard at the top.
Lower with control until elbows meet shoulder height.
breathing: Exhale as you press the handles overhead, inhale as you lower them back to shoulder height.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back off the pad to help press the weight up.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the resistance until you can keep your entire back flat against the pad for every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the top of the press.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on pressing straight up and stopping the moment your arms extend, without adding a shrug.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only pressing through a partial range near the top of the movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the handles until your elbows are level with your shoulders on every rep, adjusting the resistance if needed to keep the full range clean.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 8 to 10 reps builds solid pressing strength here, since a supported compound push like this handles moderate loads well without extra stabilizer fatigue.
Works well early in a shoulder or push session, while you're fresh enough to press with a full, controlled range.
Because the seat and backrest remove most of the balancing demand a free-weight press requires, once a week as your main overhead press is enough if you're also doing other pressing work that week.
Progress in small resistance increments once your last set's final reps stop needing a pause to reset your breath.
safetyNotes: Keep your lower back against the pad throughout; an arched back shifts strain there instead of letting your shoulders do the pressing.
Avoid locking your elbows out hard at the top of every rep, especially as the weight gets heavier.

faq.question: How many sets of machine shoulder press should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 8 to 10 reps is a solid range for building pressing strength without excess fatigue from a supported compound push.

faq.question: Machine shoulder press vs dumbbell shoulder press, which is better?
faq.answer: The machine supports your back and controls the bar path, so it's easier to press heavier with good form, especially as a beginner. Dumbbell shoulder presses demand more shoulder stability and let each arm move independently, which builds control the machine doesn't. Many lifters start on the machine and add dumbbell pressing once their shoulders can handle the extra stabilizing work.

faq.question: What can I do instead of the machine shoulder press without a gym?
faq.answer: A standing dumbbell shoulder press or a resistance band anchored under your feet and pressed overhead both train the same overhead pushing pattern without this machine.

faq.question: Why does my lower back hurt after the machine shoulder press?
faq.answer: That usually means your back arched off the pad to help finish the press, often because the resistance is a bit too heavy. Lower the weight and keep your entire back flat against the backrest through the whole set.

alternatives.name: Cable Shoulder Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead push using a cable station instead of this specific machine.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
harderVariations.reason: Removes the machine's fixed bar path, so each arm has to press and stabilize the load on its own.

summary: The band squat takes a standard barbell back squat and adds resistance bands anchored to the floor, so the bar gets heavier as you stand up instead of staying the same weight through the whole lift. Powerlifters use it to train speed out of the bottom and strength at lockout, two spots a straight-weight squat rarely challenges on their own. It works best layered onto a squat you already know well, not as a way to learn the pattern.
whyItWorks: A loaded barbell squat already gets harder as the bar sinks below parallel, since your hips and knees lose their mechanical advantage. Bands reverse that curve: the farther you stand, the more the rubber stretches and the harder it pulls the bar down. That forces your quads and glutes to keep producing force all the way through lockout instead of coasting the last few inches, which is exactly the part of the lift that stalls out when a heavy squat gets missed. The lighter effective load at the bottom also lets you drop into the hole faster without extra joint stress, so you end up training bar speed and finishing strength in the same rep.
setup: Anchor a resistance band under a loaded band peg, a pair of heavy dumbbells, or the base of a squat rack on each side
Loop the top of each band over the barbell sleeve, just inside the collar, so tension is even on both sides
Load the bar with less plate weight than your normal squat, since the bands add real resistance at the top
Set up in the rack the way you always do, bar across your traps or rear delts, and unrack with your usual walkout
execution: Unrack the bar and walk back two or three steps until the bands are taut but not pulling you off balance
Set your feet shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly, and take a full breath to brace your core
Sit back and down under control until your hip crease passes your knee, letting the bands go slack as you descend
Drive up hard through the middle of your foot, speeding up as the bands tighten instead of slowing down
Finish standing tall with hips and knees locked out against the band tension
Reset your breath at the top before starting the next rep
formCues: Keep the bar path straight up and down even as the bands pull it backward
Push the floor away through your whole foot, not just your toes
Treat the top half like a jump you're not allowed to leave the ground on
breathing: Take a full brace before you descend and hold it until you're past the sticking point, then exhale as you finish locking out against the bands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Easing off as the bar gets heavier near the top
commonMistakes.correction: Push through the band tension at the same effort you used in the hole; slowing down defeats the point of the exercise

commonMistakes.mistake: Mismatched band tension from an uneven anchor
commonMistakes.correction: Check that both bands sit on the same point of the peg or plate stack and pull with equal force before you start the set

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading the bar with your normal squat weight
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the plate load, since the bands already add significant resistance; total tension, not just bar weight, is what you're programming

programmingNotes: This belongs after your main squat work, not instead of it, since it's a speed and lockout tool layered onto a pattern you already trust
Three to five sets of two or three reps keeps the focus on bar speed rather than grinding out a tough set
Because the loaded squat is already a heavy compound lift, cap band-squat sessions at once a week unless this is the only squat work you're doing that week
Pair it with your regular squat day instead of running it as a separate session
safetyNotes: Secure the band anchor before loading the bar; a band that slips off a peg under tension can snap back hard
Use a rack with safety pins or spotter arms set just below your bottom position while you're still learning this variation

faq.question: How much band tension should I use for a squat with bands?
faq.answer: Start light, something that adds roughly a quarter of your bar weight in extra tension at lockout, and increase gradually once your bar path stays straight.

faq.question: Can I do band squats without a power rack?
faq.answer: You need a stable, heavy anchor point at floor level, so a loaded band peg or very heavy dumbbells work, but skip it entirely if you don't have one rather than anchoring to something that could shift.

faq.question: Squat with bands vs squat with chains, what's the difference?
faq.answer: Bands build tension gradually and smoothly through the whole range, while chains add weight in discrete links as they lift off the floor, so bands feel like accelerating against resistance and chains feel like the bar getting heavier in steps.

faq.question: Is the band squat safe for a beginner?
faq.answer: Not as a way to learn the squat. Get comfortable with a straight-weight barbell squat first, then add bands once your depth and bar path are consistent.

alternatives.name: Box Squat
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar speed-out-of-the-bottom quality using a box instead of bands, useful when you don't have an anchor point.

easierVariations.name: Barbell Squat
easierVariations.reason: The same back squat pattern without bands, a good way to build the base strength and bar path this variation layers on top of.

harderVariations.name: Squat with Chains
harderVariations.reason: Another accommodating-resistance tool that adds load as you stand, worth trying once bands feel comfortable, for a different tension curve.

summary: The suspended split squat hooks your rear foot into a suspension strap instead of resting it on a bench, like a rear-foot-elevated split squat with a moving base. It builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings of the front leg while the unstable rear foot adds a balance challenge. It suits anyone with some single-leg training experience who's comfortable with a standard split squat and wants more out of it without added weight yet.
whyItWorks: Your front leg does nearly all the work: the quads extend the knee, the glutes and hamstrings extend the hip, and the adductors, abductors, and calves fire to keep your knee and ankle stable as you descend and drive back up. A bench keeps the rear foot still, but a suspension strap can swing and tilt, so your front-leg stabilizers have to work harder on every rep to keep your balance centered. The rear leg still contributes a little hip extension and knee flexion rather than sitting completely passive, which is part of why this variant feels different from a regular split squat even before you consider the balance challenge.
setup: Adjust the strap so the loop sits at ankle height and face away from the anchor point.
Hook the top of one foot into the loop behind you.
Hop or step your front foot forward into a split stance, far enough that your front knee can bend to roughly 90 degrees without your heel lifting.
Keep your torso upright and your hands free or resting on your hips for balance.
execution: Start standing tall with your rear foot suspended and your front foot planted ahead of you.
Bend your front knee and lower your hips straight down, letting your rear knee drop toward the floor.
Keep your front knee tracking over your mid-foot, not caving inward or shooting far past your toes.
Lower until your rear knee is close to the floor or your front thigh is near parallel.
Drive through your front heel to stand back up to the starting position.
Keep the rear strap steady rather than letting your leg swing between reps.
formCues: Drop straight down, not forward, over your front foot.
Keep your front knee tracking toward your middle toes.
Keep your torso upright through the whole rep.
Control the rear leg so the strap doesn't swing.
breathing: Inhale as you lower into the split squat, exhale as you drive back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the front knee cave inward on the way down.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively push the front knee out so it tracks over your middle toes throughout the descent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso far forward over the front knee.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest tall and your hips dropping straight down instead of forward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bouncing off the bottom position.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause briefly at the bottom and drive up under control instead of using rebound momentum.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the rear leg swing wildly in the strap between reps.
commonMistakes.correction: Reset your rear foot position and keep the leg relaxed but still before starting the next rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking too short a stance, which jams the front knee forward past the toes.
commonMistakes.correction: Step the front foot out far enough that your shin stays closer to vertical as the knee bends.

programmingNotes: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps per leg is a reasonable starting range for this unilateral move.
As a bodyweight single-leg exercise it's demanding on balance but not heavily loaded, so most people can train it twice a week on non-consecutive days.
Place it early in a leg session, before fatigue makes the balance component harder to control.
Spend a few extra reps per side the first couple of sessions just finding a stance length that lets your front heel stay flat through the whole range.
safetyNotes: Check the strap anchor for wear before committing your weight to the suspended rear foot.
Keep something sturdy nearby to touch for balance the first few sessions, and stop if you feel sharp knee pain rather than normal muscle fatigue.
Favor a shorter range of motion over a deeper one that forces your front knee to cave inward to reach it.

faq.question: How many reps of suspended split squats should I do per leg?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps per leg is a good starting point before adding load.

faq.question: Can I do split squats without a suspension strap?
faq.answer: Yes, the regular split squat with both feet on the ground trains the same muscles without needing a strap.

faq.question: Suspended split squat vs Bulgarian split squat, what's the difference?
faq.answer: Both elevate the rear foot behind you, but a bench keeps that foot still while a suspension strap lets it move, adding an extra balance demand.

faq.question: Why does my front knee hurt during suspended split squats?
faq.answer: Knee discomfort often comes from the knee caving inward or drifting far past the toes; shorten the stance slightly and keep the knee tracking over your middle toes.

faq.question: How deep should I go on a suspended split squat?
faq.answer: Aim for your rear knee to get close to the floor or your front thigh near parallel, but only as deep as you can control without your front knee caving in; a shorter range with good tracking beats a deeper one that doesn't.

alternatives.name: Bodyweight Walking Lunge
alternatives.reason: Trains the same quads, glutes, and hamstrings through a similar split stance without needing a strap or anchor.

easierVariations.name: Split Squats
easierVariations.reason: Keeping both feet planted on the floor removes the balance demand of the suspended rear foot while you groove the split-stance pattern.

harderVariations.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
harderVariations.reason: Adding dumbbells once the suspended balance feels controlled raises the load on the same front-leg muscles.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Side Split Squat
harderVariations.reason: A barbell-loaded split pattern for lifters who want heavier, bar-based progression on the same leg drive.

summary: The cable shoulder press has you sit or stand between two pulleys set at shoulder height, press the handles straight overhead, and lower them back under control. It trains the same overhead pressing strength as a dumbbell or barbell press, and it suits anyone who wants shoulder-friendly tension that stays constant instead of unloading at lockout.
whyItWorks: Pressing overhead is mainly your front and side delts extending your arms upward, with your triceps finishing the lockout. A barbell or dumbbell press loses resistance right at the top since gravity pulls straight down and your arms are nearly vertical there, but a cable set to the side keeps a horizontal pulling angle throughout, so your shoulders stay under real tension all the way through lockout instead of coasting the last few inches.
setup: Sit or stand between two pulleys set at roughly shoulder height with handles attached.
Grab a handle in each hand and bring them up to shoulder level, elbows bent and pointed slightly forward.
Brace your core and keep your ribs stacked over your hips before you start pressing.
execution: Press both handles straight overhead until your arms are extended.
Pause briefly at full extension without locking your elbows aggressively.
Lower the handles back to shoulder height under control.
Repeat for the set, keeping your torso upright throughout.
formCues: Press the handles in a straight line overhead rather than letting them drift forward.
Keep your ribs down and avoid arching your lower back to finish the press.
Bring the handles all the way back to shoulder height on each rep instead of shortening the range.
Keep your core braced throughout to keep your torso stable as you press.
breathing: Exhale as you press the handles overhead, inhale as you lower them back to shoulder height.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back and flaring the ribs to finish the press.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core before each rep and keep your ribs stacked over your hips through the whole press.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the handles drift forward instead of pressing straight overhead.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows tracking under your wrists and press in a straight vertical line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shortening the range by not lowering the handles all the way to shoulder height.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower under control until the handles return to shoulder height on every rep.

programmingNotes: As a compound pressing movement, this can carry real load, so one focused session a week works well if you're already pressing overhead or benching elsewhere in your program.
Eight to twelve reps per set fits most goals, since the movement handles moderate to heavy resistance well.
Place it early in a shoulder or push session, since fresh shoulders let you press with better form and more weight.
safetyNotes: Keep your core braced and avoid arching your lower back to finish a rep.
Choose a weight that lets you control the full range in both directions rather than fighting the last few inches.
Stop if you feel pinching at the front of your shoulder rather than muscular fatigue.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable shoulder press should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps works well for most people building shoulder strength and size.

faq.question: What's the difference between a cable shoulder press and a dumbbell shoulder press?
faq.answer: A dumbbell press loses tension near lockout since gravity pulls straight down, while the cable's horizontal pull keeps your shoulders working through that same top range.

faq.question: Can I do this without a cable machine?
faq.answer: A dumbbell shoulder press or a shoulder press with resistance bands train the same overhead pressing pattern without a cable station.

faq.question: Why does my lower back arch during cable shoulder presses?
faq.answer: That usually means you're using your lower back to help finish the press instead of your shoulders. Brace your core, keep your ribs down, and reduce the weight until your shoulders can complete the range alone.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead press with each arm moving independently when a cable station isn't free.

easierVariations.name: Shoulder Press - With Bands
easierVariations.reason: Uses light, adjustable band resistance to learn the overhead pressing pattern before loading a full cable stack.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Shoulder Press
harderVariations.reason: Swaps the guided cable path for a free barbell, adding a real stability demand and a higher long-term load ceiling.

summary: The deficit deadlift is a standard barbell deadlift performed while standing on a low platform, usually one to three inches high, so the bar starts farther below your hands than in a conventional deadlift. That extra distance forces you to sink deeper into your hips and ankles before the pull begins, which increases the range of motion your hamstrings, glutes, and back have to work through off the floor. It is a demanding variant that builds strength out of a deeper starting position, and it asks more of your hip and ankle mobility than a standard deadlift does.
whyItWorks: A conventional deadlift already trains your posterior chain, your hamstrings, glutes, and back, through hip extension against a loaded bar. Standing on a deficit lowers the bar's starting height relative to your feet, which means your hips and knees have to bend further to reach it. That deeper starting position extends the range your hamstrings and glutes work through during the first part of the pull, the phase many lifters find hardest, so training with a deficit builds strength specifically in that bottom range. It also demands more ankle dorsiflexion and hip mobility than pulling from the floor, since your body has to fold further to reach the bar.
setup: Stand on a stable, low platform, typically one to three inches high, with the bar over your midfoot.
Set your feet hip-width apart and grip the bar just outside your legs.
Sink your hips down and back until your shins touch the bar, keeping your chest up.
Take the slack out of the bar by pulling it tight against the plates before you lift.
execution: Drive through your midfoot and extend your hips and knees together to lift the bar off the platform.
Keep the bar close to your legs as it travels up past your knees.
Finish the pull by standing fully upright, hips and knees locked out together.
Lower the bar back down under control, hinging at the hips first.
Let the bar return to the platform and reset your position before the next rep.
formCues: Keep your shins vertical and touching the bar before you pull.
Push the floor away through your midfoot rather than yanking the bar up with your arms.
Keep the bar traveling in a straight line close to your shins and thighs.
Finish the lift by squeezing your glutes, not by leaning your torso back.
breathing: Take a deep breath and brace your core before you initiate the pull, then exhale once the bar passes your knees or after you lock out at the top.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips shoot up faster than the chest at the start of the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Drive your feet into the platform and extend your hips and knees at the same rate, keeping your shoulders over the bar.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach the bar's lower starting position.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hip position first so your shins reach the bar with a flat back, and lower the platform height if you cannot maintain that.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar drift away from the shins as it rises.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the bar in contact with your legs the entire pull, dragging it up your shins and thighs.

programmingNotes: Two to four sets of three to six reps suits the deficit deadlift well as a strength-focused main lift, since the added range makes each rep more demanding than a conventional deadlift at the same weight.

This is a heavy compound pull that adds extra range and mobility demand on top of a standard deadlift, so once a week is the sensible default unless it is the only deadlift-pattern work you are doing that week.
Use a lighter load than your conventional deadlift when you first add a deficit; matching your usual deadlift weight to the deeper range is a common way lifters lose form.
safetyNotes: Start with a small deficit, around one inch, and only increase it once you can keep your back flat through the full range.
Stop the set if you feel your lower back rounding to reach the bar; that means the deficit or the load is currently too much.
Use a stable, non-slip platform that won't shift under your feet mid-lift.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of deficit deadlifts should I do?
faq.answer: Two to four sets of three to six reps works well as a main strength lift, using less weight than your conventional deadlift since the extra range makes the pull harder.

faq.question: What's the difference between a deficit deadlift and a regular deadlift?
faq.answer: Standing on a raised platform lowers the bar's starting position relative to your feet, adding extra range of motion off the floor and demanding more hip and ankle mobility than a conventional deadlift.

faq.question: How high should the deficit platform be?
faq.answer: Start around one inch and only add height once you can pull the full range with a flat back. Most lifters do not need more than two to three inches.

faq.question: Why does my lower back round at the bottom of a deficit deadlift?
faq.answer: That usually means the deficit is taller than your current hip and ankle mobility allows. Lower the platform height and work on hip and ankle mobility before building the deficit back up.

alternatives.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hip-hinge pull with a different bar and grip, useful for posterior-chain work when no deficit platform is available.

easierVariations.name: Romanian Deadlift
easierVariations.reason: Removes the deficit platform and starts from a standing hip hinge instead, cutting the extra hip and ankle mobility demand while you build hinge strength.

summary: The dumbbell lying supination trains the muscles that rotate your forearm so your palm turns to face up. You rest your forearm along a support with your wrist past the edge, grip a dumbbell near one end so it acts like a lever, and rotate your wrist from palm-down to palm-up against that resistance. It trains the exact opposite rotation from a pronation exercise, and most forearms benefit from doing both.
whyItWorks: Turning your palm face up is called supination, and it's driven by forearm muscles that are easy to overlook because everyday grip and curling movements rarely isolate them. Gripping the dumbbell off-center near one end turns the weight into a lever, so the resistance against the turn comes from the dumbbell's head swinging away from your hand instead of just its raw weight. That lever effect is what makes a light dumbbell feel demanding here, and what actually trains rotational strength rather than just grip endurance.
setup: Sit or lie with your forearm resting along a bench or your thigh, with your wrist and hand extending just past the edge.
Grip a light dumbbell near one end so the rest of it extends out past your thumb like a lever.
Start with your palm facing down or turned slightly inward, keeping your elbow bent at roughly a right angle and pinned against the support.
execution: Rotate your forearm slowly, turning your palm from facing down to facing up.
Keep your elbow pinned against the support throughout, so only your forearm rotates.
Pause briefly once your palm faces fully up.
Rotate back to the starting position with the same control, resisting the dumbbell's pull the whole way.
Complete all reps on one side before switching arms.
formCues: Keep your elbow pinned in place.
Rotate the forearm, not the shoulder.
Control the return just as much as the turn.
Grip the dumbbell near one end, not the middle.
breathing: Exhale as you rotate your palm up, inhale as you rotate back to the start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbow lift or drift away from the support during the rotation.
commonMistakes.correction: Press your elbow down into the bench or your thigh and keep it there for the entire set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rotating the whole arm from the shoulder instead of just the forearm.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arm still and let the movement happen only at your wrist and forearm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the dumbbell in the middle instead of near one end, which removes the lever effect the exercise depends on.
commonMistakes.correction: Choke up on the dumbbell so more of its length sticks out past your thumb, creating real resistance against the turn.

programmingNotes: This trains a small forearm muscle group with a light lever load, so it recovers fast and tolerates frequent training.
2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 controlled reps per arm is enough; heavy loading adds little here beyond what a lighter, well-controlled rep already provides.
It fits naturally at the end of an arm or pull session, since fresh forearms aren't necessary to perform it with good form.
Pair it with the pronation version, which trains the opposite rotation, so neither direction of forearm strength lags behind the other.
safetyNotes: Use a light dumbbell and prioritize slow, controlled rotation over speed or heavy load.
Stop if you feel sharp pain at the elbow rather than the expected forearm fatigue, and shorten the lever by choking up further on the dumbbell.

faq.question: How many sets of dumbbell lying supination should I do?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 slow, controlled reps per arm is plenty. The lever created by gripping off-center is what makes even a light dumbbell challenging.

faq.question: What muscles does dumbbell lying supination work?
faq.answer: It targets the supinator muscles of the forearm, the ones that rotate your palm to face upward, along with the grip and wrist muscles that help stabilize the movement.

faq.question: Should I train supination or pronation first?
faq.answer: Order doesn't matter much for a light accessory movement like this. Many people alternate which one they start with each session so neither arm direction consistently trains while more fatigued.

faq.question: Why does my forearm shake during this exercise?
faq.answer: Shaking is common when a small muscle group is asked to control a lever it isn't yet used to. Lighten the dumbbell or choke up further on it, and the shake usually settles as your forearm adapts over a few sessions.

easierVariations.name: Wrist Circles
easierVariations.reason: An unweighted version of forearm rotation, useful for warming up the joint before adding a dumbbell's resistance.

harderVariations.name: Wrist Roller
harderVariations.reason: Loads forearm rotation continuously through a rolling motion rather than a single controlled turn, adding more time under tension.

summary: Wrist rotations with a straight bar train forearm rotation instead of the up-and-down motion of a wrist curl. Gripping a barbell at each end and twisting your wrists back and forth works the muscles that rotate your forearm, which rarely get direct, isolated work anywhere else. It suits anyone who wants more complete forearm development or better rotational control for sports and grip-heavy lifting.
whyItWorks: Most forearm training, like a wrist curl, moves the wrist up and down through flexion and extension. Twisting a barbell back and forth instead asks your forearm to rotate around its own axis, a different muscle action (pronation and supination) that an up-and-down curl doesn't train directly. Because the bar is straight and symmetrical, both wrists rotate through the same range at the same time, which makes the movement easy to control and compare side to side.
setup: Hold a light barbell with both hands, palms facing down, hands shoulder-width apart.
Let your arms hang relaxed at your sides or hold them bent at roughly 90 degrees in front of you.
Keep your grip firm but not crushing, since you need your wrists to rotate freely.
execution: Rotate both wrists together so the bar tilts, bringing one end up and the other down.
Rotate back the other way so the opposite end lifts.
Keep the rotation smooth and controlled rather than snapping between the two positions.
Repeat for the full set, alternating which end rises each rep.
formCues: Rotate from the wrist and forearm, not by swinging your whole arm.
Keep your elbows roughly still throughout the set.
Move through a full, even rotation on both sides.
Keep your grip firm but relaxed enough to let the wrists turn.
breathing: Breathe normally through the set; there's no need to brace hard for a movement this light.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the arms or shoulders to help tilt the bar instead of rotating the wrists.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows and upper arms still and let the rotation happen at the wrist and forearm only.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a bar heavy enough that the rotation turns into a jerky, uncontrolled tilt.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can rotate smoothly through the full range on both sides.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rotating further on one side than the other without noticing.
commonMistakes.correction: Check that both directions cover the same range; an uneven rotation usually means one wrist is tighter or weaker than the other.

programmingNotes: Two to three sets of 10 to 15 rotations in each direction is plenty for this isolation movement.
Because this trains a small, specific motion with light loads, two to three sessions a week works well without much recovery concern.
Pair it with a standard wrist curl in the same session to cover both the up-and-down and the rotational sides of forearm training.
Increase the load in small increments; forearm rotators are easy to overload because the range of motion feels small compared to the effort it takes.
safetyNotes: Use a light bar until you know how your wrists respond to rotational loading; this motion can feel deceptively demanding.
Stop if you feel any pinching or sharp pain rather than normal forearm fatigue.
Keep the rotation smooth rather than snapping the bar from side to side.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for wrist rotations with a straight bar?
faq.answer: Start very light, often just the bar itself. The rotational demand on your forearms is higher than the weight suggests.

faq.question: What's the difference between wrist rotations and a regular wrist curl?
faq.answer: A wrist curl moves your wrist up and down. Wrist rotations twist your forearm around its own axis instead, training pronation and supination, a motion a curl doesn't cover.

faq.question: How many sets of wrist rotations should I do?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 10 to 15 rotations in each direction is enough for this isolation exercise.

faq.question: Can I do wrist rotations without a barbell?
faq.answer: Yes. A light dumbbell held at one end, or a similar long tool, lets you train the same rotational motion if a straight bar isn't available.

alternatives.name: Seated Palm-Up Barbell Wrist Curl
alternatives.reason: Trains the forearm through a flexion pattern instead of rotation, a useful option when a straight-bar rotation drill isn't practical.

easierVariations.name: Wrist Circles
easierVariations.reason: Practices the same rotational motion with no load at all, a gentler starting point before adding a barbell.

harderVariations.name: Wrist Roller
harderVariations.reason: Adds continuous winding resistance to the same forearm rotators once the basic rotation feels fully controlled.

summary: The standing concentration curl has you bend forward at the hips and brace your working elbow against the inside of your knee or thigh, then curl a single dumbbell with strict, isolated form. Bracing the elbow removes almost any chance of swinging or cheating the weight up, making it one of the most direct ways to isolate a single biceps.
whyItWorks: Most standing curls still let your shoulder and torso contribute a little momentum, especially once the set gets hard. Bracing your elbow against your leg fixes the upper arm in place the way a preacher bench does, but without needing any equipment beyond a single dumbbell. With the elbow locked against your leg, the only thing that can move the dumbbell is your biceps contracting, which is exactly why this variation is a go-to for isolating one arm at a time and fixing strength imbalances between sides. Working through the hinge also lets gravity pull the dumbbell straight down from the shoulder rather than out to the side, which keeps the resistance lined up with the biceps through more of the range than a fully upright curl manages.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in one hand and hinge forward at the hips, bracing your working arm's elbow against the inside of the same-side knee or thigh.
Let the dumbbell hang straight down with your arm fully extended to start.
Keep your feet planted and your core braced in the hinged position.
execution: Curl the dumbbell up toward your shoulder by bending at the elbow, keeping the elbow braced against your leg the entire time.
Squeeze your biceps hard at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbell back down slowly with control, all the way to a full elbow extension.
Repeat for the set, then switch arms.
formCues: Elbow stays braced against the leg the whole set.
Curl with the arm alone, no torso help.
Full stretch at the bottom, full squeeze at the top.
Control the lowering; don't let the dumbbell drop.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbell up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbow slide off the leg partway through the set as fatigue sets in.
commonMistakes.correction: Reset your hinge and elbow brace between reps if needed, and reduce the weight if you can't hold the brace for a full set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso to help heave the dumbbell up near the end of the set.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hinge fixed and slow the tempo down; if you need to rock, the weight is too heavy for strict form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping the curl short of full elbow extension at the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the dumbbell all the way down each rep so the biceps get a complete stretch before curling again.

programmingNotes: As a strict single-arm isolation exercise, 2 to 3 sessions a week is a sensible frequency once your form is consistent.
Because one arm works at a time, doing 8 to 12 reps per arm lets you compare both sides and catch any strength imbalance early.
It works well later in an arm session, after bigger pulling movements, since the strict bracing here doesn't need fresh legs or back.
safetyNotes: Keep your hinge supported by a braced core rather than a rounded lower back, especially as the set gets harder toward the end.
If your elbow brace keeps slipping, lower the weight rather than fighting to hold the position with a heavier dumbbell than you can control.

faq.question: How many reps should I do per arm for the standing concentration curl?
faq.answer: 8 to 12 reps per arm for three sets is a solid range. Working one arm at a time makes it easy to notice if one side is weaker or less controlled than the other.

faq.question: What makes the concentration curl different from a regular biceps curl?
faq.answer: Bracing your elbow against your leg fixes the upper arm in place, removing almost all help from your shoulder or torso. It's a stricter, more isolated version of a curl.

faq.question: Can I do this seated instead of standing?
faq.answer: Yes, the seated concentration curl braces the elbow against the inner thigh while sitting, which is actually the more traditional version and removes even more of the stabilization demand.

faq.question: Why does my form break down toward the end of the set?
faq.answer: That's usually fatigue pulling your elbow off its brace. Lower the weight slightly so you can hold strict form for every rep, rather than letting the last few reps turn into a swing.

faq.question: Should I curl both arms before switching, or alternate reps?
faq.answer: Finish the full set on one arm before switching to the other. Alternating rep by rep gives the just-worked arm a brief rest between reps, which lets you sneak in a little extra momentum without noticing.

alternatives.name: Standing Biceps Cable Curl
alternatives.reason: Trains the same biceps isolation pattern with a cable and both arms at once instead of a single braced dumbbell.

easierVariations.name: Concentration Curls
easierVariations.reason: The seated version braces the elbow against the inner thigh while sitting, removing even more stabilization demand than the standing hinge.

harderVariations.name: Standing One-Arm Cable Curl
harderVariations.reason: Swaps the braced, fixed position for a cable, which keeps tension on the biceps through the full range without the elbow brace to lean on.

summary: The dumbbell bench press is a flat-bench chest press where each arm moves independently instead of being locked to a single bar. That independence forces both sides to pull equal weight, and it lets your shoulders find a natural bottom position a fixed barbell can't offer. It's a foundational chest builder for anyone who trains at home with a pair of dumbbells or wants a barbell alternative that's gentler on cranky shoulders.
