Squeeze your glutes and lower back to lift your torso up until your body is a straight line.
Pause briefly at the top without arching past neutral.
Lower your torso back down under control to the starting position.
Repeat for the target number of reps.
formCues: Move from your hips, not by yanking with your neck.
Keep your ankles firmly anchored throughout the set.
Rise only until your body is straight, not into a deep arch.
Control the descent instead of dropping toward the floor.
breathing: Inhale as you lower your torso toward the floor, and exhale as you rise back to a straight line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using an unstable surface that shifts under your hips
commonMistakes.correction: Test the surface with your body weight before starting; a wobbly setup makes it hard to control the movement safely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching well past neutral at the top
commonMistakes.correction: Stop once your body forms a straight line from head to heels; extra arch just strains the lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the ankles slip loose mid-set
commonMistakes.correction: Check your partner's grip or the anchor point before each set, since a loose anchor turns the exercise into a balance challenge instead of a back exercise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing to add more reps before the setup feels solid
commonMistakes.correction: Spend the first session or two getting comfortable with the anchor and surface at a low rep count; a shaky setup isn't the place to chase volume.

programmingNotes: 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps is a reasonable starting point, since this variation asks more of your stabilizers than the machine version.
Works well as an accessory after a lower body or deadlift-focused session.
Once a week is enough to start, since holding your own body weight at the edge of a surface adds real core and hip demand on top of the lower back work.
Once the setup feels stable and reps stay controlled, a light dumbbell or plate held to your chest is a reasonable next step before looking for a proper bench.
safetyNotes: Only use a surface and anchor point sturdy enough to fully support your body weight; test it before loading a full set.
Stop if you feel your hips sliding or the surface shifting, since losing that stability risks a fall.

faq.question: What can I use at home instead of a hyperextension bench?
faq.answer: A bed, couch, or sturdy bench edge works, as long as a partner or something heavy anchors your ankles firmly.

faq.question: Is this exercise as effective as using a hyperextension bench?
faq.answer: It trains the same lower back and glute pattern, though a machine gives a more consistent range of motion and a steadier anchor. This version is a solid substitute when you don't have access to one.

faq.question: Why do my hamstrings feel tight the next day?
faq.answer: The hamstrings help control your hips through the movement, so mild soreness there is normal, especially the first few times you do this variation.

alternatives.name: Hyperextensions (Back Extensions)
alternatives.reason: Uses a dedicated hyperextension bench for a steadier anchor and more consistent range of motion when one is available.

summary: The scapular squeeze is a simple standing or seated drill where you draw your shoulder blades toward each other and hold the position, without moving your arms or spine. It isolates the muscles between your shoulder blades that most desk-bound days leave weak and switched off. It suits anyone working on posture, warming up before pulling exercises, or building the mind-muscle connection needed for bigger back lifts.
whyItWorks: Your middle back sits between your shoulder blades and is responsible for pulling them together and holding them there, a job that gets almost no practice if you spend your day reaching forward for a keyboard or a phone. The scapular squeeze isolates that exact motion by removing every other joint from the equation: no elbow bend, no arm swing, just your shoulder blades drawing toward your spine while your traps and rhomboids do the work. Practicing that isolated squeeze builds the awareness and strength you need to keep your shoulder blades set during rows, pull-ups, and pressing movements.
setup: Stand or sit up straight, letting your arms hang loosely by your sides.
Keep your chest lifted and your spine in a neutral position.
Let your shoulders settle into a natural, relaxed position before you begin.
execution: Draw your shoulder blades toward each other, as if you're trying to hold a pencil between them.
Hold the squeeze for 1 to 2 seconds, keeping your shoulders down away from your ears.
Release slowly back to the starting position.
Repeat for the set, keeping your arms still throughout.
formCues: Keep your shoulders pulled down, not shrugged toward your ears.
Move only your shoulder blades, not your arms or spine.
Keep your chest lifted throughout the squeeze.
Squeeze with the same effort on both sides at once.
breathing: Exhale as you draw your shoulder blades toward each other, and inhale as you release.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up instead of squeezing them back.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively keep your shoulders down and away from your ears as you draw the shoulder blades in.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to exaggerate the squeeze.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your spine neutral and let the movement come entirely from your shoulder blades.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through the reps without holding the squeeze.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause for a full 1 to 2 seconds at the top of each rep so the muscle actually contracts, not just twitches.

commonMistakes.mistake: Squeezing harder on one side than the other.
commonMistakes.correction: Check in a mirror or film yourself to confirm both shoulder blades move together evenly.

programmingNotes: This is a light, joint-friendly isolation move, so daily practice or 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps most days is reasonable.
Use it as a quick posture reset between desk sessions, or as a warm-up before rows and pull-ups to prime the same muscles.
Add a light resistance band or a short hold at the top once bodyweight squeezes stop feeling like any effort at all.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion small; this is a squeeze, not a full row.
Stop if you feel any pinching near your shoulder joint rather than tension in your mid-back.
Avoid arching your lower back to fake a bigger squeeze.

faq.question: How long should I hold the squeeze?
faq.answer: 1 to 2 seconds at the top of each rep is enough to engage the muscle without turning it into a static hold.

faq.question: Can I do this every day?
faq.answer: Yes. It's a light, low-fatigue movement, so daily practice, especially as a posture break during a desk-heavy day, works well.

faq.question: Will this fix my rounded shoulders?
faq.answer: It helps build the strength and awareness to hold better posture, but posture also depends on how you sit and move the rest of the day, so pair it with regular breaks from prolonged forward positions.

faq.question: What's a good progression once this feels easy?
faq.answer: Add light resistance with a band pull apart, or move to a scapular pull-up if you have access to a bar, since both build on the same shoulder blade pattern under more load.

alternatives.name: Band Pull Apart
alternatives.reason: Trains the same shoulder blade retraction with external band resistance instead of a bodyweight squeeze.

harderVariations.name: Scapular Pull-Up
harderVariations.reason: Adds your full hanging body weight to the same shoulder blade retraction pattern.

summary: The seated close-grip concentration barbell curl is a two-handed curl done bent over on a bench, gripping the bar with your hands close together and bracing your upper arms against your inner thighs. That braced position removes almost all body swing, forcing the biceps to do the full lifting on their own. It's a stricter alternative to a standing curl for anyone who tends to lean back or swing the hips to move the weight.
whyItWorks: The biceps flex the elbow, and they get their cleanest training stimulus when the upper arm stays fixed and the rest of the body can't help move the weight. Bracing your upper arms against your inner thighs while bent over does exactly that: it pins the shoulder in place so the only thing that can move the bar is the elbow bending, which is the biceps' actual job. The close grip on the bar also keeps both hands and forearms working through a similar, natural curling path, rather than the wider stance some barbell curls use, which some lifters find puts less strain on the wrists at the top of the rep.
setup: Sit on the edge of a bench with a barbell in front of you, feet planted and knees apart.
Bend forward at the hips and grip the bar with a close, shoulder-width or slightly narrower grip, palms facing up.
Rest the backs of your upper arms against your inner thighs, letting the bar hang with your arms extended.
Keep your back flat rather than rounded as you settle into the bent-over position.
execution: Keeping your upper arms braced against your thighs, curl the bar up by bending your elbows.
Continue until your forearms are close to vertical and your biceps are fully contracted.
Pause briefly at the top, squeezing your biceps.
Lower the bar back down slowly until your arms are fully extended again.
Keep your torso still and bent over throughout the set; only your forearms should move.
Repeat for the full set without letting your upper arms lift off your thighs.
formCues: Upper arms braced on the thighs the whole set.
Only the forearm swings, nothing else.
Full extension at the bottom of every rep.
Squeeze at the top before lowering.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the bar up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the upper arms lift away from the thighs to help swing the bar up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms pressed against your inner thighs throughout; if they lift, your shoulders and back start assisting the curl.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only curling through a short, partial range at the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the bar travel until your forearms are close to vertical each rep, so your biceps get a full, deliberate contraction.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and letting the bar drop.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the bar over two or three seconds instead of letting gravity do it; the controlled lowering is a large part of the training effect.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a grip much wider than shoulder width, which turns it into a different curl entirely.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands close together as the name suggests; a wide grip changes the angle and the exercise this movement is meant to be.

programmingNotes: As a strict isolation curl, two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps a couple of times a week fits well alongside other pulling or arm work.
Use a noticeably lighter bar than you'd use for a standing barbell curl; the braced, strict position doesn't allow the momentum that a standing curl often relies on.
This works well later in an arm-focused session, once the biceps are already warmed up from an earlier compound pull like a row.
If your lower back feels the bent-over position more than your biceps feel the curl, shorten how far forward you lean rather than pushing through discomfort.
safetyNotes: Keep the forward bend moderate; you don't need a deep hinge for the exercise to work, and a shallower lean is easier on the lower back.
Choose a weight that lets you keep the strict, braced position for every rep; if you start swinging to finish reps, the load is too heavy.
Give your wrists a moment to settle into the palms-up grip before the first rep; a rushed setup with heavy load can strain the wrist at the bottom stretch.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for the seated close-grip concentration barbell curl?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps works well, using a lighter bar than you'd choose for a standing curl since the braced position removes any help from momentum.

faq.question: What can I do if I only have dumbbells?
faq.answer: Concentration curls use the same braced-elbow setup one arm at a time with a dumbbell instead of a barbell.

faq.question: Why does my back feel this more than my biceps?
faq.answer: Check how far you're leaning forward; a moderate hinge is enough, and leaning too far can shift some strain onto the lower back instead of keeping the focus on the biceps.

faq.question: How is this different from a regular preacher curl?
faq.answer: A preacher curl braces your upper arms against a padded bench instead of your own thighs, which some lifters find locks the arm position even more strictly than this bent-over version.

alternatives.name: Concentration Curls
alternatives.reason: The classic one-arm dumbbell version of the same braced-elbow biceps isolation, useful when a barbell isn't available or one side needs extra focus.

alternatives.name: Preacher Curl
alternatives.reason: Also locks the upper arm in place to prevent swing, using a preacher bench pad instead of bracing against your own thighs.

easierVariations.name: Seated Dumbbell Curl
easierVariations.reason: A single-implement curl with a natural wrist path, a simpler way to learn a strict, controlled biceps curl before bracing a barbell between the thighs.

harderVariations.name: Spider Curl
harderVariations.reason: Braces the upper arms against an angled pad instead of your thighs, removing any hip assistance and locking the elbow position more strictly.

summary: The linear 3-part start technique breaks a standing sprint start into three separate pieces so you can practice each one on its own: the initial drive step, a handful of low acceleration steps, and the transition up into a tall running posture. Coaches use this kind of breakdown because trying to fix an entire sprint start at once is hard to feel and hard to correct. Working the parts separately, then linking them, builds a cleaner, more powerful start over time.
whyItWorks: A fast start depends on getting the body's lean angle, ground contact, and posture right in a very short window, and all three change together within the first few steps. The hamstrings and quads drive that first powerful push against the ground, while the calves help transmit force through the ankle as the foot strikes and leaves the ground. Splitting the start into three parts lets you isolate one piece of that chain at a time, so a flaw in the drive step doesn't get masked by what happens in the steps after it. Once each part is clean on its own, linking them together produces a start that's more consistent than trying to fix the whole thing at once.
setup: Mark a start line and pick a straight, clear running lane at least 10 to 15 meters long.
Warm up with light jogging and a few practice steps before working at full effort.
Decide which of the three parts you're drilling before each rep: the drive step, the acceleration steps, or the transition to upright.
Rest fully between reps so each attempt is done with fresh legs, not fatigued ones.
execution: Part 1, the drive step: from a staggered standing start, push explosively off the back foot while leaning forward, landing the first step well behind your center of mass.
Hold that low, driving body angle for the first step only, then walk out of it and reset.
Part 2, the acceleration steps: starting from the same stance, take 3 to 5 steps while keeping a strong forward lean and short, quick, powerful ground contacts.
Keep your arms driving hard front to back through these steps, matched to the rhythm of your legs.
Part 3, the transition: continue from the acceleration steps into a gradual rise, straightening your torso over 3 to 4 more steps until you reach a tall sprinting posture.
Once each part feels clean on its own, link all three together into one continuous start over 8 to 10 total steps.
formCues: Push, don't just fall forward.
Stay low through the drive and early acceleration steps.
Rise gradually, not all at once.
Arms drive front to back, not across the body.
breathing: Take one deliberate breath before each rep, then let breathing happen naturally through the short, explosive effort.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing tall too early instead of holding a forward lean through the drive and acceleration steps.
commonMistakes.correction: Practice part 1 and part 2 in isolation until the low body angle feels natural before adding the transition.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overstriding on the first step out of the start, reaching the foot too far in front of the body.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus the first step on driving backward against the ground rather than reaching forward with the foot.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the arms cross the body instead of driving straight front to back.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep elbows bent near ninety degrees and drive the hands from hip to chin height in a straight line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing all three parts together before any one of them is clean.
commonMistakes.correction: Drill each part separately across several sessions before linking them into a full start.

programmingNotes: This is a technique drill, not a loading exercise, so quality matters more than volume: 3 to 5 short reps per part, done early in a session while the legs are fresh.
Because the reps are brief and the rest between them is long, this drill can be practiced 2 to 3 times a week without adding meaningful fatigue.
Spend more sessions on whichever part feels least automatic before spending equal time on all three.
Once the full linked start feels consistent, fold it into a broader sprint or speed-day warm-up rather than training it in isolation forever.
safetyNotes: Practice on a flat, non-slip surface with proper footwear to avoid slipping during the drive step.
Keep early reps short and controlled rather than maximal effort while you're still learning the positions.

faq.question: How many reps of the 3-part start technique should I do?
faq.answer: 3 to 5 short reps per part is plenty in a single session, since this is a technique drill where quality of movement matters far more than total volume.

faq.question: Do I need any equipment for this drill?
faq.answer: No, it's a bodyweight drill that only needs a clear, straight lane of 10 to 15 meters and a flat, non-slip surface.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and the wall drill?
faq.answer: The wall drill isolates the leg drive and body lean while a wall supports your weight, while the 3-part start technique practices the same mechanics unsupported, from an actual standing start.

faq.question: Why do I keep standing up too early out of the start?
faq.answer: That usually means the drive and acceleration steps haven't been drilled enough on their own; slow down and repeat part 1 and part 2 separately before adding the transition back into a tall posture.

alternatives.name: Single-Cone Sprint Drill
alternatives.reason: Works the same acceleration mechanics with a cone as a visual target if you'd rather practice against a marker than count steps.

easierVariations.name: Linear Acceleration Wall Drill
easierVariations.reason: Practices the same forward lean and drive pattern against a wall for support, useful before removing that support and starting from a dead stop.

harderVariations.name: Wind Sprints
harderVariations.reason: Chains the same drive-and-acceleration mechanics into a full sprint once the three parts of the start feel automatic.

summary: The face pull is a cable exercise where you pull a rope attachment toward your face, elbows flaring high and wide, finishing with your hands near your ears. It targets the rear deltoids and the muscles between your shoulder blades, the ones that spend most of a desk-bound day doing nothing while the chest and front shoulders get all the work. It's a favorite for anyone who presses heavy, sits a lot, or wants their shoulders to stop rounding forward.
whyItWorks: Most people's daily posture and training both favor the front of the shoulder: pressing, typing, driving, all of it pulls the shoulders forward and rounds the upper back. The face pull directly opposes that by pulling the rope toward your face while externally rotating your shoulders at the top, a combined movement that hits the rear delts and the mid-back retractors (rhomboids and middle trapezius) at once. Because the rope splits into two handles, each side can travel its own path outward and up, letting the rotation happen naturally instead of being blocked by a fixed bar.
setup: Set a cable pulley to roughly upper-chest or face height and attach a rope handle.
Grab one end of the rope in each hand with palms facing each other.
Step back until there's tension on the cable, feet staggered or shoulder-width apart.
Stand tall with your core braced, not leaning back to use body weight.
execution: Pull the rope toward your face, leading with your elbows.
Flare your elbows out and up as the rope approaches your face.
Finish with your hands near your ears and your knuckles pointing roughly behind you.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the peak of the pull.
Return the rope slowly to the start, resisting the cable the entire way.
Repeat without letting your torso lean back to help the pull.
formCues: Elbows lead the pull, higher than your hands.
Finish with hands near your ears, not your chin.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the top.
Keep your torso still; don't lean back to cheat the weight.
breathing: Exhale as you pull the rope toward your face, inhale as you return it to the start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the rope toward the chin or chest instead of the face.
commonMistakes.correction: Aim the rope at eye or nose height and keep the elbows high throughout the pull; a lower pull turns this into a row and skips the rear-delt rotation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso backward to help move the weight.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and keep your torso upright; if you need to lean back, the weight is too heavy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drop below the hands.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows at or above hand height through the whole pull; dropped elbows shift the work toward the lats instead of the rear delts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the return and letting the cable yank the arms forward.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return at the same pace as the pull; the rear delts do real work resisting the cable on the way back too.

programmingNotes: Two to four sets of 12 to 15 reps works well, since this is light-to-moderate posture and shoulder-health work rather than a max-effort lift.
Because the load is light and the joint stress is low, most people can include it in two or three training sessions a week without it competing with recovery from heavier lifts.
Program it after your main pressing or pulling work as dedicated rear-delt and upper-back volume, not as a warm-up unless you keep the weight very light.
If you spend most of your day at a desk, this is one of the better exercises to bias slightly higher in weekly volume than the rest of your shoulder work.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light enough that you can finish each rep with your hands near your ears without straining your neck forward to meet the rope.
Stop if you feel pinching at the front of the shoulder instead of a stretch and squeeze through the rear delts and upper back.

faq.question: What muscles does the face pull work?
faq.answer: Mainly the rear deltoids, plus the rhomboids and middle trapezius between your shoulder blades. It's one of the better exercises for the muscles that counteract rounded, forward shoulders.

faq.question: How heavy should I go on face pulls?
faq.answer: Lighter than most other pulling exercises. Twelve to 15 reps with strict form, elbows high and hands finishing near your ears, matters far more here than the number on the stack.

faq.question: Can I do face pulls without a cable machine?
faq.answer: Yes, a resistance band anchored at face height works the same pattern. A dumbbell reverse fly also targets the same rear-delt muscles without any cable at all.

faq.question: Why do face pulls help with shoulder pain from bench pressing?
faq.answer: Heavy pressing biases the front of the shoulder, and face pulls directly train the opposing rear-delt and upper-back muscles. Balancing the two can ease some of the rounded-shoulder discomfort that heavy pressers often develop over time.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Reverse Fly
alternatives.reason: Hits the same rear deltoids and upper-back muscles with dumbbells when a cable machine isn't free.

easierVariations.name: Band Pull Apart
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same rear-delt pull-apart pattern with a simple band, no cable stack or rope attachment needed.

summary: This is a lying triceps isolation move where you hold a dumbbell in each hand above your chest and lower them together toward the sides of your head, then press them back up. The overhead arm position also asks your shoulders to hold steady and gives your chest a light stretch, which is why both show up as secondary muscles here even though the triceps do almost all the work. It suits anyone past the beginner stage who already curls and presses comfortably and wants a dedicated triceps finisher.
whyItWorks: Lowering the dumbbells to the sides of your head, rather than crossing them together at your forehead, keeps each arm working through its own straight line instead of sharing a single bar path. That means each triceps has to control its own dumbbell independently, which builds a bit more stability than a barbell version where the bar forces both arms to move in sync. Holding the arms overhead the entire set also keeps the shoulders working isometrically to keep the weights from drifting.
setup: Lie flat on a bench with your feet planted on the floor and a light-to-moderate dumbbell in each hand.
Press the dumbbells up above your chest so your arms are fully extended, palms facing each other.
Brace your core so your lower back stays settled against the bench.
Fix your upper arms in place before starting the first rep.
execution: Start with both dumbbells locked out directly above your shoulders.
Bend your elbows and lower the dumbbells at the same time toward the sides of your head, keeping your upper arms still.
Lower until you feel a solid stretch in the back of your upper arms, without letting the weights drop past a comfortable range.
Extend your elbows to press both dumbbells back up over your chest.
Keep the same tempo on both arms so one doesn't finish ahead of the other.
Repeat for the set.
formCues: Elbows stay narrow and pointed forward, not flared to the sides.
Lower both dumbbells at the same pace.
Keep your upper arms still, only the forearms travel.
Press back to full extension without locking the elbows out violently.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the dumbbells toward your head, exhale as you press them back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare outward as the weights lower, which shifts stress off the triceps and onto the shoulders.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the elbows tracking forward and roughly shoulder-width apart through the whole rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lowering one arm faster than the other, which can twist the torso to compensate.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down and match the pace of both arms, using a lighter weight if needed to keep them in sync.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a weight so heavy that the shoulders take over to help press it back up.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until the triceps alone can complete the full range without shoulder assistance.

programmingNotes: As a triceps isolation move, 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 12 reps once or twice a week fits most training plans well.
Place it after your heavier pressing work in a push session, since it's meant to finish the muscle rather than build raw strength.
Increase the dumbbell weight only once both arms move together smoothly for every rep.
safetyNotes: Warm your shoulders up before loading this movement, since they hold an overhead position under tension for the whole set.
Choose a bench with enough width or use a spotter for heavier loads, since dropping a dumbbell near your head is a real risk.
Stop if you feel shoulder pinching rather than pushing through a heavier weight.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for the lying dumbbell tricep extension?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 10 to 12 reps, once or twice a week, works well as a triceps finisher placed after your main pressing work.

faq.question: What can I do at home without a bench?
faq.answer: A standing dumbbell triceps extension trains the same muscle overhead without needing to lie down, and works fine on the floor or standing in open space.

faq.question: Why does one arm feel weaker during this exercise?
faq.answer: That's common and usually just reflects a real strength difference between arms. Slow the tempo down and let the weaker arm set the pace instead of rushing to match the stronger one.

faq.question: Lying dumbbell extension vs dumbbell skullcrusher: what's different?
faq.answer: Both are lying triceps moves with dumbbells. A skullcrusher usually brings the dumbbells together toward the forehead, while this version lowers them independently to the sides of the head, asking each arm to control its own path.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Skullcrusher
alternatives.reason: Covers the same lying triceps pattern with dumbbells lowered toward the forehead instead of beside the head.

alternatives.name: Cable Lying Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the triceps lying down with steady cable tension instead of dumbbells.

easierVariations.name: Standing Dumbbell Triceps Extension
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the same overhead extension pattern standing up, without needing to stabilize a bench and two dumbbells at once.

harderVariations.name: One Arm Pronated Dumbbell Triceps Extension
harderVariations.reason: Trains one arm at a time, which removes the second arm's help stabilizing the weight and demands more control.

summary: The jackknife sit-up, also known as a V-up, has you lying flat on your back and lifting your torso and straight legs at the same time, meeting in the middle so your hands reach toward your feet. Unlike a regular sit-up, which only moves your torso, this asks your upper and lower abs to fold toward each other simultaneously, which is a bigger coordination and strength demand for the same amount of floor space. It suits anyone with a decent base of core strength already, since the full-body folding motion is harder to control than it looks.
whyItWorks: Your rectus abdominis runs the full length of your torso, and most ab exercises only ask it to shorten from one end, either the ribs curling toward the pelvis in a crunch or the pelvis tilting toward the ribs in a reverse crunch. The jackknife sit-up asks both ends to move toward the middle at once, which means your upper and lower abs contract together rather than one end staying relatively still. Your hip flexors also do real work here lifting your straight legs, so this is closer to a compound core movement than a pure abdominal isolation exercise, similar to the coordination reflected in its compound mechanics rating.
setup: Lie face up on the floor, reaching your arms straight past your head and keeping your legs fully extended.
Keep your legs together and pointed toward the ceiling as you prepare to lift.
Press your lower back gently into the floor before you start moving.
Pick a fixed point ahead of you to keep your neck neutral through the rep.
execution: Lift your torso and your straight legs off the floor at the same time.
Reach your hands toward your feet as your body folds into a V shape.
Meet in the middle with your hands close to your shins or ankles if your flexibility allows.
Lower your torso and legs back down together under control.
Stop just before your shoulders and heels touch the floor to keep tension on your abs.
Repeat for your target reps, keeping the same tempo on the way up and down.
formCues: Lift your torso and legs at the same speed so you meet cleanly in the middle.
Keep your legs as straight as your hamstrings allow rather than bending your knees to cheat the range.
Lead with your chest reaching up, not just your arms flailing forward.
Control the lower on the way down instead of dropping back to the floor.
breathing: Exhale as you fold up into the V, inhale as you lower back down with control.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to jerk the torso and legs up instead of controlled strength
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the rep down and lift through your abs deliberately, even if that means fewer clean reps instead of more sloppy ones.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the legs drop faster than the torso lifts, breaking the V shape
commonMistakes.correction: Practice each half separately first if needed, then focus on lifting both halves at the same tempo once you combine them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the knees significantly to make the range easier
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a slight, natural bend at most, and regress to a tuck crunch instead if straight legs feel out of reach right now.

commonMistakes.mistake: Slamming the torso and heels back to the floor between reps
commonMistakes.correction: Lower under control and stop just short of the floor to keep your abs working through the whole set.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps work well as a core finisher once you can do a handful with clean form.
Because it's a demanding compound ab movement, two or three times a week with a day of rest between sessions is enough for most people.
Master a strict sit-up and a reverse crunch separately before combining them here, since jackknife sit-ups ask for both movements' strength and coordination at once.
If your form breaks down partway through a set, stop there rather than finishing the set with momentum.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled rather than using momentum, since a fast, jerky V-up puts unnecessary strain on your lower back.
Stop if you feel pinching or strain in your lower back rather than working through it.
Build up your rep count gradually rather than jumping straight to high volume.

faq.question: How many jackknife sit-ups should I do per set?
faq.answer: 8 to 12 clean reps for three sets is a solid target once you've built the coordination for the movement.

faq.question: What's an easier version if I can't do a full jackknife sit-up yet?
faq.answer: A tuck crunch trains the same folding motion but only moves your knees toward your chest, which is a good regression while you build strength and coordination.

faq.question: Do I need my legs completely straight for this exercise?
faq.answer: As straight as your hamstring flexibility allows is the goal, but a slight natural bend is fine, and bending more to make it easier means it's time to regress to an easier variation instead.

faq.question: Is a jackknife sit-up the same as a V-up?
faq.answer: Yes, jackknife sit-up and V-up are two names for the same exercise, lifting your torso and straight legs together to meet in a V shape.

faq.question: Why does this feel so much harder than a regular sit-up?
faq.answer: A regular sit-up only lifts your torso, while a jackknife sit-up lifts your torso and legs at the same time, which demands more coordination and strength from your entire abdominal wall at once.

alternatives.name: Cross-Body Crunch
alternatives.reason: A cross-body crunch trains your abs and obliques from the floor without the balance and coordination the V position of a jackknife demands.

easierVariations.name: Tuck Crunch
easierVariations.reason: A tuck crunch trains the same folding motion but only moves your knees toward your chest, without needing your torso and legs to lift and meet at the same time.

harderVariations.name: Hanging Leg Raise
harderVariations.reason: Hanging from a bar removes the floor's assistance entirely, so your abs control the same folding motion against your full bodyweight from a dead hang.

summary: The cable hip extension isolates your glutes and hamstrings by asking your hip alone to do the work, with an ankle cuff and a low pulley providing steady resistance through the full range of motion. It's a standing, single-leg exercise that trains hip extension without turning into a squat or a deadlift, which makes it useful when your back or knees need a break from loaded compound lifts. Anyone who wants more targeted glute work, from beginners rebuilding hip control to lifters chasing a stubborn weak point, can use it.
whyItWorks: Hip extension is the motion of driving your thigh backward from a hinged position, and it's the job your glutes and hamstrings share whenever you walk uphill, sprint, or stand up from a chair. A cable keeps tension on that motion through the entire arc, from the moment your leg is forward to the moment it's fully back, unlike a bodyweight kickback where most of the resistance fades near the top. Your glute drives the bulk of the effort as your thigh passes your torso, while your hamstring, which crosses both the hip and the knee, adds power from the hip side of that joint. Because the movement is isolated to one joint, you can load your glutes and hamstrings directly without asking your quads or your lower back to compensate, which is exactly what makes it worth adding to a program otherwise built around squats and deadlifts.
setup: Clip a cuff around your working ankle, then hook it onto a pulley set near the floor.
Face the weight stack and hold on to it or a nearby support for balance.
Stand tall with a slight bend in your standing knee and your working leg slightly forward, cable already under tension.
Brace your core so your lower back stays still through the set.
execution: Keeping a soft bend in your working knee, drive your leg straight back through your hip.
Squeeze your glute hard at the back of the motion without arching your lower back to add range.
Pause for a beat at full hip extension.
Control the leg back to the starting position, resisting the cable the whole way.
Complete all reps on one side before switching the cuff to the other ankle.
formCues: Drive from the hip, not from a rounding lower back.
Keep your standing leg soft, not locked.
Squeeze the glute at the back, don't just swing the leg.
Control the return, don't let the cable yank you back.
breathing: Exhale as you drive your leg back into hip extension, and inhale as you control it back to the start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to squeeze out a few more inches of range.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the movement where your hip runs out of extension and let your back stay neutral.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the cable yank the leg back to the start between reps.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return the same way you controlled the drive back, keeping tension on the muscle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning so far onto the support that the lower back does the work instead of the hip.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso relatively upright and let the movement come from the hip joint alone.

programmingNotes: Because it isolates one joint and one side at a time, three to four sets of twelve to fifteen reps per leg respond well, done after your main compound lower body lift rather than before it.
It fits well on a day already built around squats, hip thrusts, or deadlifts, as a finisher that targets the glute and hamstring without adding more spinal load.
Twice a week is reasonable for most lifters since the joint stress is low even though the muscle work is real, but scale the volume back on a week that's already glute-heavy elsewhere.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion within what your hip can control without your lower back taking over.
Hold the support with a firm grip so your balance doesn't depend on your working leg's momentum.
If you feel the movement in your lower back rather than your glute, shorten the range and check your posture before adding more weight.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable hip extensions should I do?
faq.answer: Three to four sets of twelve to fifteen reps per leg is a solid starting point, since the exercise is built for controlled, repeated tension rather than heavy singles.

faq.question: Can I do this at home without a cable machine?
faq.answer: Yes. A resistance band anchored low and looped around your ankle recreates the same hip-extension pattern, or you can go straight to hip extension with bands.

faq.question: What's the difference between a cable hip extension and a glute kickback?
faq.answer: A cable hip extension keeps your knee relatively straight and drives the whole leg back through the hip, while a glute kickback usually bends the knee more and emphasizes the top of the range.

faq.question: Why don't I feel this in my glutes?
faq.answer: If you feel it more in your lower back, you're likely arching to reach past your hip's real range. Shorten the motion and focus on squeezing the glute at the back instead of chasing extra distance.

alternatives.name: Glute Kickback
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hip-driven glute contraction using only bodyweight, useful when no cable machine is around.

easierVariations.name: Hip Extension with Bands
easierVariations.reason: Swaps the cable stack for a band anchored at floor level, giving you the same hip-drive pattern with resistance you can use anywhere.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
harderVariations.reason: Moves from a single-joint, single-leg isolation move to a heavy, bilateral hip extension under a loaded bar, once your glutes can handle real weight.

summary: The backward medicine ball throw has you squatting down holding a medicine ball, then explosively extending your hips and throwing the ball backward and overhead behind you. It's a full-body power exercise that trains the shoulders and hip extensors together, converting a squat into an explosive, whole-body launch rather than a controlled lift.
whyItWorks: This throw teaches your body to transfer force from the ground up through your legs and hips and out through your arms in one continuous, explosive chain, which is the same pattern behind jumping, sprinting, and many athletic movements. Because you're releasing the ball rather than controlling it through a full range like a normal lift, the exercise trains speed and power output specifically, rather than the slower grinding strength that most weight training builds. Throwing backward also removes the temptation to muscle the ball with just your arms, since the ball is moving away from your line of sight, forcing your hips to do the real work.
setup: Stand with your back to a clear, open space with enough room behind you for the ball to land safely.
Hold a medicine ball with both hands, feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down, letting the ball drop between your legs as you hinge.
execution: From the bottom of the squat, drive explosively through your hips and legs.
Extend your body upward and throw the ball backward and overhead in one continuous motion.
Release the ball as your hips and arms reach full extension.
Let your body follow through naturally after the release.
Retrieve the ball and reset your stance before the next rep.
Rest as needed between throws to keep each one genuinely explosive.
formCues: Load the hips low before exploding.
Throw comes from full-body extension, not just the arms.
Release at full extension, let it fly.
Reset fully before each throw.
breathing: Take a breath as you squat down, exhaling forcefully as you explode and release the ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to throw the ball using mostly the arms and shoulders.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on the hip and leg drive as the source of power; the arms and shoulders should feel more like they're guiding the ball's release.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not clearing the landing area behind you before throwing.
commonMistakes.correction: Always check that the space behind you is clear and appropriate for a heavy ball landing before every throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps without resetting between throws.
commonMistakes.correction: Take a moment to reset your stance and breathing before each throw; explosiveness fades quickly with fatigue and rushed setup.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a ball too heavy to throw with real speed.
commonMistakes.correction: Choose a lighter ball that you can genuinely launch explosively; a ball so heavy it barely moves defeats the purpose of a power exercise.

programmingNotes: Start with 3 sets of 5 to 6 throws, resting fully between each one to keep the effort explosive.
It works best early in a session, while your nervous system is fresh and capable of producing real power.
Progress by adding throws or slightly increasing ball weight, but never at the expense of throwing speed.
Pairs well with other explosive movements like jump squats in a power-focused training session.
safetyNotes: Always perform this exercise with plenty of clear space behind you, ideally against a wall or in an open gym area designed for ball throws.
Use a ball weight that allows a genuinely fast, explosive throw rather than a slow, heavy toss.

faq.question: What muscles does the backward medicine ball throw work?
faq.answer: The shoulders are heavily involved in the throwing motion, while the hip extensors, glutes, and legs generate the explosive power that drives the whole movement from the ground up.

faq.question: How heavy should the medicine ball be for this throw?
faq.answer: Light enough that you can throw it with genuine speed and full extension. This is a power exercise, so a ball that slows you down significantly works against the goal.

faq.question: Is the backward medicine ball throw safe to do indoors?
faq.answer: It requires real clearance behind you, so it's best done in a gym space specifically designed for ball throws, or outdoors with plenty of open room. Check your landing area every time before throwing.

faq.question: How many backward medicine ball throws should I do?
faq.answer: Five to six throws per set, for 3 sets, with full rest between throws, is a reasonable amount. Quality and explosiveness on each throw matter far more than total volume.

alternatives.name: Overhead Slam
alternatives.reason: Channels similar explosive power downward into a slam instead of backward into a throw.

alternatives.name: Supine Two-Arm Overhead Throw
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar explosive overhead throwing pattern from a lying position instead of standing.

easierVariations.name: Medicine Ball Scoop Throw
easierVariations.reason: Trains a similar hip-driven throwing pattern with a shorter, more contained range before adding the full backward arc.

harderVariations.name: Standing Two-Arm Overhead Throw
harderVariations.reason: Redirects the same explosive hip and shoulder power forward and overhead instead of behind you.

summary: The bench sprint is a standing conditioning drill where you alternate fast foot contacts on and off a low bench, closer to running in place than stepping up. It builds the same explosive push through the quads, glutes, and hamstrings that a real sprint start uses, packed into short, breathless bursts that suit a finisher or a HIIT round rather than a strength block.
whyItWorks: Sprinting comes down to how fast you can reverse direction at the ankle, knee, and hip on every ground contact, and the bench sprint isolates exactly that skill without needing a track or open space. Alternating a raised surface with the floor forces one leg to push while the other resets, which is the same push-and-recover pattern a true sprint stride uses, just compressed into a small footprint. The quads absorb most of the braking and driving force, while the calves, glutes, and hamstrings back up the hip extension on every contact.
setup: Stand tall facing a stable, flat bench or box roughly shin to knee height, close enough that a short forward lean reaches it.
Set your weight on the balls of your feet with a slight lean forward from the ankles.
Bend your elbows to roughly a right angle, ready to drive them in a running rhythm.
Clear the floor around the bench so a foot landing slightly off doesn't catch on anything.
execution: Drive one foot up onto the bench while the other stays planted on the floor.
Push off the bench foot and swap legs in the air, landing the opposite foot on the bench as the first foot returns to the floor.
Keep the exchange quick and light, closer to a running cadence than a deliberate step-up.
Pump your arms opposite your legs the way you would in an actual sprint.
Keep your torso tall with only a slight forward lean, not folded at the hips.
Hold the fastest cadence you can control for the full length of the set.
Slow the feet down and step off cleanly once the set ends, rather than stopping mid-stride.
formCues: Light, fast foot contacts, not stomps.
Slight forward lean from the ankles, chest tall.
Arms drive opposite the legs.
Soft knee on every bench landing.
breathing: Breathe in short, quick cycles that match your foot cadence, and never hold your breath through a sprint burst.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stomping the foot onto the bench with a straight, locked knee.
commonMistakes.correction: Land with a soft, slightly bent knee on every bench contact to absorb the impact through the muscle instead of the joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning forward from the hips instead of the ankles, folding the torso over.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the chest tall and let the small forward lean come from the ankles, the way a sprinter leans out of the blocks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the cadence drop but treating the set as still going.
commonMistakes.correction: Cut the set short the moment your speed drops rather than finishing the clock at half pace; a shorter, faster set trains the right quality.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting the bench too far away, forcing a reaching lunge instead of a quick foot contact.
commonMistakes.correction: Position the bench close enough that a small forward lean is all it takes to place your foot on top.

programmingNotes: Work in rounds of 20 to 30 seconds at full speed, followed by rest of equal length or longer, for four to six rounds in a session.
Because the repeated foot contacts load the front of the shin and calf, this fits best as a conditioning finisher after your main lifting is done, not as a warm-up.

Two to four sessions a week suits most people, since each round is brief and the real limiter is how well your feet and calves recover from the repeated bench contacts rather than overall training fatigue.
On days you want conditioning without the same repeated impact point, swap in fast skipping instead of adding another bench sprint session.
safetyNotes: Check that the bench sits flat and won't slide before you start; a shifting bench under a fast foot is how ankles get rolled.
Stop the set the instant your footing feels sloppy rather than pushing through the last few seconds on tired legs.

faq.question: How long should a bench sprint set last?
faq.answer: Most people do best with 20 to 30 seconds of all-out feet, followed by at least that much rest. Once your cadence drops, treat the set as done even if the clock isn't.

faq.question: What can I use if I don't have a bench?
faq.answer: A low step, a sturdy box, or a curb all work the same way. If there's no raised surface at all, fast skipping in place trains the same quick-footed conditioning.

faq.question: Bench sprint vs mountain climbers, what's the difference?
faq.answer: Mountain climbers keep both hands on the floor in a plank, so your core carries more of the load. Bench sprints keep you upright in something closer to an actual running posture, shifting the emphasis toward leg speed and cadence.

faq.question: Why does my shin hurt after bench sprints?
faq.answer: Landing with a stiff, straight leg sends the impact straight up the shin. Soften your knee on every contact, and if the ache lingers past a day, cut back the volume before your next session.

alternatives.name: Fast Skipping
alternatives.reason: Delivers the same quick-footed, quad-heavy conditioning without needing a bench, box, or step at all.

easierVariations.name: Mountain Climbers
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the same fast alternating-leg cadence but from a floor plank, so there's no bench height or footing to manage while you learn the rhythm.

harderVariations.name: Bench Jump
harderVariations.reason: Swaps the fast single-foot taps for a two-foot jump onto the bench, adding real vertical power on top of the same quad-driven pattern.

summary: The chain press is a barbell bench press with chains draped over each end of the bar, so a portion of the weight lifts off the floor as you press up and settles back down as you lower the bar. That means the bar gets lighter at your chest and heavier as your arms extend, matching the load to the strength curve of a bench press instead of staying fixed the whole way. Powerlifters use it to build speed off the chest and strength through lockout, the two spots where a straight-weight bench press tends to break down.
whyItWorks: A standard barbell load is fixed no matter where the bar is in the range, but your pressing strength isn't fixed, you're naturally strongest near lockout and weakest just off your chest. Chains fix that mismatch by adding resistance as you press higher and removing it as you lower the bar, so the load actually tracks your strength curve instead of fighting it. Your chest handles most of the work off your chest where the bar is lighter, while your shoulders and triceps take on more of the load as the chains lift off the floor and the resistance builds toward lockout. That rising resistance is also why the chain press is a common tool for building bar speed, since you have to press aggressively through the sticking point before the added chain weight catches up with you.
setup: Drape an appropriate length of chain over each end of the barbell so a portion rests on the floor at the bottom of the press.
Lie on a flat bench with your feet planted and your shoulder blades pulled back and down.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder width and unrack it over your chest.
execution: Lower the bar under control to your mid-chest, keeping your elbows at roughly a 45 degree angle from your torso.
Pause briefly at your chest without bouncing the bar.
Press the bar back up explosively, driving through the sticking point as the chains begin to lift off the floor.
Fully extend your arms at the top, feeling the chain weight add resistance right as you lock out.
Lower under control for the next rep, letting the chains settle back onto the floor as the bar descends.
formCues: Drive the bar with speed off your chest, before the chains add their full weight.
Keep your shoulder blades pinned back throughout the press.
Lower with control, don't let the chains yank the bar down.
Press in a straight line, not out over your face or down toward your waist.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace before you lower the bar, then exhale as you drive it back up past the sticking point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing at the same speed throughout the rep instead of exploding off the chest.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat the bottom of the press as the moment to move fastest, since that's before the chains add their full weight and the bar is at its lightest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the chains hit the floor with a hard clatter and bounce, which can throw off your rhythm and your spotter's timing.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the descent so the chains settle rather than crash, especially if you're training near other lifters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using so much chain weight that your speed off the chest collapses entirely.
commonMistakes.correction: Chain weight should challenge your lockout, not turn the whole rep into a grind. Scale it back if your bar speed off the chest disappears.

programmingNotes: This is a heavy compound press, so treat it like your main bench day and give the pattern a full week to recover before loading it hard again.
Three to five sets of three to five reps fits its role as a strength and bar-speed builder, chase quality reps over high volume.
If you're already pressing on other days that week, keep the chain press as your single heavy bench session and let accessory work fill the gaps rather than adding a second max-effort day.
safetyNotes: Always use a spotter or safety bars when pressing heavy, chains change the bar's feel and a missed rep can surprise you.
Keep the total chain weight reasonable relative to your working weight, start light and add gradually as the feel becomes familiar.
Check that chains are secured and can't slide off the bar mid-set.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for chain press?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of three to five reps works well for building strength and bar speed. This is a heavy compound lift, not a high-rep accessory.

faq.question: How much chain weight should I use?
faq.answer: Start light, often 10 to 20 percent of your working bar weight in chains, and add more only once the accommodating resistance feels manageable through the full range.

faq.question: What can I do instead of chain press if I don't have chains?
faq.answer: A regular barbell bench press trains the same pressing pattern and chest target. Resistance bands anchored to the bar can also mimic the rising-tension effect if chains aren't available.

faq.question: Is chain press the same as bench press with bands?
faq.answer: They both add rising resistance as you press up, but chains add weight through a physical mass lifting off the floor, while bands add tension through stretch. Many lifters find chains feel smoother, since the resistance changes more gradually.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders feel the chain press more than a regular bench press?
faq.answer: The added resistance near lockout asks your shoulders and triceps to finish the rep against more load than a straight-weight bench, so some extra fatigue there is expected. Back off the chain weight if it turns into joint discomfort rather than muscle fatigue.

alternatives.name: Barbell Bench Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same horizontal press pattern and primary chest target without needing chains at all.

easierVariations.name: Floor Press with Chains
easierVariations.reason: Shortens the range of motion by pressing from the floor, a good way to learn how the accommodating resistance feels before pressing through a full bench stroke.

harderVariations.name: Bench Press with Chains
harderVariations.reason: Uses a heavier total chain load once the accommodating-resistance feel is familiar, adding even more tension at the top of the press.

summary: The banded hip extension has you standing, band anchored low in front of you, driving one leg straight back against the resistance. It isolates hip extension, the glutes' main job, while you stay upright and stable on the other leg. It needs only a band and something to anchor it to, which makes it one of the easiest standing glute exercises to do anywhere, home or gym alike.
whyItWorks: Standing on one leg while the other drives backward asks your glute to do its primary job, extending the hip, without help from momentum or a lying position doing some of the work for you. The band's resistance increases the further your leg travels back, which happens to match where your glute is naturally strongest in this motion, so the exercise gets harder exactly where you're most capable of handling it. Balancing on the stance leg at the same time adds a stability challenge most floor-based glute exercises skip entirely.
setup: Anchor a resistance band low to the ground on a post or door anchor.
Loop the other end around your ankle and face the anchor, standing a step or two back so there's tension.
Hold onto something stable for balance if needed, and keep a slight bend in your standing knee.
execution: Keeping your working leg mostly straight, drive it backward against the band's resistance.
Squeeze your glute hard as your leg reaches its furthest point back.
Keep your torso upright rather than leaning forward to help the leg move.
Hold the squeeze briefly at the back of the movement.
Return your leg forward with control, resisting the band the whole way.
Complete all reps on one side before switching legs.
formCues: Torso stays tall, no forward lean.
Squeeze the glute at the back of the movement.
Standing knee soft, not locked.
Controlled return, don't let the band snap the leg forward.
breathing: Exhale as you drive the leg back and squeeze, inhale as it returns forward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso forward to help swing the leg back.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and let the hip do the work; leaning forward turns the exercise into momentum instead of a glute squeeze.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to gain extra range.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the leg when your lower back would otherwise arch; the range that matters is what your glute controls, not how far the leg swings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps and letting the band snap the leg forward.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return over about two seconds; that resisted portion is doing real work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wobbling badly on the standing leg and losing the squeeze.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold something stable for balance while you learn the movement, and remove the support once your stance feels solid.

programmingNotes: Start with 2 or 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps per side, two or three days a week.
It works well as glute activation before squats or lunges, or as standalone glute work at the end of a session.
Increase difficulty with a stronger band or by adding a hold at the back of the movement, rather than swinging faster.
Pairs naturally with the glute bridge and kickback for a well-rounded glute routine without weights.
safetyNotes: Check the band and anchor before each set; a slipping band is the main hazard here.
If balance is shaky, hold a wall or sturdy chair rather than risking a fall while chasing an unsupported set.

faq.question: How many hip extensions with bands should I do?
faq.answer: Twelve to fifteen reps per side, for 2 or 3 sets, works well for most people. A slow, controlled tempo matters more than a high count here.

faq.question: Hip extension with bands vs glute bridge: which is better?
faq.answer: The bridge is easier to balance in and simpler to load heavier over time; the standing band version adds a balance challenge and trains the glute in a more functional, upright position. Using both covers more ground than either alone.

faq.question: Why can't I feel this in my glutes?
faq.answer: Check for a forward-leaning torso or an arching lower back, both of which shift the work away from the glute. Stand tall, keep the range modest, and squeeze deliberately at the back of the movement.

faq.question: What band strength should I use for hip extensions?
faq.answer: Start light enough to complete 12 to 15 controlled reps with a clean squeeze at the back. Move up in band strength only once that becomes easy, not before.

alternatives.name: Glute Kickback
alternatives.reason: The same hip extension pattern from all fours instead of standing, if a band anchor isn't available.

alternatives.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
alternatives.reason: Works the same single glute lying down, useful for comparing strength side to side.

easierVariations.name: Glute Bridge
easierVariations.reason: Works the same glutes lying on your back with both feet planted, an easier position to keep steady.

harderVariations.name: One-Legged Cable Kickback
harderVariations.reason: Moves the same standing hip extension onto a cable stack, where resistance is easier to increase precisely.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
harderVariations.reason: A heavier, bench-supported version of hip extension once band tension stops being enough.

summary: The feet-elevated push-up is a standard push-up with your feet resting on a step, bench, or box instead of the floor. Raising your feet tilts more of your bodyweight over your hands, so your chest and shoulders carry more load with every rep than they would in a flat push-up. It's a simple way to make a push-up harder without adding any external weight, useful once regular push-ups stop feeling challenging.
whyItWorks: A push-up is essentially an incline press using your own bodyweight as the resistance, and how much of that weight lands on your upper body depends on the angle of your torso. When your feet sit higher than your hands, your shoulders end up carrying a larger share of your total bodyweight through the same range of motion, which increases the demand on the chest and front shoulders, and asks the core to work harder to keep your hips from sagging on that tilted line.
setup: Place a stable step, bench, or box behind you and rest your toes on top of it.
Walk your hands out until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to heels at that incline.
Set your hands slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers pointing forward.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes before starting the first rep.
execution: From the elevated plank position, bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor.
Keep your elbows at roughly a 45-degree angle from your torso rather than flaring straight out.
Lower until your chest is close to the ground or your shoulders reach a comfortable stretch.
Press through your palms to straighten your arms and return to the starting plank.
Keep your hips level with your shoulders throughout, no sagging or piking.
Repeat for the set, resetting your foot placement on the step if it shifts.
formCues: One straight line from shoulders through heels, even on the incline.
Elbows at roughly 45 degrees, not flared wide.
Hips stay level, no sagging toward the floor.
Chest leads the movement down and up.
breathing: Inhale as you lower your chest toward the floor, exhale as you press back up to the starting plank.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag below the line of the shoulders and feet as fatigue sets in.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes before each rep, and end the set once you can no longer hold a straight line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a surface so high that the movement turns into more of a shoulder press than a chest-dominant push-up.
commonMistakes.correction: Start with a low step, around knee height, and raise it only once you can do a full set with strict form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the head drop and the neck crane forward to look at the floor.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your gaze slightly ahead of your hands so your neck stays in line with your spine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the descent and bouncing off the bottom instead of controlling it.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower for a slow count of two before pressing back up; a controlled descent builds more strength than a fast, bouncy one.

programmingNotes: This is still a bodyweight movement, so it tolerates more frequent practice than a loaded lift; 3 sets of 8 to 15 reps, two to three times a week with a day of rest between sessions, works well for most people.
Raise the surface height gradually over weeks rather than jumping straight to a high box; a few inches at a time keeps the shoulders adapting without overloading them.
Pair it with a rowing or pulling movement in the same workout to balance the extra pushing volume.
safetyNotes: Choose a step or bench that won't slide or tip when your toes press into it.
If your shoulders feel pinchy or sharp at the bottom of the rep, shorten the range or lower the foot height until it feels clean again.

faq.question: How high should my feet be for elevated push-ups?
faq.answer: Start with a step around knee height. Going too high shifts the movement toward a shoulder press and can strain the shoulders before your chest gets a proper workout, so raise the height gradually as strict reps get easier.

faq.question: Are feet-elevated push-ups harder than regular push-ups?
faq.answer: Yes, tilting your feet above your hands shifts more of your bodyweight onto your chest and shoulders, so the same number of reps feels noticeably harder than a flat push-up.

faq.question: What can I use if I don't have a step or bench?
faq.answer: A sturdy chair, stairs, or a low wall all work, as long as the surface is stable and won't slide when you push off it. A flat push-up on the floor is also a fine substitute when nothing stable is available.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders feel it more than my chest?
faq.answer: That's usually a sign the surface is too high for your current strength. Lower the step so your torso angle is less steep, which shifts more of the work back toward the chest.

faq.question: How many reps should I do before raising the step higher?
faq.answer: Once you can complete all your planned sets with strict form and a straight body line, that's the signal to raise the surface by a small amount, a few inches at a time, rather than jumping straight to the highest box you can find.

alternatives.name: Pushups
alternatives.reason: Trains the same chest, shoulder, and triceps pattern at ground level, a direct swap when you don't have a step, bench, or box to elevate your feet on.

easierVariations.name: Incline Push-Up
easierVariations.reason: Flips the incline so your hands are raised instead of your feet, taking bodyweight off the chest and shoulders until you're ready to load them more.

harderVariations.name: Push-Ups With Feet On An Exercise Ball
harderVariations.reason: Swaps the fixed step or bench for an unstable ball under your feet, adding a balance and core-control demand on top of the same elevated-feet loading.

summary: The rickshaw deadlift has you stand inside a loaded frame and lift it by gripping handles at your sides, similar in feel to a trap bar deadlift but usually loaded and walked as a strongman event rather than performed for straight reps off the floor. Because the handles sit level with your hips rather than out in front of your shins, the lift favors a more upright torso and a bigger role for the quads than a conventional barbell deadlift. It suits lifters who already deadlift confidently and want a variation with more available equipment options and a slightly different loading pattern.
whyItWorks: Where a barbell sits in front of your shins and pulls your torso forward as you set up, the rickshaw frame surrounds you, with handles positioned right at your sides near hip height. That position lets you keep a more upright torso through the lift, which shifts more of the workload onto the quads and reduces how far your hips need to travel compared to a conventional deadlift. Because the frame swings freely on some equipment, your grip and stabilizing muscles also have to control any side-to-side sway, adding a balance and bracing demand on top of the raw pulling strength the lift already requires. The neutral, hammer-style grip the handles allow is also easier on the wrists and biceps than pulling a straight bar, which is part of why some lifters use it as a heavier-loading alternative on weeks when a conventional deadlift feels rough on the joints.
setup: Load the rickshaw frame evenly on both sides before stepping in.
Stand inside the frame with feet roughly hip-width apart, gripping a handle firmly in each hand.
Bend your knees and hips to lower into position, lifting your chest and holding a flat spine.
Take a full breath and brace your core before initiating the lift.
execution: Drive through your legs to lift the frame off the ground, keeping your torso upright.
Extend your hips and knees together until you're standing fully tall, with the frame hanging at your sides.
Pause briefly at the top without leaning back or hyperextending your lower back.
Lower the frame back down under control by bending your hips and knees together.
Reset your grip and your brace before starting the next rep.
formCues: Chest up, torso stays tall through the lift.
Drive through the legs, not just the back.
Full lockout at the top, no lean-back.
Lower with the same control you used to lift.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace before each rep, exhaling once you reach the top of the lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to get the frame moving off the ground.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hips and chest position before the pull starts, and keep a flat back from setup through lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning back or hyperextending the spine at the top of the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the movement once your hips are fully extended and you're standing tall; there's no need to lean past that point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the frame swing side to side during the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and keep even pressure on both handles to keep the frame moving in a straight vertical line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading the frame unevenly, causing the lift to feel lopsided.
commonMistakes.correction: Double-check that both sides carry equal weight before you begin the set.

programmingNotes: This is a genuinely loaded compound pull, so treat it like a main lower body lift and keep it to once a week if it's your primary deadlift-pattern movement that week.
Three to five sets of 3 to 6 reps builds strength well for this pattern, since the neutral grip and upright torso let most lifters handle heavier loads than a conventional deadlift.
Place it early in a lower body session while your bracing and grip are fresh, since both fatigue quickly under this loading pattern.
If your gym has both a rickshaw frame and a trap bar, alternate between them across training blocks rather than doing both in the same week.
safetyNotes: Keep the lower back flat throughout the lift; the more upright torso here doesn't remove the need for solid spinal bracing.
Start with a conservative load until you're comfortable with how the frame balances and swings under weight.

faq.question: What's the difference between a rickshaw deadlift and a trap bar deadlift?
faq.answer: They share a similar neutral-grip, straddled stance, but the rickshaw frame is typically strongman equipment used for heavier loads and event-style training, while the trap bar is a more common gym tool. The movement pattern and muscles worked are very similar.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of rickshaw deadlifts should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of 3 to 6 reps is a solid range for building strength, treating it like a main compound lift rather than a light accessory movement.

faq.question: What muscles does the rickshaw deadlift work?
faq.answer: The quads take on a bigger share of the work than in a conventional deadlift, thanks to the more upright torso position, with the glutes, hamstrings, lower back, traps, and forearms all contributing as well.

faq.question: Can I do a rickshaw deadlift without a rickshaw frame?
faq.answer: A trap bar deadlift trains a nearly identical neutral-grip, straddled-stance pattern and is available at most gyms that don't carry strongman equipment.

alternatives.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same neutral-grip, quad-dominant deadlift pattern when a rickshaw frame isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
easierVariations.reason: Uses the same neutral-grip, straddled-frame stance as the rickshaw but on more widely available equipment, a good place to build the pattern first.

summary: The standing low-pulley deltoid raise has you stand beside a low cable station and raise the handle out and up to shoulder height, working the side of the shoulder through a path a dumbbell can't quite match. Because the cable pulls across your body instead of straight down, it keeps tension on the shoulder even at the bottom of the rep, where a dumbbell raise would otherwise go slack.
whyItWorks: The side deltoid lifts your arm out to the side, and a dumbbell raise loads that muscle hardest only near the top, since gravity pulls straight down and barely resists the first part of the lift. A low pulley changes the angle of resistance: because the cable runs up and across your body rather than straight down, it keeps real tension on the shoulder from the very first inch of the raise, not just the top half. Standing a step or two away from the machine, rather than right next to it, increases that cross-body angle and makes the early part of the rep even harder, which is why small changes in where you stand noticeably change how the exercise feels.
setup: Set a low pulley to the lowest setting and attach a single handle.
Stand sideways to the machine, a step or two away, holding the handle in the hand farther from it.
Let your arm hang down and slightly across your body to start, with a soft bend in your elbow.
execution: Raise your arm out and up until your hand reaches roughly shoulder height.
Lead with your elbow rather than your hand or wrist.
Pause briefly at the top without shrugging your shoulder up toward your ear.
Lower the handle back down under control, letting the cable pull your arm back across your body.
Repeat for the set, then switch sides.
formCues: Lead with the elbow, not the hand.
Raise to shoulder height, no higher.
Keep your shoulder down, don't shrug.
Control the lowering phase, don't let the cable yank your arm back.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the handle out and up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the whole body to swing the weight up instead of isolating the shoulder.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso still and let the deltoid alone lift the handle; swinging means the weight is too heavy for a strict raise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear at the top of the raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulder pressed down and away from your ear throughout, even at the top of the movement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too close to the machine, which shortens the cable angle and the range of real tension.
commonMistakes.correction: Stand a step or two away from the pulley so the cable pulls across your body for more of the rep.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 12 to 15 reps per side suits this isolation exercise well.
Twice or three times a week works for most people, since it's a light, single-joint movement that recovers quickly.
Place it after your main pressing work in a shoulder session, since it's better suited to finishing the shoulder than to moving heavy loads.
safetyNotes: Keep the raise at or just below shoulder height; going higher shifts stress onto the front of the shoulder joint without adding much benefit.
Ease off the weight if you feel pinching at the top of the shoulder instead of fatigue in the muscle on the side of it.

faq.question: How many reps should I do for the standing low-pulley deltoid raise?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 12 to 15 reps per side is a solid range, two or three times a week.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and a dumbbell lateral raise?
faq.answer: The cable keeps tension on the shoulder through the whole range, including the bottom, where a dumbbell raise loses most of its resistance; the dumbbell version is simpler to set up and a fine place to start.

faq.question: What can I do without a cable machine?
