harderVariations.reason: Returns to two legs but adds a barbell, trading the balance challenge for heavy loading.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Hip Thrust
harderVariations.reason: Elevating your shoulders lengthens the range and lets you keep adding weight for years.

summary: The Floor Glute-Ham Raise kneels you on a padded floor with your ankles anchored, then has you lower your torso forward under control before pulling yourself back upright using your hamstrings and glutes. It trains the hamstrings through a full range that few other exercises hit, working them both as knee flexors and hip extensors in the same rep. Anyone who wants stronger, more resilient hamstrings without a glute-ham machine can use this version.
whyItWorks: Most hamstring exercises isolate just one of their two jobs, a leg curl bends the knee, a deadlift extends the hip. The glute-ham raise asks the hamstrings to do both at once: as you lower your torso forward from kneeling, the hamstrings work eccentrically to control your knees straightening under your bodyweight, then as you pull back upright, they work together with the glutes to flex the knees and extend the hips again. That combined demand is closer to what the hamstrings do while sprinting or decelerating than an isolated curl, which is part of why the movement shows up in hamstring injury prevention work.
setup: Kneel on a pad with your ankles anchored under something solid or held firmly by a partner.
Keep your knees roughly hip-width apart and your torso upright, in a straight line from knees to head.
Cross your arms over your chest or keep your hands loose in front, ready to catch yourself if needed.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes before you start moving.
execution: Keeping your hips extended and your body in a straight line, slowly let your torso tip forward from the knees.
Resist the fall the entire way, using your hamstrings to control the descent as long as you can.
Once you can no longer control the lean, catch yourself with your hands and lower the rest of the way to the floor.
Push off the floor and use your hamstrings and glutes to pull your torso back to the upright kneeling position.
Keep your hips extended throughout the pull, don't let them pike backward.
Reset at the top and repeat for the set.
formCues: Straight line from knees to shoulders, no piking at the hips.
Resist the fall, don't just drop.
Push through the floor to start the pull back up.
Glutes squeezed at the top of every rep.
breathing: Inhale as you lower under control, exhale as you drive back up to kneeling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips pike backward during the lowering phase.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a straight line from knees to head by actively squeezing the glutes as you lean forward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping fast instead of resisting the lean.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the descent as much as your hamstrings allow before catching yourself with your hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to pull back up from the floor with the arms doing most of the work.
commonMistakes.correction: Use your hands only to push off the floor, then let the hamstrings and glutes finish the pull.

commonMistakes.mistake: Anchoring the feet under something that can slip or lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Have a partner hold your ankles firmly, or wedge them under a fixed, heavy object.

programmingNotes: Start with 2 to 3 sets of 4 to 6 controlled reps; the eccentric demand is high even without added weight.
Once a week is enough for most people early on, since the deep hamstring load can leave you sore for several days.
Program it early in a lower body session, before your legs are fatigued from squats or deadlifts.
Progress by increasing how far you lower before catching yourself, rather than adding reps too quickly.
safetyNotes: Stop the descent and catch yourself with your hands the moment your hamstrings can no longer control the lean.
Use a well padded surface for your knees, and stop if you feel any hamstring strain rather than pushing through it.

faq.question: How many reps of floor glute-ham raise should a beginner do?
faq.answer: Start with 2 to 3 sets of 4 to 6 reps, catching yourself with your hands partway down. The eccentric control is demanding even at low reps, and quality matters more than quantity here.

faq.question: Can I do a glute-ham raise without a partner or a machine?
faq.answer: Yes, you can anchor your ankles under a heavy piece of furniture, a loaded barbell resting on the floor, or a sturdy fixed bar instead of using a partner or a glute-ham developer machine.

faq.question: Floor glute-ham raise vs Nordic curl, are they the same?
faq.answer: They're close cousins. A Nordic curl usually stays purely at the knee with the hips locked, while the glute-ham raise lets the hips extend too, adding the glutes into the pull back up.

faq.question: Why can't I pull myself back up from the floor?
faq.answer: That's normal at first, the concentric pull is one of the hardest parts of the movement. Keep lowering under as much control as you can and use your hands to help on the way back until your hamstrings and glutes catch up in strength.

alternatives.name: Romanian Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hamstrings through hip extension with a barbell instead of bodyweight and an anchor point.

easierVariations.name: Lying Leg Curls
easierVariations.reason: A machine leg curl trains the knee-flexion half of the same movement with support and adjustable resistance, a gentler entry point.

harderVariations.name: Glute Ham Raise
harderVariations.reason: The machine version lets you dial in the range and add support as you build toward a full unassisted floor rep.

summary: The seated band hamstring curl is a seated exercise where you loop a resistance band around your ankle and curl your heel back and down against the band's pull. It isolates your hamstrings without needing a leg curl machine, making it easy to do at home or while traveling. It suits anyone building hamstring strength for the first time, or rehabbing after time off from harder posterior-chain work.
whyItWorks: Your hamstrings cross both your hip and knee joints, but when you're seated with your hip already bent, the only job left for them is bending your knee, which is exactly what this exercise isolates. Anchoring the band in front of you and looping it around your ankle creates resistance that increases as you curl your heel back, so your hamstrings work hardest right at the point in the range where they're usually weakest. Because the resistance comes from a band rather than a fixed machine cam, your hamstrings also have to control the curl on the way back out, adding a controlled eccentric to every rep.
setup: Sit in a sturdy chair or on a bench with your feet flat on the floor.
Anchor a resistance band to a low point in front of you, like a table leg or a doorframe anchor.
Loop the other end of the band around one ankle, keeping some tension in the band at the start.
execution: Keeping your thigh still, curl your heel back and down, bending your knee against the band's resistance.
Squeeze your hamstring at the end of the range.
Slowly straighten your leg back out, controlling the band the whole way.
Complete all reps on one side before switching legs.
formCues: Keep your thigh pressed against the chair rather than lifting it to help the curl.
Curl through a full range rather than a short, partial motion.
Control the return instead of letting the band snap your leg back out.
Keep your upper body relaxed and still throughout.
breathing: Exhale as you curl your heel back, and inhale as you straighten your leg back out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the thigh off the seat to help complete the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your thigh pressed down; if you need to lift it, the band tension is too high for your current strength.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the band yank the leg back to the start.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return phase at the same speed as the curl itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a band with too little tension to feel any resistance.
commonMistakes.correction: Shorten the band or anchor it further away to add enough resistance to challenge the hamstring through the full curl.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps without pausing at the end range.
commonMistakes.correction: Add a brief squeeze at the most bent position of each rep before returning.

programmingNotes: As a light band isolation exercise, 2 to 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps per leg most lower-body training days works well.
Use it as accessory work after your main lower-body lift, or as a standalone hamstring session on a day without equipment access.
Increase the challenge by shortening the band or moving the anchor point further away rather than by rushing the tempo.
safetyNotes: Check the band anchor is secure before starting; a band that slips can snap back unexpectedly.
Stop if you feel any sharp pain behind the knee rather than muscular fatigue in the hamstring.
Choose a band tension you can control through the full range without your thigh lifting off the seat.

faq.question: How many sets should I do?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps per leg is a good starting point for a band-based isolation exercise like this.

faq.question: Can I do this without any equipment other than a band?
faq.answer: Yes, that's the appeal of the exercise; a chair and a resistance band anchored to something sturdy is all you need.

faq.question: What's a good alternative if I don't have a band?
faq.answer: The standing leg curl works the same knee-flexion pattern using your own body weight and a wall or machine for support instead of band resistance.

faq.question: Why don't I feel much resistance at the start of the curl?
faq.answer: Bands provide less resistance when they're less stretched, so the beginning of the movement will always feel lighter than the end; that's normal and different from the more even resistance of a machine.

alternatives.name: Standing Leg Curl
alternatives.reason: Isolates the same knee-flexion movement standing, using your own body weight and a support instead of band resistance.

harderVariations.name: Seated Leg Curl
harderVariations.reason: Trains the same seated knee-flexion pattern on a machine with adjustable, progressive resistance instead of a band.

summary: The standing dumbbell upright row pulls two dumbbells straight up your body to roughly chest height, elbows leading the way. It builds the traps first, with the side delts picking up a good share of the work too. It's a solid pick for anyone chasing broader-looking shoulders and a thicker neck-to-shoulder line, especially if a barbell version has ever bothered their wrists.
whyItWorks: Pulling a weight up close to the body with the elbows rising above the hands is what puts the traps, which run from your neck down to your shoulder blades, under real tension, since they're the muscles responsible for shrugging the shoulder blades upward. The side delts assist because the upper arm is also abducting away from the body as the elbows rise. Because dumbbells let each hand find its own angle instead of locking to a bar's fixed width, you get this trap and shoulder work with less strain on the wrists than a barbell version.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, palms facing your body.
Stand with your feet hip-width apart and a soft bend in your knees.
Let the dumbbells hang close to your body rather than out in front.
Brace your core so your lower back doesn't arch as you pull.
execution: Pull both dumbbells straight up along your body, leading with your elbows.
Stop once your elbows reach roughly shoulder height.
Keep the dumbbells close to your torso the entire way up.
Lower the weights back down with control, don't let them drop.
Pause briefly at the bottom before starting the next rep.
formCues: Let your elbows lead the pull, not your hands.
Keep the dumbbells brushing close to your body as they rise.
Stop at shoulder height, pulling higher adds strain without adding benefit.
Keep your shoulders down away from your ears until the very top of the pull.
breathing: Exhale as you pull the dumbbells up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the elbows above shoulder height.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the pull once your elbows reach shoulder level, going higher just adds joint strain.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the dumbbells drift away from the body.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the dumbbells close enough to brush your torso on the way up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up before the elbows start the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Lead with the elbows first, and let the traps finish the movement at the top instead of starting with a shrug.

programmingNotes: This is a loaded compound pull for the upper traps and shoulders, so once a week with real weight is enough if you're also training shoulders or back that week.
3 sets of 10 to 12 reps builds the traps and side delts well without needing heavy loads.
Pair it with a pressing exercise earlier in the session, since the shoulders handle this move better when they aren't already fatigued from other pulling work.
If shoulder pinching shows up at any weight, switch to the one-arm dumbbell version and find the angle that feels clean for each side.
safetyNotes: Stop pulling above shoulder height, since that position is where most shoulder pinching during this exercise starts.
If you feel pinching at the front of the shoulder even at a moderate height, lower the weight and shorten the range for that session.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of standing dumbbell upright rows should I do?
faq.answer: 3 sets of 10 to 12 reps works well. Keep the weight moderate since the traps and shoulders respond fine without needing to go heavy.

faq.question: What can I use instead of dumbbells for upright rows?
faq.answer: A barbell, an EZ-bar, or a resistance band anchored under your feet all train the same pulling pattern. Dumbbells just let each wrist find its own comfortable angle.

faq.question: Dumbbell upright row vs barbell upright row, which is better?
faq.answer: Dumbbells let your wrists rotate to a more natural angle, which many people find easier on the shoulders. A barbell locks your grip width but lets you load more total weight once your shoulders handle the movement well.

faq.question: Why does my shoulder pinch during upright rows?
faq.answer: It usually happens when the elbows pull above shoulder height. Stop the pull lower, around chest to collarbone height, and the pinching often disappears.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell One-Arm Upright Row
alternatives.reason: Training one arm at a time lets you pick a grip angle for each shoulder and fix side-to-side strength gaps.

easierVariations.name: Upright Row - With Bands
easierVariations.reason: Bands get lighter at the bottom and only build tension near the top, which is more forgiving on the shoulders while you learn the pull path.

harderVariations.name: Upright Row
harderVariations.reason: A barbell locks both hands to a fixed grip width and lets you load more total weight than a pair of dumbbells.

summary: The kneeling cable triceps extension isolates the triceps by having you kneel facing away from a low pulley, elbows bent overhead, and extend your arms to press the rope up and forward. Kneeling removes the ability to lean back or use your legs to help the lift, which keeps the tension squarely on the triceps throughout the set. It's a useful finishing movement for anyone whose triceps tend to get overshadowed by shoulders or chest during pressing exercises.
whyItWorks: The triceps' main job is straightening the elbow, and this exercise isolates exactly that motion by keeping the upper arms fixed near the head while only the forearms move through the extension. Because kneeling takes away the stable base a standing position would offer for leaning or driving with the legs, the torso has less opportunity to compensate, which keeps the effort concentrated on the triceps rather than spreading across other muscles. Extending the arms from behind the head also puts the long head of the triceps, the portion that crosses the shoulder joint, into a stretched starting position, which many lifters find makes the muscle work harder through the first part of each rep compared with a pushdown that starts with the arms already close to the body.
setup: Attach a rope handle to a low pulley and kneel facing away from the machine, a few feet in front of it.
Reach back and take the rope with both hands, elbows bent and pointing up near your ears.
Brace your torso upright with your core tight.
Set the weight light enough to start; your arm position here gives you very little mechanical advantage to force through a load that's too heavy.
execution: Keeping your upper arms still and close to your head, extend your elbows to press the rope up and forward.
Straighten your arms until your elbows reach full extension.
Pause briefly at the top of the extension.
Bend your elbows back to return to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the set.
formCues: Keep your elbows pinned near your ears.
Only your forearms should move.
Exhale as you extend.
Don't let your elbows flare outward.
Keep your torso still, resisting any temptation to help with your back.
breathing: Exhale as you extend your arms, inhale as you bend your elbows back to the start. Keep the tempo unhurried enough that your breathing stays matched to the movement rather than getting ahead of it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward or flare out to the sides during the extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms fixed close to your head throughout the set, checking their position if your form starts to slip.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the shoulders or leaning the torso to help finish the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso upright and still, letting your triceps complete the extension on their own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only extending partway and calling it a full rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Straighten your elbows all the way at the top of each rep to get the full range this exercise is meant to train.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 10 to 12 reps works well as a single-joint finisher.
Place it after a bigger pressing movement, since this is an isolation exercise meant to finish off the triceps rather than lead a session.
This single-joint movement recovers quickly enough that most people can train it comfortably two or three times within a week.
Add weight in small increments; because your elbows have so little help from other muscles here, even a modest jump in load can wreck your form.
safetyNotes: Keep the load light enough that you can maintain elbow position without flaring.
Stop if you feel pinching in the elbow joint; that's a sign the load or range needs adjusting.
Avoid locking the elbows out forcefully at the top; a controlled full extension is enough.

faq.question: What does the kneeling cable triceps extension work?
faq.answer: It isolates the triceps, the muscle on the back of the upper arm responsible for straightening the elbow.

faq.question: Why kneel instead of stand for this exercise?
faq.answer: Kneeling removes the ability to lean back and use body momentum, keeping the tension focused directly on the triceps.

faq.question: Can I do this exercise standing instead?
faq.answer: Yes, a standing overhead cable extension works the same muscle if kneeling isn't comfortable for your knees.

faq.question: Why does this exercise feel harder than a triceps pushdown at the same weight?
faq.answer: Extending from overhead starts the triceps in a longer, more stretched position than a pushdown does, which tends to make the same load feel more demanding through the first part of the rep.

alternatives.name: Triceps Pushdown - Rope Attachment
alternatives.reason: Works the triceps through a downward cable path instead of overhead, a different elbow angle on the same muscle.

easierVariations.name: Cable Rope Overhead Triceps Extension
easierVariations.reason: Uses the same overhead cable path from a standing position, which is easier on the knees while you learn the elbow-pinned technique.

summary: The cable iron cross has you standing between two high pulleys, arms spread wide like the shape of the movement's name, then sweeping both handles down and together in front of your body. It isolates your chest through a long, arcing path that a pressing exercise can't match, with constant cable tension replacing the momentum a dumbbell fly relies on. It's a good pick for anyone looking to finish a chest workout with a deep stretch and a hard squeeze, rather than more pressing volume.
whyItWorks: Your chest's fibers run in a fan shape from your sternum out to your upper arm, and their job is pulling your arm across your body, which is exactly the arcing path a cable cross traces. Standing between two pulleys set high means the cable pulls down and in from above, so your chest stays under real tension even at the very start of the movement, unlike a dumbbell fly where gravity does most of the work once your arms drop below shoulder height. Keeping a slight, fixed bend in your elbows throughout the sweep also takes your triceps mostly out of the equation, so the work stays concentrated in your chest instead of leaking into a pressing pattern. The wide starting position gives your pecs a deep stretch before every rep, which is the part of a fly that a straight pushing movement like a bench press never really provides.
setup: Set both pulleys to a high position and attach single handles.
Stand centered between the two stacks, one foot slightly forward for a stable base.
Grip one handle per hand and step forward until your arms sit wide and the cables load up.
Set a slight forward lean and a small, fixed bend in both elbows before your first rep.
execution: Keeping your elbow bend fixed, sweep both handles down and together in front of your hips.
Squeeze your chest hard as your hands meet or cross in front of your body.
Control the handles back out to the wide starting position, resisting the cables the whole way.
Stop the return once you feel a full stretch across your chest, without letting your shoulders roll forward.
Repeat the sweep for the full set without pausing at the top.
formCues: Keep a slight, fixed bend in your elbows the whole set.
Sweep in an arc, don't press straight forward.
Squeeze your chest together at the bottom.
Feel the stretch wide, don't let your shoulders round to chase more range.
breathing: Exhale as you sweep the handles down and together, and inhale as you control them back out to the stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows more as the set gets tiring, which turns the fly into a press.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your elbow angle at the start and keep it locked through every rep, using a lighter weight if you can't maintain it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders roll forward to reach a wider stretch at the start.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest open and shoulder blades gently set back, stopping the stretch where your shoulder position stays stable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the return trip and letting the cables snap the arms back out.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return at the same pace as the squeeze, keeping tension on your chest through the entire rep.

programmingNotes: As a chest isolation move, three sets of twelve to fifteen reps placed after your pressing work make a solid finisher, since your chest is already warm and this move asks for control rather than raw strength.
It fits naturally at the end of a push or chest day, giving your pecs a deep stretch and squeeze that a flat or incline press doesn't provide on its own.
Twice a week suits most chest-focused programs, since the joint stress is low but the muscle can still feel it if you go too heavy too soon.
safetyNotes: Keep the stretch at the start comfortable rather than maximal, especially in the first few sessions.
Avoid letting your shoulders round forward to chase extra range, that shifts strain onto the front of the shoulder joint.
Use a weight light enough that you can keep your elbow bend fixed for every rep in the set.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable iron cross should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of twelve to fifteen reps at the end of a chest session works well, since this move is built to finish the muscle with a deep stretch and squeeze.

faq.question: Can I do this chest fly pattern without a dual cable station?
faq.answer: Yes. Two bands anchored high on either side recreate the same sweep, as does a set of dumbbell flyes lying on a bench.

faq.question: What's the difference between a cable iron cross and a regular cable crossover?
faq.answer: They're close variations on the same arm-cross pattern. The names are often used loosely for the same standing dual-pulley fly, though some gyms use iron cross for a wider or lower starting arm position.

faq.question: Why do I feel this more in my shoulders than my chest?
faq.answer: If your elbows bend more as the set goes on or your shoulders round forward, the load shifts off your chest. Lock your elbow angle and keep your chest open through the full range.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Flyes
alternatives.reason: Trains the same chest fly pattern with dumbbells instead of a dual cable station, useful when the crossover machine is busy.

easierVariations.name: Cross Over - With Bands
easierVariations.reason: Swaps the cable stack for bands anchored high, giving you the same wide arm-cross pattern with resistance that's easy to keep light while you learn the shape.

harderVariations.name: Flat Bench Cable Flyes
harderVariations.reason: Moves the same wide, arcing chest path onto a bench where you can add real load, once the standing version feels controlled.

summary: The rack pull with bands starts the bar on pins set around knee height, so you skip the deadlift's floor-to-knee pull and go straight to the lockout portion. Bands looped under the bar and anchored to the floor add extra tension as you stand tall, so the last few inches get harder instead of easier. It's a lockout and grip builder for lifters who already deadlift, not a replacement for the full lift. Your lower back, traps, and forearms do most of the work.
whyItWorks: A full deadlift is hardest off the floor and easiest at lockout, since your body settles into a stronger pulling position as your hips and knees straighten. Starting from pins removes that hard floor pull and hands you a bar that's already partway up, so your lower back and hips only finish the top half of the range. Looping bands under the bar changes the resistance curve again: as you drive the bar upward, the bands stretch and pull harder, so the lockout, normally the easiest part, becomes the hardest. That combination trains your body to grind through a stubborn top end sticking point and builds grip and upper back strength from holding a heavier than usual load at the top.
setup: Set the safety pins or blocks just below or at knee height inside a power rack.
Loop a resistance band under each end of the loaded bar, then anchor the other end beneath a rack post or a stack of loaded plates.
Load the bar so the added band tension still lets you complete every rep with a full lockout.
Grip the bar just outside your knees with hips back and chest up, like the top half of a deadlift.
execution: Brace your core and pull your shoulders back before the bar leaves the pins.
Drive through your heels and pull the bar up along your shins as the pins release it.
Push your hips forward as the bar passes your knees, fighting the growing band tension.
Stand fully tall, squeezing your glutes and pulling your shoulders back at the top.
Hold the locked out position for a full second before reversing the movement.
Lower the bar back to the pins under control, letting the bands go slack as it lands.
formCues: Keep the bar dragging up your shins and thighs, not drifting forward.
Finish by squeezing your glutes, not by leaning your torso back.
Keep your lats tight so the bar stays close through the whole pull.
Reset your grip and brace fully between reps instead of bouncing off the pins.
breathing: Take a deep breath and brace before the bar leaves the pins, then exhale once you've locked out at the top.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso back at lockout to finish the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes instead of arching your lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting the pull with slack in the bands, so the resistance jumps suddenly mid rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Set the band anchor so there's already light tension with the bar resting on the pins.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking the bar off the pins instead of pulling in a straight line.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace first, then pull the bar up smoothly along your shins.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar drift away from the body during the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the bar in contact with your legs for the entire movement.

programmingNotes: This is a heavy, grip and lockout taxing pull, so once a week is plenty unless it's the only pulling work you're doing that week.
Three to five sets of three to five reps fits best, since the added band tension makes higher rep counts unnecessary.
Program it after your main deadlift work, or on a separate day, so fatigue from a full deadlift session doesn't blunt your lockout strength here.
Add band tension or bar weight in small steps; a stronger lockout builds over weeks, not one big jump in load.
safetyNotes: Keep the bar path close to your body throughout the lift to protect your lower back.
Check that band anchors are secure before loading the bar, since a band that slips under tension can snap back hard.
Stop the set if your lower back rounds under the load instead of staying braced.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for rack pulls with bands?
faq.answer: Start lighter than your regular deadlift and add band tension gradually. Most lifters can handle more total weight here than in a full deadlift, since the range is shorter.

faq.question: Can I do rack pulls with bands without a power rack?
faq.answer: You need pins, blocks, or a rack to set the bar at the right height, so a standard power rack is the easiest setup. Without one, a regular deadlift or a deficit deadlift trains similar muscles.

faq.question: What's the difference between rack pulls and rack pulls with bands?
faq.answer: Both start the bar on pins for a partial range, but bands add extra resistance as you stand up, making the lockout the hardest part instead of the easiest.

faq.question: Do rack pulls with bands help my regular deadlift?
faq.answer: They can strengthen a weak lockout and build grip endurance, both of which carry over to pulling a heavier deadlift from the floor.

alternatives.name: Barbell Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same lower back, hips, and grip through a full range of motion when pins or bands aren't available.

easierVariations.name: Rack Pulls
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the same partial-range pull from pins without the added band tension, a simpler way to learn the lockout position first.

harderVariations.name: Deadlift with Bands
harderVariations.reason: Applies the same growing band resistance to a full-range pull from the floor once your lockout and band technique are solid.

summary: Seated leg tucks work your abdominals by pulling your knees toward your chest while you balance on your seat bones, with no machine or added load involved. It is a floor-friendly way to build core control for people who find a full sit-up or a hanging raise too much too soon. The exercise doubles as a stability drill, since holding the balanced position between reps is half the challenge.
whyItWorks: Pulling your knees toward your chest shortens your hip flexors and abdominals together, and the seated position adds an extra layer: because you are balanced on your seat bones rather than lying on a mat, your abdominals also work isometrically to keep your torso from tipping backward between reps. That combination, a dynamic knee tuck plus a static torso hold, is what separates this move from a floor-based crunch or reverse crunch.
setup: Sit near the front edge of a bench or a sturdy chair.
Lean your torso back slightly and place your hands on the bench beside your hips for support.
Lift your feet off the floor and extend your legs out in front of you.
Brace your core to find your balance point before the first rep.
execution: Pull your knees up and in toward your chest, rounding through your midsection.
Hold the tucked position for a moment, keeping your balance on your seat bones.
Extend your legs back out to the starting position without letting your feet touch the floor.
Keep your torso leaned back at a steady angle throughout the set.
Repeat for the full set, breathing steadily between reps.
formCues: Round through the midsection, not just the hips.
Keep your feet off the floor the whole set.
Use your hands for balance, not for lifting.
Move at a controlled pace, no swinging.
breathing: Exhale as you tuck your knees toward your chest, inhale as you extend your legs back out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rocking backward and using momentum to swing the knees in.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and pull the knees in with your abdominals rather than swinging your torso.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the lower back round onto the bench between reps.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a slight lean without collapsing your spine; find a stable angle and hold it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the bench so hard that the arms do most of the work.
commonMistakes.correction: Use your hands lightly for balance and let your core drive the knee tuck.

commonMistakes.mistake: Touching the feet down between reps to rest.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your feet elevated for the entire set, or use shorter sets if you need a real rest.

programmingNotes: As a bodyweight core move, 2 or 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps a few times a week is a reasonable amount to start with.
It pairs well as a finisher after a lower-body or upper-body session, since it does not add much fatigue to the rest of your training.
Once holding the tucked position at the top feels easy, add a one or two second pause there before moving on to a hanging variation.
If balance is the limiting factor rather than ab fatigue, practice the seated hold on its own before chaining full reps together.
safetyNotes: If your lower back rounds excessively or aches, shorten the lean-back angle until your core catches up.
Keep the movement slow and controlled; a fast, swinging tempo shifts the work from your abs to momentum.

faq.question: How many reps of seated leg tucks should I do?
faq.answer: Start with 2 or 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps. Once that feels easy, add a short pause at the top of each rep instead of rushing to more reps.

faq.question: Can I do seated leg tucks without a bench?
faq.answer: Yes. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your hands planted slightly behind your hips for support, then tuck your knees the same way.

faq.question: What is an easier alternative if I cannot keep my feet off the floor?
faq.answer: A reverse crunch lets you lie down instead of balancing, which removes the stability demand while you build ab strength.

faq.question: Why does my hip flexor cramp during this exercise?
faq.answer: Your hip flexors assist the knee tuck alongside your abs, so cramping usually means they are fatigued or tight. Slow the tempo and shorten the range slightly if it keeps happening.

alternatives.name: Cable Reverse Crunch
alternatives.reason: Trains the same lower-ab region with adjustable cable resistance instead of a balance challenge.

easierVariations.name: Reverse Crunch
easierVariations.reason: Lets you lie down instead of balancing on your seat bones, removing the stability demand while you build ab strength.

harderVariations.name: Hanging Leg Raise
harderVariations.reason: Removes the bench entirely, hanging from a bar so your core has to control your full body weight instead of a seated lean.

summary: The Tire Flip is a strongman movement where you deadlift a large tire off the ground, drive it up and over with your hips and shoulders, and flip it forward. It builds raw, full-body power, mostly through the quads, hamstrings, glutes, and upper back, with grip and shoulders along for the ride.
whyItWorks: The lift works in two distinct phases. The first is a hip-hinge pull, close to a deadlift, that gets the tire off the ground and up to about knee or thigh height, loading the quads, hamstrings, and lower back hard because the tire's bulk keeps your hands far from your center of mass. The second phase is a drive and push, where you shift your hips under the tire and extend through the legs and shoulders to send it over. Because the load is awkward and unevenly shaped, your whole body, not just one muscle group, has to coordinate the lift.
setup: Stand close to the tire with your feet roughly shoulder-width apart, toes near or slightly under the bottom edge.
Grip the underside of the tire with both hands, fingers curled under the lip.
Set your back flat and your hips low, similar to a deadlift stance.
Clear the space in front of you so the tire has room to flip.
execution: Pull the tire upward by driving through your legs and extending your hips, keeping your back flat.
Once the tire reaches thigh height, shift your hands lower and drive your knee or hip underneath it.
Press upward and forward through your legs and shoulders to lift the tire onto its edge.
Finish by pushing through your arms and shoulders to flip the tire forward onto the ground.
Reset your feet and repeat the same sequence for each rep.
formCues: Keep your back flat through the whole pull, the same way you'd guard it in a deadlift.
Get your hips, not just your arms, underneath the tire before you drive it up.
Drive through your heels on the initial pull.
Let your legs do the work in the final push, not just your lower back.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace your core before the initial pull, then exhale forcefully as you drive the tire up and over.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back during the initial pull off the ground.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hips low and your chest up before you pull, exactly like setting up for a deadlift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to muscle the tire up with the arms instead of driving with the legs.
commonMistakes.correction: Get your hip underneath the tire's edge and push through your legs; your arms and shoulders only finish the flip.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too far from the tire, which stretches the pull out and strains the lower back.
commonMistakes.correction: Start with your toes close to the base of the tire so the pull stays short and vertical.

programmingNotes: Because this loads the hip hinge as hard as a heavy deadlift, treat it as the one heavy pull of the week rather than something you repeat daily.
Three to six flips per set is typical, since each rep is taxing on grip and the lower back.
Fits well on a strongman or posterior-chain day, usually placed early in the session while you're fresh.
If you're using a lighter tire purely for conditioning, two sessions a week is reasonable, but drop straight back to one heavy session if you move up in tire size.
safetyNotes: Keep your lower back flat on the first pull; this is where most strain happens.
Use a tire sized to your current strength level rather than the biggest one available.

faq.question: How many tire flips should I do per set?
faq.answer: Most programs call for 3 to 6 flips per set, since each rep demands a near-maximal pull and push.

faq.question: Is Tire Flip the same as a deadlift?
faq.answer: The first phase is a deadlift-style pull, but the second phase adds a push and flip that a straight deadlift doesn't have. If you don't have a tire, a regular deadlift trains the pulling half of the movement.

faq.question: Why does my lower back feel it the most?
faq.answer: The initial pull off the ground puts the tire far from your body, which loads the lower back and hamstrings heavily, similar to a deadlift with a wide grip. Keeping your hips low and back flat at the start reduces that strain.

faq.question: Can I flip a tire without strongman equipment?
faq.answer: You need an actual tire for this specific movement, but a deadlift or sandbag load trains the same raw pulling strength if you don't have access to one.

alternatives.name: Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hip-hinge pull off the ground with a barbell when you don't have access to a tire.

alternatives.name: Sandbag Load
alternatives.reason: Another ground-to-overhead strongman lift that builds the same awkward-object strength without needing a truck tire.

easierVariations.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same ground-to-hip pull pattern without the awkward bear-hug grip or the flip at the top.

easierVariations.name: Sled Push
easierVariations.reason: A gentler way to build the full-body drive needed for a tire flip, without lifting dead weight off the ground first.

harderVariations.name: Atlas Stones
harderVariations.reason: Raises the bar further: lifting an odd, rolling object from the ground demands even more grip and full-body coordination than a tire.

summary: The bent-arm barbell pullover has you lying across a bench, holding a barbell over your chest with elbows slightly bent, then lowering it back behind your head in an arc before pulling it back over your chest. It's a compound pull for the lats, with the chest, shoulders, and triceps assisting through the movement, and it stands apart from most lat work by loading the muscle in a long, overhead stretch rather than a simple down-and-back pull.
whyItWorks: Most lat exercises pull a handle toward your torso, which trains the lats mainly in a shortened position. The pullover flips that: as the bar arcs behind your head, your lats lengthen under load at the same time your rib cage expands to make room for the stretch, which is a range of tension most pulling movements never ask for. Keeping the elbows bent, rather than locked straight, shortens the lever arm slightly and shifts more of the work onto the lats and chest together instead of turning it into a pure shoulder-mobility test, which is why this version is the more approachable of the two pullover styles.
setup: Lie across a flat bench so only your upper back and shoulders are supported, feet flat on the floor.
Hold a light barbell over your chest with hands shoulder-width apart, elbows bent at roughly 90 degrees.
Brace your core so your hips don't sag or your ribs flare as the bar moves.
Start with noticeably less weight than you'd use for a bench press; this movement rewards control, not load.
execution: Lower the bar in an arc back behind your head, keeping your elbows bent at the same angle throughout.
Go only as far as your shoulders can move without your lower back arching or your ribs popping up.
Pause briefly at the deepest comfortable stretch behind your head.
Pull the bar back over your chest along the same arc, leading with your lats rather than your arms.
Keep your core braced and hips level for the entire rep, in both directions.
Reset your grip and breathing before starting the next rep.
formCues: Elbows stay bent at the same angle the whole time.
Stop the stretch where your ribs stay down, not where your back arches.
Lead the pull back with your lats, not your arms.
Hips and core stay braced throughout, no sagging.
breathing: Inhale as the bar lowers behind your head into the stretch, exhale as you pull it back over your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the ribs flare up and the lower back arch as the bar lowers.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent at the point where your rib cage stays down and your core stays braced, even if that means a shorter range at first.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using too much weight, turning the movement into a slow, shaky press instead of a controlled pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load significantly; this exercise is about the stretch and the lat contraction, not how much you can lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Changing the elbow angle mid-rep, straightening or bending further than the starting position.
commonMistakes.correction: Fix your elbow bend at the start and keep it consistent through the entire arc, both lowering and returning.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the bar back with the arms and shoulders instead of the lats.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on driving your elbows down and back toward your hips to initiate the return, rather than just bending your arms.

programmingNotes: This is an isolation-leaning pull that doesn't need heavy loading to be effective; 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps at a light weight is plenty.
Place it after your main pulling or pressing work, since it works well as a stretch-focused finisher rather than a first exercise.
Because the load stays light and the joint stress is moderate, two sessions a week is reasonable for most lifters.
Pair it with a rowing movement in the same session to balance the long-lever stretch with a shortened, contraction-focused pull.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light and the range shallow until you're confident in your shoulder mobility for this overhead position.
Stop the descent well before any point where your shoulders feel like they're being forced past a comfortable range.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for bent-arm barbell pullovers?
faq.answer: 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps at a light weight works well. This exercise trades heavy loading for a deep stretch, so more reps with strict control beats fewer reps with heavy weight.

faq.question: What can I do instead of the bent-arm barbell pullover?
faq.answer: A rope straight-arm pulldown on a cable machine trains the same lat stretch-to-contraction pattern without needing a bench or a barbell, which makes it a good swap when you don't have both available.

faq.question: Bent-arm vs straight-arm pullover, what's the difference?
faq.answer: The bent-arm version keeps a slight bend at the elbows throughout, which shares the work between the lats and chest. The straight-arm version locks the elbows nearly straight, lengthening the lever and turning it into a more isolated lat stretch.

faq.question: Why does the pullover feel like it's in my shoulders instead of my back?
faq.answer: If the stretch feels concentrated in the front of the shoulder rather than the lats, the range is likely too deep for your current mobility. Shorten how far you lower the bar until the stretch shifts toward your back and ribs instead.

alternatives.name: Rope Straight-Arm Pulldown
alternatives.reason: Trains the same lat stretch-to-contraction pattern on a cable, without needing a bench or a loaded barbell.

easierVariations.name: Bent-Arm Dumbbell Pullover
easierVariations.reason: Uses a single lighter dumbbell instead of a loaded bar, which is more forgiving on the shoulders while you learn the arc.

harderVariations.name: Straight-Arm Dumbbell Pullover
harderVariations.reason: Straightens the arms for a longer lever and a deeper lat stretch once the bent-arm version feels controlled.

summary: The flat bench leg pull-in has you sitting at the end of a bench, hands gripping behind you for support, knees drawing in toward your chest and then extending back out. It's a compound core move that trains the lower abdominals through a full range of hip flexion, using your own body weight as the only resistance. It suits beginners building core control as well as anyone who wants an equipment-free ab exercise with a longer range of motion than a standard crunch.
whyItWorks: Bringing your knees toward your chest is hip flexion, and your abdominals, especially the lower fibers of the rectus abdominis, work alongside your hip flexors to pull your legs in and keep your pelvis from tipping forward as they move. Sitting on the edge of the bench with your hands behind you for support removes your legs from the floor entirely, so there's no assistance from pushing off the ground, which means your core has to control the entire arc from extended to tucked and back again.
setup: Sit near the end of a flat bench, hands gripping the edge behind your hips for support.
Lean back slightly and lift your feet off the floor, legs extended out in front of you.
Brace your core before your first rep.
Keep your chest up rather than collapsing forward.
execution: Draw your knees in toward your chest, curling your hips and lower back slightly as they come in.
Pause briefly with your knees pulled in close.
Extend your legs back out to the starting position under control.
Keep your feet off the floor for the entire set.
Repeat without letting your lower back arch as your legs extend.
formCues: Curl the hips in, don't just bend the knees.
Keep your feet off the floor the whole set.
Chest stays up, not collapsing forward.
Control the extension; don't let your legs drop.
breathing: Exhale as you draw your knees in, inhale as you extend your legs back out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the feet touch the floor between reps.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your feet hovering off the ground for the entire set; touching down gives your abs a rest the exercise isn't meant to offer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back as the legs extend out.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a slight posterior pelvic tilt throughout and stop extending your legs at the point where your lower back would start to arch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing the legs in and out quickly.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down; a controlled pull-in trains the abs far more than a fast swing that relies on momentum.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning too far back and collapsing the chest.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and your arms only slightly behind your hips rather than reclining flat.

programmingNotes: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps works well as core-focused work, and two or three times a week is a reasonable frequency for a bodyweight ab exercise like this.
Place it alongside other core work like planks rather than as a standalone session; the abs recover quickly enough to train fairly often.
Progress by slowing the tempo or adding a brief pause at the tucked position before adding an unstable surface.
If your hip flexors fatigue faster than your abs, that's normal at first, since both muscle groups share the pulling-in motion.
safetyNotes: Stop the leg extension before your lower back starts to arch off its neutral position.
If you feel strain in the lower back rather than effort in the abs, shorten the range of motion or try the floor-based regression.

faq.question: How many reps of leg pull-ins should I do?
faq.answer: 10 to 15 controlled reps for 2 or 3 sets is a solid target. Slow, controlled reps build more core strength here than fast, momentum-driven ones.

faq.question: Why does my lower back arch during leg pull-ins?
faq.answer: Extending the legs too far, or too fast, can pull the pelvis forward if the core isn't controlling the movement. Shorten the range and slow down until you can keep the lower back from arching.

faq.question: Can I do leg pull-ins without a bench?
faq.answer: Yes, doing the same knee tuck seated or lying on the floor works the same pattern with a slightly shorter range of motion.

faq.question: What's harder than the flat bench leg pull-in?
faq.answer: The exercise ball pull-in, which uses an unstable ball under your feet, adds a balance challenge on top of the same core movement.

alternatives.name: Leg Raise
alternatives.reason: Works the same lower abs on the floor with no bench required.

easierVariations.name: Leg Pull-In
easierVariations.reason: Does the same knee tuck lying on the floor instead of a bench, a shorter and more supported range to start with.

harderVariations.name: Exercise Ball Pull-In
harderVariations.reason: Places your feet on an unstable exercise ball instead of a fixed bench, adding a balance challenge to the same pull-in.

summary: The seated bent-over two-arm dumbbell triceps extension is a two-handed triceps kickback done from a seated, hip-hinged position. You hold a dumbbell in each hand, pin your upper arms against your ribs, and extend your elbows straight back to isolate the triceps at the end of the movement. It suits lifters who want a controlled, seated alternative to standing kickbacks, since the bench takes lower-back and balance demands out of the equation and lets you focus purely on the elbow extension.
whyItWorks: Your triceps exist to straighten your elbow, and they get their strongest, most isolated contraction when the upper arm is held still and slightly behind the torso, which is exactly the position this exercise locks you into. Bending forward at the hips and pinning your upper arms against your ribs removes the shoulders from the movement almost entirely, so nearly all the work falls on the triceps as they extend the forearm against the dumbbell's resistance. Because it's a single-joint push movement, it lets you fatigue the triceps directly without any help from the chest or shoulders, which is useful once a pressing exercise has already worn those bigger muscles down but the triceps still have more work left in them.
setup: Take a seat toward the front edge of a bench, holding one dumbbell in each hand with your palms turned toward you.
Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is close to parallel with the floor, keeping your back flat rather than rounded.
Bend your elbows to about 90 degrees and tuck your upper arms against your ribs so they stay still throughout the set.
Brace your core lightly to support the hinged position before your first rep.
execution: Keeping your upper arms pinned against your ribs, extend your elbows to straighten your arms behind you.
Continue until your arms are fully extended and your triceps are fully contracted.
Pause for a moment at full extension, squeezing your triceps.
Bend your elbows again, guiding the dumbbells down to that same 90-degree bend you began from, moving with control.
Keep your torso still and hinged throughout the set; only your forearms should move.
Repeat for the full set without letting your upper arms drift away from your ribs.
formCues: Elbows pinned to your ribs the whole set.
Only the forearm moves, not the shoulder.
Flat back, hips hinged, not rounded.
Squeeze at full extension before lowering.
breathing: Exhale as you extend your elbows back, inhale as you bend them to lower the weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the upper arms swing away from the ribs during the extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows tucked and stationary; if they drift away from your body, the shoulders start doing work that belongs to the triceps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to hinge forward instead of bending at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hips back and keep your spine flat before you start the set, the same way you'd set up for a hip hinge in a deadlift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing the dumbbells backward.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and control the extension; a slower rep keeps tension on the triceps instead of letting the swing do the work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only partially extending the elbows at the top of the movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Straighten your arms fully on every rep so the triceps get the full contraction; a short range of motion trains less muscle.

programmingNotes: This is a light isolation movement, so two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps a couple of times a week is a reasonable starting point for most people.
Place it after a compound pressing exercise like a bench press or shoulder press, when the triceps are already warm from assisting but not yet fatigued from direct work.
Because both arms extend together, it's easy to notice if one side lags behind the other; slow the tempo down on the weaker side rather than simply adding more weight.
A light dumbbell goes a long way here; the tucked-elbow position limits how much load your triceps can safely handle before your shoulders start compensating.
safetyNotes: Keep the hip hinge modest if your lower back feels strained during the setup; a shallower forward lean still trains the triceps effectively.
Choose a lighter dumbbell than you'd expect; once the weight forces your shoulders to help, the exercise loses most of its isolation benefit.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for the seated bent-over two-arm dumbbell triceps extension?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps works well for most people, using a light dumbbell that lets you keep your elbows pinned to your ribs for every rep of the set.

faq.question: What's a good substitute if I don't have dumbbells?
faq.answer: A cable rope overhead triceps extension trains the same overhead-extension pattern with constant tension from a cable stack instead of a bent-over dumbbell position.

faq.question: Why can't I feel this in my triceps?
faq.answer: Check that your upper arms stay tucked against your ribs through the whole set; if they swing away from your body even slightly, your shoulders take over and the triceps barely fire.

faq.question: How is this different from the one-arm version?
faq.answer: The one-arm version lets you focus fully on each side and add a slight rotation at the top for extra contraction, while the two-arm version trains both sides at once and takes less total time to finish a set.

alternatives.name: Cable Rope Overhead Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead stretch on the triceps using a cable stack and rope handle instead of dumbbells.

easierVariations.name: Triceps Pushdown
easierVariations.reason: A cable version with a fixed, guided path that's easier to control than two free dumbbells held in a bent-over position.

harderVariations.name: Lying Close-Grip Barbell Triceps Extension Behind The Head
harderVariations.reason: Loads both arms together on a single barbell lying on a bench, letting you add more total weight than a pair of dumbbells allows.

summary: The kneeling forearm stretch targets the wrist flexors and forearm muscles by having you kneel with your hands pressed into the ground and your fingertips turned back toward your body, then shift your weight backward until you feel a stretch. It's a simple way to release tension that builds up in the forearms from gripping, whether that's from lifting, climbing, or a day spent typing.
whyItWorks: Turning your palms so your fingers point back toward your knees while they're pressed flat on the floor puts the wrist into extension while the fingers stay flexed against the ground, which lengthens the wrist flexor muscles running through the forearm. Shifting your weight backward increases that stretch gradually, letting you control exactly how deep it goes just by how far back you lean.
setup: Kneel on a mat with both hands pressed against the ground in front of you.
Turn your hands so your fingertips face backward, aimed at your body.
Press your full palm evenly into the mat.
execution: With your palms still flat on the floor, gently shift your weight back toward your heels.
Continue shifting back until you feel a clear stretch through your forearms and wrists.
Hold at the point where the stretch feels noticeable but comfortable.
Slowly shift your weight forward again to release the stretch.
formCues: Keep the whole palm flat, don't let it lift.
Shift your weight back slowly.
Breathe steadily through the hold.
Ease off if you feel any pinching at the wrist.
breathing: Breathe slowly and steadily while you hold the stretch; there's no need to force your breath.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the palm lift off the floor as you shift your weight back.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep constant, even pressure through the whole palm as you shift, adjusting how far back you go if the palm starts to lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shifting your weight back too quickly, causing a sharp pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Ease into the position gradually instead of dropping your weight back all at once.

programmingNotes: Hold for 20 to 30 seconds and repeat two or three times per hand.
Since this is a gentle static stretch rather than loaded work, it's fine to do daily.
It pairs naturally with grip-heavy training like rows, pull-ups, or deadlifts, either before or after the session.
safetyNotes: Stop shifting your weight back at the first sign of sharp wrist pain.
This should feel like a stretch, not a joint strain; back off if it crosses into discomfort.

faq.question: How long should I hold the kneeling forearm stretch?
faq.answer: Around 20 to 30 seconds per side works well, repeated two or three times.

faq.question: When should I do this stretch?
faq.answer: It fits well before or after exercises that load your grip and forearms, like rows, pull-ups, or deadlifts.

faq.question: Is this the same as a wrist flexor stretch?
faq.answer: Yes, this position specifically targets the wrist flexors and the forearm muscles that run into them.

alternatives.name: Wrist Circles
alternatives.reason: A gentler, dynamic option for the same forearms and wrists if the static kneeling position feels like too much pressure.

summary: The bench jump has you standing in front of a flat bench, dipping into a quarter squat, then jumping both feet up and over it before landing on the other side, or hopping back and forth over it depending on the variation your program calls for. It's a plyometric drill for the quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings, built around one skill: converting a fast dip into an explosive jump and absorbing the landing without your knees caving in.
whyItWorks: Jumping over a fixed object forces your legs to produce force fast rather than grinding through a slow squat. The short dip before takeoff loads your quads and glutes eccentrically, then your nervous system has to convert that stored tension into an explosive concentric push within a fraction of a second, which is the stretch-shortening cycle that makes plyometrics build power differently than a slow strength lift. The bench itself adds a real consequence to a sloppy jump: clip it with a foot and you know immediately, which keeps most people honest about lifting their knees and clearing the height rather than skimming over it.
setup: Stand facing the long side of a flat, sturdy bench with feet hip-width apart.
Pick a spot roughly a foot back from the bench so your takeoff has room.
Keep your eyes on the far side of the bench, not down at your feet.
execution: Dip quickly into a quarter squat, swinging your arms back behind you.
Drive up and forward explosively, swinging your arms up and forward to help the jump.
Tuck your knees enough to clear the bench with both feet.
Land on the far side already sinking into your hips and knees, letting your legs quiet the impact rather than your joints.
Stand tall for a moment to reset before the next rep.
Repeat for the prescribed number of jumps, resting fully between sets.
formCues: Fast dip, explosive drive, no hesitation between the two.
Land quiet, not flat-footed and loud.
Knees track over your toes on landing, not caving in.
Reset fully before every jump, this isn't a race.
breathing: Exhale sharply on the jump up, inhale as you reset your stance before the next rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing with stiff, locked knees instead of absorbing the impact.
commonMistakes.correction: Bend your knees and hips on landing like you're catching a fall, letting your legs act as shock absorbers rather than pillars.

commonMistakes.mistake: Knees collapsing inward on takeoff or landing.
commonMistakes.correction: Cue your knees to stay stacked over your second toe on both ends of the jump, and drop the height if you can't control it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing from one rep straight into the next without resetting.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause and stand tall between jumps until your balance settles, treating each rep as its own separate effort.

commonMistakes.mistake: Jumping for height alone and clipping the bench with a trailing foot.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on tucking your knees up and forward through the jump, not just jumping higher than the bench requires.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arms hanging still instead of swinging with the jump.
commonMistakes.correction: Swing your arms back on the dip and drive them up and forward on takeoff; the timing of that swing adds real upward force when it matches the leg drive.

programmingNotes: Plyometric work like this asks more of your joints per rep than it looks like on paper, so low volume wins: 3 to 5 sets of 5 to 8 jumps is plenty.
Rest close to a full minute or more between sets. The point is a fast, powerful jump every time, not a conditioning burn.
Place it early in a session, right after your warm-up and before heavy lifting, while your legs are still fresh and fast.
Because the landing loads your joints repeatedly, once a week is enough for most people unless a coach has built a specific plyometric block around it.
Only raise the bench height once your landings stay quiet and controlled at the current one; a louder or wobblier landing means the height already outpaced your control.
safetyNotes: Use a bench you're confident won't tip or slide, and clear the landing zone of anything you could trip over.
Stop the set if your landings start getting sloppier or louder; that's your legs telling you they're fatigued before your set count is.
Wear shoes with real cushioning and grip; repeated landings on a hard floor in flat, worn-out soles add unnecessary strain to your knees and ankles.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of bench jumps should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of 5 to 8 jumps is plenty. This is a power drill, not a conditioning one, so quality per rep matters far more than total volume.

faq.question: What can I do instead of bench jumps if I don't have a bench?
faq.answer: A freehand jump squat trains the same explosive hip and knee extension without anything to clear, and it's a fair swap when you don't have a sturdy bench or box available.

faq.question: Are bench jumps hard on the knees?
faq.answer: They can be if you land stiff-legged or let your knees cave inward. Landing softly with bent knees and hips, tracking your knees over your toes, is what keeps the impact manageable.

faq.question: How high should the bench be for bench jumps?
faq.answer: A standard flat bench height works for most people who can already do a controlled bodyweight squat. If clearing it consistently feels risky, drop to a lower step or box until your jump and landing are both clean.

alternatives.name: Freehand Jump Squat
alternatives.reason: Trains the same explosive hip and knee extension without needing a bench to clear.

easierVariations.name: Bodyweight Squat
easierVariations.reason: Builds the same hip and knee bend pattern you land in, without the landing impact or the height to clear.

harderVariations.name: Box Jump (Multiple Response)
harderVariations.reason: Adds repeated jumps onto a box in sequence, asking your legs to reset and fire again with almost no rest between reps.

summary: The box squat with bands anchors resistance bands to the floor and loops them over the bar, so tension stays low while you're seated on the box and rises sharply as you stand toward lockout. It's a dynamic effort tool built to train how fast you can move a submaximal load, layered on top of the same paused, dead-stop box squat pattern.
whyItWorks: Bands stretch the most exactly where a barbell squat's mechanical advantage is most favorable, near the top, which forces you to keep accelerating instead of decelerating into lockout the way you naturally would with plates alone. Combined with the box squat's dead-stop pause, your quadriceps and glutes have to fire explosively from a genuine standstill against a load that keeps climbing as you rise, which trains rate of force development rather than raw maximal strength. Your lower back, adductors, and abductors still do the same stabilizing work they do in any box squat, holding your position steady while the band tension pulls unevenly at the top of the lift if your bar path drifts.
setup: Anchor a resistance band to the floor on each side of the rack, or loop them around secure pins.
Loop the top of each band over the bar sleeves so the tension is even on both sides.
Set a box behind you at a height where your hip crease drops to about knee level when seated.
Load a lighter bar weight than your usual box squat, since the bands will add real resistance as you rise.
Unrack the bar and walk back until the box is directly behind you, feet set in your normal squat stance.
execution: Sit back and down toward the box under control, feeling the band tension go slack as you descend.
Sit fully onto the box for a brief pause, keeping your torso braced even though the bands are light at the bottom.
Drive up off the box as explosively as you can the instant your weight settles.
Keep accelerating through the entire rise as the band tension increases, don't let the bar slow down near the top.
Finish every rep at full lockout with intent, then walk the tension back down under control before the next descent.
formCues: Explode off the box, the bands only get heavier from there.
Keep speeding up, not slowing down, as you near lockout.
Torso stays braced through the light bottom position too.
Bar path stays straight even as the bands pull unevenly.
breathing: Brace and hold your breath through the seated pause and the drive up, then exhale once you're standing at lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the bottom position as a free rest since the bands feel light there.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso braced through the pause on the box regardless of how light the bar feels, your position still needs to be sound before you drive up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing bar speed near the top as the band tension climbs.
commonMistakes.correction: Think about accelerating hardest right as the bands stretch the most, that's the entire point of the tool.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using bands so heavy that your normal squat depth and box pause fall apart.
commonMistakes.correction: Choose a band tension light enough that your position on the box and your bar path still match your regular box squat.

programmingNotes: Bands are a speed tool layered on submaximal weight, so this fits well as a weekly dynamic effort session at lighter bar loads rather than a heavy strength day, with the band tension providing the real challenge.
Typical dynamic effort work uses eight to twelve total reps across several sets of two to three, resting enough between sets to keep every rep genuinely fast.
Because the demand is on speed and coordination more than grinding strength, this pairs well earlier in a session before accessory work rather than at the end when you're already tired.
safetyNotes: Check both band anchors are secure before loading the bar, an anchor slipping mid-set changes the resistance suddenly and unevenly.
Keep the plate weight light enough that a missed rep is still manageable, the point of this variation is speed, not a maximal grind.
Stop the session if your form on the box starts to break down as fatigue sets in, dynamic effort work is meant to stay clean and fast.
Recheck band tension after a few sets, a band that's crept off center changes the resistance without you noticing mid-set.

faq.question: How much band tension should I use for box squats?
faq.answer: Start light enough that your bar speed stays fast through the entire rise, then add tension gradually once you can accelerate cleanly against the current setup.

faq.question: Do I need less bar weight when I add bands?
faq.answer: Yes, since the bands add real resistance by lockout, most lifters drop the plate weight well below their usual box squat working weight.

faq.question: Box squat with bands vs chains, which should I use?
faq.answer: Both add resistance as you rise, but bands ramp up faster and pull harder right at the top, while chains build resistance more gradually and feel closer to a normal bar until near lockout.

faq.question: Why does the bar feel like it's pulling to one side?
faq.answer: That usually means the bands aren't anchored or looped evenly on both sides. Check both anchor points and band lengths before your next set.

alternatives.name: Box Squat with Chains
alternatives.reason: Swaps bands for chains as the accommodating-resistance tool, useful if you don't have anchor points for bands but still want added tension near lockout.

easierVariations.name: Box Squat
easierVariations.reason: Removes the band tension entirely so you can groove the seated pause and stand-up pattern with a predictable, constant load first.

harderVariations.name: Speed Box Squat
harderVariations.reason: Keeps the same speed-focused intent but removes the band variable, asking you to hit fast bar speed against a fixed submaximal load alone.

summary: The bodyweight mid row has you lean back at a moderate angle under a fixed bar, straps, or rings, then pull your chest up to your hands using your own bodyweight as the resistance. It sits between an easy, near-vertical row and a fully horizontal inverted row, which makes the angle itself the main way you adjust the difficulty. It's a compound pulling movement that trains your middle back hard, with your lats and biceps helping drive the pull.
whyItWorks: The further your body leans back from vertical, the more of your bodyweight the row has to pull against, so the mid-row angle is really a way to dial in resistance that a barbell row would otherwise need external plates for. Your middle back does the primary job of pulling your shoulder blades together and driving your elbows back, while your lats add pulling power through your upper arms and your biceps assist at the elbow. Because you control the angle yourself, you can make each set as easy or as hard as you need without changing equipment.
setup: Set a bar, straps, or rings at around waist height.
Grip with both hands and walk your feet forward until your body leans back at roughly a 45-degree angle.
Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Set your heels firmly on the floor before starting the first rep.
execution: Pull your chest up toward your hands by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull.
Pause briefly at the top before lowering.
Lower back down under control to a full arm extension.
Keep your body rigid throughout; don't let your hips sag.
formCues: Lead the pull with your elbows, not your hands.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Keep a straight line from head to heels the whole set.
breathing: Exhale as you pull up, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag during the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and glutes to keep a straight line from head to heels through the entire rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a body angle that's too easy or too hard for your current strength.
commonMistakes.correction: Walk your feet closer to under the anchor for an easier angle, or further out for a harder one, until you find a range where you can complete your target reps with good form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking with the arms instead of driving the elbows back.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on pulling your elbows behind you and squeezing your shoulder blades together, letting your arms follow.

programmingNotes: This works well as your main pulling exercise on an upper-body day.
Three sets of 8 to 12 reps at a body angle that's genuinely challenging by the last few reps is a good target.
Two or three days a week is fine, since you control the load through your body angle rather than adding external weight.
safetyNotes: Check that your bar, straps, or rings are securely anchored before loading your full bodyweight onto them.
Stop the set once your shoulder blades stop squeezing together at the top; that's usually a sign your back is fatigued and your arms are starting to take over.

faq.question: How do I make the bodyweight mid row harder or easier?
faq.answer: Change your body angle. Walking your feet further out and leaning back more makes it harder, while standing more upright makes it easier.

faq.question: What equipment do I need?
faq.answer: A fixed bar, gymnastics rings, or suspension straps set around waist height all work, as long as they can hold your full bodyweight securely.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and an inverted row?
faq.answer: They're close relatives. An inverted row usually sets you closer to horizontal under a fixed bar, while the mid row uses a more moderate angle, which is often a more approachable starting point.

faq.question: Can I do this without straps or rings?
faq.answer: Yes, a secured bar at the right height, like in a squat rack, works the same way. A seated cable row is a good alternative if you don't have any of these options.

alternatives.name: Inverted Row
alternatives.reason: Trains the same pulling pattern off a fixed bar for anyone without straps or rings to set up a mid row.

alternatives.name: Seated Cable Rows
alternatives.reason: Trains the same middle-back pull with a cable stack when no bar, straps, or rings are available.

harderVariations.name: Suspended Row
harderVariations.reason: Swaps the fixed anchor for hanging straps, adding instability that raises the demand on the same row pattern.

summary: The cable seated lateral raise has you sit sideways next to a low pulley, hold the handle in your outside hand, and raise your arm out to the side up to shoulder height. It isolates your side delts with steady cable resistance, and it suits anyone who wants fuller shoulder width without relying on dumbbells, which lose tension right where this exercise needs it most.
whyItWorks: Your side delts lift your arm out to the side, and the resistance they need to fight changes as your arm rises. A dumbbell only resists gravity, which pulls straight down, so tension drops off near the top of the raise when your arm is closest to horizontal. A low pulley pulls at a different angle, keeping meaningful tension on your side delts through the top portion of the raise where a dumbbell goes nearly slack.
setup: Sit sideways on a bench next to a low pulley with a handle attached.
Grab the handle with your outside hand, letting your arm hang across the front of your body.
Sit up tall with your torso stable and your inside hand braced on the bench if needed.
execution: Raise your arm out to the side until it reaches roughly shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top of the raise.
Lower your arm back down slowly, resisting the cable the whole way.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch and repeat on the other.
formCues: Lead with your elbow, keeping a slight bend throughout the raise.
Raise to shoulder height, not higher, to keep the load on your delts rather than your traps.
Keep your torso still and avoid leaning away from the cable to help lift the weight.
Control the lowering phase instead of letting the cable yank your arm back down.
breathing: Exhale as you raise your arm out to the side, inhale as you lower it back down.
