Adding a jump and a mid air leg switch forces your quadriceps to fire explosively out of a lunge, then asks the same muscles, along with your calves, glutes, and hamstrings, to control the landing on the opposite leg. That combination of producing power and absorbing it under bodyweight is what makes split jumps a useful plyometric building block, even though the pattern itself is simple.
setup: Start in a lunge stance, one foot forward and one foot back, both knees bent to roughly 90 degrees.
Keep your torso upright and your front knee tracking over your front foot.
Set your arms in a ready position to help drive the jump.
execution: Bend both knees slightly to load, then push forcefully through both feet to jump straight up.
Switch your legs in the air, bringing your back foot forward and your front foot back.
Land softly in the opposite lunge stance, absorbing the impact through your knees and hips.
Reset briefly if needed, then repeat the jump, switching legs again each time.
Keep your chest up and your landings controlled throughout the set.
formCues: Land soft and quiet, not with a hard thud.
Front knee stays over the front foot on landing.
Chest stays up through the jump and landing.
Push off both feet evenly to jump straight up, not forward.
breathing: Exhale as you jump and switch legs, inhale as you reset in the landed lunge position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the front knee cave inward or shoot past the toes on landing.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on landing with your front knee tracking straight over your front foot, absorbing the impact through your hips and knees together.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing stiff legged with a loud, hard impact.
commonMistakes.correction: Bend your knees more on landing so your legs absorb the force instead of your joints.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso forward during the jump.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and your torso close to upright through the jump and the landing.

programmingNotes: Work it in sets of 6 to 10 jumps per leg, for 2 to 3 rounds, once or twice a week given the impact on the joints.
Fits well in a power or conditioning block, but skip it on days your knees or ankles already feel beat up from other training.
Progress by focusing on jump height and a cleaner landing before chasing more total reps.
safetyNotes: Master the stationary lunge and a controlled landing pattern before adding the jump if lunges are new to you.
Stop if you feel sharp knee pain on landing; a quiet, controlled landing shouldn't hurt.

faq.question: How many split jumps should I do per set?
faq.answer: 6 to 10 jumps per leg is a solid range, for 2 to 3 rounds. Quality landings matter more than a high count.

faq.question: Can I do split jumps every day?
faq.answer: It's better to leave a day or two between sessions, since the repeated landings add real impact to your knees and ankles.

faq.question: What's an easier version of the split jump if the landing feels unstable?
faq.answer: Practice the stationary lunge first to build strength and balance in the position, then add the jump once landings feel controlled without it.

faq.question: Why do my knees hurt when I do split jumps?
faq.answer: Check that you're landing with soft, bent knees tracking over your feet rather than stiff legged or with your knee drifting past your toes. If pain continues, scale back to the stationary lunge for now.

alternatives.name: Freehand Jump Squat
alternatives.reason: The same explosive jump and soft landing pattern, using a symmetric squat stance instead of a split lunge stance.

easierVariations.name: Split Squats
easierVariations.reason: The same split stance without the jump, useful for building strength and balance in the position before adding impact.

harderVariations.name: Lunge Sprint
harderVariations.reason: Moves the same split stance pattern forward through space instead of jumping in place, adding a traveling power demand.

summary: The side bridge, better known as the side plank, has you support your bodyweight on one forearm and the edge of one foot while keeping your torso and legs rigid in one long, level line. It's an isometric hold that targets the obliques and deep core muscles on the side facing down, while your shoulder works to keep you stable through the hold.
whyItWorks: Your obliques and the deep core muscles along your side exist to resist your torso bending or collapsing sideways, but most core exercises train the front of the abs instead. Holding a side bridge puts gravity directly against that sideways collapse, forcing the obliques and the smaller stabilizing muscles around your spine to fire continuously just to keep your hips from dropping. That's a demand very few other exercises create as directly.
setup: Lie on your side with your elbow directly under your shoulder and your forearm flat on the floor.
Rest one foot directly above the other, or offset them slightly if that feels more stable.
Rest your top hand on your hip or extend it toward the ceiling.
execution: Push through your forearm and the side of your bottom foot to lift your hips off the floor.
Keep your torso rigid in one level line, running from the crown of your skull to your ankles.
Hold the position, keeping your hips lifted and your body from sagging.
Lower back down with control after your set time is up, then switch sides.
formCues: Straight line, head to heels.
Hips lifted, not sagging toward the floor.
Elbow stacked directly under the shoulder.
Look straight ahead, don't drop your head.
breathing: Breathe steadily throughout the hold; don't hold your breath just because the position is static.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag toward the floor instead of staying lifted.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively squeeze your obliques to keep your hips up in line with your shoulders and ankles for the entire hold.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the top shoulder or hip forward, turning the side bridge into a half-twisted plank.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulders and hips stacked directly on top of each other, facing straight out to the side.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing the elbow too far forward or behind the shoulder.
commonMistakes.correction: Line your elbow up directly beneath your shoulder before you lift your hips, so your shoulder joint stays stable under load.

programmingNotes: Since this is a bodyweight isometric hold, two or three sessions a week is plenty to build real oblique endurance.
Start with two or three holds of 20 to 30 seconds per side and build hold time gradually from there.
Pair it with a front plank in the same core circuit to train bracing from both the front and the side.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel sharp pain in the supporting shoulder or wrist rather than muscle fatigue in your side.
Keep the hold time realistic; shaking or a dropping hip is a sign to end the set rather than push through with bad form.

faq.question: How long should I hold a side bridge?
faq.answer: Twenty to thirty seconds per side is a solid starting point. Build up gradually rather than jumping straight to long holds, since form tends to break down before the muscles truly fatigue.

faq.question: What's the difference between a side bridge and a side plank?
faq.answer: They're the same exercise; side bridge and side plank are two names for the identical position, forearm and foot supporting your bodyweight in a straight line.

faq.question: Why does my shoulder hurt during side bridges?
faq.answer: This is usually a sign your elbow isn't stacked directly under your shoulder, which shifts extra load onto the joint. Check your elbow position first, and consider shortening your hold time if discomfort continues.

alternatives.name: Plank
alternatives.reason: Trains the same isometric core bracing from a front-facing position instead of a side one, useful if a side bridge irritates your shoulder or wrist.

harderVariations.name: Push Up to Side Plank
harderVariations.reason: Adds a dynamic rotation out of a push-up into the same side-bridge position, once holding it still stops being a real challenge.

summary: A weighted sit-up with bands loops a resistance band behind you and across your chest or shoulders, so the band pulls you back down as you curl your torso up. The added tension means your abdominals have to keep working through the whole sit-up instead of just the first few degrees off the floor, where a plain sit-up gets easy fast. It suits anyone who already has bodyweight sit-ups down cold and wants more resistance without loading a bar or a plate across their chest.
whyItWorks: A regular sit-up is hardest in the first inch or two off the floor, where your torso has the least mechanical advantage, and gets progressively easier as you sit upright. A band anchored behind you reverses that curve: it pulls the least while you're lying flat and stretches tighter the higher you curl, so your abdominals keep fighting resistance all the way to the top instead of coasting through the back half of the rep. That constant tension is what makes the band version a genuine strength progression rather than just a harder-feeling version of the same motion. It also means you can keep progressing the exercise for a long time just by moving to a thicker band, long after a bodyweight sit-up alone has stopped feeling challenging.
setup: Anchor a resistance band behind you at roughly chest height, or loop it around a sturdy post or rack.
Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Pass the band across your upper back and hold one end in each hand near your chest, or cross it over both shoulders.
Take up the slack in the band so it already has light tension while you're lying flat.
execution: Curl your torso up off the floor, leading with your chest rather than your chin.
Keep driving upward against the band until your torso is close to vertical.
Pause briefly at the top, where the band pulls hardest.
Lower your torso back down under control, resisting the band the whole way instead of letting it snap you back to the floor.
Keep your feet flat and your lower back in light contact with the floor at the bottom of each rep.
Reset the band tension before starting the next rep.
formCues: Lead the curl with your chest, not your chin.
Control the lowering phase, don't let the band fling you down.
Keep your feet flat and heels pressed into the floor.
Exhale fully at the top to deepen the contraction.
breathing: Exhale as you curl up against the band, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap the torso back down instead of controlling the descent.
commonMistakes.correction: Resist the band on the way down just as hard as you pushed against it on the way up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling on the band with the arms instead of curling with the abs.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your arms fixed near your chest and let your torso do the work of curling against the band.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum from the head and neck to start the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Lead with the chest and keep your chin slightly tucked so the neck stays out of the lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting the band too loose, so the first few reps feel like a plain bodyweight sit-up.
commonMistakes.correction: Take up the slack before you lie down so the band is already working from the first rep.

programmingNotes: As a single-joint movement for the midsection, two or three sessions a week is sustainable since it doesn't tax the lower body or nervous system the way a squat or deadlift does.
Three or four sets of 10 to 15 reps is a reasonable target once the band tension makes the last few reps genuinely hard.
A thicker band or a shorter anchor point raises the resistance, the equivalent of adding plates to a bar.
Pair it with a rotational core movement, like a cable twist, so the trunk gets trained in more than one plane that session.
safetyNotes: Keep your lower back pressed lightly into the floor through the rep rather than arching it to gain height, which shifts load from the abs onto the spine.
Choose a band and anchor point that let you finish every rep with a controlled descent; if the band yanks you down, it's too strong for the rep range you're using.

faq.question: How many reps of weighted sit-ups with bands should I do?
faq.answer: Three or four sets of 10 to 15 reps works well once the band is tight enough that the last few reps are genuinely hard.

faq.question: Can I do weighted sit-ups without a resistance band?
faq.answer: Yes, drop the band and do a plain bodyweight sit-up, or hold a light plate against your chest for a similar added challenge.

faq.question: Do sit-ups with bands work the lower abs?
faq.answer: They mainly target the upper abdominals through spinal flexion. For the lower abs, pair them with a reverse crunch or a leg raise.

faq.question: Why does my lower back hurt during weighted sit-ups?
faq.answer: That usually means your lower back is arching to gain height instead of staying lightly pressed into the floor. Lighten the band tension until you can keep it flat.

alternatives.name: Cable Crunch
alternatives.reason: Swaps the band for a cable machine, keeping the same idea of resistance that increases as you curl forward.

alternatives.name: Weighted Crunches
alternatives.reason: A shorter range crunch with a held weight, useful when a band or anchor point isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Sit-Up
easierVariations.reason: The same sit-up pattern without the band, a good way to groove the motion before adding resistance.

harderVariations.name: Jackknife Sit-Up
harderVariations.reason: Adds a simultaneous leg raise to the sit-up, asking the abs to work through a longer range in one rep.

summary: The barbell shrug is a straightforward isolation move: hold a loaded bar at arm's length and lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears, then lower them back down. It targets the trapezius almost exclusively, since your elbows stay locked and only your shoulder girdle moves. It's a simple way to add direct trap size and strength on top of whatever back or pulling work you already do.
whyItWorks: The trapezius elevates the shoulder blades, which is exactly the motion a shrug isolates by keeping the elbows straight and moving only at the shoulder joint. Because there's no rowing or pulling motion involved, the biceps and forearms are limited to just gripping the bar, which keeps essentially all of the working load on the traps rather than sharing it with other pulling muscles the way a row or deadlift does.
setup: Take an overhand grip on the barbell at roughly shoulder width, arms hanging straight down.
Stand with your feet hip-width apart and the bar resting against your thighs.
Keep a slight bend in your knees and your chest up before the first rep.
execution: Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears, keeping your elbows locked.
Avoid rolling your shoulders forward or backward, the motion is straight up and down.
Pause briefly at the top of the shrug.
Lower your shoulders back down under control to the starting hang.
Let the bar settle fully before starting the next rep.
Keep your grip firm throughout so the bar doesn't shift in your hands.
formCues: Straight up and down, no rolling the shoulders.
Elbows locked, the movement comes only from the shoulder girdle.
Pause at the top before lowering.
Full lower each rep, don't shortcut the range.
breathing: Exhale as you lift your shoulders up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward instead of moving them straight up and down.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on lifting your shoulders directly toward your ears without any circular motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum by bouncing the bar off the thighs to start each rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the bar come to a full stop at the bottom before lifting again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows to help the bar rise higher.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the elbows locked throughout so the traps do all the lifting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutting the range short at the top instead of shrugging fully.
commonMistakes.correction: Lift until your shoulders are as close to your ears as they'll go before pausing.

programmingNotes: This is a light isolation movement for a muscle that recovers quickly, so two to three sessions a week works well for most lifters.
Three sets of 12 to 15 reps with a full range builds more trap size than heavier sets that only move the bar a few inches.
It fits naturally at the end of a pulling day, after your rows or deadlifts have already warmed up your upper back.
Grip strength is often the limiting factor before the traps are, so straps can help once the bar starts slipping before your traps are fatigued.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion controlled rather than using a heavy jerking bounce, which shifts strain toward the neck.
If you feel tension in your neck rather than your traps, lighten the load and slow the tempo down.

faq.question: How many sets of barbell shrugs should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 12 to 15 reps with a full range of motion is a solid amount, done two or three times a week.

faq.question: Do barbell shrugs work the whole upper back or just the traps?
faq.answer: Mostly just the upper traps, since the elbows stay locked and the only motion is lifting the shoulder blades straight up. Rows and deadlifts do more for the rest of your upper back.

faq.question: Why can't I feel barbell shrugs in my traps?
faq.answer: Usually the range is too short, or momentum from bouncing the bar is doing some of the work. Slow down, let the bar come to a full stop at the bottom, and shrug all the way up before pausing.

faq.question: Should I do shrugs in front or behind my back?
faq.answer: In front is the standard, more shoulder-friendly version most lifters should default to. The behind-the-back version works the traps at a slightly different angle but asks more of your shoulder mobility.

alternatives.name: Cable Shrugs
alternatives.reason: Trades the barbell for a cable, keeping constant tension on the traps through the whole range instead of easing off at the bottom.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Shrug
easierVariations.reason: Lets each shoulder move independently with a lighter, easier-to-grip load, a good starting point before loading a barbell.

summary: The heaving snatch balance is an Olympic weightlifting drill that isolates the catch phase of the snatch. You start with the bar racked behind your neck, drive it up off your shoulders with a short leg heave, then pull yourself down fast underneath it into a full overhead squat. It's built for lifters who already snatch and want to sharpen the speed and stability of their catch, not a beginner introduction to overhead lifting.
whyItWorks: Catching a snatch overhead is less about arm strength and more about how fast you can drop your body under a bar that's already moving. The heave off your shoulders gives the bar a brief moment of upward travel, and that window is what you have to pull your feet into a wide squat stance and punch your arms straight overhead. Your quadriceps and glutes drive both the heave and the catch squat, while your shoulders and upper back lock the bar in place once you're under it, which is exactly the sequence a real snatch demands under a heavier, faster-moving bar. Training this drill separately from the full lift lets you repeat that catch far more often than a heavy snatch session allows, since the bar stays light enough to reset for another rep almost immediately instead of needing a full pull from the floor each time.
setup: Set the bar in a squat rack at shoulder height, or clean it into position behind your neck.
Grip the bar in your snatch-width grip, well outside your shoulders.
Stand with feet at your normal squat stance, bar resting across your upper traps.
Brace your abs and set your feet before the first rep.
execution: Dip slightly by bending your knees a few inches, keeping your torso upright.
Drive up through your legs to heave the bar a short distance off your shoulders.
The instant the bar leaves your shoulders, pull yourself down underneath it, jumping your feet into a wide squat stance.
Punch your arms straight overhead as you drop, catching the bar with locked elbows.
Receive the bar in a full overhead squat, hips below knee height if your mobility allows.
Stand up out of the squat while keeping the bar locked directly overhead.
Lower the bar back to your shoulders under control before the next rep.
formCues: Heave the bar up, don't just lift your body.
Punch your arms straight the moment the bar clears your shoulders.
Get your feet flat and wide the instant you land.
Keep your eyes forward, not down at the bar.
breathing: Take a breath and brace before the dip, hold it through the heave and catch, then exhale once you stand up out of the squat.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing the bar up with the arms instead of driving it with the legs.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the heave short and let your legs do the work; your arms only need to lock, not push.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the bar with bent elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Punch your elbows fully straight the instant your feet land, before you try to stand up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing with feet too narrow to support an overhead squat.
commonMistakes.correction: Practice the footwork on its own first: dip, then jump straight into your widest comfortable squat stance.

programmingNotes: This is a technical drill, not a strength builder, so keep the bar light, well under your snatch max, and focus entirely on speed and position.
Three to five sets of two or three reps once a week is enough; more than that just grooves fatigue into your technique.
Program it early in a session, right after your warm-up, while your legs and reflexes are fresh.
safetyNotes: Only attempt this with a bar and plates you can safely miss under; practice in a rack or with a spotter if you're new to overhead catches.
Stop for the day if your overhead lockout starts breaking down; a soft catch under load is how shoulders get hurt.

faq.question: What's the difference between a snatch balance and a heaving snatch balance?
faq.answer: A regular snatch balance drops straight down under the bar with minimal leg drive. The heaving version adds a short upward push off the shoulders first, which is closer to the timing of a real snatch.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of heaving snatch balance should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of two or three reps once a week, with the bar kept light. This is a speed and position drill, not a max-effort lift.

faq.question: Do I need to be able to snatch before doing this?
faq.answer: Yes. This drill assumes you already know the overhead squat catch position; it's meant to sharpen an existing snatch, not teach the lift from scratch.

faq.question: Why does my overhead squat feel unstable when I catch the bar?
faq.answer: That's usually a mobility or footwork issue rather than a strength one. Drill the catch position with an empty bar and work on ankle and hip mobility before adding weight.

faq.question: How is this different from a power snatch?
faq.answer: A power snatch is the full lift, pulling the bar from the floor and catching it in a partial squat. The heaving snatch balance skips the pull entirely and starts from the shoulders, so all the practice goes into the drop and catch instead of the pull.

easierVariations.name: Snatch Balance
easierVariations.reason: Drops straight down under the bar without the extra upward heave, so you can learn the fast footwork and overhead catch before adding leg drive.

harderVariations.name: Snatch
harderVariations.reason: Takes the same overhead catch position and builds it into a full pull from the floor once your footwork and lockout are reliable.

summary: The spider curl has you lying face down on an inclined bench with your arms hanging straight down, curling an EZ-bar up toward your shoulders. Lying prone removes any chance of swinging your torso to help the lift, so the biceps do the work through the entire range without momentum. It suits anyone who wants a strict, isolated biceps exercise once basic curls stop being a challenge on their own.
whyItWorks: A standing curl lets your hips and lower back sway to help move the weight once it gets heavy, which takes real work away from the biceps without you noticing. Lying face down on an incline pins your torso and upper arms against the bench, so there's no surface to push off of and no momentum to borrow. The biceps have to lift and lower the bar on their own the entire time, which makes the spider curl one of the stricter ways to isolate them.
setup: Set an incline bench to a steep angle and lie face down against it, chest and stomach supported.
Let your arms hang straight down, holding an EZ-bar with an underhand grip at the angled part of the bar.
Keep your upper arms pinned against the bench for the whole set.
execution: Curl the bar up toward your shoulders by bending your elbows.
Keep your upper arms pressed against the bench as you curl.
Squeeze the biceps at the top of the curl.
Lower the bar back down with control until your arms are straight again.
Repeat for the set without letting your torso lift off the bench.
formCues: Upper arms glued to the bench the whole rep.
Curl with the elbows, not the shoulders.
Full stretch at the bottom, full squeeze at the top.
No swinging the torso to start the curl.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the bar up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the upper arms drift forward off the bench to help the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms pressed against the bench throughout the set, even if it means using less weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a weight heavy enough that only a partial range of motion is possible.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can curl through the full range, from a straight arm to a full squeeze, on every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and letting the bar drop.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the bar on the way down just as deliberately as the way up; that portion builds strength too.

programmingNotes: 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps works well, once or twice a week alongside other biceps or pulling work.
It fits best after a compound pulling movement, since it isolates the biceps once they're already somewhat fatigued from bigger lifts.
Increase the weight in small steps once every rep in a set looks clean through the full range.
safetyNotes: Avoid letting the elbows flare out to the sides; keep them tracking in the same line as your upper arms.
Stop short of full lockout tension at the bottom if you feel any pinching at the front of the elbow.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for spider curls?
faq.answer: Start light enough to complete every rep through the full range of motion without your upper arms lifting off the bench. Add weight in small steps from there.

faq.question: Spider curl vs preacher curl: what's the difference?
faq.answer: Both remove momentum by supporting the upper arms, but the spider curl has you face down with your arms hanging, which keeps tension on the biceps even at the top of the curl. The preacher curl angles the arms in front of you and eases off tension near full contraction.

faq.question: Can I do spider curls with a dumbbell instead of an EZ-bar?
faq.answer: Yes, a dumbbell in each hand works the same way. The EZ-bar's angled grip is just easier on the wrists for some lifters.

faq.question: Why don't I feel spider curls in my biceps?
faq.answer: Check that your upper arms are staying pinned to the bench and that the weight isn't so heavy you're only moving it a few inches. Both let other muscles sneak in and take over.

alternatives.name: Hammer Curls
alternatives.reason: Works the same biceps with a neutral grip and no bench required, useful when an incline bench isn't free.

alternatives.name: Barbell Curl
alternatives.reason: The standard standing version of the same curling motion, for when no bench is available at all.

easierVariations.name: Preacher Curl
easierVariations.reason: Also supports the upper arms to remove momentum, but the angled pad gives a bit more support than hanging face down on an incline bench.

summary: The front plate raise lifts a weight plate, held by its edges, straight out in front of your body to about shoulder height. It trains the front deltoid just like a dumbbell front raise, but the flat, edge-gripped plate adds a real forearm and grip demand on top of the shoulder work. It's a step up from the standard dumbbell version, suited to lifters who've built a solid base of shoulder strength and want a new stimulus. It also doubles as a practical move for anyone who trains with plates and doesn't always have dumbbells free.
whyItWorks: Holding a plate by its edges puts your grip in a mechanically weaker position than wrapping fingers around a dumbbell handle, so your forearms and hands work harder just to keep the plate from tipping. That extra grip demand doesn't change what the front deltoid is doing, raising a straight arm forward against gravity, but it does mean the set often ends because the grip or the shoulder gives out first, whichever is the weaker link that day. The flat shape also removes the momentum trick some lifters use with a dumbbell, since there's no comfortable place to let the weight swing from.
setup: Choose a plate light enough to hold comfortably by the edges, 5 or 10 pounds to start.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding the plate with both hands at the outer edges.
Brace your core and keep a slight bend in the knees.
execution: Hold the plate against your thighs, arms straight, hands gripping the outer edges.
Keeping your arms straight, raise the plate forward and up together.
Stop once your arms reach about shoulder height, plate roughly vertical.
Hold briefly, keeping the grip firm and the shoulders down.
Lower the plate under control until it rests against your thighs again.
Continue for the full set without letting the plate drift or tilt.
formCues: Grip the edges firmly the entire set, a loose grip lets the plate tilt.
Raise to shoulder height, no higher.
Keep the arms straight but not locked, elbows soft.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the plate, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the plate too loosely, letting it wobble mid-air.
commonMistakes.correction: Squeeze the edges hard enough that the plate stays flat and still through the whole rep; a wobbling plate means the grip needs work before the weight goes up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the torso to launch the plate upward.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your ribs stacked over your hips and let only the arms move; if the plate needs a swing to get moving, it's too heavy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a plate heavier than your grip can safely control.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until the shoulder, not the grip, is the limiting factor; a dropped plate is a real hazard for your feet.

programmingNotes: Two to three sets of 8 to 10 reps is enough, since grip fatigue often ends the set before the shoulder is fully worked.
This fits best after a standard front raise, once the front deltoid is already warm, rather than as the first shoulder move of the day.
Once a week is usually plenty for this specific variation; use dumbbells or cables on other days and save the plate version for variety.
safetyNotes: Keep bare feet or open-toe shoes well clear of where the plate would land if your grip slips.
Choose a plate with worn or textured edges rather than a slick, painted one that's harder to hold securely.

faq.question: What muscle does the front plate raise work?
faq.answer: The front deltoid does the main work, the same as a dumbbell front raise, with the forearms and grip working harder because of how the plate is held.

faq.question: How heavy a plate should I use for front plate raises?
faq.answer: Start with 5 or 10 pounds. The awkward grip makes even a light plate feel harder than the same weight in a dumbbell.

faq.question: Is the plate raise harder than the dumbbell front raise?
faq.answer: Yes, mostly because of the grip. The shoulder work is nearly identical, but holding a plate by its edges adds a real forearm challenge.

faq.question: Can beginners do front plate raises?
faq.answer: It's fine to try with a very light plate, but most beginners get more out of a dumbbell front raise first, then add the plate version once the movement feels automatic.

alternatives.name: Front Cable Raise
alternatives.reason: Delivers the same front-delt raise with constant cable tension when no plate is free or the grip demand isn't wanted that day.

easierVariations.name: Front Dumbbell Raise
easierVariations.reason: Swaps the plate's awkward edge grip for a dumbbell handle, letting you focus purely on the shoulder without the extra grip demand.

harderVariations.name: Standing Front Barbell Raise Over Head
harderVariations.reason: Moves to a barbell for a heavier bilateral load once the plate's grip challenge feels manageable.

summary: The dumbbell one-arm shoulder press has you press a single dumbbell overhead from shoulder height while your other hand stays free, standing or seated. Because only one side is loaded, your core and obliques have to work hard just to keep your torso from tipping toward the weight, on top of the shoulder and triceps doing the actual pressing. It builds overhead strength and anti-rotation core control at the same time, which makes it a step up in difficulty from a standard two-arm press.
whyItWorks: Pressing a dumbbell overhead with both arms lets your body stay balanced, since the load is even on both sides. Loading only one side removes that balance entirely, and your body has to resist tipping and rotating toward the loaded arm for the whole set, not just at the top of the press. That anti-rotation demand recruits your obliques and deep core muscles in a way a two-arm press barely touches, so the same shoulder gets trained alongside a genuine core challenge instead of two separate exercises.
setup: Stand or sit with a dumbbell held at shoulder height in one hand, elbow bent and palm facing forward or slightly inward.
Brace your core firmly before the first rep, as if you were about to take a light punch to the stomach.
Keep your feet planted roughly hip-width apart if standing, or sit tall against a bench back if seated.
execution: Press the dumbbell straight up overhead, finishing with a fully straight elbow.
Avoid leaning or tipping your torso toward the working side as the dumbbell rises.
Pause briefly at the top with the dumbbell stacked roughly over your shoulder.
Lower the dumbbell back down to shoulder height with control.
Complete all reps on one side before switching to the other arm.
formCues: Brace your core before every rep.
Press straight up, not out and up.
Keep your torso from leaning sideways.
Stack the dumbbell over your shoulder at the top.
breathing: Exhale as you press the dumbbell overhead, inhale as you lower it back to your shoulder.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso sideways away from the loaded arm to help start the press.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core hard before the rep begins and keep your ribcage stacked over your hips throughout the press.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing the dumbbell out and away from the body instead of straight up.
commonMistakes.correction: Picture a straight line from the dumbbell to the ceiling and press directly along it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a weight so heavy that only a short, incomplete press is possible.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until you can lock the arm out fully overhead on every rep with your torso staying upright.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps without resetting the core brace between them.
commonMistakes.correction: Take a breath and reset your brace at the top or bottom of each rep rather than letting tension leak out mid-set.

programmingNotes: This is a genuinely loaded overhead pressing movement with an added core-stability demand, so treat it like your one heavy pressing exercise for the week rather than a second full-intensity session days later.
3 sets of 6 to 10 reps per arm at a challenging weight builds real pressing strength while keeping the core brace manageable.
If shoulder pressing already appears elsewhere in your week at high intensity, drop this to a lighter, higher-rep accessory set instead of stacking two heavy overhead sessions.
New lifters should master the two-arm dumbbell shoulder press first, since the added anti-rotation demand here is easier to learn once the pressing pattern itself feels automatic.
safetyNotes: Choose a weight you can control through the full range without your torso tipping sideways.
Keep your lower back from arching excessively as the dumbbell reaches the top; a tight core brace helps prevent that.

faq.question: How many sets of dumbbell one-arm shoulder presses should I do?
faq.answer: 3 sets of 6 to 10 reps per arm at a challenging weight is a solid range. Because only one side is loaded at a time, expect the total set time to run longer than a two-arm press for the same total reps.

faq.question: What can I use instead of the dumbbell one-arm shoulder press?
faq.answer: The two-arm dumbbell shoulder press trains the same overhead pattern with more balance and less core demand, a good option while you're still building pressing strength or core control.

faq.question: One-arm vs two-arm dumbbell shoulder press: which is better?
faq.answer: The one-arm version adds a genuine core anti-rotation challenge on top of the shoulder work, useful once your overhead pressing strength is solid. The two-arm version lets you use more total weight and is the better place to start for beginners.

faq.question: Why does my torso lean to the side during this press?
faq.answer: That usually means either the weight is too heavy or your core brace isn't tight enough before the rep starts. Lighten the dumbbell and take a moment to brace firmly before every single rep.

alternatives.name: Alternating Cable Shoulder Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same single-arm overhead press pattern from a cable station when a dumbbell heavy enough isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
easierVariations.reason: Pressing both arms together removes the single-side core-bracing demand of the one-arm version, a simpler place to build pressing strength first.

summary: The upward stretch reaches both arms straight overhead with your fingers interlaced and palms turned up, lengthening your shoulders along with your lats and chest. It's a simple way to counter the rounded, arms-down posture most of the day puts you in, and it needs nothing but a few feet of space above your head.
whyItWorks: Reaching your arms overhead and pressing your palms upward pulls your shoulder blades into an extended, upward-rotated position, which lengthens the shoulder muscles along with the lats running down your sides and the chest across the front. Interlacing your fingers and turning the palms up locks your arms into that reaching position so the stretch holds steady instead of drifting, and a gentle lean to either side adds more length down that same side of your torso.
setup: Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart.
Interlace your fingers and raise your arms overhead, turning your palms to face up.
Keep your shoulders relaxed down and away from your ears before you start reaching.
execution: Press your palms upward, straightening your arms as much as feels comfortable.
Reach a little higher and feel the stretch through your shoulders and sides.
Hold the reach for 15 to 20 seconds, breathing normally.
Optionally, lean gently to one side to add a stretch down that side of your torso, then switch sides.
Lower your arms slowly and shake them out when you're done.
formCues: Push palms up, not just arms up.
Shoulders stay down, away from the ears.
Lean sideways gently, don't force it.
Reach, don't strain.
breathing: Inhale as you reach up, then breathe steadily while you hold the stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hunching the shoulders up toward the ears while reaching.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively relax your shoulders down even as your arms reach overhead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to gain extra height.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your core gently engaged so the reach comes from your shoulders and upper back, not from arching your spine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning so far to one side that you lose balance.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the sideways lean small and controlled; the stretch doesn't need a dramatic angle to work.

programmingNotes: Hold for 15 to 20 seconds per side, for 2 rounds.
Works well daily, especially first thing in the morning or during a break from sitting.
A simple way to open up the shoulders and lats before an upper-body workout.
safetyNotes: If you feel any pinching or sharp sensation in the shoulder, lower your arms slightly and reach within a comfortable range instead.
Keep the sideways lean gentle; this is a reach and stretch, not a balance challenge.

faq.question: What does the upward stretch target?
faq.answer: Mainly your shoulders, with your lats and chest stretching too as your arms extend overhead.

faq.question: How long should I hold the upward stretch?
faq.answer: 15 to 20 seconds is enough, for 1 or 2 rounds, with an optional side lean for each side.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch every day?
faq.answer: Yes, it's a gentle bodyweight stretch that works well as a daily habit, especially after sitting for a while.

faq.question: Is it normal to feel this stretch down the side of my body?
faq.answer: Yes, especially when you add the sideways lean, since that brings your lats and the side of your torso into the stretch along with your shoulders.

alternatives.name: Doorway Chest Stretch
alternatives.reason: Uses a doorway for a deeper chest-focused stretch, useful when the chest, not the shoulders, is what feels tight.

alternatives.name: Chest And Front Of Shoulder Stretch
alternatives.reason: Targets the front of the shoulder and chest more directly, a good option when overhead reaching doesn't reach the tightness you're feeling.

harderVariations.name: Round The World Shoulder Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Moves the arms through a full circular path instead of a single overhead reach, a more dynamic shoulder stretch once the static version feels too easy.

summary: Rack pulls set the bar on pins inside a power rack, usually around knee height, so you pull only the top portion of a deadlift instead of starting from the floor. Because the range is shorter, most lifters can load the bar heavier than their full deadlift and still finish the rep. That extra load makes rack pulls a straightforward way to build a stronger lockout, a tougher grip, and a thicker upper back.
whyItWorks: The hardest part of a deadlift is usually the first few inches off the floor, where your back angle is most disadvantaged. Rack pulls remove that section entirely and start you with the bar already at or above knee height, in a stronger position. Because you're no longer limited by your weakest point in the range, you can handle noticeably more weight, and that heavier load forces your lower back, traps, and forearms to work harder than they would under a normal deadlift's max weight. Over time, that overload builds strength and confidence in the top half of the pull, the part that decides whether a heavy deadlift locks out or stalls.
setup: Set the safety pins in a power rack to about knee height, or slightly above.
Load the bar heavier than your usual deadlift working weight, since the shorter range allows it.
Walk up so the bar sits over the middle of your feet, hips back and chest tall.
Take a firm double overhand or mixed grip just outside your knees.
execution: Brace your core and take the slack out of the bar before pulling.
Push the floor away through your heels as you straighten your hips and knees together.
Keep the bar in contact with your thighs as it travels upward.
Finish by standing tall, with your hips fully extended and shoulders back.
Pause for a moment at the top with everything locked in place.
Lower the bar back to the pins with control instead of dropping it.
formCues: Push your hips through to lockout rather than pulling with your arms.
Keep your shins close to vertical, since you're not reaching down to the floor.
Brace your midsection before the bar moves and hold that brace through the rep.
Set the bar down under control so each rep starts from a dead stop on the pins.
breathing: Inhale and brace hard just before you pull, then exhale after you've locked out at the top of the rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading the bar so heavy that the lower back rounds to get it moving.
commonMistakes.correction: Pick a weight you can pull with a flat back for every rep, then add load once that's consistent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bouncing the bar off the pins between reps instead of resetting.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the bar come to a complete stop on the pins, rebrace, then start the next rep fresh.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hyperextending the lower back at the top to add extra range.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the movement once your hips are fully extended and your body is upright, not leaned back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar swing away from the legs as it rises.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the bar sliding up your thighs so the load stays close to your center of mass.

programmingNotes: Because the load is heavier than a full deadlift, one session a week for rack pulls is enough for most lifters.
Sets of three to six reps suit the goal here, which is building top end strength rather than conditioning.
Rack pulls work well as the second heavy pull of the week if your main deadlift day is a few days apart, but skip stacking both in one session.
Track the bar weight over time rather than chasing reps, since a stronger lockout shows up as more weight moved through the same short range.
If your grip gives out before your back or hips do, spend a few weeks building grip endurance separately rather than switching to lifting straps every session.
safetyNotes: Never pull a weight that forces your lower back to round just to get the bar off the pins.
Use collars to keep plates secure, since a heavier than usual load makes a shifting plate more dangerous.
Skip rack pulls on days your grip or lower back already feels fatigued from other pulling work.

faq.question: How heavy should rack pulls be compared to my deadlift?
faq.answer: Many lifters can handle 10 to 20 percent more than their deadlift max, since the range is shorter and starts from a stronger position. Add weight gradually and let your form set the limit.

faq.question: Do rack pulls build my deadlift or just my grip?
faq.answer: Both. The heavier load builds real grip and upper back strength, and the lockout practice carries over directly to finishing heavy deadlifts.

faq.question: Rack pulls or deadlifts, which is better?
faq.answer: They train different things. Deadlifts build strength through the entire range, including the hardest part off the floor, while rack pulls overload the lockout. Most lifters benefit from doing both, not choosing one.

faq.question: How high should I set the pins for rack pulls?
faq.answer: Around knee height is the standard setting. Pins set higher shorten the range further and let you handle even more weight, while pins just below the knee keep more of the pull intact.

faq.question: Will rack pulls hurt my lower back?
faq.answer: Not if you keep the load light enough to maintain a flat back through every rep. Rack pulls become risky only when the heavier weight tempts you into rounding to finish a rep your form can't support.

alternatives.name: Stiff-Legged Barbell Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Loads the same lower back and hamstrings with a hip hinge pattern when a rack or pins aren't available.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Deadlift
harderVariations.reason: Extends the pull down to the floor, adding back the hardest part of the range once your lockout and grip can handle heavier weight.

summary: The seated one-arm dumbbell palms-down wrist curl trains the muscles on the top of your forearm, the wrist extensors, by lifting a light dumbbell using only your wrist while your palm faces the floor. It is the reverse of the more common palms-up wrist curl, and most lifters need noticeably less weight for it, since the extensors are smaller and weaker than the flexors on the underside of the forearm. Training one arm at a time lets you match the load and range to each wrist individually.
whyItWorks: Your forearm has two opposing muscle groups: flexors on the palm side that curl the wrist down, and extensors on the back side that lift it up. Most grip-focused training, from deadlifts to pull-ups, biases the flexors heavily, so the extensors are often the weaker, more neglected half of the forearm. Resting your forearm on your thigh with your palm down and lifting the dumbbell using only your wrist isolates that extensor group directly, without your fingers, elbow, or shoulder getting involved.
setup: Sit on a bench and rest your forearm along your thigh, palm facing down, wrist and hand hanging just past your knee.
Hold a light dumbbell with your fingers wrapped loosely around the handle.
Brace your forearm against your thigh so only your wrist moves.
Start with your wrist relaxed and slightly bent downward.
execution: Lift the back of your hand up as high as your wrist allows, keeping your forearm pinned to your thigh.
Pause briefly at the top of the lift.
Lower the dumbbell back down slowly, letting your wrist bend past neutral into a light stretch.
Keep the motion isolated to the wrist; do not let your forearm roll or your elbow bend.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch arms.
formCues: Forearm stays pinned to your thigh the whole rep.
Lift with the wrist only, not the fingers or elbow.
Pause briefly at the top of each rep.
Lower slowly into the stretch.
breathing: Exhale as you lift the back of your hand up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using too much weight and swinging the forearm to help lift it.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until your forearm can stay completely still against your thigh for the full set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps without pausing at the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold the top position for a full second so the extensors do the work instead of momentum.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the wrist drop too fast on the way down.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the dumbbell on a slow two-count instead of letting gravity snap the wrist down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the dumbbell too tightly with the fingers.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a loose, relaxed grip so your fingers are not compensating for the wrist extensors.

programmingNotes: This is a small, single-joint muscle group, so keep the weight light and build up slowly rather than chasing heavier dumbbells quickly.
Two or three sets of 12 to 15 reps per arm, two or three times a week, is enough for most people since it is isolation work on a small muscle group.
Give the extensors at least a day of rest between sessions early on; they fatigue and tighten faster than most lifters expect from such a light exercise.
If you also train the palms-up version, do the extensor work first while your wrist is fresh, since the extensors are the weaker half of the pair.
safetyNotes: Start with a lighter dumbbell than you would guess; the wrist extensors are a small muscle group and overloading them can aggravate the tendons near your elbow.
Stop the set if you feel sharp pain on the outside of your elbow rather than pushing through it.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for the palms-down wrist curl?
faq.answer: Start lighter than feels necessary, often just 2 to 5 kilograms per hand. The wrist extensors are small and weak compared to the flexors, and using a similar weight to your palms-up curl usually means the load is too heavy.

faq.question: Why is this exercise also called a reverse wrist curl?
faq.answer: Because the palm faces down instead of up, the motion runs in the opposite direction of a standard wrist curl, working the extensors on the back of the forearm instead of the flexors underneath.

faq.question: What can I do if I do not have dumbbells at home?
faq.answer: A cable wrist curl at a low pulley works the same motion with adjustable resistance if a gym cable station is available.

faq.question: Why does the outside of my elbow hurt after wrist curls?
faq.answer: That usually means the extensor tendons near your elbow are working harder than they are ready for. Lower the weight and shorten your range of motion, and stop the exercise if sharp pain continues.

alternatives.name: Cable Wrist Curl
alternatives.reason: Keeps constant tension through the cable instead of relying on gravity alone for resistance.

easierVariations.name: Seated Dumbbell Palms-Down Wrist Curl
easierVariations.reason: Trains both wrists together, which is more stable and forgiving while you learn the extensor pattern.

harderVariations.name: Seated Palms-Down Barbell Wrist Curl
harderVariations.reason: Moves to a barbell once single-arm control is solid, allowing more total load across both wrists.

summary: This is a close-grip EZ bar curl with a resistance band looped under your feet and attached to the bar, adding extra tension as you curl higher. The band makes the top of the curl harder while the bottom stays lighter, which is the opposite of how a plain bar feels. It's a beginner move that suits anyone who wants to add variety to biceps training or push through a sticking point near the top of the curl.
whyItWorks: A plain barbell curl is hardest around the middle of the range and gets easier near the top as your elbow straightens out mechanically. A band stretched under your feet fights that natural easing, since it pulls harder the more you stretch it, which happens right as your arm approaches full flexion. That shifts the toughest part of the rep to the top of the curl instead of the middle, forcing your biceps to keep working hard through the exact range a plain bar would let them coast through.
setup: Loop a resistance band under both feet, standing on it with a stable, shoulder-width stance.
Attach the other end of the band to the center of the EZ bar, or hold both in the same hand grip.
Grip the bar on the inner angled section, hands close together.
Take up the slack in the band before your first rep so tension starts right away.
execution: Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbow, keeping your upper arms pinned to your sides.
Fight through the extra band tension as you approach the top, rather than jerking through it.
Squeeze at the top for a full second.
Lower under control, resisting the band's pull the whole way back down.
Reset your stance on the band if it shifts off-center between reps.
formCues: Feet stay planted on the band, don't let it slide.
Elbows stay pinned to your sides throughout.
Fight the band's pull on the way down too, not just up.
Squeeze hardest right at the top where the band is strongest.
breathing: Exhale as you curl up against the band's resistance, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing on the band unevenly so one foot bears more tension than the other.
commonMistakes.correction: Center the band under both feet at the start of every set and check your stance if the bar starts pulling to one side.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a band so strong that form breaks down near the top of the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Choose a lighter band than you think you need; the band should make the top challenging, not force your elbows forward to finish the rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar snap back down once the band's pull peaks.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the lowering phase the whole way; releasing tension lets the band jerk the bar and puts sudden strain on the elbow.

programmingNotes: As a light isolation exercise, it fits well two to three times a week without much recovery cost.
Sets of 12 to 15 reps suit this movement, since the band makes the top range hard even at moderate bar loads.
Use a lighter bar than your regular EZ bar curl to account for the added band resistance near lockout.
It travels well, so it's a solid choice when you're training with limited equipment away from a gym.
safetyNotes: Check the band for nicks or wear before each use; a band that snaps under tension can whip back toward your face.
Anchor the band securely under both feet before pulling; a slipping band can throw you off balance mid-rep.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for close-grip EZ bar curl with band?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 12 to 15 reps, two to three times a week, works well given the added resistance near the top of each rep.

faq.question: What band tension should I use for this curl?
faq.answer: Start lighter than you think. The band adds real resistance at the top of the curl, and a band that's too strong will force your elbows forward to finish the rep.

faq.question: Can I do this curl without a band?
faq.answer: Yes, dropping the band turns it into a standard close-grip EZ bar curl, which feels heavier through the stretched bottom position instead of the top.

faq.question: What kind of band works best for this curl?
faq.answer: A closed-loop fabric or rubber resistance band you can stand on comfortably works best. Choose one light enough that you can still curl the bar smoothly through the last few degrees of the top position.

alternatives.name: Resistance Band Lat Pulldown
alternatives.reason: Not a curl, but a band-only pulling option for the same travel bag or home setup that has no EZ bar available.

harderVariations.name: Close-Grip EZ Bar Curl
harderVariations.reason: Dropping the band leaves a flat resistance curve, which feels heavier through the stretched bottom position the band was covering for you.

summary: The medicine ball chest pass has you drive a weighted ball forward from your chest with both hands, training your chest, shoulders, and triceps to produce force fast instead of just under a slow, controlled load. Unlike a chest press, the ball leaves your hands entirely, so the movement trains speed and power output as much as raw strength. It works well with a partner or against a solid wall, and it's a natural way to add an explosive element to an upper-body session.
whyItWorks: A regular chest press builds strength by moving a fixed load through a controlled range, but it never asks your muscles to produce force fast enough to launch anything, since the bar stays in your hands the whole time. The chest pass is a compound push where the ball actually leaves your grip, so your chest, shoulders, and triceps have to fire together and accelerate through the whole range instead of decelerating near the end the way a press does. That specific quality, power rather than pure strength, is what a throw trains and a press can't.
setup: Stand a few steps from a solid wall or a partner, feet shoulder-width apart and knees slightly bent.
Hold the medicine ball at chest height with both hands, elbows out to the sides.
Choose a ball weight light enough that you can throw it with real speed, not just push it.
execution: Load your chest by pulling the ball in slightly toward your body.
Drive the ball forward explosively by extending your arms and pushing through your chest.
Release the ball at full arm extension, letting it leave your hands completely.
Catch the rebound off the wall, or receive the return pass from your partner, with soft elbows.
Absorb the catch by letting your elbows bend back toward your chest before the next throw.
Repeat for the set, resetting your stance between throws if your balance drifts.
formCues: Load the chest before you throw, don't just push from a dead stop.
Extend fully and let the ball leave your hands.
Catch with soft elbows, absorbing the impact.
Reset your stance between throws.
breathing: Exhale sharply as you drive the ball forward, inhale as you absorb the catch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pushing the ball with a slow, even tempo instead of throwing it with speed.
commonMistakes.correction: Treat the release like a real throw, accelerating through the whole motion instead of decelerating near full extension.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the rebound with stiff, locked elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your elbows bend back toward your chest on the catch to absorb the impact safely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a ball too heavy to throw with real speed.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop to a lighter ball; the point of this exercise is speed, not maximum load.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 6 to 8 explosive throws is plenty, since power work depends on quality speed, not high volume.
Best done early in a session, right after your warm-up, while your nervous system is fresh enough to produce real speed on every rep.
As an explosive, technique-dependent throw, twice a week with a rest day between sessions lets your nervous system recover between bouts.
Rest close to a full minute or more between sets so fatigue doesn't turn the throws into a slow push.
safetyNotes: Stop the set if your throws start slowing down noticeably; that fatigue is exactly when form and catch control break down.
Use a wall or partner setup with enough space that a missed catch doesn't send the ball into anything fragile.

faq.question: How many reps of medicine ball chest pass should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 6 to 8 explosive throws is enough, since the goal is speed and quality on every rep, not high volume.

faq.question: Medicine ball chest pass vs regular chest press, which is better for building power?
faq.answer: The chest press builds raw strength under a controlled load, but the bar never leaves your hands, so it never trains your muscles to accelerate through release. The chest pass lets the ball leave your grip entirely, training the explosive power a press can't. Most people benefit from both: press for strength, pass for speed.

faq.question: Can I do a medicine ball chest pass without a partner?
faq.answer: Yes, throwing against a solid, unobstructed wall works just as well and lets you set your own pace and rest between throws.

faq.question: What weight medicine ball should I use for a chest pass?
faq.answer: Light enough that you can throw it with real speed and still catch the rebound safely, usually 2 to 6 kilograms for most beginners. If the ball is slowing your throw down to a push, it's too heavy.

alternatives.name: Supine Chest Throw
alternatives.reason: Trains the same explosive chest-pass pattern lying down, which reduces the leg and balance demands if you don't have room to stand and throw.

easierVariations.name: Cable Chest Press
easierVariations.reason: A slower, controlled push through the same chest, shoulder, and triceps pattern, useful for building base strength before adding the explosive release.

summary: The squat-style Turkish get-up takes you from lying on the floor to standing tall with a kettlebell locked out overhead, moving through your forearm, hand, and a kneeling position along the way. Instead of standing up out of a lunge, this style sweeps your back leg all the way through to a parallel stance and finishes with a squat. It suits lifters who already move comfortably through floor transitions and want to build shoulder stability and total-body coordination under load.
whyItWorks: Every position in the get-up asks your shoulder to keep the kettlebell stacked directly over your wrist while the rest of your body changes shape underneath it, from lying down, to propped on a forearm, to a bridge on one hand, to kneeling, to standing. Your shoulder stabilizers have to hold that lockout through each transition without losing the line, while your core resists the sideways pull of the offset load. Sweeping the trailing leg through to a parallel stance instead of stopping in a lunge asks your hips to rotate under load, which is what makes the squat-style finish feel different from the lunge-style version even though both end in the same standing lockout.
setup: Lie on your back with the kettlebell locked out straight above your shoulder in one hand.
On the kettlebell side, bend your knee and set that foot flat on the floor.
Spread your other arm and leg out to about 45 degrees to give yourself a wide base.
Fix your eyes on the kettlebell before you start moving.
execution: Press through your planted heel and free hand to roll up onto your opposite forearm, keeping the kettlebell locked out overhead.
Push off that forearm onto a flat hand, straightening your arm so your hips lift into a bridge.
Sweep your straight leg back and underneath your body into a kneeling position, kettlebell still locked out overhead.
Sweep your back leg all the way through so both feet land parallel in a squat stance, pivoting on your front foot as you turn.
Stand straight up out of the squat stance, keeping the kettlebell stacked overhead the whole time.
Pause standing with the kettlebell locked out directly above your shoulder.
Reverse the sequence step by step to return to the floor under control.
formCues: Track the kettlebell with your eyes through every transition, not your feet or the floor.
Keep the arm holding the kettlebell locked out the entire time, don't let the elbow bend.
Pivot on your front foot as you sweep the back leg through, rather than dragging it.
Stand up out of the squat evenly through both legs, not by shifting weight to one side.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace before you start moving, then breathe steadily through each transition instead of holding your breath the whole way up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the kettlebell drift away from directly over the shoulder during a transition.
commonMistakes.correction: Check that your wrist, elbow, and shoulder stay stacked under the kettlebell at every position, correcting the angle before moving to the next step.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dragging the back leg through instead of pivoting on the front foot.
commonMistakes.correction: Push off the ball of your front foot as you sweep the back leg through, letting your hips rotate into the squat stance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing up unevenly, pushing mostly through one leg.
commonMistakes.correction: Once your feet are parallel, drive up through both legs at the same time, like a standard squat.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a kettlebell too heavy to control smoothly through every transition.
commonMistakes.correction: Practice the full sequence with a light kettlebell or no load until every position feels stable before adding weight.

programmingNotes: Two or three reps per side, for two or three sets, is plenty since the technical demand matters more than the rep count.
This works best early in a session, while you're fresh enough to control every transition with good form.
Two sessions a week with a light to moderate kettlebell is enough to build the skill and shoulder stability without overloading the joint.
safetyNotes: Practice the full movement without weight, or with just your hand, until every transition feels controlled before adding a kettlebell.
Stop and reset if the kettlebell wobbles or drifts off line at any point; that's a sign to slow down or reduce the weight.

faq.question: What's the difference between the squat-style and lunge-style Turkish get-up?
faq.answer: Both share the same floor-to-kneeling sequence. The squat style sweeps the back leg through to a parallel stance and stands up with a squat, while the lunge style stands up out of a half-kneeling lunge by driving through the front leg.

faq.question: How heavy should the kettlebell be for a Turkish get-up?
faq.answer: Start light, or even with no weight, until every transition feels controlled. The get-up rewards good positioning far more than heavy load, so most people use a lighter kettlebell than they would for a press or squat.

faq.question: How many reps of Turkish get-up should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three reps per side, for two or three sets, is a solid range since the technical demand of each transition matters more than doing many reps.

faq.question: Why does the squat-style get-up feel harder than the lunge style?
faq.answer: Sweeping the back leg through to a parallel stance asks your hips to rotate under an offset overhead load, which takes more hip mobility and control than stepping straight up out of a lunge.

alternatives.name: Kettlebell Turkish Get-Up (Lunge style)
alternatives.reason: Reaches the same standing overhead position through a lunge transition instead of a squat, a good alternate technique for the same skill.

easierVariations.name: Kettlebell Windmill
easierVariations.reason: Isolates the overhead anti-lateral-flexion hold and hip hinge on their own, without the full sequence of floor-to-standing transitions in the get-up.

harderVariations.name: One-Arm Overhead Kettlebell Squats
harderVariations.reason: Takes the same locked-out overhead position and parallel foot stance into a full repeated squat, once the get-up transition feels solid.

summary: The standing inner biceps curl has you hold dumbbells with your arms angled out to the sides instead of straight down, then curl them up while holding that same angle. Standing without a backrest means your shoulders and core have to hold that outward position themselves, a stability demand the seated and incline versions don't ask for. It fits lifters who already curl regularly and want a detail-focused move for the outer part of the biceps, once their torso control is solid.
whyItWorks: The biceps has two heads, and the angle your upper arm hangs at changes how much tension each one carries. Letting your arms drift out to the sides rather than hanging flush against your torso puts your shoulder in a position that stretches the long head of the biceps more than a close, standard curl does. Doing this standing removes the bench that would otherwise lock your shoulders in place, so your mid-back and shoulder stabilizers have to hold that outward arm angle steady on their own while your biceps handle the actual curl. That combination makes the standing version a stricter test of control than the same curl done seated or reclined.
setup: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand, feet shoulder-width apart.
Let your arms hang out to the sides at roughly a 30 to 45 degree angle from your torso, palms facing forward.
Brace your core and keep your shoulders back rather than letting them round forward.
execution: Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders while holding that same outward arm angle.
Keep your elbows from drifting in toward your ribs as the weight rises.
Squeeze the biceps briefly at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbells slowly back to a full stretch before the next rep.
Keep your torso still throughout; don't rock or lean to help lift the weight.
formCues: Hold a steady arm angle the whole set.
Curl straight up, don't let the dumbbells drift inward.
Keep your torso still, no rocking for momentum.
Lower all the way to a full stretch each rep.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbells up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift back toward the torso mid-curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold your arms at the same outward angle for the whole set; drifting inward turns this into a standard standing curl.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using body momentum, a small hip or shoulder swing, to start the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso still and let your biceps do the lifting; if you need to swing, the weight is too heavy for this strict angle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a weight too close to your regular curl load.
commonMistakes.correction: Use lighter dumbbells than your standard curl, since holding the outward angle without a backrest makes the same load feel heavier.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 10 to 12 reps suits this detail-focused move well.
Twice a week is enough for a single-joint arm exercise like this, spaced a few days apart from your other pulling work.
Place it after your main curling movement in an arm session, since the balance demand makes it a poor choice to load heavy early in a workout.
safetyNotes: Keep the outward arm angle moderate, around 30 to 45 degrees; pushing it wider adds unnecessary strain to the front of the shoulder.
Drop the weight and reset your stance if you feel your shoulders rounding forward to compensate for fatigue.

faq.question: How many reps should I do for the standing inner biceps curl?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 12 reps works well. Use less weight than your usual curl, since the outward angle and the lack of a backrest both make it harder.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and the incline version?
faq.answer: The incline bench pins your shoulders in place, so the standing version asks your torso and shoulders to hold the same outward angle on their own, a harder stability challenge at the same weight.

faq.question: What can I do if I can't balance the outward angle yet?
faq.answer: The seated dumbbell inner biceps curl holds the same arm path with a backrest, a steadier way to start.

faq.question: Why does this feel so much harder than a normal curl with the same dumbbells?
faq.answer: The outward angle changes which part of the biceps does the work, and standing without support means your shoulders have to hold that angle themselves instead of resting on a bench.

alternatives.name: Hammer Curls
alternatives.reason: Trains the biceps and forearms with a neutral grip when you'd rather not hold an outward arm angle under load.

alternatives.name: Concentration Curls
alternatives.reason: Isolates the same biceps with your elbow braced against your leg, trading the balance demand for a seated, locked-in position.

easierVariations.name: Seated Dumbbell Inner Biceps Curl
easierVariations.reason: Adds a backrest that holds the same outward arm angle for you, removing the balance demand while you learn the position.

harderVariations.name: Incline Inner Biceps Curl
harderVariations.reason: Reclines further back on an angled bench, stretching the long head of the biceps even more at the bottom of each rep.

summary: The decline dumbbell triceps extension has you lie back on a bench set to a slight decline, holding a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, then bend your elbows to lower the weights toward your temples before pressing back up. The decline angle changes the direction your arms travel relative to gravity, which keeps tension on your triceps through a longer stretch at the bottom of the rep than a flat or incline bench allows. It is a single-joint isolation move, so it works best as an accessory to build arm size and lockout strength rather than as your main pressing exercise.
whyItWorks: Your triceps' only real job is elbow extension, and this move isolates exactly that by keeping your shoulders fixed while only your forearms travel. Lying on a decline bench points your upper arms slightly behind your head instead of straight up, which puts the long head of the triceps, the portion that crosses your shoulder joint, into a deeper stretch at the bottom of each rep than a flat-bench version does. Loading a muscle near that stretched position is part of what makes lying extensions a favorite for building tricep size, and holding the decline angle keeps that stretch in play for the whole set instead of just the bottom inch.
setup: Set an adjustable bench to a slight decline and lie back with your head at the low end.
Hook your feet or knees under the bench pad so your body stays anchored.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand and press them straight up over your chest, palms facing each other.
Turn your upper arms in slightly so your elbows point toward the ceiling, not out to the sides.
execution: Keeping your upper arms still, bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells toward your temples.
Stop the descent once your forearms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Press through your forearms to extend your elbows and return the dumbbells overhead.
Pause briefly at the top without locking out hard, then start the next rep.
formCues: Keep your elbows pointed at the ceiling the whole rep, not flared out.
Move only at the elbow, your upper arms should not swing.
Lower the dumbbells to the sides of your head, not straight down toward your face.
Control the descent instead of dropping into the stretch.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the dumbbells toward your temples, and exhale as you press them back overhead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift outward as the weight gets heavier.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a mental picture of your elbows staying narrow and pointed up, and drop the weight if you cannot hold that line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the shoulders to help press the dumbbells up.
commonMistakes.correction: Fix your upper arms in place before the first rep and check that only your forearms move.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and losing control near the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the descent to about two seconds so the triceps, not momentum, control the weight.

programmingNotes: Two to three sets of ten to fifteen reps at the end of a push or arm day gives the triceps a solid isolation finisher after compound pressing.
Because it is a single-joint move with a light-to-moderate load, most lifters recover from it within a day or two, so training it twice a week alongside other pressing work is reasonable.
Pair it with a horizontal or overhead press earlier in the session; the triceps are already partly fatigued from those compound lifts, so this move finishes the job rather than pre-exhausting them.
safetyNotes: Choose a dumbbell weight you can lower under full control before adding more load; a dropped dumbbell near your head is the real risk with this exercise.
Keep your elbows pointed up rather than flared, which reduces strain on the elbow joint itself.
Warm up your elbows with a lighter set first if they feel stiff, since this move loads the joint near full flexion.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of decline dumbbell triceps extensions should I do?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of ten to fifteen reps works well as an accessory move after your main pressing exercise for the day.

faq.question: Can I do triceps extensions without a decline bench?
faq.answer: Yes. A standing dumbbell triceps extension trains the same muscle with the same range of motion and needs no bench at all, or a flat bench works if a decline one is not available.

faq.question: What's the difference between the decline and flat versions of this exercise?
faq.answer: The decline angle points your upper arms slightly behind your head, which stretches the triceps a bit more at the bottom of the rep than a flat bench does; the movement pattern and muscles trained are otherwise the same.

faq.question: Why do my elbows hurt during triceps extensions?
faq.answer: That is often the elbows flaring outward under load or the weight being too heavy to control through the full stretch. Keep your elbows narrow and pointed at the ceiling, and drop the weight until you can complete every rep with that position held.
