This is a light, bodyweight plyometric drill, so two to three sessions a week works well, ideally with a day of rest between explosive-focused sessions.
Perform it early in a session, right after your warm-up, since jump quality drops quickly once your legs are fatigued from other training.
Rest fully between sets, aiming for something close to your best jump on every rep rather than grinding through tired, lower-quality ones.
safetyNotes: Land on a surface with some give, like a gym floor or turf, rather than concrete, to reduce impact on your joints.
Stop the session if your landings start feeling unstable or your knees cave inward, since that's a sign of fatigue outpacing your control.

faq.question: What muscles does the rocket jump work?
faq.answer: Mainly the quadriceps, with the calves and hamstrings assisting to generate the explosive upward drive and to help control the landing.

faq.question: How many rocket jumps should I do per set?
faq.answer: Five to eight jumps per set is a good range. Because this is an explosive power exercise, quality reps done while fresh matter more than a high total count.

faq.question: Is the rocket jump good for beginners?
faq.answer: Yes, it's a beginner-friendly plyometric drill that needs no equipment. Just focus on a soft, controlled landing every rep rather than jumping for maximum height right away.

faq.question: How is the rocket jump different from a regular vertical jump?
faq.answer: They're very similar; the rocket jump specifically cues an overhead arm reach at the top, which adds a bit of extra height through arm drive and gives you an easy visual target to gauge your jump against.

alternatives.name: Star Jump
alternatives.reason: Trains the same explosive, bodyweight vertical jump pattern with an added arm and leg spread, a comparable beginner-level substitute.

harderVariations.name: Linear Depth Jump
harderVariations.reason: Adds a step down before the jump, increasing the eccentric landing demand once a standard vertical jump feels easy.

summary: The atlas stone trainer is a rubber-coated or textured practice stone used to learn the atlas stone lift safely: hinging down to hug the stone, rolling it into your lap, then standing and loading it onto a platform. It trains the lower back and hips as the primary movers, with the biceps, forearms, glutes, hamstrings, and quadriceps all sharing the load. It's built specifically so beginners can learn the technique before moving to a real competition stone.
whyItWorks: Lifting a round, handle-free object is fundamentally different from a barbell deadlift, since there's nothing to grip cleanly, forcing you to hug the load close to your body and use your whole torso rather than just your hands and arms. The atlas stone trainer keeps that same awkward-object challenge while offering a more forgiving, grippier surface than a real stone, which lets you focus on learning the hip hinge, the roll into your lap, and the stand-and-load sequence without fighting the surface itself at the same time.
setup: Position the training stone on the floor in front of a loading platform or target height.
Stand close to the stone with your feet outside it, hips back and chest up.
Wrap both arms fully around the stone before attempting to lift.
execution: Hinge down and hug the stone tightly against your torso.
Drive through your legs and hips to lift the stone off the floor, keeping it pulled in close.
Roll the stone up onto your thighs as you stand more upright.
Use the momentum from that roll to help lift the stone toward your chest.
Extend your hips and legs fully to stand up with the stone secured against your torso.
Load the stone onto the platform with control, rather than dropping it from height.
formCues: Hug the stone tight to your body.
Hips back, chest up on the initial pull.
Roll onto the thighs before standing tall.
Load with control, don't drop from height.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace before initiating the lift, exhaling as you stand and load the stone onto the platform.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to lift with a rounded back instead of hinging at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hips back and your chest up before gripping the stone; a rounded back under this kind of load is the main injury risk.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keeping the stone away from your body during the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Hug the stone as tightly as possible against your torso; the closer it stays, the less strain on your lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the platform loading step and just holding the stone at the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Practice the full loading motion onto a platform, since that final placement is part of the actual skill being trained.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attempting a stone that's too heavy before the lifting pattern is comfortable.
commonMistakes.correction: Start with a lighter training stone and only increase weight once the hinge, hug, and roll feel smooth and repeatable.

programmingNotes: Start with 3 to 5 lifts at a manageable weight, focusing entirely on technique rather than speed.
This exercise fits well as a skill-building session on its own rather than being crammed into the end of an unrelated workout.
Progress the stone's weight gradually, and only once the current weight feels controlled and repeatable.
Rest fully between lifts; this is a demanding, whole-body effort each time.
safetyNotes: Keep your back flat and hinge from the hips throughout; this lift places real demand on the lower back if the spine rounds under load.
Learn this movement with a lighter training stone before attempting a real competition stone, and ideally with someone experienced watching your first attempts.

faq.question: What muscles does the atlas stone trainer work?
faq.answer: The lower back and hips drive the lift, with the glutes, hamstrings, and quadriceps powering the stand, and the biceps and forearms working hard just to hold the stone against your body.

faq.question: Is the atlas stone trainer safe for beginners?
faq.answer: It's specifically designed to be a safer, more forgiving entry point than a real competition stone, thanks to its grippier surface. It's still a demanding lift, so start light and prioritize technique over weight.

faq.question: Atlas stone trainer vs real atlas stones: what's the difference?
faq.answer: The trainer typically has a textured or rubber-coated surface that's easier to grip and hug than a real stone's smooth, heavy surface. It's meant as a stepping stone to build the lifting pattern before progressing to genuine competition stones.

faq.question: How heavy should my first atlas stone trainer be?
faq.answer: Light enough that you can complete the full hinge, hug, roll, and load sequence with control and without straining. Technique matters far more than weight when you're learning this lift.

alternatives.name: Keg Load
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar awkward-object lift and load pattern with a keg instead of a stone-shaped implement.

alternatives.name: Farmer's Walk
alternatives.reason: Builds the same total-body strength and grip demand common to strongman training, in a carrying pattern instead of a lift and load.

easierVariations.name: Sandbag Load
easierVariations.reason: Uses a softer, easier-to-grip load to practice the same lift-and-load pattern before moving to a rounder stone shape.

harderVariations.name: Atlas Stones
harderVariations.reason: Moves to a genuine competition-style stone once the trainer's lift-and-load pattern feels solid and controlled.

summary: The suspended row uses straps or a TRX anchored overhead: you lean your bodyweight back, then pull your chest toward the handles. It trains the middle back, lats, and biceps the same way a bent-over row does, except the resistance comes from your own lean angle instead of a barbell. It's a beginner-friendly pulling move for anyone without access to a cable machine or free weights.
whyItWorks: Pulling your chest toward your hands draws your shoulder blades together and bends your elbows, which is exactly the job of the middle back, lats, and biceps in any rowing movement. The steeper you lean back, the more of your bodyweight the straps have to support, which raises the resistance without changing the movement pattern at all, so you can scale the exercise just by moving your feet. Because the handles hang freely instead of sitting on a fixed bar, your shoulders also have to control the handle path through the whole pull, which keeps the surrounding rotator cuff muscles engaged in a way a machine row doesn't ask for.
setup: Anchor the straps overhead and adjust the handles to roughly chest height.
Grip the handles with palms facing each other and walk your feet forward until your arms are extended and your body leans back.
Keep your heels planted and your body in a straight line from head to ankles.
Choose a lean angle: more upright is easier, closer to horizontal is harder.
execution: Start with arms extended and your body leaning back in a straight line.
Pull your chest toward the handles by driving your elbows back and down.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull.
Keep your body rigid, don't let your hips sag or lead the movement.
Lower back under control to the extended-arm starting position.
Reset your body line before the next rep.
formCues: Drive your elbows back, don't just bend at the wrist and hand.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of every rep.
Keep your body one straight line from head to ankles.
Keep your core braced so the pull comes from your back, not your hips.
breathing: Exhale as you pull your chest toward the handles, inhale as you lower back out. Keep the breathing steady rather than holding it, since a held breath tends to show up as the hips sagging under the extra tension.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders round forward at the bottom of the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest up and shoulder blades set even as your arms fully extend.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning the row into mostly a biceps curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Lead with your elbows driving back, not just your hands bending toward your shoulders.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag below the body line.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to keep your torso rigid through the pull.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking the handles with jerky momentum.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo so your back muscles, not momentum, do the pulling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning the head to look up or around mid-pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your neck in line with your spine and your eyes forward so your body line stays honest.

programmingNotes: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps is a solid range, adjusting the lean angle to land in that rep count.
Because the lean angle lets you dial the load up or down instantly, this holds up to 2 to 3 sessions a week without the fatigue cost of a loaded barbell row.
Pair it with a pushing exercise like a suspended push-up in the same session to balance pull and push volume.
Try a brief pause at the top of each pull once the basic tempo feels controlled; the extra time under tension at full contraction adds difficulty without changing the angle.
safetyNotes: Check the strap anchor and handles for wear before leaning your bodyweight into them.
Stop if you feel sharp pain at the front of the shoulder and reduce the lean angle.
Keep both straps set to equal lengths so one shoulder doesn't end up carrying more of the lean than the other.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of suspended rows should I do?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps works well; lean back further once the current angle feels easy for all reps.

faq.question: What can I use instead of a TRX for suspended rows?
faq.answer: Gymnastics rings or suspension straps anchored to a secure overhead point, like a sturdy pull-up bar, both work.

faq.question: Suspended row vs bent-over barbell row, what's the difference?
faq.answer: Both train the middle back, lats, and biceps the same way; the suspended version loads with a bodyweight lean instead of a fixed external weight.

faq.question: Why does my lower back feel tired after suspended rows?
faq.answer: That usually means your hips are sagging and your lower back is working to hold the body line instead of your core; brace tighter and keep the body straight through the pull.

faq.question: Can suspended rows build real back strength, or are they just a warm-up move?
faq.answer: They can build real strength, especially for beginners and intermediates; leaning closer to horizontal increases the load substantially, and once that stops being enough, you can add a weighted vest or move to a loaded barbell row.

alternatives.name: Seated Cable Rows
alternatives.reason: A seated, fixed-path row that hits the same middle back and biceps without needing an anchor point.

alternatives.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
alternatives.reason: A supported, single-arm row that works the same muscles when only dumbbells are on hand.

easierVariations.name: Inverted Row
easierVariations.reason: A fixed bar instead of swinging straps removes the instability so you can focus purely on the pulling pattern.

harderVariations.name: Bent Over Barbell Row
harderVariations.reason: A loaded barbell lets you keep adding weight once bodyweight leans no longer feel challenging.

summary: You set an incline bench to a steep angle, stand beside it, and drape your working arm down over the raised pad so the upper arm hangs straight toward the floor. From that dead-hang position you curl a single dumbbell, which stretches the long head of the biceps harder than a standard standing curl allows. It's a finishing move for lifters who already have the basic curl pattern down and want more stretch under load.
whyItWorks: Your biceps' long head crosses the shoulder joint, so it gets a deeper stretch when your arm hangs behind the plane of your torso instead of at your side. Draping your arm over the incline pad puts the shoulder in that extended position before you even start curling, so every rep begins from a longer muscle length than a standard curl does. That extra stretch under load is where a lot of the growth stimulus from curl variations comes from, and it's also why your working weight will usually need to drop compared to a plain standing curl.
setup: Set an incline bench to roughly 45 to 60 degrees and stand next to the high end.
Hold a dumbbell in the hand nearest the bench and drape that arm over the pad so your upper arm hangs straight down, shoulder slightly behind your torso.
Brace your free hand on the bench or your hip for balance.
Let the dumbbell hang at full arm extension before the first rep.
execution: Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow, keeping your upper arm pinned against the pad.
Continue until your forearm is roughly vertical and you feel a strong peak contraction in the biceps.
Squeeze briefly at the top without shrugging your shoulder to help the lift.
Lower the dumbbell slowly back to a full hang, resisting the weight the whole way down.
Finish all reps on one side before switching arms.
formCues: Keep the upper arm glued to the pad the entire rep.
Let the weight hang fully at the bottom before curling again.
Squeeze, don't shrug, at the top.
Lower slower than you lift.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbell up, inhale as you lower it back to the hang.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbow drift forward off the pad to cheat the weight up.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can keep the upper arm pressed against the pad for every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a bench angle that's too shallow, which turns this into a regular standing curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Set the bench steep enough that your arm genuinely hangs behind your torso at the bottom.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and letting the dumbbell drop.
commonMistakes.correction: Count two or three seconds on the way down; the stretched position is the whole point of this variation.

programmingNotes: This is a single-joint stretch-focused move, so 3 sets of 10 to 12 reps per arm near the end of an arm or pull session works well.
Because the stretched bottom position is more demanding than a standard curl, expect to use a noticeably lighter dumbbell than your usual curl weight.
Twice a week is plenty for most lifters, since it's isolated work layered on top of whatever rowing or pulling already hits the biceps.
Pair it with a compound pull earlier in the session and save this for when your grip and elbows are already warm.
safetyNotes: Keep the bench angle steep enough that your shoulder doesn't feel pinched at the bottom of the stretch.
Stop short of pain in the front of the shoulder; mild biceps stretch is expected, joint pain is not.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for the standing one-arm dumbbell curl over incline bench?
faq.answer: Three sets of 10 to 12 reps per arm, using a lighter dumbbell than your normal curl since the stretched position makes the exercise harder at the same weight.

faq.question: What can I do instead if I don't have an incline bench?
faq.answer: A seated incline dumbbell curl gives you nearly the same stretched long-head position without needing to balance standing next to the bench.

faq.question: Why does this version feel so much harder than a regular dumbbell curl?
faq.answer: Draping your arm over the bench stretches the biceps' long head before the rep even starts, so you're curling from a longer, weaker muscle length than you would standing upright.

alternatives.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
alternatives.reason: Sitting back on the incline bench hits the same stretched long-head position without needing to balance your weight against the pad while standing.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Bicep Curl
easierVariations.reason: The regular standing curl drops the stretch position and the balance demand of leaning over a bench, so you can focus on the basic curling pattern first.

harderVariations.name: One Arm Dumbbell Preacher Curl
harderVariations.reason: Pinning the upper arm against a preacher pad removes any chance of swinging the torso, forcing the biceps to handle the full stretch and the full lockout alone.

summary: The dumbbell alternate bicep curl is exactly what it sounds like: you curl one dumbbell up while the other arm hangs still, then switch. Working one side at a time lets you focus your full attention on each rep and often lets you use a bit more weight per arm than curling both together, since the resting arm gets a short break. It's one of the first arm exercises most people learn, and one of the easiest to do sloppily without noticing.
whyItWorks: Your biceps flex the elbow and help rotate your forearm, and a dumbbell curl loads both of those jobs directly. Alternating sides means each rep gets your undivided attention instead of splitting it between two arms moving at once, which makes it easier to catch a wandering elbow or a swinging torso before it becomes a habit. The brief pause while one arm rests also means you can typically curl a slightly heavier dumbbell per rep than you could curling both arms together for the same total volume.
setup: Stand tall holding one dumbbell in each hand, feet planted about hip-width apart.
Let your arms hang fully at your sides, palms facing your thighs.
Brace your core and pin your elbows close to your ribs before the first rep.
execution: Keeping your right elbow pinned at your side, curl the right dumbbell up toward your shoulder.
Rotate your palm to face your shoulder as the dumbbell rises.
Squeeze your biceps at the top without letting the elbow drift forward.
Lower the right dumbbell back down under control to full arm extension.
As the right arm finishes, curl the left dumbbell using the same path.
Continue alternating arms until you've completed all reps on both sides.
formCues: Elbow stays pinned at your side, not drifting forward.
Rotate your palm up as you curl for a full biceps squeeze.
Lower on a slow two-count instead of dropping the weight.
The resting arm hangs straight and still, no swinging.
breathing: Exhale as you curl each dumbbell up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso backward to help swing the dumbbell up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your ribs stacked over your hips and drop the weight until you can curl without any body English.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbow drift forward, turning the curl into a front raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arm glued to your side for the whole rep; only your forearm should move.

commonMistakes.mistake: Curling both dumbbells at the same time out of habit.
commonMistakes.correction: Let one arm fully rest while the other works; that's the point of the alternating pattern.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the weight quickly on the way down.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the lowering phase down; the eccentric is where a lot of the growth stimulus happens.

programmingNotes: As a beginner-friendly isolation move, it fits well two or three times a week as accessory work after your main pressing or pulling.
Two to three sets of 10 to 12 reps per arm is a solid starting point; add weight once you can finish every rep with strict form.
Pair it with a triceps move on the same day for a simple, balanced arm session.
Because the fatigue cost per set is low compared to a compound lift, it's fine to program it more often than a heavy pressing or pulling exercise.
safetyNotes: Keep your wrists straight through the curl; a bent wrist under load is an easy way to irritate a tendon over time.
Avoid relying on back momentum to move the weight; if you need to lean or heave, the dumbbell is too heavy for strict reps.

faq.question: Alternating dumbbell curls vs curling both arms together: which is better?
faq.answer: Neither is strictly better. Alternating lets you focus fully on each rep and often use slightly more weight per arm since the resting side gets a break. Curling both together saves time and forces stricter symmetry since you can't lean on your stronger arm without it showing.

faq.question: How much weight should I start with for dumbbell curls?
faq.answer: Pick a weight you can curl for 10 to 12 strict reps per arm without swinging your torso or letting your elbow drift forward. It's easy to overestimate this lift; start lighter than feels impressive and add weight once the form holds up.

faq.question: Can I do alternating dumbbell curls sitting down?
faq.answer: Yes, sitting on a bench removes any leg drive and makes it harder to cheat with body momentum, which is a useful way to make the exercise stricter without adding weight.

faq.question: Does alternating build bigger arms than curling both at once?
faq.answer: The muscle-building signal comes from total volume and effort, not from whether you alternate. Pick whichever version lets you keep the strictest form for the most reps, and switch it up over time if you like variety.

alternatives.name: Barbell Curl
alternatives.reason: Trains the same biceps with a barbell when dumbbells aren't available.

alternatives.name: EZ-Bar Curl
alternatives.reason: An angled bar grip that's kinder to the wrists if straight-bar curls bother yours.

harderVariations.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
harderVariations.reason: Pins your shoulders back on an incline bench, removing any body swing and adding a deeper stretch at the bottom.

harderVariations.name: Concentration Curls
harderVariations.reason: Isolates one arm at a time with your elbow braced against your leg, for a stricter squeeze once alternating feels easy.

summary: This drill has a partner toss you a medicine ball, which you catch and immediately fire back overhead in one continuous motion. It's built around the catch, not just the throw. Absorbing the incoming ball loads your lats and shoulders the instant before you reverse direction and throw, which trains the kind of fast, reactive power that a standalone throw from a dead stop can't teach.
whyItWorks: Catching a moving ball forces your lats, chest, and shoulders to decelerate it eccentrically, which pre-loads those same muscles right before they have to reverse and produce force in the other direction. That stretch-and-fire sequence is what makes the exercise reactive rather than just strong. Your abdominals brace hard through the catch to stop the ball's momentum from folding you forward, and then stay engaged as your arms drive the ball back overhead. Because the catch and the throw happen in one continuous motion instead of two separate ones, your nervous system gets practice producing power on a much shorter timeline than a standing throw from rest ever demands.
setup: Stand facing your partner or a sturdy wall, far enough apart that the ball travels through the air rather than being handed off.
Hold a light to moderate medicine ball ready position, arms slightly bent, eyes on the incoming ball.
Set a stable, shoulder-width stance so you can absorb the catch without stepping back.
execution: Track the ball as your partner tosses it toward you.
Catch it with both hands, letting your arms and lats give slightly to absorb the force.
Immediately reverse direction, bringing the ball back behind your head in one continuous motion.
Drive through your legs and torso and throw the ball back overhead to your partner or against the wall.
Reset your stance and repeat for the next catch.
formCues: Catch soft, let your arms absorb the ball instead of stopping it dead.
Turn the catch into the throw in one motion, don't pause between them.
Brace your core through the catch so your torso doesn't fold forward.
Drive the throw from your legs and hips, not just your arms.
breathing: Exhale sharply as you release the throw, and take your next breath in during the moment you're tracking the incoming ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the ball dead still and pausing before starting the throw.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the catch flow straight into the throw, the whole value of this drill is in that one continuous, reactive motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting your torso fold forward when the ball lands in your hands.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core before the catch arrives so your body can absorb the force without collapsing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing with just your arms while your legs stay passive.
commonMistakes.correction: Drive the throw from the ground up, letting your legs and hips add power instead of leaving it all to your shoulders.

programmingNotes: This is a reactive power drill, so quality reps matter more than quantity. Three to five sets of five to eight throws is a solid dose.
Twice a week is enough for most people, placed early in a session while your nervous system is fresh and your catch reflexes are sharp.
Use a ball light enough that you can catch and reverse it in one smooth motion. If the catch turns into a fight to control the ball, it's too heavy for this drill.
safetyNotes: Warm up your shoulders and wrists before adding real throwing speed.
Use a soft medicine ball and enough space that a missed catch doesn't put you or your partner at risk.
Stop the set if your catching technique breaks down and the ball starts jarring your wrists or shoulders.

faq.question: How many reps of catch and overhead throw should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of five to eight throws is a good starting dose. This is a power drill, so stop a set once your catches or throws start losing snap.

faq.question: Do I need a partner for this drill?
faq.answer: A partner is ideal, but a sturdy wall works too. Throw the ball against the wall at an angle so it bounces back for you to catch.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and a standing overhead throw?
faq.answer: A standing overhead throw starts from a dead stop with the ball already in your hands. This drill adds a catch first, so you're training your muscles to absorb force and reverse it immediately, which is a more reactive skill.

faq.question: Why does my lower back or shoulders feel it the next day?
faq.answer: The catch loads your lats and shoulders eccentrically right before the throw asks them to fire again, which is more demanding than a throw alone. Keep the ball light and the reps low while you build up tolerance.

alternatives.name: Supine Two-Arm Overhead Throw
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar lat-loaded overhead throwing pattern lying on your back, useful when you're working solo against a wall at a low angle.

easierVariations.name: Standing Two-Arm Overhead Throw
easierVariations.reason: Removes the catch, letting you groove the overhead throwing motion on its own before adding a reactive catch in front of it.

summary: The side-lying floor stretch has you lie on your side and reach your top arm overhead and across your body, lengthening the whole side of your torso from your ribs to your armpit. It's a gentle, floor-based way to open up the lats and the side body without needing to stand, balance, or hold any weight.
whyItWorks: Your lats run from your lower back up to your upper arm bone, and they shorten every time you pull something down or toward you, which is most of what upper-body pulling exercises and everyday reaching involve. Reaching your arm overhead and across your body while lying on your side puts the lat through the opposite motion, lengthening it along its full path instead of shortening it. Doing this from the floor removes the balance demands a standing overhead reach would add, so the muscle can relax into the stretch instead of also working to keep you upright.
setup: Lie on your side with your legs stacked and slightly bent for stability.
Rest your bottom arm along the floor or use it to support your head.
Keep your hips stacked, not rolled forward or back.
execution: Reach your top arm straight overhead, then let it drift down and across toward the floor in front of you.
Let your rib cage follow the stretch slightly, opening the side of your torso toward the ceiling.
Hold the position, breathing steadily, without forcing the reach further than feels comfortable.
Release slowly and bring your arm back to your side.
Switch sides and repeat the same stretch on the other arm.
formCues: Keep your hips stacked and still; the stretch should come from your arm and rib cage.
Reach long through your fingertips rather than just bending at the shoulder.
Let your breath guide small increases in the stretch instead of pulling harder with your arm.
Keep your neck relaxed and in line with your spine, don't crane it toward the stretch.
breathing: Breathe slowly and evenly throughout the hold, letting each exhale soften into a slightly deeper stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the hips forward or backward to chase a deeper stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hips stacked directly on top of each other; let the stretch come from the reaching arm and rib cage instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Holding your breath while reaching for the stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep breathing steadily throughout the hold. Tension in the breath usually shows up as tension in the muscle you're trying to relax.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bouncing the arm to try to reach farther.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold the stretch still instead of bouncing. A static, steady hold lengthens the muscle more safely than repeated small tugs.

programmingNotes: This is a gentle static stretch, so it's fine daily, or as part of your warm-up or cool-down whenever your lats or upper back feel tight.
Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds, and repeat two or three times per side if the area still feels tight after the first hold.
It pairs well after any pulling session, rows or pull-ups, or before overhead work like a shoulder press.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel sharp pain rather than a gentle pulling sensation along your side.
Support your head with a small cushion or your bottom arm if lying flat on the floor feels uncomfortable on your neck.

faq.question: How long should I hold the side-lying floor stretch?
faq.answer: Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds, and repeat two or three times per side if the muscle still feels tight afterward.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch without lying on the floor?
faq.answer: Yes, standing and reaching your arm overhead and across your body works the same muscles, though it adds a small balance demand the lying version avoids.

faq.question: Why do I feel this stretch more on one side than the other?
faq.answer: It's common for one lat to be tighter, often on the side you use more for pulling or reaching overhead. Hold both sides for equal time rather than matching how tight each one feels.

faq.question: What does this stretch help with besides the lats?
faq.answer: It also opens the side body and intercostal muscles between your ribs, which can feel stiff after a lot of sitting or after chest and shoulder training.

alternatives.name: Latissimus Dorsi-SMR
alternatives.reason: Releases tension in the same lat muscle with a foam roller instead of a static stretch, a good option when you want more direct pressure on tight spots.

harderVariations.name: Side Wrist Pull
harderVariations.reason: Moves the same lat and side-body stretch to standing and adds an active wrist pull, which deepens the stretch once the lying version feels easy.

summary: The overhead cable curl places you between two high pulleys, arms starting out to the sides near shoulder height, and asks you to curl both handles in toward your head at the same time. Unlike a standing dumbbell curl, where gravity only resists the lift directly below the weight, the cable's angle keeps real tension on your biceps even near the top of the range, where a free weight would otherwise go slack. It's a two-arm isolation move built for people who already have curl technique down and want a variation that challenges the biceps differently through the movement.
whyItWorks: A standing dumbbell curl loses tension as your forearm approaches vertical, because gravity is pulling straight down and the weight pulls less on your elbow the closer your forearm gets to vertical. Cables don't work that way: the pulley keeps pulling along a fixed line no matter where your arm is, so positioning two high pulleys and curling inward keeps your biceps under real load through a larger share of the range, including the portion where a dumbbell curl would otherwise coast. Curling with both arms at once, from a slightly stretched starting position with your arms out to the sides, also asks your biceps to work through more of their length than a curl that starts with your arms hanging straight down.
setup: Set two pulleys to a high position and attach a single handle to each.
Stand centered between the two towers, roughly equidistant from both pulleys.
Take a handle in each hand and step forward slightly to create tension in the cables.
Start with your arms extended out to your sides at roughly shoulder height, elbows slightly bent.
execution: Keep your upper arms roughly stationary as you begin the curl.
Curl both handles in toward your head, bending at the elbow.
Continue until your hands approach your temples or forehead.
Squeeze your biceps briefly at the top of the movement.
Lower back out to the starting position with control, resisting the cables the entire way.
Keep the tempo even between both arms so neither side does more of the work.
formCues: Keep the upper arms still; only the forearms move.
Curl both hands toward your head, not out to the sides.
Squeeze at the top before lowering.
Control the stretch back to the start; don't let the cables snap your arms straight.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the handles toward your head, inhale as you extend back to the starting position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the upper arms forward or letting the elbows drift to help complete the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms fixed in place throughout the set; if you need to swing them to finish a rep, the weight is too heavy for strict form.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping short at the top instead of bringing the hands close to the head.
commonMistakes.correction: Curl until your hands are near your temples and pause briefly there, since that's where the cable angle provides some of the most useful tension.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the cables yank the arms back out too quickly on the return.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return phase at the same pace as the curl; a fast, uncontrolled stretch wastes the tension advantage cables give you over a free weight.

programmingNotes: As a biceps isolation exercise, it fits best later in an upper-body or pull session, after your compound rows or pull-ups have already been trained.
Two to three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a reasonable range for building biceps size and endurance without needing especially heavy loading.
Because two pulleys are required at once, this exercise works best in a gym with a dedicated cable crossover station rather than a single-pulley setup.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled on both the curl and the return; jerking the cables can strain the elbow or shoulder joints.
Choose a load you can curl with both arms moving in sync; letting one arm dominate can create uneven strain across your shoulders.
Warm up your elbows and shoulders with a lighter set first, since the stretched starting position asks more of both joints than a standard curl does.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of overhead cable curls should I do?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a solid range, since this is a biceps isolation move meant to finish a session rather than build maximum strength.

faq.question: What can I do instead if my gym only has one cable pulley free?
faq.answer: A reverse cable curl from a single low pulley or a standard EZ-bar curl both train the same biceps flexion pattern without needing two overhead stations.

faq.question: Overhead cable curl vs standing dumbbell curl, which is better?
faq.answer: The cable version keeps tension on your biceps closer to the top of the curl, where a dumbbell curl tends to go slack; the dumbbell version is simpler to set up and still builds the same muscle effectively, so either is a reasonable choice depending on what equipment you have.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders feel this exercise more than my biceps?
faq.answer: Check that your upper arms are staying still and your elbows aren't drifting forward as you curl; if your shoulders are doing extra work to hold your arms in place, the resistance may be too heavy for the position.

alternatives.name: Reverse Cable Curl
alternatives.reason: Uses a single low pulley instead of the overhead double-pulley setup, a good swap when only one cable station is free.

alternatives.name: EZ-Bar Curl
alternatives.reason: Trains the same biceps flexion pattern with a fixed bar and no cable machine required at all.

easierVariations.name: Concentration Curls
easierVariations.reason: Trains one arm at a time with a dumbbell instead of two overhead pulleys, an easier setup for learning the curl before adding cable positioning.

harderVariations.name: Drag Curl
harderVariations.reason: Keeps the elbows pinned back and drags the bar up the torso, a strict-technique variation that demands more shoulder stability under load.

summary: The triceps stretch raises one arm overhead, bends the elbow, and gently pulls it further back with the other hand to lengthen the muscle along the back of your upper arm. It also pulls on the lats along your side, making it a quick way to open up the shoulder and upper back after pressing work or a day spent at a desk.
whyItWorks: Bending the elbow and reaching the hand down behind your head puts the triceps into a fully lengthened position, since the muscle crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints. Adding gentle overhead pressure with your other hand takes up the remaining slack in the shoulder, which is why this stretch reaches into the lats along your side as well as the back of your arm.
setup: Stand or sit tall with your shoulders relaxed and down.
Raise one arm straight overhead.
Bend that elbow so your hand drops behind your head, fingers pointing toward your opposite shoulder blade.
execution: Reach your other hand up and place it on the bent elbow.
Gently pull the elbow back and slightly behind your head until you feel a stretch along the back of your upper arm.
Hold the position without bouncing, keeping your breathing steady.
Release slowly and lower both arms.
Switch sides and repeat with the other arm.
formCues: Keep shoulders down, not hunched toward your ears.
Pull gently, don't yank the elbow.
Chest stays open, don't round forward.
Breathe steadily through the hold.
breathing: Breathe slowly and steadily throughout the hold instead of holding your breath.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking the elbow back sharply to deepen the stretch faster.
commonMistakes.correction: Apply steady, gentle pressure instead; a slow build gets you just as deep without risking the joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders creep up toward the ears during the hold.
commonMistakes.correction: Consciously drop your shoulders away from your ears before and during the stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to compensate for a tight shoulder.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your ribs stacked over your hips and let the stretch happen at the shoulder and arm, not the spine.

programmingNotes: Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds, and repeat once or twice per side.
This is gentle enough to do daily, especially after any pressing or overhead work.
Use it as part of a cool-down rather than before heavy lifting, since cold triceps don't need a deep stretch before load.
safetyNotes: Stop pulling if you feel sharp pain rather than a mild stretch; back off to a lighter pull.
Skip this stretch on a shoulder that's currently injured or recently had surgery without clearance.

faq.question: How long should I hold a triceps stretch?
faq.answer: Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds, and repeat once or twice if it still feels tight.

faq.question: How often can I do the triceps stretch?
faq.answer: It's gentle enough for daily use, particularly after pressing exercises or a long day with your arms overhead.

faq.question: What if raising my arm overhead hurts my shoulder?
faq.answer: Try the triceps side stretch instead, which pulls the arm across your body rather than straight overhead.

faq.question: Why does this stretch also pull on my side, not just my arm?
faq.answer: The triceps and the lats share a connection through the shoulder, so pulling the bent elbow back and overhead naturally stretches both at once.

alternatives.name: Tricep Side Stretch
alternatives.reason: Pulls the arm across from the side instead of overhead, a useful option if raising your arm straight up bothers your shoulder.

summary: The power snatch from blocks starts the bar resting on elevated blocks and finishes with a shallow overhead catch above parallel instead of a full overhead squat. Shortening the pull and keeping the catch shallow lets you focus reps on the fastest, most technical part of the snatch, the turnover and the overhead lockout, without also managing a floor-level start or a deep receiving squat. It suits lifters refining their snatch technique who already have a reliable overhead position and want more reps of the finish.
whyItWorks: A full snatch asks you to pull the bar from the floor with your widest grip, accelerate it overhead in one continuous motion, and catch it in a deep squat. Power snatch from blocks strips out the slower floor-level pull and the deep catch, leaving the part of the lift that actually separates a clean rep from a missed one, the violent hip extension and the fast pull-under into a locked-out overhead position. Because the wide grip and standing pull recruit your hips, back, and shoulders together, the muscle demand spreads across your whole posterior chain and shoulders rather than concentrating in one joint.
setup: Set blocks or a rack so the bar sits at or just below your knees.
Take your widest comfortable snatch grip and stance.
Set your hips down, chest up, and shoulders slightly ahead of the bar.
Brace your core and pull your shoulder blades back before you start the pull.
execution: Pull the bar off the blocks with control, keeping it close to your legs.
As the bar passes your knees, extend your hips explosively while keeping the bar tight to your body.
Finish the pull with a hard shrug, letting the bar rise as high as your extension allows.
Pull yourself under the bar fast, punching your arms straight overhead.
Catch the bar overhead in a shallow dip, well above parallel, with your arms locked.
Stand up out of the dip immediately, then lower the bar back to the blocks under control.
formCues: Keep the bar close from the blocks all the way up.
Hips finish the pull before your arms bend.
Catch high, arms locked, not in a deep squat.
Shoulders stay active and locked, not shrugged up at the ears.
Stand tall the moment you catch it.
breathing: Brace and hold your breath through the pull, then exhale once the bar is locked out overhead and you're standing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the catch sink into a deep overhead squat instead of a shallow dip.
commonMistakes.correction: Absorb the bar with a short, shallow bend at the knees and stand immediately; a deep catch turns this into a full snatch and works against the point of the power version.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling with the arms too early instead of letting the hips finish first.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your arms long and relaxed until your hips have fully extended, then use them only to pull yourself under the bar.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the bar with soft, unlocked elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Punch your arms fully straight the instant you catch the bar; a bent elbow overhead is unstable under any load.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting the blocks too high, turning the lift into mostly an arm pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the bar at or just below knee height so there's still a real leg drive to finish the pull.

programmingNotes: This is fast, technical pulling work with a real skill component, so keep it early in a session while you're fresh and focused.
Sets of 2 to 3 reps protect the speed and precision the lift depends on; higher reps just add fatigue-driven technique breakdown.
Given the technical and total-body demand of the overhead catch, once a week as your main pulling variation is a reasonable default unless you're specifically drilling turnover.
Warm up with the empty bar and light loads to rehearse the overhead position before adding weight for working sets.
safetyNotes: If you can't lock the bar out overhead cleanly, drop the weight rather than catching it with bent arms.
Set the blocks at a height you can actually control; too high removes the pull, too low reintroduces the floor-level demands this variation is meant to avoid.
Learn the overhead catch position with a coach or experienced training partner before loading this movement heavily.

faq.question: How high should the blocks be for power snatch from blocks?
faq.answer: Set them so the bar sits at or just below your knees. That keeps a real pull in the lift while shortening it compared to starting from the floor.

faq.question: What's the difference between a power snatch from blocks and a regular power snatch?
faq.answer: Both use the same shallow, above-parallel catch overhead. A power snatch pulls from the floor, while the blocks version shortens that first pull so you can focus reps on the fast finish and the overhead catch.

faq.question: How many reps and sets should I do for power snatch from blocks?
faq.answer: Two to three reps per set keep the bar speed and catch precision high. Three to five sets is typical for a main pulling movement.

faq.question: Is the power snatch easier than a full snatch?
faq.answer: The catch is shallower, above parallel instead of a full overhead squat, so many lifters find it more forgiving on the hips and knees, but the overhead lockout and turnover speed still demand real technique.

faq.question: Do I need special coaching before trying this?
faq.answer: Yes. The overhead catch carries real risk if your positioning is off, so build the pattern with light loads and, ideally, an experienced coach before adding real weight.

alternatives.name: Muscle Snatch
alternatives.reason: Trains the overhead pull and lockout without receiving under a dip, useful for isolating arm and shoulder speed.

harderVariations.name: Snatch from Blocks
harderVariations.reason: Adds a deeper, full overhead-squat catch to the same shortened pull once the shallow catch feels automatic.

harderVariations.name: Power Snatch
harderVariations.reason: Extends the pull all the way from the floor while keeping the same shallow overhead catch.

summary: The Tricep Dumbbell Kickback is a single-joint isolation move where you extend a dumbbell backward from a bent-over position, working the triceps through a controlled arc. It's a common finisher for arm day, isolating the triceps without any help from the chest or shoulders.
whyItWorks: Bending over and keeping your upper arm fixed parallel to the floor removes your shoulder from the movement entirely, so the only joint doing work is the elbow. Extending the forearm against the dumbbell's resistance isolates the triceps through its full range, and because the weight sits at the far end of your forearm, the resistance is toughest right at full extension, which is exactly where the triceps often feel weakest.
setup: Hold a dumbbell in one hand and hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor.
Support yourself with your free hand on a bench, or brace your knee against it.
Raise your upper arm so it's parallel to the floor, elbow bent at roughly 90 degrees.
Keep your back flat rather than rounded in this bent-over position.
execution: Keeping your upper arm still and parallel to the floor, extend your forearm back until your arm is straight.
Pause briefly at full extension and squeeze the triceps.
Bend the elbow to return the dumbbell to the starting position with control.
Repeat for the prescribed reps, then switch arms.
formCues: Keep your upper arm pinned at your side; only your forearm should move.
Extend all the way to a straight arm instead of stopping short.
Keep your back flat and your core braced in the bent-over position.
Control the lowering phase instead of letting the dumbbell drop.
breathing: Exhale as you extend the arm back, inhale as you bend the elbow to return to the start.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the upper arm swing or drift away from the body during the extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Pin your upper arm against your side and only move from the elbow.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing the weight instead of a controlled extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the movement down and use only the triceps to extend the arm, not a swinging motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the back to compensate for a weak hip hinge in the bent-over position.
commonMistakes.correction: Hinge from the hips with a flat back, and use a bench for support if balance is an issue.

programmingNotes: A light isolation exercise like this works well for 2 to 3 sessions a week when training arms.
Three sets of 10 to 15 reps per arm is a common range since the triceps respond well to higher reps in this position.
Place it later in an arm or upper-body session, after any heavier pressing work, since it isolates a muscle that's already been working.
Pair with a biceps isolation move to balance out an arm-focused session.
safetyNotes: Keep the back flat during the bent-over position rather than rounding under the weight of the dumbbell.
Use a weight light enough that you can keep your upper arm still throughout the set.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of Tricep Dumbbell Kickback should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 10 to 15 reps per arm is a common range, since this isolation move responds well to higher reps.

faq.question: Why don't I feel this in my triceps?
faq.answer: Usually the upper arm is swinging instead of staying fixed. Pin your upper arm parallel to the floor and let only the forearm move to isolate the triceps.

faq.question: Can I do Tricep Dumbbell Kickback without a bench?
faq.answer: Yes, you can hinge forward freestanding, but using a bench for support makes it easier to keep your back flat and your upper arm still.

faq.question: Is Kickback or Pushdown better for triceps?
faq.answer: Both isolate the triceps well. Pushdowns keep more constant cable tension through the cable, while kickbacks let you focus on one arm at a time and feel the squeeze at full extension.

alternatives.name: Triceps Pushdown
alternatives.reason: A cable alternative that keeps constant tension on the triceps if dumbbells aren't available.

alternatives.name: Standing Dumbbell Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: A different dumbbell angle on the same muscle, useful for variety or if the bent-over position bothers your lower back.

easierVariations.name: Body Tricep Press
easierVariations.reason: A bodyweight tricep isolation move with no added load, useful while you build the mind-muscle connection before adding a dumbbell.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Skullcrusher
harderVariations.reason: A bench-supported position that lets you load the triceps more heavily than the bent-over kickback position allows.

summary: The sit-up is a bodyweight core exercise where you curl your torso all the way up from lying on your back to sitting upright, using your hip flexors and abdominals together. It's one of the oldest core exercises around, and it still works as a simple way to build the strength to get your torso off the ground with control, whether that's for sport, for getting up off the floor, or just for training your midsection without equipment.
whyItWorks: Your abdominals contract to curl your spine, while your hip flexors take over for the second half of the movement, pulling your torso up and over your hips. Training this full range, rather than only the crunch portion, builds strength through the whole motion of sitting up, which is a movement you repeat dozens of times a day getting out of bed, off a couch, or up from the floor. Because the resistance is only your own body weight, the exercise scales naturally with your own strength: your first rep and your five-hundredth rep use the same technique, just at different levels of control.
setup: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Cross your arms over your chest or rest your fingertips lightly by your ears.
Keep your feet flat and, if needed, hook them under something sturdy for support.
Engage your core before you move, rather than starting from a completely relaxed position.
execution: Brace your abdominals as if you're about to be tapped in the stomach.
Curl your chin toward your chest and lift your shoulders off the floor.
Continue curling your torso up and forward until you're sitting fully upright.
Pause briefly at the top without throwing your body forward.
Reverse the motion, lowering your torso back down one vertebra at a time.
Let your shoulders touch the floor lightly before starting the next rep.
formCues: Curl up, don't yank up.
Keep your chin tucked slightly, not jutting forward.
Exhale on the way up like you're blowing out a candle.
Lower with the same control you used to rise.
breathing: Exhale as you curl up toward sitting, and inhale as you lower back down to the floor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling on your neck with your hands to yank yourself up.
commonMistakes.correction: Rest your fingertips lightly by your ears and let your abdominals do the lifting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing up instead of curling.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the rep down until you can feel your abs working through the first few inches off the floor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the lower back slam into the floor on the way down.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower under control and let your back touch down softly, one section at a time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Holding your breath through the entire rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Exhale as you rise and inhale as you lower, so your core has a steady rhythm to work with instead of tensing against held air.

programmingNotes: Since this is an unloaded core movement rather than a heavy compound lift, 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps most days it's programmed is realistic for most people.
It pairs well with a rotational or anti-extension core move, like a plank, so your midsection gets trained from more than one angle in the same session.
Two to three times a week works for most people, since the main limiter here is technique and control rather than heavy fatigue.
safetyNotes: Skip sit-ups on days your lower back is already irritated, since the hip flexor pull can load the lower back if form breaks down.
Keep the motion slow enough to stop at any point instead of relying on momentum to finish the rep.
If you feel the movement mainly in your neck instead of your abs, stop and reset your hand position.

faq.question: How many sit-ups should I do a day?
faq.answer: Three sets of 10 to 15 controlled reps, two to three days a week, is a solid amount for most people; more reps done sloppily add less than fewer reps done with good form.

faq.question: Are sit-ups bad for your back?
faq.answer: Sit-ups are safe for most people when the motion is slow and controlled and the lower back doesn't slam into the floor. If you already have lower back pain, talk with a professional before adding them.

faq.question: What's the difference between a sit-up and a crunch?
faq.answer: A crunch lifts just your shoulders and upper back off the floor, while a sit-up continues all the way up to a full sitting position, which brings the hip flexors into the movement.

faq.question: Can I do sit-ups without anchoring my feet?
faq.answer: Yes. Keeping your feet free makes your abdominals work harder to control the movement, since you can't lean on your hip flexors pulling against anchored feet as much.

faq.question: Why do sit-ups get easier the more I do them?
faq.answer: As your abdominals and hip flexors get stronger, the same bodyweight resistance takes less relative effort, which is a normal sign of progress and a good time to add reps or slow the tempo.

alternatives.name: Reverse Crunch
alternatives.reason: Trains the abdominals through spinal flexion from the opposite end, without pulling on the neck.

easierVariations.name: Crunches
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same abdominal contraction through a shorter range, without the hip flexor demand of sitting all the way up.

harderVariations.name: Weighted Sit-Ups - With Bands
harderVariations.reason: Adds resistance to the same full range of motion once bodyweight reps feel easy.

summary: The incline push-up trains your chest and triceps with your hands elevated on a bench, step, or bar while your feet stay on the floor. The upward angle takes weight off your arms, so it's a natural starting point if a full floor push-up still feels too heavy. It builds the same pressing pattern as the standard push-up: hands under shoulders, straight body line, full range of motion. Anyone rebuilding upper body strength after time off, or working toward their first floor push-up, can use it as a stepping stone.
whyItWorks: Elevating your hands raises your body's center of mass relative to your base of support, which shifts more of your bodyweight onto your legs and less onto your arms and chest. Your pectorals still drive the pressing motion, with your shoulders and triceps locking out the top of each rep, but you're pushing a smaller share of your total weight than you would on the floor. Because the incline lowers the load, you can groove the mechanics of a good push-up, a straight body line, elbows tracking back rather than flaring, full range of motion, before you add the extra resistance of a flat or decline position. The steeper the incline, the lighter the exercise; the lower the surface, the closer it gets to a standard floor push-up.
setup: Find a stable bench, step, or bar around knee to hip height.
Place your hands shoulder-width apart on the edge, fingers pointing forward.
Walk your feet back until your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes so your hips don't sag or pike.
Keep your neck neutral, eyes toward the bench, not straight down or forward.
execution: Start with arms straight and your body rigid in one line.
Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the bench.
Keep your elbows at roughly a 45 degree angle from your torso as you descend.
Lower until your chest is a couple inches from the surface.
Pause briefly at the bottom without letting your hips drop.
Press through your palms to straighten your arms.
Exhale as you push back up to the starting position.
formCues: Keep your body one straight line from shoulders to ankles.
Point elbows back at about 45 degrees, not flared out to the sides.
Drive through your whole palm, not just your fingers.
Keep your head in line with your spine.
Move at a steady pace instead of dropping quickly and bouncing up.
breathing: Inhale as you lower your chest toward the bench, and exhale as you press back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag toward the floor
commonMistakes.correction: Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs so your torso stays rigid through the whole rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows closer to your body, tracking back at roughly 45 degrees.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only lowering halfway
commonMistakes.correction: Bring your chest close to the bench on every rep so you get the full range of motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing hands too high on a tall surface
commonMistakes.correction: Use a bench or step around knee to hip height so your torso stays close to horizontal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the head drop forward and chin jut out
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your neck in line with your spine and your gaze toward the bench, not the floor ahead of you.

programmingNotes: Because the incline reduces the load, most people can handle higher rep ranges, think 12 to 20 reps per set.
Use it as a chest and triceps accessory on a push day, or as your main pressing exercise if floor push-ups are still too hard.
Two or three sets, two to three times a week, works well since the joint stress is low compared to a loaded press.
Lower the incline height over time, a shorter step and then eventually the floor, as sets get easy with strict form.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel sharp pain in your wrists or shoulders instead of pushing through it.
Keep your wrists stacked under your hands rather than letting them collapse to one side.
Use a surface that won't slide, tip, or wobble under your hands.

faq.question: How many reps of incline push-ups should I do?
faq.answer: Most people can aim for 12 to 20 reps per set once the surface height matches their strength. If you can't hit 8 clean reps, raise the surface a little; if 20 feels easy with good form, lower it.

faq.question: Is the incline push-up easier than a regular push-up?
faq.answer: Yes. Elevating your hands shifts more of your bodyweight onto your legs, so you're pressing less of your total weight than you would on the floor.

faq.question: Can I do incline push-ups without a bench?
faq.answer: A sturdy step, low wall, or the edge of a couch works fine as long as it won't slide or tip while you push.

faq.question: What muscles does the incline push-up work?
faq.answer: It's mainly a chest exercise, with your shoulders and triceps helping lock out the top of each rep and your core working to keep your body straight.

faq.question: When should I move from incline push-ups to floor push-ups?
faq.answer: Once you can do 15 to 20 incline reps with strict form and no sagging in the hips, try a set on the floor and see how many clean reps you get.

alternatives.name: Incline Push-Up Wide
alternatives.reason: A wider hand placement on the same incline shifts more emphasis onto the outer chest.

harderVariations.name: Push Up
harderVariations.reason: A flat push-up removes the incline, so you press a larger share of your bodyweight.

harderVariations.name: Decline Push-Up
harderVariations.reason: Elevating your feet instead of your hands adds even more load to your chest and shoulders.

summary: The supine one-arm overhead throw has you lying on your back, winding a medicine ball back with one arm, then using your core and shoulder together to fling it up and over your head to a partner. Because only one arm drives the throw, your abdominals have to work harder to transfer force evenly instead of letting both arms share the load. It is a power drill built for speed, not a strength exercise you load up heavy, and it usually shows up in athletic conditioning sessions rather than general strength programs.
whyItWorks: Flinging a medicine ball overhead with one arm from a lying position asks your core to connect the force from your hips and shoulder into a single fast release, since there is no second arm to help square up the throw. Your abdominals work to control and transfer that one-sided force, while your lats, chest, and shoulder drive the arm through its overhead arc. Because the ball starts from a dead stop on the floor each time, there is no run-up or elastic bounce to borrow power from, so your throwing arm and core have to generate the entire effort from scratch on every rep.
setup: Lie on your back with your head pointing toward your throwing partner or target area.
Hold a medicine ball in one hand, with that arm resting back near your shoulder or slightly behind your head.
Plant your feet and bend your knees to give your hips a stable base to drive from.
Keep your non-throwing arm relaxed on the floor beside you rather than using it to push off.
Face your partner or target directly so the throw does not need to curve or angle across your body.
execution: Drive your hips slightly into the floor and swing your arm forward and up in one fast motion.
Release the ball as your arm reaches full extension above your head.
Let your core brace through the release instead of collapsing to one side.
Watch the ball leave your hand and travel toward your partner or target before relaxing.
Reset the ball in your throwing hand before starting the next rep.
formCues: Keep the throw moving in a straight line toward your target, not veering off to the side.
Brace your core through the whole throw instead of letting your hips twist loose.
Finish the throw with a full arm extension, not a half-hearted release.
breathing: Exhale as you release the ball, and take a full breath while you reset the ball for the next throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the opposite hip lift off the floor to help muscle the ball up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep both hips grounded and let your core and arm generate the power instead of twisting your lower body.

commonMistakes.mistake: Releasing the ball too early, before full arm extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold the release until your arm is fully extended for a cleaner, more powerful throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a ball that is too heavy to throw with real speed.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop to a lighter ball if the throw turns into a slow push, since speed is the whole point of this drill.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing every rep toward the same exact spot without checking your target is clear.
commonMistakes.correction: Confirm your partner or landing zone is ready before each throw, since a distracted catch is how most drops and near misses happen.

programmingNotes: Keep sets short and explosive, around 5 reps per arm, since the point is speed and not volume.
Rest fully between sets, closer to 60 to 90 seconds, so each throw stays fast instead of turning into a slow grind.
This pairs well early in a session, right after your warm-up, when your nervous system is fresh enough to produce a crisp, fast release.
safetyNotes: Check your overhead space before throwing so the ball has a clear path and nothing is in the way of your arm.
Stop if you feel your lower back arching uncomfortably off the floor during the throw, and shorten the range until your core control catches up.

faq.question: What does the supine one-arm overhead throw train?
faq.answer: It mainly trains your abdominals to transfer power, with your chest, lats, and shoulders driving the arm through the throw.

faq.question: Do I need a partner for this throw?
faq.answer: A partner to catch and return the ball makes this much easier, though you can also throw against an open wall of space and retrieve it yourself if no partner is available.

faq.question: Can I do this with two arms instead?
faq.answer: Yes, the two-arm version is an easier variation that lets both sides share the load evenly.

faq.question: How many reps should I throw per side?
faq.answer: Around five explosive throws per arm is typical, since this is a power drill rather than a high-volume exercise.

faq.question: What size medicine ball should I use for this throw?
faq.answer: Start with a light ball, often lighter than you would use for the two-arm version, since one arm has to generate and control all of the force by itself.

faq.question: Which shoulder muscles does this throw emphasize most?
faq.answer: The throwing shoulder works through a long overhead arc, so it gets more direct demand than in the two-arm version, where the load is shared evenly between both sides.

alternatives.name: Catch and Overhead Throw
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar overhead throwing pattern with a catch-and-release rhythm if lying on your back is not practical.

easierVariations.name: Supine Two-Arm Overhead Throw
easierVariations.reason: Lets both arms share the load, which is an easier way to learn the overhead release before isolating one side.

harderVariations.name: Standing Two-Arm Overhead Throw
harderVariations.reason: Adds a standing base that requires more full-body coordination and hip drive once the lying version feels controlled.

summary: The lying cambered barbell row has you lie face down on an incline bench with a cambered bar hanging beneath you, rowing it up toward your torso with your chest supported the entire time. Because the bench takes your lower back out of the equation, you can focus every bit of effort on pulling with your middle back, lats, and biceps instead of stabilizing your spine. It's a beginner-friendly way to build back strength for anyone who wants a rowing movement without the balancing act of a standing bent-over row.
whyItWorks: Rowing a weight toward your torso trains your middle back and lats to draw your shoulder blades together and pull your upper arm back, with your biceps assisting as the elbow bends. A standing row asks your lower back and core to hold your torso steady against the pull at the same time, which can limit how hard you're able to row before fatigue elsewhere ends the set. Lying face down on an incline bench removes that stabilization job entirely, so your back muscles can work through a fuller range and a heavier load than they might otherwise handle safely.
setup: Set an adjustable bench to a steep incline and lie face down on it, chest against the pad.
Let a cambered bar hang straight down from your arms, gripping it with hands slightly wider than shoulder width.
Keep your feet braced against the floor or bench supports for stability.
execution: Row the bar straight up toward your torso by driving your elbows back and up.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement.
Pause briefly, keeping your chest pressed into the pad the whole time.
Lower the bar back down slowly until your arms are fully extended.
Let your shoulder blades separate slightly at the bottom before starting the next rep.
formCues: Elbows drive back, not out to the sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades at the top of every rep.
Keep your chest pinned to the pad throughout.
Lower the bar as slowly as you lifted it.
breathing: Exhale as you row the bar up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare wide out to the sides instead of driving straight back.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows tracking close to your body as they travel back, which keeps the middle back doing the work instead of the shoulders.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a short, partial range that skips the full stretch at the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the bar until your arms are fully extended each rep, so your back gets the complete range this setup is meant to provide.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the chest off the pad to help heave the bar up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest pressed into the bench for the entire set; if you need to lift off the pad to finish a rep, the weight is too heavy.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps is a solid range for building back strength and size with this setup.
Because your lower back is fully supported, this can handle slightly heavier loads than a standing row before fatigue elsewhere becomes the limiting factor.
Pairs well with a vertical pulling movement like a lat pulldown in the same session, since the two together train the back through both a horizontal and vertical pattern.
safetyNotes: Keep your neck in a neutral position, looking down at the pad rather than craning it up to see the bar.
Choose a weight you can control through the full range without needing to jerk the bar or lift your chest off the bench.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for the lying cambered barbell row?
faq.answer: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps works well for building back strength and size, since the chest support lets you focus the effort entirely on the pull.

faq.question: What can I do without an incline bench or cambered bar?
faq.answer: A one-arm dumbbell row using a flat bench for chest and knee support trains the same chest-supported rowing pattern one side at a time.

faq.question: Lying cambered barbell row vs bent-over barbell row, which is better?
faq.answer: Neither replaces the other; the lying version removes lower-back stabilization so you can focus purely on the pull, while the bent-over row adds a real core and lower-back demand on top of the same rowing motion. Many lifters use the lying version when they want to isolate the back without extra fatigue elsewhere.

faq.question: Why do I feel this more in my biceps than my back?
faq.answer: That usually means you're initiating the pull by bending your elbows first instead of driving them back with your shoulder blades. Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of each rep, and let your biceps assist rather than lead.

alternatives.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
alternatives.reason: Uses a bench for chest and knee support one side at a time, useful for training each side of the back evenly.

alternatives.name: Lying T-Bar Row
alternatives.reason: Trains the same chest-supported rowing pattern on a T-bar row machine when a cambered bar and incline bench aren't available.

easierVariations.name: Seated Cable Rows
easierVariations.reason: Braces your feet and torso in a fully seated position, an easier setup while you learn to pull with your back instead of your arms.

harderVariations.name: Bent Over Barbell Row
harderVariations.reason: Removes the chest support, adding a real lower-back and core stability demand on top of the same rowing motion.

summary: The reverse grip bent-over row is a barbell row done with an underhand, palms-up grip instead of the usual overhand hold, hinging forward at the hips and pulling the bar toward your waist. Flipping the grip shortens the range at the top and pulls the elbows in closer to the body, which pulls more of the lats and biceps into a movement that a standard grip leans more on the middle back and rear delts to perform. It suits lifters who already have solid hinge control from deadlifts or standard rows and want a back-builder that leans harder on the lats.
whyItWorks: An underhand grip changes the angle your elbows travel through as you pull, bringing them closer to your sides rather than flaring out to the sides the way an overhand grip encourages. That closer elbow path shifts a larger share of the pulling work onto the lats, the broad muscles running down the sides of your back, and the biceps, which are in a stronger position to assist when the palms face up. The middle back and rear delts still work to retract the shoulder blades at the top of each rep, but the underhand grip changes where along that chain the heaviest demand falls, which is why the same weight can feel different on the biceps and lats compared with a standard bent-over row.
setup: Load a barbell on the floor or on a rack at a height you can hinge down to safely.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, take an underhand grip just outside your hips, and hinge forward until your torso is close to a 45-degree angle or flatter.
Keep a soft bend in your knees and a neutral spine, with your chest lifted and your gaze slightly ahead of your feet.
Brace your core firmly before lifting the bar off the floor or the rack.
execution: Pull the bar upward toward your lower ribs or upper waist, leading with your elbows and keeping them close to your sides.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull without standing upright or losing your hinge.
Pause briefly at the top of the row, feeling the contraction across your lats and middle back.
Lower the bar back down under control to a full arm extension, keeping the hinge position steady.
Reset your brace at the bottom of each rep rather than letting your spine round as fatigue builds.
Keep your torso angle consistent throughout the set instead of standing up a little with each rep.
formCues: Elbows tucked close to your sides.
Hinge angle stays fixed all set.
Pull to the waist, not the chest.
Reset your brace every rep.
breathing: Brace and inhale before pulling the bar up, exhale as you row it toward your waist, inhale again as you lower it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing up gradually with each rep instead of holding a fixed hinge.
commonMistakes.correction: Lock in your torso angle at the start of the set and hold it. If you notice yourself standing taller by the last few reps, the weight is too heavy for your current hinge control.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the elbows-out path of a standard overhand row instead of tucking them in.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows traveling close to your ribs as you pull; letting them flare out cancels the lat and biceps emphasis the underhand grip is meant to create.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to help the bar off the floor.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and set your hinge before the pull starts. If your lower back rounds under the starting weight, reduce the load until you can keep it neutral.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking the bar upward with a jerking motion rather than pulling it with the back.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the pull down and drive your elbows back deliberately; a controlled tempo trains the back muscles far more than a fast, jerky pull does.
