execution: Brace your core and begin bending your knees while letting your feet slide outward evenly on the discs
Lower until your thighs are roughly parallel to the floor, feet now in a wide stance with the discs tracking straight out, not twisting
Pause briefly at the bottom to confirm control before reversing
Drive your feet back together by actively pulling with your inner thighs while your quads straighten your knees
Return to the starting stance with the discs back under you and stand to full extension
Reset your stance and breath before the next rep
formCues: Let both feet slide out at the same rate so your hips stay level and square
Keep your knees tracking over your toes even as your stance widens
Pull your feet back with intention instead of letting momentum do it
breathing: Brace before you start sliding out and keep that brace through the bottom, exhaling as you pull your feet back together and stand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sliding one foot out farther or faster than the other
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down until both discs move at the same pace and your hips stay level

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading the bar with a normal squat weight
commonMistakes.correction: Load far lighter than your usual squat, since the sliding stance limits how much force you can produce safely

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the knees cave inward as the stance widens
commonMistakes.correction: Actively push your knees out over your feet through the whole slide, not just at the bottom

programmingNotes: Treat this as an accessory movement for hip control, placed after your main squat work rather than as your primary squat for the day
Two to three sets of six to eight slow, controlled reps build the stabilization pattern without turning it into a grind
Since the load stays light and the real challenge is coordination rather than raw force, two sessions a week is reasonable if your floor surface and discs stay consistent
Skip the bar entirely for your first few sessions and groove the sliding pattern with just body weight first
safetyNotes: Use discs rated for your floor surface; the wrong pairing can grip unevenly and twist a knee mid-slide
Keep the slide width within a range where your knees stay comfortable, this isn't a movement to force into a wider stance than your hips allow

faq.question: What can I use instead of real plate movers?
faq.answer: Furniture sliders or a folded towel on a smooth floor work for light loads, as long as they glide evenly under both feet.

faq.question: How wide should my stance slide in this squat?
faq.answer: Only as wide as you can control without your knees caving in or your hips rocking, usually somewhere around shoulder-width to one and a half times that.

faq.question: Can I do a squat with plate movers without a barbell?
faq.answer: Yes, start with body weight only or hold a light dumbbell at your chest until the sliding pattern feels controlled before adding a bar.

faq.question: Does this replace regular squats?
faq.answer: No, it's a hip-control accessory on top of a standard squat, not a stand-in for your main lower-body strength work.

alternatives.name: Goblet Squat
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar quad-dominant squat pattern with a front-loaded hold, useful when you don't have gliding discs on hand.

easierVariations.name: Barbell Squat
easierVariations.reason: The same knee-bend pattern with a fixed stance, a good base to own before adding a sliding component.

summary: The hanging bar good morning is a barbell hip hinge where you hold the bar with straight arms in front of your thighs instead of resting it across your back. That single change shifts extra work onto your grip and upper back while your hamstrings, glutes, and lower back do the actual hinging. It suits lifters who already know a standard good morning or Romanian deadlift and want a fresh way to load the same hip hinge pattern.
whyItWorks: Your hamstrings and glutes cross the hip joint, so they control how fast you lower into the hinge and how hard you drive back up to standing. Because the bar hangs from straight arms rather than sitting on your traps, your upper back and forearms work isometrically to keep it close to your legs the whole time, and your abs brace to stop your spine from rounding as your torso tips forward. The result trains the same muscles as a standard good morning while adding a grip and upper-back demand you don't get with the bar racked on your shoulders. It also changes where the load sits relative to your spine: a racked bar pushes straight down through your upper back, while a hanging bar pulls forward on your shoulders and hands, so your lats and rear shoulders have to fight to keep your arms from being dragged out of position as you hinge.
setup: Load a barbell on the ground or pull it from a rack set at hip height.
Grip it just outside your hips with both hands, arms fully extended.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, chest up.
Brace your abs before the first rep.
execution: Keep your arms straight and the bar close to your thighs throughout the rep.
Push your hips back as you hinge forward, letting your torso lower toward parallel with the floor.
Let your knees bend slightly, but keep the movement centered at your hips, not your knees.
Stop when you feel a stretch through your hamstrings, usually around mid-shin height.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up, squeezing your glutes at the top.
Keep the bar tracking straight up and down along your legs the whole rep.
formCues: Push your hips back first, not straight down.
Keep the bar brushing your thighs on the way down.
Lock your lower back flat, not rounded.
Drive through your heels to stand up.
breathing: Inhale as you hinge back, exhale as you drive your hips forward to stand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the knees like a squat instead of hinging at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Send your hips back first and let your knees bend only a little as you lower.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar drift away from your legs.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your arms straight and the bar brushing your thighs through the whole rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back near the bottom of the descent.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent as soon as your lower back wants to round, even if that means a shorter range.

programmingNotes: This is a loaded barbell hip hinge, so treat it as your main posterior-chain lift for the week: two or three sets of six to eight reps once a week is enough to drive adaptation without wrecking your next squat or deadlift session.
Because your grip and upper back fatigue fast in the hanging position, do it early in a session, right after your warm-up.
Start with less weight than your usual good morning until your grip strength and hip hinge timing catch up.
safetyNotes: Stop the set if your lower back rounds under load; that's your range-of-motion limit for the day, not a target to push past.
Keep the weight moderate while you're learning the hanging grip. A slipping bar is a bigger risk here than in a racked good morning.

faq.question: How is a hanging bar good morning different from a regular good morning?
faq.answer: In a regular good morning the bar rests across your upper back like a squat. Here you hold it with straight arms in front of your thighs instead, which adds a grip and upper-back challenge to the same hip hinge.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of six to eight reps once a week is plenty for most lifters, since it's a heavy compound hip hinge.

faq.question: What can I use instead if I don't want to hang a barbell from straight arms?
faq.answer: A Romanian deadlift trains the same hamstring and glute hinge with the bar in a more familiar grip position.

faq.question: Is the hanging bar good morning safe for my lower back?
faq.answer: It can be, if you stop the hinge before your lower back rounds and start light until your hips find the pattern. Skip it if you have an existing lower back issue and check with a professional first.

faq.question: Why does my grip give out before my hamstrings on this exercise?
faq.answer: The hanging arm position puts continuous tension on your forearms with no rest between reps, so if your grip strength lags behind your hip hinge strength it will fatigue first. Straps can help you finish a set once your legs are still the limiting factor, not your hands.

alternatives.name: Romanian Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hamstring and glute hinge with the bar held in a more familiar grip if the hanging-arm position bothers your shoulders.

easierVariations.name: Band Good Morning
easierVariations.reason: Same hip hinge pattern with a resistance band instead of a loaded barbell, so you can groove the movement before adding weight.

harderVariations.name: Stiff-Legged Barbell Deadlift
harderVariations.reason: Adds a full pull from the floor to the same hamstring-dominant hinge once your hips and grip can handle heavier loads.

summary: The dumbbell incline shoulder raise has you lie back on an angled bench and raise a dumbbell in each hand up and forward, straight-armed, until they're roughly overhead. Sitting back into the bench removes any chance of swinging the weight up with your hips or lower back, so the front of your shoulders has to do the lifting on its own. It's a beginner-friendly isolation move for anyone building shoulder size or strength who wants a strict version of a front raise.
whyItWorks: A standing front raise is easy to cheat by leaning back or bouncing the dumbbells off your thighs to get them moving. Lying back against an incline bench takes that shortcut away completely, since your torso is already pinned to the pad and there's nothing left to swing. With the cheat removed, the front deltoids have to generate the entire lift on their own, with your triceps helping keep the elbows locked and steady through the top of the range.
setup: Set a bench to a moderate incline, around 45 to 60 degrees, and sit back with your shoulders and head against the pad.
Hold a light dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging down at your sides with palms facing your thighs.
Plant your feet flat on the floor and settle your back fully into the bench before the first rep.
execution: Keeping your elbows nearly straight, raise both dumbbells forward and up in a smooth arc.
Continue the raise until your arms reach roughly shoulder height to overhead, whichever feels controlled for your shoulders.
Pause briefly at the top without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears.
Lower the dumbbells back down along the same path with control.
Keep your shoulder blades pinned against the bench for the entire set.
formCues: Raise with straight, relaxed elbows.
Keep your shoulders pinned to the pad.
Lead with the dumbbells, not your chest.
Lower slower than you raise.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the dumbbells forward and up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows more as the set gets harder, turning the raise into a partial press.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight and keep your elbows nearly straight through the whole range, even on the last rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Raising the dumbbells so fast that momentum, not the shoulder, does most of the work.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the lift down to about two seconds up and two seconds down so the deltoid stays under tension the whole time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears near the top of the raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulders pressed down against the bench and stop the raise before you feel the shrug creeping in.

programmingNotes: This isolates a small muscle group, so it recovers quickly and can be trained two or three times a week without the joint feeling beat up.
3 sets of 10 to 15 reps with a light to moderate dumbbell is enough; the front delts also get plenty of work from pressing movements.
Place it after your main pressing exercise for the day, since a fatigued front deltoid makes the strict raise even harder to fake.
Increase reps toward 15 before adding weight, since strict form tends to break down first when the load goes up too quickly on this raise.
safetyNotes: Start with a light dumbbell; the front shoulder is a small muscle and the joint doesn't need heavy loading to grow.
Stop the raise before your shoulders start to shrug, since that's usually the first sign the weight is too heavy.

faq.question: How many sets of dumbbell incline shoulder raises should I do?
faq.answer: 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps with a light dumbbell is plenty. This move works best as an accessory to your main pressing exercises, not as the centerpiece of a shoulder day.

faq.question: What can I do instead of the dumbbell incline shoulder raise without a bench?
faq.answer: A standing front dumbbell raise trains the same front-shoulder pattern with no equipment beyond the dumbbells themselves, though it's easier to cheat with your hips if you're not paying attention.

faq.question: Dumbbell incline shoulder raise vs standing front raise: what's the difference?
faq.answer: The incline version pins your torso to the bench so the front deltoid does all the lifting with no help from momentum. The standing version needs no bench and is easier to fit into a workout, but it takes more discipline to keep your hips still.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders shrug up during this exercise?
faq.answer: That usually means the weight is too heavy or you're raising too high. Lower the dumbbell and stop the raise around shoulder height instead of pushing all the way overhead.

alternatives.name: Front Cable Raise
alternatives.reason: Keeps constant tension on the front shoulder through the same raising path when an incline bench isn't free.

easierVariations.name: Front Dumbbell Raise
easierVariations.reason: The standing version of the same forward-raise pattern needs no bench, a simple place to learn the motion before adding an incline.

harderVariations.name: Standing Dumbbell Straight-Arm Front Delt Raise Above Head
harderVariations.reason: Extends the same raise further overhead, adding a longer lever arm and a bigger demand on the front shoulder.

summary: The standing dumbbell triceps extension is an overhead isolation move where you lower a dumbbell behind your head and press it back up, elbow staying fixed in place. It puts the triceps in a deep stretch at the bottom that most pushdown-style exercises never reach. Anyone chasing triceps size, or whose lockout is lagging on pressing lifts, benefits from adding it.
whyItWorks: The triceps crosses the elbow and, for the long head, the shoulder too, so stretching the arm overhead before you extend puts that long head under more tension than a pushdown done with the arm at your side. Because the shoulder stays raised and fixed throughout, nearly all the movement happens at the elbow, which keeps the exercise a clean, targeted isolation rather than a compound lift that recruits the shoulders and chest.
setup: Hold one dumbbell with both hands, cupping the top plate with your palms.
Press the dumbbell overhead until your arms are straight.
Keep your elbows pointed forward, close to your ears.
Stand with feet hip-width apart and your core braced.
execution: Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending only at the elbows.
Keep your upper arms still and close to your head the whole way down.
Lower until your forearms are roughly parallel to the floor, or as far as feels controlled.
Extend your elbows to press the dumbbell back to the starting position.
Pause briefly at the top before lowering again.
formCues: Keep your elbows pointed forward, not flared out to the sides.
Move only at the elbow, your upper arms shouldn't travel much at all.
Keep your ribs down so your lower back doesn't arch as the dumbbell lowers.
Control the descent, this is where the triceps do the most work.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the dumbbell behind your head, exhale as you press it back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare out to the sides.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows pointed forward and close to your ears throughout the lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Moving at the shoulder instead of the elbow.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms fixed in place and only let your forearms swing at the elbow joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using too much weight and cutting the range short.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until you can lower the dumbbell to a full, controlled stretch behind your head.

programmingNotes: This is a single-joint isolation move, so 2 to 3 times a week is fine if your triceps aren't already worked hard from pressing that day.
3 sets of 10 to 15 reps builds size well without needing heavy weight.
Place it after your main pressing work, since fresh triceps hold the overhead position better than fatigued ones.
Use a lighter dumbbell than you'd guess, the stretched position limits how much weight you can control safely.
safetyNotes: Keep a firm grip on the dumbbell at all times, since it's held directly above your head.
Stop if you feel strain in the elbow joint itself rather than the muscle, and check that your elbows stay pointed forward instead of flaring.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for standing dumbbell triceps extensions?
faq.answer: 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps works well for most people. Keep the weight light enough to control the full stretch behind your head.

faq.question: What can I use instead of a dumbbell for this exercise?
faq.answer: A cable with a rope attachment set behind your head, or an EZ-bar held overhead with both hands, both train the same overhead stretch position.

faq.question: Overhead triceps extension vs triceps pushdown, which is better?
faq.answer: The overhead version stretches the triceps more at the bottom, which is useful for the long head specifically. The pushdown lets you use more weight safely and is easier on the shoulders. Doing both covers more of the muscle.

faq.question: Why does my elbow hurt during overhead triceps extensions?
faq.answer: It's often too much weight for the stretched position, or elbows that drift out to the sides instead of staying forward. Lighten the load and keep your elbows pointed straight ahead and close to your ears.

alternatives.name: EZ-Bar Skullcrusher
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead triceps stretch with a bar instead of a single dumbbell held overhead.

easierVariations.name: Triceps Pushdown
easierVariations.reason: The cable guides the path for you, which takes the balance and overhead-stability demand out of the movement.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Skullcrusher
harderVariations.reason: Lying down removes the need to balance the weight overhead, so you can push the stretch and load further.

summary: The side jackknife has you lie on your side and fold your upper body and legs toward each other at the same time, closing the gap between your ribs and hips like a jackknife closing. It's a dynamic, bodyweight way to train the obliques through a full range of motion, rather than just holding them isometrically like a side plank does.
whyItWorks: The obliques run diagonally along your sides, and their main job is bending your torso sideways and rotating it. Lying on your side and folding your ribcage and legs toward each other puts those muscles through their actual shortening action against gravity, rather than just asking them to resist movement the way a static hold does. That's what separates the side jackknife from an isometric side bridge: it trains the obliques to actively produce the bending motion, not just resist it. Most core training leans heavily on movements that flex the spine forward or hold it still, so a side-bending exercise like this one fills a gap that a typical crunch or plank routine leaves untouched, which matters since real-world twisting and side-bending tasks, reaching sideways for something, catching yourself off balance, rely on exactly this muscle action.
setup: Lie on your side with your legs stacked and fully extended, body in a straight line.
Rest your bottom arm along the floor for light support, or place your hand lightly behind your head.
Keep your top arm resting along your side or lightly touching your top leg.
execution: Simultaneously lift your legs and your upper torso off the floor, folding your ribs toward your hips.
Reach your top hand toward your feet as you fold, if that's comfortable, to help you feel the contraction.
Pause briefly at the top of the fold, feeling the squeeze through your obliques.
Lower back down with control until your body is straight again.
Complete the full set on one side before switching to the other.
formCues: Fold from the ribs and hips together, not just the legs.
Keep the movement in the same plane, no rolling forward or back.
Pause and squeeze at the top of each fold.
Lower with control, don't just drop back down.
breathing: Exhale as you fold your torso and legs together, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling slightly onto the back or front to make the fold easier.
commonMistakes.correction: Stay strictly on your side throughout the movement; rolling takes the load off the obliques and onto other muscles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only lifting the legs or only lifting the torso instead of folding both together.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on closing the distance from both ends at once, ribs coming down to meet the hips as the hips lift to meet the ribs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing up rather than a controlled fold.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and pause briefly at the top; a controlled fold trains the obliques far more than a fast, swinging one.

programmingNotes: Since this is a bodyweight core movement, two or three sessions a week is a reasonable frequency.
Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps per side is a solid target once you can complete the fold with good control.
Pair it with a front-facing core move like a crunch or jackknife sit-up to balance oblique and rectus abdominis work in the same session.
safetyNotes: If your lower back rounds or strains during the fold, shorten the range slightly until your oblique strength catches up.
Keep the hip you're lying on cushioned with a mat; the bony point of the hip can get uncomfortable on a hard floor.

faq.question: How many side jackknives should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps per side is a solid range once your form is controlled. Prioritize a clean fold over a high rep count.

faq.question: What's the difference between a side jackknife and a side bridge?
faq.answer: A side bridge is a static hold, your obliques resist movement the whole time. A side jackknife is dynamic, your obliques actively shorten to fold your ribs and hips together and then lengthen back out, training a different part of their job.

faq.question: Can I do the side jackknife if I have lower back pain?
faq.answer: This isn't medical advice, but if your lower back rounds or aches during the fold, that's usually a sign to shorten the range or build oblique strength with a static side bridge first before adding the dynamic version.

faq.question: Why do side jackknives feel harder on one side than the other?
faq.answer: It's common for one set of obliques to be stronger than the other, often the side opposite your dominant hand. Train both sides for equal reps rather than matching effort, and the strength gap will usually close over time.

alternatives.name: Jackknife Sit-Up
alternatives.reason: Uses the same folding, knees-to-chest motion but from your back instead of your side, working the front of the abs more than the obliques.

easierVariations.name: Side Plank
easierVariations.reason: Holds the same side-lying position isometrically instead of folding through it, a gentler way to build oblique strength before adding the dynamic fold.

summary: The close-grip EZ bar curl is a biceps curl done on the angled EZ bar with your hands set closer than shoulder width. The angled grips let your wrists sit at a more natural angle than a straight bar while the narrow hand position shifts a bit more emphasis onto the long head of the biceps. It's a beginner-friendly isolation move that suits anyone building arm strength who wants a wrist-friendlier grip than a straight barbell curl.
whyItWorks: The biceps has two heads, and hand position changes how evenly they share the work. Bringing your grip in closer than shoulder width stretches the long head of the biceps a bit more at the bottom of the curl, which is part of why lifters use a close grip to target the outer sweep of the arm. The EZ bar's zigzag shape lets your wrists tilt slightly inward through the curl instead of staying locked straight, which takes pressure off the wrist joint compared to a straight bar without changing what the biceps and forearms are doing.
setup: Grip the EZ bar on the inner angled section, hands close together but not touching.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding the bar with your arms extended down in front of your thighs.
Pin your elbows lightly against your sides and keep them there for the whole set.
Set your shoulders back and down so your torso stays upright, not leaned back.
execution: Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbow, keeping your upper arms still.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top without letting your elbows drift forward.
Lower the bar slowly, taking about twice as long as the lift.
Stop just short of fully locking out your elbows at the bottom to keep tension on the muscle.
Repeat without swinging your torso to help the bar up.
formCues: Elbows stay pinned to your sides the whole set.
Only the forearm moves, the upper arm stays still.
Squeeze at the top for a full second.
Lower slower than you lift.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the bar up, inhale as you lower it back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the torso and hips to help heave the bar up.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can curl it with your back against a wall; momentum from the body defeats the point of an isolation curl.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward and up as the set gets tiring.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a light touch of your elbows against your sides throughout; if they start floating forward, that's your cue to end the set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping so narrow the wrists cross the centerline of the body.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands on the angled grips of the EZ bar, roughly fist-width apart, not jammed together in the middle.

programmingNotes: As an isolation move for a single muscle group, two to three sessions a week works well, spaced with at least a day of rest between arm-focused sessions.
Sets of 10 to 15 reps let you feel the stretch and squeeze without needing to load up heavily.
Pair it with a pressing movement in the same session so your arms get balanced pulling and pushing volume.
Save it for after your bigger back or pulling exercises, since fatigued biceps make rows and pull-ups harder to do well.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel a sharp pinch at the front of the elbow rather than muscle fatigue in the biceps.
Keep the weight light enough that your lower back stays neutral instead of arching to help the lift.

faq.question: How many reps and sets for close-grip EZ bar curl?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 10 to 15 reps, two to three times a week, is a solid starting point for building arm size and strength.

faq.question: What can I use instead of an EZ bar for this curl?
faq.answer: A straight barbell with the same narrow grip works as a substitute, though the EZ bar's angle is easier on the wrists.

faq.question: Close-grip EZ bar curl versus regular EZ bar curl: what changes?
faq.answer: A regular EZ bar curl uses the outer, wider grips. Moving your hands to the inner, narrower grips shifts a bit more of the work onto the long head of the biceps.

faq.question: Why does my wrist hurt during EZ bar curls?
faq.answer: Check that you're on the angled inner grips, not the flat center of the bar. If pain continues, your grip may be too narrow, forcing an unnatural wrist angle.

faq.question: Should I curl with a close grip every arm session?
faq.answer: No, rotate it with a wider grip or a different curl variation across the week. Sticking to one hand position every session trains the same narrow range of the biceps and skips the rest.

alternatives.name: Close-Grip Standing Barbell Curl
alternatives.reason: A straight bar in the same narrow grip, useful when an EZ bar isn't free at your gym.

easierVariations.name: Close-Grip EZ-Bar Curl with Band
easierVariations.reason: A band deloads the hardest stretched position at the bottom, making the same close grip easier to learn before you add a fixed bar load.

summary: This floor variation of the oblique crunch skips the twist and instead has you reach one hand straight down toward your heel while your shoulders lift, training the obliques through side bending rather than rotation. It's a beginner bodyweight move, done flat on the floor with no equipment, and pairs naturally with rotational ab work for a fuller side-core routine.
whyItWorks: The obliques don't just rotate the torso, they also bend it sideways, and a straight reach toward the heel isolates that side-bending function without any twist mixed in. Because the movement stays in one plane, it's easier to feel exactly which side is working, which makes it a useful teaching tool for beginners still learning to control their core rather than just their arms and hips.
setup: Lie flat on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Rest your arms straight down at your sides, palms facing your legs.
Brace your core gently so your lower back doesn't arch off the floor.
execution: Lift your shoulder blades a few inches off the floor, curling straight up rather than to one side.
As you curl, slide one hand along the floor toward the heel on the same side.
Reach as far as your range allows without twisting your ribcage or lifting your hips.
Hold the top position for a brief squeeze on that side of your waist.
Lower back down with control until your shoulder blades touch the floor.
Repeat the reach toward the other side, alternating for the set.
formCues: Reach straight down the side, don't rotate the ribcage.
Keep both hips glued to the floor the whole time.
Move slow enough to feel the side of your waist working.
Small, controlled lift, not a big sit-up.
breathing: Exhale as you curl and reach toward your heel, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Twisting the ribcage instead of reaching straight down the side.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest facing the ceiling the entire time; only your reaching arm and the side of your torso should move.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting one hip lift off the floor to help the reach.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep both hips pressed down and shorten the reach if that's what it takes to keep them still.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the free arm to push off the floor for momentum.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the resting arm relaxed at your side and let the working side do all the lifting.

programmingNotes: Start with 2 to 3 sets of 10 to 12 reps per side, since it's a small, low-fatigue isolation move.
It suits the end of a workout or a short standalone core session, since it needs no warm-up load.
Once the reach feels easy at full range, slow the tempo instead of adding weight, since a controlled lateral flexion is harder to fake than a fast one.
safetyNotes: If you feel the reach in your neck rather than your side, shorten the range and focus on the curl coming from your ribs.
Stop and reset if your lower back arches instead of staying gently pressed down.

faq.question: How is this different from a regular oblique crunch?
faq.answer: This version reaches straight toward your heel with no twist, training side bending. The classic oblique crunch adds rotation, turning your ribcage toward the opposite knee.

faq.question: How many reps of floor oblique crunches should I do?
faq.answer: 10 to 12 reps per side for 2 to 3 sets is a reasonable starting point. Slow the tempo down before adding any load.

faq.question: Can beginners do oblique crunches on the floor?
faq.answer: Yes, it's one of the more approachable oblique exercises since there's no rotation to coordinate, just a straight reach down one side.

faq.question: Why can't I feel this in my obliques?
faq.answer: You may be twisting instead of bending straight to the side, or reaching too far and using your hip to help. Keep your chest facing up and shorten the reach until you feel the side of your waist working.

alternatives.name: Oblique Crunches
alternatives.reason: Swaps the straight reach for a twisting crunch toward the opposite knee, useful once you want to add rotation to your oblique work.

easierVariations.name: Crunches
easierVariations.reason: Drops the side reach entirely, a simpler starting point if the straight lateral flexion still feels awkward.

harderVariations.name: Cross-Body Crunch
harderVariations.reason: Adds a dynamic elbow-to-knee reach once the straight side bend feels easy to control.

summary: The farmer's walk is a loaded carry: you pick up a heavy weight in each hand, usually from trap-bar-style handles, and walk a set distance or time while keeping your torso tall and your grip locked on. It trains your forearms and grip directly, while your core, glutes, hamstrings, quads, and traps all work isometrically just to keep you upright and moving under load. It suits anyone who wants real-world carrying strength, not just lifters chasing a bigger deadlift.
whyItWorks: Carrying a heavy weight at your sides is one of the most honest tests of total-body strength there is, because nothing about it lets you cheat with momentum or a shortened range of motion. Your grip has to hold the handles for the entire distance without resetting, which is why the forearms take the brunt of the fatigue, while your core and lower back fight to keep your spine upright against the weight pulling you sideways and forward with every step. Your legs and glutes do the actual walking, but under a heavy enough load even that simple task becomes a full-body bracing exercise, which is exactly why the farmer's walk carries over to so many other lifts and daily tasks that involve carrying something heavy.
setup: Load two farmer's handles or heavy dumbbells to a weight you can carry for the full distance without stopping.
Stand between the handles, hinge at the hips, and grip each one with a flat back.
Brace your core before you stand up with the weight.
Stand fully upright with your shoulders back before taking your first step.
execution: Stand up with the weight using your legs, not your lower back.
Walk forward with short, controlled steps, keeping your torso tall.
Keep your shoulders back and down rather than letting the weight round them forward.
Breathe steadily throughout instead of holding your breath the entire walk.
Cover the set distance or time without setting the weight down.
Lower the weight with control at the end by hinging at the hips, not by dropping it.
formCues: Chest up, shoulders back, the whole walk.
Short, quick steps beat long, lurching ones.
Grip locked; don't let the handles roll in your hands.
Breathe steadily instead of holding your breath.
breathing: Take a deep breath before you stand up with the weight, then breathe steadily and evenly through the walk instead of holding it the whole way.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the shoulders forward as the arms fatigue.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively pull your shoulders back and down before you start walking, and reset that position anytime it slips.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking long, lurching strides that swing the weights.
commonMistakes.correction: Use short, quick steps instead; a controlled, almost choppy stride keeps the weights from swaying and throwing off your balance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting the weight down the moment the grip starts to fail instead of finishing the set distance.
commonMistakes.correction: Grip fatigue is part of the exercise; push through it for the planned distance and let grip strength catch up over time rather than cutting every set short.

commonMistakes.mistake: Holding the breath for the entire walk.
commonMistakes.correction: Take a strong brace before lifting, then breathe steadily as you walk; holding your breath the whole distance spikes blood pressure for no benefit.

programmingNotes: Two to four sets of 30 to 60 seconds, or 20 to 40 meters, is a solid range for most people, and once a week is enough given how demanding a heavy carry is on the grip and lower back.
Because it taxes the same grip and posterior chain that heavy deadlifts and rows use, schedule it away from your heaviest pulling day rather than stacking both in the same session.
Increase the challenge by adding weight before adding distance; a shorter, heavier carry still builds the grip and bracing strength that make this exercise valuable.
Works well as a finisher at the end of a strength session, when the fatigue in your grip and core doesn't interfere with your main lifts.
safetyNotes: Set the weight down by hinging at the hips with a flat back, the same way you picked it up; don't just drop it or bend forward from the waist.
If your lower back rounds under the load partway through the walk, the weight is too heavy or the distance too long for where your strength is right now.

faq.question: How heavy should farmer's walks be?
faq.answer: Heavy enough that the last 10 to 15 seconds of the carry genuinely challenge your grip, but light enough that your posture stays tall the whole way. Many people can handle more weight here than they'd guess, since the movement itself is simple.

faq.question: How far or how long should a farmer's walk set be?
faq.answer: 20 to 40 meters, or 30 to 60 seconds, is a solid target for most people. Shorter, heavier carries and longer, lighter ones both build useful strength, just with a slightly different emphasis.

faq.question: Can I do farmer's walks without farmer's handles?
faq.answer: Yes, a pair of heavy dumbbells or kettlebells works just as well. What matters is a weight you can grip firmly and carry with tall posture for the full distance.

faq.question: Why do my forearms fail before my legs on farmer's walks?
faq.answer: Grip strength is usually the limiting factor in a loaded carry, since your hands hold the weight continuously with no chance to reset. That's normal, and it's also exactly why the exercise is such a good grip builder.

alternatives.name: Rickshaw Carry
alternatives.reason: Carries a similar total-body load with the weight positioned at your sides in a slightly different grip, when farmer's handles aren't free.

harderVariations.name: Yoke Walk
harderVariations.reason: Loads the same walking-under-load pattern onto your back instead of your hands, letting you move far heavier total weight.

summary: The decline oblique crunch has you lie back on a decline bench with your feet anchored at the top, then curl your torso up and rotate to bring one shoulder toward the opposite knee. The decline angle adds extra resistance compared with a flat floor crunch, since you are now curling your torso up against gravity pulling you back down the slope. It targets your obliques, the muscles along the sides of your torso responsible for trunk rotation, and works well as a finisher for a core-focused day.
whyItWorks: Your obliques rotate and side-bend your trunk, and this move trains both actions at once by combining a curl with a twist. On a flat floor, a crunch only fights gravity through a short range near the top of the movement. Tilting the bench into a decline extends that range: your torso starts lower than your hips, so you are curling and rotating up against a steeper pull the whole way, which keeps your obliques under tension longer per rep than a flat version does.
setup: Set the bench to a moderate decline and secure your feet under the ankle pads.
Lie back with your hands lightly touching your temples, elbows out to the sides.
Engage your core and flatten your lower back against the bench before the first rep.
execution: Curl your torso up off the bench, leading with your chest.
Rotate your torso as you curl, bringing one shoulder toward the opposite knee.
Pause briefly at the top of the twist.
Lower back down under control to the starting position.
Alternate sides each rep, or complete a full set on one side before switching.
formCues: Lead the rotation from your ribs, not by yanking with your hands on your head.
Curl before you twist, don't just rotate a flat torso.
Keep your lower back pressed to the bench through the whole rep.
Move slowly enough to feel the obliques working on both the way up and down.
breathing: Exhale as you curl and rotate up, and inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling on the head or neck to generate the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands as a light resting point only and let your abdominal muscles do the lifting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rotating from the hips instead of the ribs, so the whole body swings.
commonMistakes.correction: Anchor your hips and feet still and focus the twist on your upper torso.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing up instead of a controlled curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the rep down and pause at the top before lowering, which removes the swing.

programmingNotes: Two to three sets of ten to fifteen reps per side fits well at the end of a core or lower-body session.
As a bodyweight isolation move for a smaller muscle group, it recovers quickly, so training obliques two or three times a week is fine even alongside other ab work.
Pair it with a straight-plane move like a plank or a standard crunch so your core gets trained through both rotation and stability in the same session.
safetyNotes: Keep the motion controlled rather than snapping up, since a fast twist under a decline load can strain your lower back.
If you feel the movement in your neck rather than your obliques, lighten the effort and rebuild the curl pattern first.
Choose a decline angle you can control fully before increasing it.

faq.question: How many reps of decline oblique crunches should I do?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of ten to fifteen reps per side is a solid starting point, done at the end of a core workout.

faq.question: Can I do oblique crunches without a decline bench?
faq.answer: Yes, an oblique crunch on the floor trains the same rotating curl without any equipment, just with less resistance than the decline version.

faq.question: What's the difference between an oblique crunch and a regular crunch?
faq.answer: A regular crunch curls your torso straight up and mainly works the abdominals down the center. An oblique crunch adds a twist toward one knee, which shifts more of the work to the muscles along the sides of your torso.

faq.question: Why do I feel this more in my hip flexors than my abs?
faq.answer: That usually means the hips are helping lift the torso instead of the abs doing the curl. Keep your feet anchored and focus on curling your ribs toward your pelvis before you add the twist.

alternatives.name: Russian Twist
alternatives.reason: Trains rotational core strength through a seated twisting pattern that needs no bench at all.

easierVariations.name: Oblique Crunches - On The Floor
easierVariations.reason: Moves the same curl-and-twist pattern to the floor, removing the decline bench's added resistance while you learn to lead the rotation from your ribs.

harderVariations.name: Kneeling Cable Crunch With Alternating Oblique Twists
harderVariations.reason: Adds adjustable cable resistance to the same twisting curl, letting you keep increasing the load once bodyweight decline reps stop being challenging.

summary: The vertical swing loads a dumbbell with both hands and drives it from between your knees up toward chest height using a hard hip hinge, not your arms. It trains the same explosive glute-and-hamstring extension as a kettlebell swing, while the dumbbell's shape keeps the weight close to your body through the whole arc. It suits anyone who wants a conditioning move that trains hip power without a barbell or a full Olympic-lift setup.
whyItWorks: The power in a vertical swing comes from snapping your hips open, not from lifting with your shoulders. Your hamstrings and glutes decelerate the hinge at the bottom and then fire to drive the dumbbell upward, while your quads help stabilize your knees through that same hinge. Your shoulders only catch and redirect the weight once hip drive has already sent it moving, which is why they show up as a secondary mover rather than the engine of the movement. Because the dumbbell travels in a straight vertical line instead of swinging out and away from your body the way a kettlebell can, this version asks for slightly less grip and wrist control, making it a reasonable entry point into ballistic hip-hinge training.
setup: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, dumbbell held with both hands in front of your hips.
Hinge at your hips, pushing them back while keeping a soft bend in your knees.
Let the dumbbell hang between your knees as your torso leans forward.
Keep your chest up and your spine long, not rounded.
execution: Hinge back until the dumbbell swings behind your knees.
Drive your hips forward explosively, squeezing your glutes at the top.
Let the hip drive, not your arms, send the dumbbell upward toward chest height.
Keep your arms relatively relaxed, acting as ropes that guide the weight rather than lift it.
Let the dumbbell fall back down under control as your hips hinge back again.
Repeat for the set, keeping a smooth, continuous rhythm between reps.
formCues: Hips open before the dumbbell rises, not the other way around.
Arms stay relaxed; they guide the weight rather than row it up.
Glutes squeeze hard at the top of each hip drive.
Spine stays long through the hinge, with no rounding at the bottom.
breathing: Exhale sharply as your hips snap forward and the dumbbell rises, then inhale as you hinge back to load the next rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Squatting down and up instead of hinging at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your knees only softly bent; the movement should feel like your hips are closing and opening, not your knees bending deeply.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the dumbbell with your shoulders and arms.
commonMistakes.correction: Let hip drive do the work and keep your arms loose enough that the weight feels like it floats up on its own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding your lower back at the bottom of the hinge.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the backswing a little earlier and keep your chest lifted so your spine stays in a neutral line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the dumbbell out away from your body like a kettlebell.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the path close and vertical, tracking roughly over your shins and up the midline of your body.

programmingNotes: Because this is an explosive hip-hinge movement, it asks more of your nervous system and connective tissue than its light to moderate dumbbell load suggests, so once a week as a power or conditioning focus is a sensible default rather than something to chase daily.
Sets of 10 to 15 reps work well, with full recovery between sets, since the goal is a crisp hip snap rather than grinding through fatigue.
It pairs naturally with a lower-body strength day, placed early in the session while your hip drive is still fresh and explosive.
safetyNotes: Stop the set if your lower back rounds or aches rather than your glutes and hamstrings doing the work.
Keep the dumbbell's path close to your body; letting it drift forward or outward adds unnecessary strain through your shoulders and low back.

faq.question: Is the vertical swing the same as a kettlebell swing?
faq.answer: It uses the same hip-hinge pattern, but a dumbbell's shape keeps the weight traveling in a straighter, more vertical path than a kettlebell's horn allows, which makes it a slightly more controlled entry point into swing training.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do?
faq.answer: Ten to fifteen reps per set, for 2 to 4 sets, with a short rest between sets so each rep stays explosive rather than fatigued.

faq.question: What can I do if I don't have a dumbbell?
faq.answer: A bodyweight hip-hinge drill like the glute bridge builds the same hip-opening pattern without any equipment, and a kettlebell swing is a direct substitute if one is available.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders feel it more than my glutes?
faq.answer: That usually means you're lifting the dumbbell with your arms instead of letting hip drive send it upward. Slow the movement down and focus on snapping your hips open first.

alternatives.name: Good Morning
alternatives.reason: Trains the same hamstring-driven hip hinge under a barbell load, useful when you want to build hinge strength without the explosive swing component.

easierVariations.name: Glute Bridge
easierVariations.reason: Builds the same hip-opening, glute-driven pattern from the floor with no weight involved, a good place to start before adding a swinging dumbbell.

harderVariations.name: One-Arm Kettlebell Swings
harderVariations.reason: Moves the same hip-hinge power into a single-arm kettlebell swing, which adds a grip and anti-rotation demand on top of the hip drive.

summary: Lower back self-myofascial release, or SMR, uses a foam roller to apply slow, sustained pressure to the muscles along your spine, aiming to ease tightness rather than build strength. You control your own bodyweight over the roller, so the pressure is easy to adjust just by shifting how much weight you let sink into it. It's a common way to loosen up before a workout that involves bending or twisting, or to unwind a stiff lower back at the end of the day.
whyItWorks: Sustained pressure over a tight muscle encourages it to relax in a way that quick stretching often doesn't, partly because your body eases tension faster when it isn't also being asked to move through a range at the same time. Rolling slowly along the muscles beside your spine, rather than directly over the spine itself, lets you find and settle into the tighter spots without putting pressure on the bony structures that don't respond well to it.
setup: Sit on the floor with a foam roller placed horizontally behind you, at the base of your lower back.
Lean back onto the roller, bend your knees, and plant your feet flat on the floor.
Support your upper body with your hands behind you or crossed over your chest, whichever keeps you stable.
execution: Lift your hips slightly so your weight rests on the roller instead of the floor.
Roll slowly up and down across the muscles just to either side of your spine, staying off the spine itself.
Pause on any spot that feels notably tighter than the rest for 20 to 30 seconds.
Breathe steadily while you hold each spot rather than tensing up against the pressure.
Shift your weight slightly side to side to reach the muscles on either side of your lower spine.
formCues: Roll the muscles beside the spine, not the spine itself.
Move slowly, don't rush across tight spots.
Let your breath stay slow and even.
Ease off if any spot feels sharp rather than tight.
breathing: Breathe slowly and steadily throughout, letting each exhale coincide with easing further into a tight spot.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling directly over the spine instead of the muscles beside it.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the roller shifted slightly to one side of your spine at a time, targeting the muscle tissue rather than the bones and joints of your spine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling quickly back and forth instead of pausing on tight areas.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down and hold steady pressure on any spot that feels tight for at least 20 seconds before moving on.

programmingNotes: This is gentle enough to do daily, either before training as a warm-up or afterward to help your lower back settle down.
One to two minutes total is usually enough; more time on the roller doesn't necessarily bring more relief once a spot has eased.
It works well right before hip and lower-back mobility work, since the muscles are already more receptive to stretching afterward.
safetyNotes: Stop immediately if you feel any sharp, shooting, or radiating pain rather than a dull, tolerable pressure; that's a sign to see a professional rather than keep rolling.
Avoid rolling directly over your spine or lower back if you have a diagnosed spinal condition; check with a healthcare provider first.

faq.question: How long should I foam roll my lower back?
faq.answer: One to two minutes total is usually plenty, pausing 20 to 30 seconds on any spot that feels notably tighter than the rest.

faq.question: Can I do lower back SMR without a foam roller?
faq.answer: A firm massage ball or a rolled towel can substitute in a pinch, though a full-size foam roller spreads the pressure more evenly and is usually more comfortable to start with.

faq.question: Why does rolling my lower back sometimes make it feel worse?
faq.answer: Rolling directly on the spine or joints rather than the muscle tissue beside it can irritate rather than help, and pressing too hard too fast can leave a muscle sore the way any new pressure might. Ease up, shift slightly off the spine, and stop if sharp pain shows up instead of dull tightness.

alternatives.name: Rhomboids-SMR
alternatives.reason: Targets the muscles just above the lower back, a good option if tightness runs higher between your shoulder blades rather than lower down.

alternatives.name: Piriformis-SMR
alternatives.reason: Releases a deep hip muscle that often refers tightness into the lower back, worth trying if rolling the lower back itself doesn't bring much relief.

summary: The dumbbell scaption has you raising a pair of light dumbbells out and slightly forward, along a diagonal roughly halfway between a front raise and a side raise, up to about shoulder height. That angle matches the natural plane of your shoulder blade, which is why the movement is often called scaption in the first place. It's a beginner-friendly way to build the front and middle deltoids and works well for anyone who wants shoulder work that feels gentler on the joint than a straight-out-to-the-side raise.
whyItWorks: Your shoulder blade doesn't sit flat against your back, it angles forward by roughly 30 to 45 degrees, and raising your arm along that same diagonal keeps the ball of your shoulder joint centered in its socket more evenly than a raise directly out to the side does. That centered path is why scaption tends to feel smoother on the shoulder, particularly for anyone who's felt pinching during a standard lateral raise. The angle still targets the same deltoid fibers as a side raise, so you're not sacrificing much muscle work for the more comfortable path.
setup: Stand tall holding a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Turn your thumbs slightly upward so your palms angle inward.
Keep a soft bend in your elbows before the first rep.
execution: Raise both arms out and slightly forward, along a diagonal about halfway between straight out to the side and straight ahead.
Lift until your arms reach roughly shoulder height, no higher.
Keep the slight elbow bend and thumbs-up angle throughout the lift.
Lower the dumbbells back down slowly and under control.
Reset your shoulders before starting the next rep rather than letting them creep upward.
formCues: Raise on a diagonal, not straight out to the side.
Stop at shoulder height, no higher.
Thumbs tilt slightly up through the whole lift.
Lower slowly, don't just drop the arms.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the dumbbells, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Raising the arms past shoulder height to try to get more range.
commonMistakes.correction: Cap the lift at shoulder height. Going higher shifts the work onto the traps and can pinch the shoulder joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up instead of lifting with the shoulder.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo and use a lighter dumbbell if you notice yourself using your legs or back to help start the lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders creep up toward the ears during the raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your neck long and your shoulders down away from your ears throughout the movement, resetting between reps if they start to rise.

programmingNotes: Twelve to fifteen light reps for two or three sets builds solid shoulder strength without overloading a small stabilizing muscle group.
Two or three times a week works well for strength building, and a light daily set is fine too if you're using this as a shoulder warm-up or maintenance move.
Keep the weight light. This exercise is about the quality of the raise, not how much you can lift.
Works well early in a shoulder session as a warm-up for the joint before heavier pressing work.
safetyNotes: Stop the raise at shoulder height rather than pushing higher, which is where most shoulder pinching happens in overhead-style raises.
If you feel any catching or pinching sensation at any point in the range, lower the weight and shorten the range until it's fully pain free.

faq.question: What's the difference between scaption and a lateral raise?
faq.answer: A lateral raise lifts the arm straight out to the side, while scaption lifts it on a diagonal about halfway between the side and the front, matching the natural angle of your shoulder blade. Many people find the scaption angle noticeably more comfortable on the shoulder joint.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for scaption?
faq.answer: Start light. This is an isolation move for smaller shoulder muscles, and most people find 12 to 15 reps with a fairly light dumbbell is plenty of challenge.

faq.question: Can I do scaption every day?
faq.answer: Yes, a light set most days is fine, especially if you're using it as a shoulder warm-up or general shoulder health movement rather than a strength-building exercise. For building strength, two or three focused sessions a week is enough.

faq.question: Why is scaption recommended over a regular shoulder raise?
faq.answer: Because the diagonal path matches the natural angle of the shoulder blade, it tends to keep the shoulder joint more centered, which many people find reduces pinching compared to raising the arm straight out to the side.

alternatives.name: Front Dumbbell Raise
alternatives.reason: Raises the arm on a nearby path in front of the body, useful variety for the same front-of-shoulder muscles.

easierVariations.name: Lateral Raise - With Bands
easierVariations.reason: Band resistance is lightest right at the bottom of the lift, which is easier on the shoulder while you learn the raise.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
harderVariations.reason: Moves the arm further out to the side instead of the diagonal scaption angle, a slightly more demanding lever for the same muscles.

summary: The lying supine dumbbell curl has you flat on your back on a bench, curling dumbbells up toward your shoulders. Lying down removes the ability to swing your torso or drive your elbows forward to help the lift, so the biceps handle nearly the entire movement on their own. It's a straightforward option for anyone who wants a strict curl variation without needing a preacher bench or cable stack.
whyItWorks: A standing dumbbell curl gives you room to lean back slightly or swing your elbows forward as the weight gets heavy, both of which let momentum help move the dumbbell instead of your biceps doing all the work. Lying flat on a bench takes that room away: your torso and shoulders are pressed against a fixed surface, so the biceps are the only muscle group that can flex your elbow and raise the weight. That strict setup makes it a reliable way to isolate the biceps, especially for lifters who tend to cheat a standing curl once the reps get hard.
setup: Lie flat on your back on a bench, feet planted on the floor or bench for stability.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with your arms extended down toward the floor on either side of the bench.
Keep your upper arms close to your torso as your starting position.
Brace your shoulders against the bench so they can't shift during the set.
execution: Curl the dumbbells up toward your shoulders, bending only at the elbow.
Keep your upper arms still, close to your sides, throughout the movement.
Squeeze your biceps briefly at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbells back down under control to a full arm extension.
Avoid letting the dumbbells swing or drift away from your sides.
Repeat for the full set at a controlled, even pace.
formCues: Elbows stay pinned to your sides.
Curl comes from the elbow, not the shoulder.
Squeeze the biceps at the top.
Lower with control, don't let the weight drop.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbells up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward or away from the torso during the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms pinned to your sides for the whole set, moving only from the elbow joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a weight heavy enough that the shoulders roll forward to help lift it.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until your shoulders can stay flat against the bench through every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and letting the dumbbells drop.
commonMistakes.correction: Take at least as long lowering the weight as you did curling it up; the controlled negative is part of the work.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a solid dose for building bicep strength and size, since this is a lighter isolation movement rather than a heavy compound lift.
It works well as one of the first exercises in an arm-focused session, since the strict setup rewards fresh muscles over fatigued ones.
Most lifters can train biceps like this twice a week without issue, given how quickly a small isolation movement like this recovers.
Add reps toward 15 before increasing the dumbbell weight, since strict elbow position matters more here than how much you're lifting.
safetyNotes: Keep the dumbbells under control on both the lift and the lowering phase; letting them drop can strain the elbow joint.
If you feel the movement in your shoulders instead of your biceps, lighten the load and reset your upper arm position against your sides.

faq.question: How many reps should I do for the lying supine dumbbell curl?
faq.answer: Three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a good starting point. Move toward 15 reps before adding weight, since strict elbow position matters more here than heavy load.

faq.question: Lying dumbbell curl vs standing dumbbell curl, what's the difference?
faq.answer: The lying version pins your shoulders and torso against a bench, removing any chance to swing or lean into the lift. The standing version needs no bench and is quicker to set up, but it's easier to cheat with momentum as the reps get harder.

faq.question: Can I do this curl without a bench?
faq.answer: Yes, lying flat on the floor works the same way. You'll lose a small amount of range at the bottom since the floor stops your arm sooner than a bench edge would, but the movement pattern stays the same.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders hurt during lying dumbbell curls?
faq.answer: This usually means the weight is heavy enough that your shoulders are rolling forward to help the lift. Lighten the dumbbells and keep your shoulder blades pressed flat against the bench throughout the set.

faq.question: Is the lying dumbbell curl better than a standing curl for building biceps?
faq.answer: Neither is strictly better; they train the same muscle with a different level of strictness. The lying version removes almost every way to cheat the lift, which makes it a good check on your form, while the standing version is quicker to set up and lets you use slightly more weight since your whole body can help stabilize it.

alternatives.name: Hammer Curls
alternatives.reason: Works the biceps and forearms with a neutral grip, a useful swap if lying flat isn't comfortable or a bench isn't free.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Bicep Curl
easierVariations.reason: The standing version of the same curl, no bench needed, and easier to set up when you just want a quick set of bicep work.

harderVariations.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
harderVariations.reason: Keeps the arms hanging behind the torso for a deeper stretch on the biceps under load, a step up in difficulty from lying flat.

summary: A medium grip bench press is the standard hand spacing on a barbell bench press, sized so your forearms are vertical when the bar touches your chest. It spreads the work fairly evenly across the chest, shoulders, and triceps, rather than shifting the emphasis heavily toward one muscle the way a much wider or narrower grip does.
whyItWorks: Grip width changes how far the bar travels and which muscle does the most work at each point along that path. A grip sized so your forearms sit vertical at the bottom keeps your wrists stacked directly under the bar for the entire lift, which is the most mechanically efficient position for transferring force from your chest and shoulders into the bar without extra strain on the wrist joint.
setup: Lie back on the bench with your eyes roughly under the bar.
Unrack a light warm-up set first and check that your forearms are vertical when the bar is at your chest, adjusting your hand spacing in or out until they are.
Once you find that spacing, grip the bar there for every working set, keeping both hands the same distance from center.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench before unracking your working weight.
execution: Unrack the bar and hold it with arms extended directly over your shoulders.
Lower the bar under control to the middle of your chest, letting your elbows track to roughly 45 to 70 degrees from your torso.
Check that your forearms stay vertical as the bar nears your chest.
Press the bar back up along the same path to full arm extension.
Keep your shoulder blades pinned to the bench for the entire rep.
Rerack the bar only once the set is complete and the bar is fully locked out.
formCues: Forearms vertical when the bar reaches your chest.
Both hands the same distance from the center knurl.
Shoulder blades pinned back, not rolling forward.
Elbows at 45 to 70 degrees, not flared to 90.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the bar to your chest, exhale as you press it back up to lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picking a hand spacing by eyeballing the bar's rings instead of checking the forearm angle at the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Test your grip on a light warm-up set first, adjusting until your forearms sit vertical when the bar touches your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the bar slightly asymmetric, one hand a little wider than the other.
commonMistakes.correction: Use the barbell's knurl marks or center line to place both hands the exact same distance from the middle every time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the grip width drift rep to rep within the same set.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands fixed on the same spot for the entire set once you have set your grip.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows out to a full 90 degrees at this grip width.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the elbows track to roughly 45 to 70 degrees, which keeps the shoulder joint in a safer position at a medium grip.

programmingNotes: Since a medium grip is usually the version lifters use to track their heaviest top set, keep that top effort to once a week, with wide-grip or close-grip variations as lighter accessory work later in the week.
3 to 5 sets of 3 to 8 reps builds strength on this grip well, since it is the most balanced position for moving heavy loads.
Use this grip as the reference point when comparing bench press progress over time, since a shifting grip width makes strength comparisons across sessions unreliable.
Recheck your forearm angle every few months, since flexibility and shoulder position can shift the ideal spacing slightly over time.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or set safety bars in the rack for any set that approaches your limit.
Keep the grip symmetric; an uneven grip can twist the bar path and put uneven strain on one shoulder.

faq.question: What counts as a medium grip on the bench press?
faq.answer: A grip where your forearms are vertical, straight up and down, when the bar touches your chest. For most lifters that lands close to shoulder width, but the forearm angle matters more than any fixed measurement.

faq.question: Medium grip vs wide grip bench press, what is the difference?
faq.answer: A wider grip shortens the distance the bar travels and shifts more of the load onto the chest. A medium grip spreads the work more evenly across the chest, shoulders, and triceps.

faq.question: Medium grip vs close grip bench press, what is the difference?
faq.answer: A close grip lengthens the bar path and shifts more of the work onto the triceps. A medium grip keeps the chest as the clear prime mover while the shoulders and triceps share the rest.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do with a medium grip bench press?
faq.answer: 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 8 reps works well for building strength, since this grip is the most efficient position for moving your heaviest weights.

alternatives.name: Close-Grip Barbell Bench Press
alternatives.reason: Narrows the grip from this baseline, shifting more of the work onto the triceps for a session focused on arm strength.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
easierVariations.reason: Lets each arm find its own comfortable path, gentler on the shoulders while you learn where a medium grip should feel balanced.

harderVariations.name: Wide-Grip Barbell Bench Press
harderVariations.reason: Widens the grip from this baseline, shortening the range and shifting more of the load onto the chest.

summary: Flat bench cable flyes have you lying on a bench between two low cable pulleys, sweeping your arms in a wide arc to bring the handles together over your chest. Unlike a dumbbell flye, the cable keeps tension on your chest through the entire range, including the top of the movement where a dumbbell usually goes slack. It's a solid isolation move for anyone who's already built some pressing strength and wants to add chest-specific volume with less shoulder strain than heavy pressing.
whyItWorks: The chest's main job is to bring your arm across your body, and a flye trains exactly that arc without your triceps helping the way they do in a press. A dumbbell flye loses tension near the top since gravity stops pulling the weight away from your body once your arms are vertical, but a cable pulls at an angle from the machine the whole time, so your pecs stay under real load even at full contraction. That constant tension is what makes cable flyes a favorite chest-isolation finisher once your pressing strength is already established.
setup: Set both cable pulleys to a low position and attach single handles.
Place a flat bench centered between the two pulleys.
Lie back on the bench holding a handle in each hand, arms extended out to your sides with a slight bend in the elbows.
Start with your arms roughly in line with your chest, not stretched too far behind you.
execution: Sweep your arms up and together in a wide arc, keeping the slight elbow bend fixed throughout.
Bring the handles together over your chest, squeezing your pecs at the top.
Pause briefly once the handles meet.
Lower your arms back out to the sides under control, resisting the cables the entire way.
Stop the descent once your upper arms are roughly level with your torso.
Repeat for the full set without letting the elbows bend more or less as you go.
formCues: Keep a slight, fixed bend in the elbows the whole set.
Squeeze your chest at the top, don't just let the handles clack together.
Lower with control; don't let the cables yank your arms back.
Lead the movement with your hands, not your shoulders rounding forward.
breathing: Inhale as you lower your arms out to the sides, exhale as you bring the handles together over your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows more on the way up, turning the flye into a press.
commonMistakes.correction: Fix your elbow angle at the start and keep it constant throughout; a press works different muscles and defeats the point of an isolation flye.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stretching too far back at the bottom of the movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent once your upper arms reach roughly torso level; going further loads the front of the shoulder joint more than the chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the cables pull the arms back quickly instead of controlling the eccentric.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower at the same speed you raised the handles; the controlled lowering is where a lot of the chest tension happens.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the shoulders forward to reach further at the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulder blades pulled back against the bench and let your hands do the traveling instead of your upper back rounding forward.

programmingNotes: 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps fits well as chest isolation work after your main pressing exercises.
Because it's a single-joint move for a muscle group that also gets worked by pressing, once or twice a week is usually enough on top of your regular chest volume.
Use a lighter weight than you'd guess; the constant cable tension makes this exercise feel harder at a given weight than a comparable dumbbell flye.
Pairs well as a finisher after bench press or incline press, when your chest is already warm but you want a few extra isolated reps.
safetyNotes: Keep the stretch at the bottom moderate; going too far back can strain the front of the shoulder, especially with heavier cable weight.
If you feel shoulder pinching rather than a chest stretch, shorten the range of motion and check your elbow bend.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for cable flyes?
faq.answer: Less than you'd guess. The constant tension from the cable makes a given weight feel heavier through the whole range than the same weight on dumbbells, so start light and build up.

faq.question: What's the difference between cable flyes and dumbbell flyes?
faq.answer: Cable flyes keep tension on your chest through the entire range, including at the top, while dumbbell flyes lose tension near the top once gravity stops pulling the weight sideways.

faq.question: Should I bend my elbows during cable flyes?
faq.answer: Yes, keep a slight, fixed bend throughout. A completely straight arm puts more strain on the elbow joint, while a bend that changes mid-rep turns the flye into a press.

faq.question: Can I do cable flyes without a cable machine?
faq.answer: Yes, dumbbell flyes on a flat bench train the same chest-isolation pattern, or a machine pec fly if you prefer a guided path.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Flyes
alternatives.reason: Trains the same chest-isolation arc with free weights when a dual cable stack isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Butterfly
easierVariations.reason: Swaps the free cable arc for a guided machine path, an easier way to feel the same chest squeeze.

harderVariations.name: One-Arm Flat Bench Dumbbell Flye
harderVariations.reason: Trains one side at a time with a dumbbell, demanding more shoulder stability than the two-handed cable version.

summary: Knee across the body is a lying rotational stretch that reaches the glutes, the outer hip, and the lower back in one position. You bend one knee and let it fall across your torso toward the opposite side while your shoulders stay flat on the floor, which twists the hip and spine just enough to release tension without any equipment. It works well as a cooldown after lower body training or as a quick reset for a stiff lower back.
whyItWorks: Letting a bent knee drop across the midline pulls the hip into internal rotation and draws the pelvis and lumbar spine along with it. That combination lengthens the glute on the working side and puts a gentle rotational stretch through the lower back at the same time, which is why one position covers both areas rather than needing two separate stretches.
setup: Lie on your back with both legs extended.
Bend one knee to roughly 90 degrees, lifting that foot off the floor.
Rest your arms out to the sides for balance, palms down.
execution: Keeping your bent knee at roughly 90 degrees, guide it across your body toward the floor on the opposite side.
Let your hip rotate as the knee lowers, keeping the opposite shoulder pressed flat against the floor.
Stop at the point where you feel a clear stretch through your glute, outer hip, or lower back.
Hold that position, breathing steadily.
Bring the knee back to center with control.
Repeat on the other side.
formCues: Keep both shoulders flat on the floor.
Let the knee's weight do the work instead of forcing it down.
Stop before any pinch, not after it.
Keep the bent knee angle steady through the hold.
breathing: Exhale as the knee lowers across your body, then breathe slowly through the hold.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the opposite shoulder off the floor to let the knee drop further.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep that shoulder pinned down and treat the shoulder staying flat as your actual range limit, not the knee height.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the knee down with your hand to force a deeper stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Let gravity do the work first; only add light hand pressure once the passive stretch already feels easy.

programmingNotes: Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds and repeat two or three rounds.
This is gentle static stretching, so it fits well as a daily cooldown after lower body or running sessions.
Pair it with a hip flexor stretch for a fuller lower body cooldown routine.
safetyNotes: Stop the rotation the moment you feel a pinch rather than a stretch in your lower back.
Keep the movement slow; this position shouldn't be bounced into.

faq.question: How long should I hold the knee across the body stretch?
faq.answer: Around 20 to 30 seconds per side is enough, repeated for two or three rounds.

faq.question: What does the knee across the body stretch work?
faq.answer: It reaches the glutes, the outer hip through the abductors, and the lower back, all through one rotational position.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch every day?
faq.answer: Yes, it's a light static stretch, so it's safe to include daily as part of a warm-up or cooldown.

faq.question: Why do I only feel this stretch in my lower back and not my glute?
faq.answer: Everyone rotates a little differently, so the emphasis shifts based on your hip mobility. If you want more glute and less lower back, try keeping the rotation smaller and more controlled.

alternatives.name: Ankle On The Knee
alternatives.reason: A seated figure-four position that reaches the same glute without needing to rotate through the lower back.

alternatives.name: Cat Stretch
alternatives.reason: Targets the lower back directly through flexion and extension instead of rotation, useful if twisting bothers your back.

harderVariations.name: IT Band and Glute Stretch
