harderVariations.reason: Uses a seated crossed-leg position to reach deeper into the same outer hip and glute tissue once the lying version feels easy.

summary: The one-arm kettlebell jerk starts with the bell already racked at your shoulder and sends it overhead using a short dip, an explosive leg drive, and a quick re-bend of the knees to catch the lockout. It moves more weight overhead than a strict press because your legs, not your shoulder, are doing most of the work, which is why it's a staple lift in kettlebell sport training.
whyItWorks: The dip and drive generate upward momentum from your legs, the biggest and strongest muscles you have, and that momentum does most of the work of getting the bell moving toward lockout. The re-bend right after the drive lets you drop your body slightly under the bell as it arrives overhead, shortening the distance your arm has to travel and catching the weight in a stable, locked position rather than pressing it the whole way up with the shoulder alone.
setup: Pull the kettlebell into the rack at your shoulder with a clean, or start with it already sitting there.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, torso upright, grip firm on the handle.
Set your feet flat and stable; the drive needs a solid base to push against.
Take a breath and brace lightly before the first dip.
execution: Dip your knees a short distance, keeping your torso vertical and the bell steady in the rack.
Drive up explosively through your legs, using that upward force to launch the bell off your shoulder.
As the bell rises, quickly re-bend your knees slightly and drop under it.
Punch your arm straight to lock the bell out overhead as you catch it in that lower position.
Stand back up to full height once the bell is locked out and stable.
Lower the bell back to the rack with control before starting the next rep.
formCues: Short dip, explosive drive.
Drop under the bell, don't just press it.
Feet stay flat through the drive.
Stand tall once it's locked out.
breathing: Inhale before the dip, exhale sharply as you drive the bell up and catch the lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing the last portion of the lift with the shoulder instead of dropping under the bell.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on the quick re-bend right after the drive; catching low under the bell should do more work than the shoulder does.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dipping too deep before driving, which slows down the whole lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the dip short and quick; a shallow, fast dip transfers more force than a deep, slow one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the heels come up off the floor during the drive.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your feet flat and push through the whole foot, which gives you a more stable base to drive from.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the lockout with a bent elbow instead of fully extended.
commonMistakes.correction: Finish the punch to a straight arm as you drop under the bell, so the joint, not the muscle, is holding the weight.

programmingNotes: Three to five sets of 3 to 6 reps per arm is a reasonable range while you're building the timing of the dip and re-bend.
This is a demanding, technical compound lift, so once a week per arm at a real working weight is enough for most people building strength.
If you want the longer, higher-rep sets used in kettlebell sport conditioning, treat those as a separate lighter-weight session rather than adding volume onto your strength day.
Grip fatigue often shows up before your legs do; if your hand is the limiting factor, that's normal and not a sign to push through poor form.
safetyNotes: Make sure you have clear overhead space and a stable floor before attempting heavier jerks.
Stop the set if the catch feels unstable rather than trying to muscle a shaky lockout into place.

faq.question: How many reps of the kettlebell jerk should I do?
faq.answer: Three to six reps per arm across three to five sets works well while you're learning the dip, drive, and catch.

faq.question: What's the difference between a kettlebell jerk and a push press?
faq.answer: A push press uses one continuous drive and lockout without a re-bend, while the jerk adds a quick drop under the bell after the drive, letting you move more weight overhead.

faq.question: Can I do a kettlebell jerk without cleaning the bell first?
faq.answer: Yes, you can start with the bell already racked, either handed to you or set up with a clean beforehand, and just practice the dip-drive-catch on its own.

faq.question: Why does my kettlebell jerk feel unstable at the top?
faq.answer: That usually means the elbow isn't fully locked or the re-bend under the bell was too shallow. Focus on dropping lower under the weight and finishing the arm to a straight lockout.

alternatives.name: Push Press
alternatives.reason: Uses the same leg dip and drive to move a barbell overhead if a kettlebell isn't what you have on hand.

easierVariations.name: One-Arm Kettlebell Push Press
easierVariations.reason: Uses the same leg-driven start but finishes with a single continuous lockout instead of the jerk's re-bend and catch, which is easier to time.

harderVariations.name: One-Arm Kettlebell Split Jerk
harderVariations.reason: Catches the overhead lockout in a split stance instead of parallel feet, letting you stabilize heavier weight overhead.

summary: Incline Hammer Curls have you lean back on an angled bench and curl a pair of dumbbells straight up while keeping your palms facing each other the whole rep. That neutral grip shifts some of the work from the biceps onto the brachialis, a muscle underneath the biceps that adds thickness to the upper arm, plus the forearms. The incline position stretches the arm further at the bottom than a standing hammer curl does, which makes the same weight feel noticeably harder.
whyItWorks: Keeping your palms facing each other instead of turning them up changes which muscles do most of the lifting. A standard curl relies heavily on the biceps, which twists the forearm as it flexes the elbow. A neutral grip removes that twisting job, so more of the load shifts to the brachialis and to the forearm muscles that don't care which way your palm faces. Leaning back on the incline bench also pulls your shoulder behind your hip, which puts your arm in a longer starting position than it would have standing straight up, adding a deeper stretch before the curl even begins.
setup: Set an incline bench to a moderate angle, around 45 to 60 degrees.
Sit back with your shoulders and upper back against the pad, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Let your arms hang straight down, slightly behind your torso, with palms facing each other.
execution: Curl both dumbbells straight up toward your shoulders, keeping your palms facing each other the whole way.
Keep your upper arms still, without letting the elbows drift forward.
Squeeze briefly at the top of the curl.
Lower the dumbbells slowly back to a full arm extension before starting the next rep.
Repeat for the target number of reps.
formCues: Keep your palms facing each other the entire rep.
Let your upper arms stay still, curl only from the elbow.
Keep your shoulders pinned to the backrest.
Lower all the way to a full stretch each rep.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbells up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the wrists rotate so the palms turn upward during the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a firm neutral grip with your palms facing each other for the whole set, or the exercise turns into a standard curl and loses its point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward as the dumbbells rise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms fixed against your sides through the whole rep; forward drift shortens the range and lets the shoulders take over.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a bench angle so shallow it barely differs from standing.
commonMistakes.correction: Set the bench closer to 45 to 60 degrees so your arms actually hang behind your torso for a real stretch.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a solid range for this arm exercise.
Twice a week works fine if you give it a day or two of rest between sessions, since it's a light, single-joint movement.
Use lighter dumbbells than your standard curl the first time you try this angle, since the added stretch catches most people off guard.
Pairs well with a triceps exercise on an arm-focused day, working opposite muscle groups back to back.
safetyNotes: Set the bench angle gradually rather than jumping to the steepest setting, since a deep stretch under load feels different than it looks.
Ease off the weight if you feel a sharp pull at the front of the shoulder instead of a stretch through the arm.

faq.question: How many reps should I do for incline hammer curls?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 12 reps is a good starting point. Use less weight than your usual curl, since the deeper stretch on an incline bench makes it feel harder.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and a regular incline dumbbell curl?
faq.answer: The neutral grip in a hammer curl keeps your palms facing each other the whole rep, which shifts more work onto the brachialis and forearms instead of the biceps alone.

faq.question: What can I do without an incline bench?
faq.answer: Standing hammer curls train the same neutral-grip pattern without needing a bench.

faq.question: Why do my forearms get tired faster with this variation?
faq.answer: The neutral grip recruits your forearm muscles more directly than a standard curl does, so grip fatigue often shows up before your biceps feel fully worked.

alternatives.name: Cable Hammer Curls - Rope Attachment
alternatives.reason: A rope attachment keeps the same neutral grip under constant cable tension if a bench or dumbbells aren't available.

easierVariations.name: Hammer Curls
easierVariations.reason: Standing removes the need for a bench and skips the deeper shoulder stretch of the incline start.

harderVariations.name: Zottman Curl
harderVariations.reason: Adds a grip rotation on the way down, turning the same neutral-grip curl into extra forearm work too.

summary: The elevated back lunge loads a single-leg lunge pattern with a barbell while your rear foot rests on a bench or box behind you. Elevating the back foot lets your front leg sink through a deeper range than a standard lunge, putting more direct demand on the quadriceps while the glutes and hamstrings stabilize the hip.
whyItWorks: Resting your rear foot on an elevated surface removes it almost entirely from the work of supporting your weight, which forces your front leg to do nearly all the lifting through a longer range of motion than a lunge where both feet are on the floor. That combination of a single working leg and a deeper range is what makes the quadriceps work so hard here, while the front hip and glutes have to control the knee and torso through the whole descent, building the kind of single-leg strength and stability that carries over to running, cutting, and stairs.
setup: Set a bench or box about knee height behind you and load a barbell on a rack at shoulder height.
Step under the bar and position it across your upper back, gripping it wide for stability.
Unrack the bar, step forward, and rest the top of your rear foot on the bench behind you.
Set your front foot far enough forward that your shin stays roughly vertical at the bottom of the descent.
Brace your core before starting the first rep.
execution: Keeping your torso upright, lower your body by bending your front knee and hip.
Let your rear knee drop straight down toward the floor behind you.
Descend until your front thigh is close to parallel with the floor or as deep as your hips allow with good control.
Drive through your front foot to return to the starting position.
Complete all reps on one side before switching legs and repeating.
formCues: Keep your torso tall, don't lean forward over your front knee.
Track your front knee in line with your toes, not caving inward.
Drive evenly through your whole front foot, not just the toes.
Set the bench distance so your shin stays close to vertical at the bottom.
breathing: Inhale and brace before you descend, exhale as you drive back up to standing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing the bench too far forward, which pushes the shin far past vertical and puts extra strain on the front knee.
commonMistakes.correction: Shorten the stance until your shin stays roughly vertical when your thigh is parallel to the floor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso forward over the front knee instead of staying upright.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and your torso stacked over your hips throughout the descent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the front knee cave inward as you push back up, especially on the last few reps of a set.
commonMistakes.correction: Consciously push the knee out in line with your toes and drop the weight if the knee starts collapsing inward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the descent instead of lowering with control.
commonMistakes.correction: Take about two seconds to lower on each rep so the front leg does the work rather than gravity.

programmingNotes: This is a heavily loaded single-leg quad movement, so plan for 3 sets of 6 to 10 reps per leg with a weight that challenges the last couple of reps.

Because the front leg does nearly all the work here, once a week per leg is enough recovery time between sessions if this is your main quad-focused lift that week; twice a week only makes sense if your other training that week is light on the quads.
Start with just the barbell or a light load to dial in the bench distance and balance before adding weight; the single-leg setup punishes sloppy positioning more than a two-legged squat does.
safetyNotes: Keep a spotter or safety pins nearby when using heavier loads, since stepping out of a failed rep is harder on one leg.
Stop the descent at a depth where your knee tracks cleanly over your toes; forcing extra depth once the knee caves in raises injury risk without adding benefit.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for the elevated back lunge?
faq.answer: Start with just the bar to get the bench distance and balance right, then add weight in small increments once you can complete every rep with a controlled descent and no knee cave.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of elevated back lunge should I do?
faq.answer: 3 sets of 6 to 10 reps per leg is a solid range for building single-leg quad strength. Keep the weight challenging enough that the last two reps of each set are genuinely hard.

faq.question: Elevated back lunge vs regular barbell lunge, what's the difference?
faq.answer: The elevated back lunge parks your rear foot on a bench so your front leg does nearly all the work through a deeper range, which builds more raw single-leg quad strength. The regular barbell lunge keeps both feet on the floor and adds a walking or stepping component, which trains balance and coordination more directly.

faq.question: Why does my front knee hurt during elevated back lunges?
faq.answer: It's often a stance that's too short, which pushes the knee far past the toes on the way down. Move the bench back a bit and check that your knee tracks in line with your toes rather than caving inward.

alternatives.name: Barbell Lunge
alternatives.reason: Uses the same barbell setup and single-leg quad-and-glute pattern, but walking forward instead of holding one leg elevated behind you.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Rear Lunge
easierVariations.reason: Drops the elevated back foot and the barbell for a standard rear lunge with dumbbells, cutting the balance demand while keeping the same forward-leg pattern.

summary: The V-bar version of the triceps pushdown swaps the straight bar or rope for an angled, fixed handle that your palms face each other on. That locked neutral grip gives you a more secure hold than a straight bar, which usually means you can push a bit more weight once your elbows are warmed up and your form is dialed in.
whyItWorks: A V-bar fixes your hands in a neutral, palms-facing-each-other position and keeps them close together, which gives most people a stronger, more stable grip than an overhand hold on a straight bar. A more secure grip means less of your effort leaks into just hanging onto the handle, so more of it goes directly into extending the elbow, the same job every pushdown variation asks of the triceps. The fixed angle of the handle also removes a layer of coordination the straight bar and rope both require, since there's no wrist position to manage once your hands are set, which makes the V-bar a good default when you simply want to add weight without thinking about grip.
setup: Attach a V-bar to the high pulley and set the weight.
Stand close to the machine with feet shoulder-width apart and a slight forward lean.
Grip the angled sides of the V-bar with palms facing each other.
Pin your upper arms against your ribs with elbows bent around 90 degrees.
execution: Keeping your upper arms locked against your sides, push the V-bar straight down.
Extend your elbows fully without letting your shoulders roll forward.
Pause briefly at full extension and squeeze the triceps.
Let the bar rise back under control until your forearms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Keep your grip firm on the angled handles throughout, without letting your wrists bend.
Repeat for the set, keeping your elbows pinned the entire time.
formCues: Elbows pinned to your sides.
Push straight down, not out and away.
Squeeze at full extension.
Let the handle rise under control, not a free drop.
breathing: Exhale as you push the bar down, inhale as you let it rise back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare out to the sides instead of staying pinned to the ribs.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms glued against your body for the whole rep; flaring elbows shifts the work toward the shoulders.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso down into the bar instead of extending from the elbow.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your forward lean small and fixed, and let the elbow joint do all the moving.

commonMistakes.mistake: Loading more weight than you can control through the full range.
commonMistakes.correction: Since the V-bar grip can handle more weight, it's easy to overload it; drop the load if you're cutting the range short to compensate.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the handle snap back up quickly at the top of each rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the return at a similar pace to the push so the triceps stay under tension both directions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the V-bar too wide, near the outer edges, instead of on the angled grip sections.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands on the angled part of the handle close together, which is what gives the V-bar its stable, neutral grip in the first place.

programmingNotes: Place this after your main pressing work as an arm finisher, the same as any pushdown variation.
Four sets of 8 to 12 reps suits this version well, since the secure grip supports slightly heavier loads than the rope or straight bar.
If your grip tends to fail before your triceps do on other pushdown variations, this is the version to default to.
Add a short pause at full lockout on your final set when you want more time under tension without adding weight.

Because the fixed handle removes the wrist variability of a rope, it's also a reasonable choice for tracking strength progress over time, since the movement pattern stays identical rep to rep and week to week.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel sharp elbow pain rather than muscle fatigue; reduce the load or the range rather than pushing through it.
Avoid snapping the elbows into a hard lockout on fast reps, which can jar the joint over a full set.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do with the V-bar pushdown?
faq.answer: Four sets of 8 to 12 reps works well, since the secure grip on the V-bar usually lets you handle a bit more load than the rope or straight bar.

faq.question: Is the V-bar better than the rope for triceps pushdowns?
faq.answer: They serve different needs. The V-bar's fixed neutral grip is more secure and supports heavier loads, while the rope lets your wrists rotate, which is gentler on sensitive elbows.

faq.question: What can I use if the V-bar attachment is taken?
faq.answer: A dumbbell triceps extension with a pronated grip gives a similar locked-hand feel and trains the same elbow-extension movement.

faq.question: Why does the V-bar feel more stable than the straight bar?
faq.answer: The angled, neutral grip keeps your hands close together in a naturally strong position, so less effort goes into just holding on and more goes into extending the elbow.

faq.question: Can I use the V-bar for a wider variety of triceps exercises?
faq.answer: It's built for pushdown-style movements with a fixed neutral grip. For other angles, like overhead extensions, the rope attachment usually fits better since it allows more hand rotation.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Tricep Extension -Pronated Grip
alternatives.reason: Gives you the same locked, neutral-ish grip feel on a single dumbbell when the V-bar attachment is taken.

easierVariations.name: Triceps Pushdown - Rope Attachment
easierVariations.reason: The rope's rotating grip is gentler on the elbows while you build up pressing strength before locking into the V-bar's fixed hand position.

harderVariations.name: Cable One Arm Tricep Extension
harderVariations.reason: Working one arm at a time demands far more core and shoulder stability than the two-handed V-bar version.

summary: Cable shrugs have you stand facing a low pulley, hold the handle or bar attachment with both hands, and lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears. It isolates your traps with constant cable tension, and it suits anyone building upper trap thickness or looking for a shoulder-friendly alternative to heavy barbell shrugs.
whyItWorks: Your traps' main job in a shrug is elevating your shoulder blades straight up, without any rotation or forward roll. A cable pulls straight down from a fixed low point, which keeps the resistance path simple and constant, unlike a barbell where the bar can drift forward or back as your grip and stance shift, giving your traps a cleaner, more consistent line to work against.
setup: Stand facing a low pulley with a straight bar or handle attached.
Grab the attachment with both hands, arms fully extended, and stand tall with your knees soft.
Let the weight stack lift slightly off the rest so there's tension in the cable before you start.
execution: Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears, keeping your arms fully extended.
Pause briefly at the top of the shrug.
Lower your shoulders back down slowly, letting them stretch down under control.
Repeat for the set without bending your elbows to help lift the weight.
formCues: Move only your shoulders, keep your elbows locked and arms straight the whole set.
Lift straight up rather than rolling your shoulders forward or backward.
Pause at the top for a moment instead of bouncing straight back down.
Let your shoulders stretch down fully between reps instead of stopping short.
breathing: Exhale as you lift your shoulders up, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the shoulders forward or backward instead of lifting them straight up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the motion a straight vertical shrug, your traps work best moving in one direction without rotation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows to help heave the weight up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your arms straight throughout and let your traps do all the lifting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using so much weight that the range shortens to a small pulse near the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until you can lift your shoulders through their full range and lower them just as fully.

programmingNotes: Traps recover quickly and tolerate frequent training, so two to three sessions a week works well for most lifters.
Twelve to fifteen reps per set with a brief pause at the top tends to build trap thickness better than very heavy, low-rep shrugs.
Place it near the end of a back or shoulder session, since traps rarely need to be fresh for other lifts.
safetyNotes: Avoid rolling your shoulders, straight up and down protects your shoulder joint better than a circular motion.
Choose a weight that lets you complete the full range instead of relying on a short, heavy pulse.
Stop if you feel sharp pain in your neck rather than muscular fatigue in your traps.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable shrugs should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 12 to 15 reps with a brief pause at the top works well for building trap thickness.

faq.question: What's the difference between cable shrugs and barbell shrugs?
faq.answer: A barbell can drift forward or back as your grip and stance shift, while a cable pulls from a fixed low point, giving your traps a more consistent straight-up path to work against.

faq.question: Can I do this without a cable machine?
faq.answer: Dumbbell shrugs train the same straight-up motion without needing a cable station.

faq.question: Why does my neck hurt during cable shrugs?
faq.answer: That usually means you're rolling your shoulders instead of lifting them straight up, or using too much weight and jerking the reps. Slow down, keep the motion vertical, and drop the load if the strain shows up in your neck.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Shrug
alternatives.reason: Trains the same straight-up shoulder elevation with dumbbells when a cable station isn't free.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Shrug
harderVariations.reason: Trades the fixed cable path for a barbell, which typically allows heavier loading once cable weight stops challenging your traps.

summary: The guillotine bench press lowers the bar down to your neck or upper chest instead of the middle of your chest, with your elbows flared out wide the whole rep. That bar path shifts more of the work onto the upper chest and front shoulders than a standard bench press, but it also puts the shoulder joint in a far more vulnerable position, which is why it's an advanced variation reserved for lifters with healthy, mobile shoulders.
whyItWorks: Lowering the bar to your neck line, rather than your mid chest, changes the angle your upper arm makes with your torso at the bottom of the lift. With elbows flared wide, more of the pressing work shifts to the upper portion of the chest and the front of the shoulders, and the triceps get involved as they lock the elbow out at the top. That same flared elbow position, though, puts the shoulder joint near the end range of external rotation under load, which is the tradeoff for the different muscle emphasis.
setup: Lie on the bench with your eyes roughly under the bar, feet flat on the floor.
Grip the bar wider than your standard bench press grip, since the elbows will flare out during the lift.
Unrack the bar and hold it steady over your neck and upper chest before starting the first rep.
Retract your shoulder blades against the bench and keep them pinned there through the set.
execution: Lower the bar slowly and under control toward your neck or the very top of your chest, letting your elbows flare out to the sides.
Stop the bar just above your neck, never letting it touch or rest there.
Press the bar back up along the same path, keeping your shoulder blades pinned to the bench.
Lock your elbows out fully at the top without shrugging your shoulders forward.
Reset your shoulder position briefly before starting the next rep.
formCues: Bar stops just above the neck, never touches down.
Elbows flare wide, following the bar path.
Shoulder blades stay pinned to the bench.
Lower slowly, this isn't a bar to drop under control.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the bar toward your neck, exhale as you press it back up to lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lowering the bar too fast and losing control near the neck.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the descent down deliberately and use a lighter weight than your standard bench press until the path feels fully controlled.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulder blades come off the bench to chase extra range.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the shoulder blades retracted and pinned throughout; range should come from the arms and shoulder joint, not from the upper back lifting off.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attempting this variation with a heavy load before building shoulder mobility and control on a standard bench press.
commonMistakes.correction: Spend time on standard and close-grip bench presses first, and only add the guillotine variation once your shoulders move well and stay pain-free under load.

programmingNotes: Given the shoulder demand, keep this as an accessory movement, 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 10 reps at a moderate weight rather than a max-effort lift.
Once a week is enough, since the exposed shoulder position adds joint stress beyond what a standard bench press session already provides that week.
Place it after your main pressing exercise for the session, once your shoulders are warm but not so fatigued that control breaks down.
Drop the weight noticeably compared to your standard bench press; chasing the same number here isn't the goal.
safetyNotes: Reserve this variation for lifters with healthy, mobile shoulders and solid control on a standard bench press first.
Stop the set immediately if you feel any pinching or sharp discomfort at the front of the shoulder; that joint position leaves little margin for pushing through pain.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for the guillotine bench press?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 6 to 10 reps at a moderate weight works well as an accessory movement. This isn't a lift to chase a heavy single on, given the exposed shoulder position.

faq.question: Is the guillotine bench press safe for the shoulders?
faq.answer: It puts the shoulder joint in a more vulnerable position than a standard bench press, so it's best reserved for lifters with healthy, mobile shoulders and solid pressing experience already.

faq.question: What's the difference between the guillotine press and a regular bench press?
faq.answer: The guillotine press lowers the bar to the neck or upper chest with flared elbows, shifting emphasis to the upper chest and front shoulders. A standard bench press lowers to the mid chest with elbows tucked closer, which is easier on the shoulder joint.

faq.question: Can I do a guillotine press with dumbbells instead of a barbell?
faq.answer: A standard dumbbell bench press lets each arm find its own natural path and can build similar upper chest emphasis without fixing a bar directly over your neck.

faq.question: How much lighter should the guillotine press be than a regular bench press?
faq.answer: Expect to use noticeably less weight, often 20 to 30 percent under your standard bench press, since the wider elbow flare and neck-line bar path put you in a mechanically weaker position. Chasing the same number here defeats the point of the exercise.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
alternatives.reason: Lets each arm settle into its own natural path, building similar upper chest emphasis without fixing the bar over your neck.

easierVariations.name: Barbell Bench Press - Medium Grip
easierVariations.reason: Lowers the bar to the mid chest instead of the neck, keeping the shoulders in a far less exposed position at the bottom.

summary: Platform hamstring slides are a floor-based hamstring exercise where you lie on your back, heels resting on sliding discs, hips lifted in a bridge, and curl your heels in toward your hips using only your hamstrings and glutes. No machine required, just a smooth surface and something for your heels to slide on.
whyItWorks: Your hamstrings do two jobs: bending the knee and extending the hip. Most leg curl machines only train the knee-bending half. Sliding your heels in while your hips stay lifted asks the hamstrings and glutes to hold hip extension and pull the knee at the same time, closer to how they actually work together when you run or sprint.
setup: Lie on your back on a smooth floor with a slider disc, folded towel, or furniture mover under each heel.
Bend your knees slightly and place your feet hip-width apart.
Press through your heels and lift your hips into a bridge position.
Keep your arms flat on the floor at your sides for support.
execution: From the bridge position, slide your heels slowly toward your hips by bending your knees.
Keep your hips lifted and level throughout the slide, don't let them sag toward the floor.
Pause briefly once your heels are as close to your hips as you can get without your hips dropping.
Slide your heels back out to a straight-leg bridge with the same control.
Keep your hips up the entire set, only lowering them once the set is complete.
formCues: Hips stay up the whole time, this isn't a bridge that rises and falls.
Slide slow enough that you could stop and hold at any point.
Drive the slide from your hamstrings and glutes, not by arching your lower back.
Keep your core braced so your hips don't sag as your legs bend.
breathing: Breathe steadily throughout, exhaling gently as you curl your heels in and inhaling as you slide back out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips drop as the knees bend.
commonMistakes.correction: Squeeze your glutes to keep your hips level and lifted through the entire slide, treating the bridge height as non-negotiable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sliding fast and using momentum instead of muscle.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down until you can feel your hamstrings working the whole way in and the whole way back out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Starting without a slick enough surface, so the feet catch instead of glide.
commonMistakes.correction: Use real sliders, a smooth towel on a hard floor, or furniture movers, not carpet or grippy shoes that stop the slide.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 slow slides work well as a hamstring accessory, either after squats and deadlifts or on their own lower-body day.
Because the hips have to stay lifted the entire set, this fatigues quickly; shorter, cleaner sets beat grinding out extra reps with sagging hips.
A great option for home training days when there's no leg curl machine available.
safetyNotes: Stop the set once your hips start sagging on every rep instead of pushing through with poor position, since that's usually the point your hamstrings have done their real work for that set.
If you feel this in your lower back rather than your hamstrings and glutes, check that your hips are lifting from a glute squeeze and not from arching your spine.

faq.question: What muscles do hamstring slides work?
faq.answer: Mainly your hamstrings, with your glutes working hard to keep your hips lifted the whole time. It trains both halves of what the hamstrings actually do: bending the knee and extending the hip.

faq.question: Can I do hamstring slides without slider discs?
faq.answer: Yes. A smooth towel on a hardwood or tile floor, or furniture movers under your heels, work just as well. Socks on a smooth floor can work in a pinch, though grippier flooring will stop the slide.

faq.question: Are hamstring slides good for beginners?
faq.answer: Yes, they need no equipment beyond something for your heels to glide on, and the bodyweight resistance makes them approachable while still building real hamstring and glute strength.

faq.question: Why do my hips sag during hamstring slides?
faq.answer: Usually your glutes are fatiguing before your hamstrings finish the rep, or your core isn't braced enough to hold the bridge. Shortening the set and focusing on a tight glute squeeze from the very first rep usually fixes it.

alternatives.name: Ball Leg Curl
alternatives.reason: Trains the identical hip-lifted, knee-curling pattern using a stability ball instead of sliders.

alternatives.name: Seated Band Hamstring Curl
alternatives.reason: A seated, equipment-light alternative when you don't have a smooth enough floor for sliding.

easierVariations.name: Single Leg Glute Bridge
easierVariations.reason: Builds the hip-lifting strength and control this exercise needs, without adding the sliding knee-bend component yet.

summary: The dumbbell skullcrusher, also called a lying triceps extension, isolates the triceps by bending only at the elbow while lying on a bench. Two dumbbells replace the usual barbell or EZ-bar, letting each arm move through its own natural path while your triceps handle nearly all of the work.
whyItWorks: The triceps has one main job across all three of its heads: straighten the elbow. Lying down and keeping the upper arms still removes the shoulders from the movement almost entirely, so the elbow-extension motion falls squarely on the triceps instead of getting shared with the chest or shoulders the way a close-grip bench press would share it. That isolation is exactly why the skullcrusher tends to build the lockout strength that carries over to pressing movements like the bench press and shoulder press.
setup: Lie back on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand, arms extended straight up over your chest.
Turn your palms to face each other, keeping the dumbbells close together.
Plant your feet flat on the floor for stability.
Keep your upper arms vertical and still; only your forearms will move.
execution: Bend your elbows and let the dumbbells travel down near your temples, keeping your upper arms fixed in place.
Stop just before the dumbbells reach your head, or when you feel a full stretch in the triceps.
Pause briefly at the bottom without letting your elbows drift outward.
Extend your elbows to press the dumbbells back up to the starting position.
Keep the motion isolated to the elbow joint throughout the entire set.
formCues: Elbows stay fixed, only the forearms move.
Lower toward your temples, not your chest.
Keep elbows tucked in, not flared out to the sides.
Full extension at the top without slamming the elbows straight.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the dumbbells toward your head, exhale as you press them back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the upper arms drift backward toward the face as the elbows bend.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms vertical and still throughout the set; only the forearms should travel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows out to the sides instead of keeping them pointed toward the ceiling.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows tracking straight up and down, tucked closer to a shoulder-width position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using too much weight and turning the movement into a partial-range press.
commonMistakes.correction: Lighten the load until you can lower the dumbbells through a full, controlled range without your shoulders taking over.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and losing control near your head.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down the descent, especially in the last few inches, since this is where the risk of losing control is highest.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps works well as a targeted triceps finisher after a pressing movement.
As a single-joint isolation exercise, training it two or three times a week is reasonable if your elbows feel good.
Because control near the head matters more than load here, add weight gradually and only once the full range feels stable.
Fits naturally at the end of a chest or shoulder day, since your triceps are usually already warmed up from pressing.
safetyNotes: Use a spotter or start with lighter dumbbells until you're confident controlling the bottom position near your head.
Stop the descent higher up if you feel any elbow discomfort, and build the range back up gradually over time.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for dumbbell skullcrushers?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps is a solid range for building triceps strength and size with this exercise.

faq.question: Are dumbbell skullcrushers safe?
faq.answer: They're safe with a controlled range and appropriate weight. The main risk is losing control near your head, so start lighter than you think you need and build up once the movement feels stable.

faq.question: Skullcrusher or tricep extension, what's the difference?
faq.answer: They train the same muscle through a similar bending motion; the skullcrusher usually refers to the lying version done to a point near the head, while standing or overhead tricep extensions change the body position and the angle of stretch on the triceps.

faq.question: What can I use instead of dumbbells for skullcrushers?
faq.answer: An EZ-bar or straight barbell works for the same movement pattern and often feels more stable since both arms move together.

alternatives.name: Cable Rope Overhead Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Keeps constant tension on the triceps via the cable, useful if a bench isn't available.

alternatives.name: Machine Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: A guided path that removes the balance demand of holding two dumbbells overhead near your face.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Tricep Extension -Pronated Grip
easierVariations.reason: Done standing with more shoulder involvement for stability, an easier introduction to the same elbow-extension pattern.

harderVariations.name: EZ-Bar Skullcrusher
harderVariations.reason: A fixed bar lets you load more total weight and keeps both arms moving together through the same path.

summary: Atlas stones have you lifting a genuinely heavy, round stone off the floor by hinging down, hugging it tight against your torso, rolling it up onto your thighs, and standing to load it onto a platform. It's a classic strongman event that trains the lower back and hips as primary movers, with the biceps, forearms, glutes, hamstrings, quadriceps, and traps all sharing serious load. This is an expert-level lift, not a beginner exercise, and it demands real preparation before attempting it with heavy weight.
whyItWorks: A stone has no handles, no knurling, and no predictable shape to grip, which means every ounce of control comes from hugging it tightly against your body and using your entire torso as the gripping surface. That total-body squeeze, combined with a hip-driven lift and a roll into the lap that helps carry momentum upward, is what makes atlas stones one of the most complete strength tests in strongman training. The stone's awkward, shifting weight also demands constant core bracing throughout the lift, well beyond what a fixed-shape barbell or dumbbell requires.
setup: Position the stone in front of a loading platform at your target height.
Stand close with your feet outside the stone, hips back and chest lifted.
Wrap both arms fully around the stone, gripping underneath it before attempting to lift.
execution: Hinge down and hug the stone tightly against your chest and stomach.
Drive through your legs and hips explosively to break the stone off the floor.
Roll the stone up onto your thighs as you rise toward standing.
Use that momentum to help drive the stone further up your torso.
Extend your hips and legs fully to stand tall with the stone secured against you.
Load the stone onto the platform with control, setting it down rather than dropping it.
formCues: Hug the stone tight, no gaps.
Hips back, chest lifted on the pull.
Roll onto the thighs, don't muscle it straight up.
Load with control, every time.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace hard before the lift, exhaling forcefully as you stand and load the stone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the back during the initial hinge and pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your hips back and chest up before gripping the stone; a rounded spine under this kind of load is the single biggest risk in this lift.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attempting a stone heavier than your technique can currently handle.
commonMistakes.correction: Master the atlas stone trainer and lighter stones first; this is an expert-level lift that punishes attempting too much weight too soon.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the stone drift away from the body during the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the stone hugged tight against your torso throughout; distance from your body multiplies the strain on your lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the stone from height instead of loading it with control.
commonMistakes.correction: Place the stone onto the platform deliberately; a controlled load is part of the actual skill and protects both the platform and your form.

programmingNotes: Treat this as a low-rep, high-focus lift: 3 to 5 lifts per stone, with full recovery between attempts.
This belongs in a dedicated strength or strongman-style session, not tacked onto the end of unrelated training.
Only progress stone weight once the current one is fully controlled through the entire lift, from floor to platform.
Given the expert difficulty here, having an experienced coach or training partner watch your early attempts is strongly worthwhile.
safetyNotes: This is an expert-level, high-injury-risk lift if attempted with poor technique or too much weight. Build a strong deadlift and master the atlas stone trainer before attempting a real competition stone.
Never attempt a heavy stone alone the first several times; have someone experienced present to check your setup and technique.

faq.question: What muscles do atlas stones work?
faq.answer: The lower back and hips drive the lift, with the glutes, hamstrings, quadriceps, and traps powering the stand, while the biceps, forearms, and core work hard to hug and control the stone's awkward shape throughout.

faq.question: Are atlas stones safe for beginners?
faq.answer: No, this is an expert-level strongman lift. Beginners should build general strength with deadlifts and squats, then learn the specific technique on an atlas stone trainer before ever attempting a real, heavy stone.

faq.question: How do I avoid hurting my back doing atlas stones?
faq.answer: Hinge from the hips with a flat back, hug the stone tight against your body the entire lift, and never attempt a weight beyond what your technique can currently handle. A rounded back under a heavy, awkward load is the clearest path to injury here.

faq.question: Atlas stones vs deadlift: what's the difference?
faq.answer: A deadlift moves a fixed-shape barbell with clear handles and a predictable bar path. Atlas stones involve a round, handle-free object that must be hugged and controlled with your whole torso, which is why the skill and total-body demand are considerably higher.

alternatives.name: Keg Load
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar awkward-object lift and load with a keg instead of a stone.

alternatives.name: Axle Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Covers a similar total-body pulling demand with a thick bar instead of a round, handle-free stone.

easierVariations.name: Atlas Stone Trainer
easierVariations.reason: The grippier practice version of this exact lift, the recommended place to build the technique before a real stone.

easierVariations.name: Sandbag Load
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same hinge-hug-and-load pattern with a softer, more forgiving load.

summary: The cable rear delt fly has you stand between two low pulleys (or face a single one with crossed arms) and pull the handles out and back in a wide arc, targeting the rear third of your shoulder. It isolates a muscle that pushing exercises like bench press and shoulder press barely touch, and it suits anyone building shoulder health or working on posture.
whyItWorks: Your rear delts pull your arms backward and rotate your shoulders externally, the opposite job of the front delts that most pressing movements hammer. A cable keeps tension on that muscle through the entire arc, from the stretched position in front of your chest to the fully contracted position with your arms out to the sides, which a dumbbell fly loses at the top once gravity stops pulling on the weight.
setup: Stand between two low pulleys, or face a single low pulley with a handle attached.
Cross your arms so your left hand grabs the right-side cable and vice versa, or grab a single handle with the opposite hand across your body.
Stand tall with a slight forward lean and soft knees, arms extended in front of you at chest height.
execution: Pull both handles out and back in a wide arc, leading with your elbows.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together as your hands reach the sides of your body.
Pause for a moment at full contraction.
Return slowly to the starting position, letting the cables stretch your arms back across your chest.
Repeat for the set without letting momentum take over.
formCues: Lead the movement with your elbows, not your hands.
Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout the arc.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the back of the movement.
Control the return instead of letting the cables snap your arms forward.
breathing: Exhale as you pull the handles back and out, inhale as you let them return across your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning the fly into a rear delt row by bending the elbows and pulling like a row.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows only slightly bent and let your arms travel in a wide arc instead of tucking them toward your ribs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using so much weight that your torso swings to help start the pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until your torso stays still and your shoulder blades do the work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping the arc at shoulder height instead of finishing with your hands past your sides.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep pulling until your hands are level with or slightly behind your torso before you pause.

programmingNotes: This is a small, easily fatigued muscle group, so aim for higher reps, around 12 to 20, rather than chasing heavy loads.
Because the joint stress here is low, two to four short sessions a week tend to add up to more total work than one heavy session.
Pair it after your main pressing or pulling work, since fresh rear delts rarely need to lead a session.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light enough that your shoulder blades, not your neck and traps, do the pulling.
If you feel pinching in the front of your shoulder, narrow the arc and stop just before your hands cross the midline.
Avoid locking out your elbows at the start position under tension.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable rear delt fly should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 15 to 20 reps works well, since this small muscle responds better to volume than to heavy singles.

faq.question: What muscles does the cable rear delt fly work?
faq.answer: It isolates your rear deltoids, the back third of your shoulder muscle, with your middle back assisting to retract your shoulder blades.

faq.question: Can I do a rear delt fly without a cable machine?
faq.answer: Yes, a band rear delt fly or a bent-over dumbbell rear delt raise trains the same arc without a cable stack.

faq.question: Why does my upper trap take over instead of my rear delt?
faq.answer: That usually means the load is too heavy or you're shrugging as you pull. Drop the weight and keep your shoulders down and away from your ears through the whole arc.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Lying One-Arm Rear Lateral Raise
alternatives.reason: Trains the same rear-delt arc lying on a bench with a single dumbbell when a cable station isn't free.

alternatives.name: Bent Over Dumbbell Rear Delt Raise With Head On Bench
alternatives.reason: Adds head support on an incline bench for anyone whose lower back feels the standing bent-over version too much.

summary: The double kettlebell windmill has you hold one kettlebell locked out overhead while hinging sideways at the hips to reach the other kettlebell, or a light load, toward the floor with your opposite hand. It's less about moving heavy weight and more about controlling your torso and hips through a long, loaded side bend, which makes it a core and hip mobility exercise as much as a strength one. Because it demands real shoulder stability and hip control at the same time, it's best approached after you're comfortable holding a kettlebell locked out overhead on its own.
whyItWorks: Keeping one kettlebell locked overhead while you hinge sideways at the hips forces your obliques, deep core muscles, and shoulder stabilizers to work together to keep that overhead arm stacked and your spine from collapsing to one side. The sideways hip hinge itself is a hip mobility pattern most people rarely train, since most hinging happens straight forward and back rather than to the side. Holding a second load in the lower hand adds resistance to that hinge without changing the core demand of the overhead side, which is what makes the double kettlebell version more challenging than doing the movement with just one bell.
setup: Clean one kettlebell overhead and lock your elbow out, with your palm facing forward or slightly rotated.
Turn your feet out roughly 45 degrees on the side of the overhead arm.
Hold the second kettlebell, or a lighter weight, in your opposite hand hanging at your side.
execution: Keep your eyes on the overhead kettlebell throughout the movement.
Push your hips back toward the overhead side as you hinge sideways at the hips.
Let your opposite hand travel down toward the floor as your torso tips sideways, keeping the overhead arm locked and stacked.
Reach only as far down as you can control while keeping the overhead shoulder stable.
Reverse the hinge, driving your hips back under you to return to standing.
Keep the overhead arm locked out the entire rep, from start to finish.
formCues: Eyes stay on the overhead bell the whole time.
Hips hinge sideways, not the spine bending alone.
Overhead arm stays locked and stacked throughout.
Reach only as far as you can control.
breathing: Take a breath and brace before hinging down, exhale as you drive your hips back to return to standing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending mainly through the spine instead of hinging at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on pushing your hips toward the overhead side first, letting the torso follow rather than folding the lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the overhead elbow bend or the shoulder round forward as you reach down.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep watching the overhead bell and actively push it toward the ceiling throughout the hinge, resetting the rep if the elbow starts to bend.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching further down than your hip mobility currently allows.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent as soon as you feel your form or balance start to break down, even if that's a shorter range than you'd like.

programmingNotes: Because the load is usually light to moderate and the goal is control rather than maximal effort, 2 sessions a week of 3 to 5 slow reps per side fits well into most programs.
Master the single kettlebell windmill and a comfortable overhead lockout before adding the second bell in the lower hand.
Treat it as accessory or mobility work early in a session, since the balance and coordination demand is high and fades quickly with fatigue.
safetyNotes: Stop the rep immediately if the overhead shoulder starts to shake or the elbow bends; that's your body telling you the range or load has gone past what you can stabilize.
Build the hip hinge and overhead hold separately before combining them, since either one breaking down under load can pull you off balance.

faq.question: What muscles does the kettlebell windmill work?
faq.answer: Mainly the obliques and deep core muscles that control the side bend, along with the shoulder stabilizers holding the overhead arm locked out. It also opens up hip mobility in a sideways direction that most training rarely touches.

faq.question: Do I need to be flexible to do the windmill?
faq.answer: Some hip and hamstring mobility helps, but you only need to hinge as far as you can control. Reaching a shorter distance with good form and a locked overhead arm is more useful than forcing a deeper reach and losing control.

faq.question: Is the double kettlebell windmill harder than the single kettlebell version?
faq.answer: Yes. Holding a second kettlebell in the lower hand adds load to the hip hinge itself, on top of the shoulder and core demand of keeping the first bell locked overhead, so most people should master the single-bell version first.

alternatives.name: Weighted Ball Side Bend
alternatives.reason: Trains the same side-bending core control without needing a kettlebell locked out overhead.

easierVariations.name: Kettlebell Windmill
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same hip hinge and overhead hold with a single kettlebell, so you can focus on balance before managing a second bell.

harderVariations.name: Advanced Kettlebell Windmill
harderVariations.reason: Builds on the same hip-hinge-under-an-overhead-load pattern with a technique change that increases the balance and mobility demand further.

summary: The standing hip flexors stretch puts you in a split stance, one foot forward and one back, and has you tilt your pelvis to lengthen the front of the back leg's hip. It works the hip flexors and the upper quadriceps without needing to get down on the floor, which makes it convenient between sets, before a run, or during a desk break. Anyone who sits for long stretches of the day, or who feels a pinch at the front of the hip during squats and lunges, is a good candidate for it.
whyItWorks: Your hip flexors, including the portion of the quadriceps that crosses the front of the hip, work to lift your knee toward your chest with every stride and every step up a curb. Spending most of the day sitting holds that same group in a shortened position for hours, and when you finally stretch it, it has to relearn how to lengthen under its own tension. Tucking your back hip underneath you and squeezing the glute on that side tilts the pelvis backward, which opens the front of that hip joint and puts a direct stretch on the flexors without kneeling or using a mat.
setup: Stand in a long split stance, one foot well in front of the other, both feet pointing forward.
Bend your front knee slightly and keep your back leg straight, heel lifted.
Rest a hand on a wall or chair if you need help balancing.
Keep both hips facing forward rather than letting the back hip rotate open.
execution: Tuck your back hip underneath you by squeezing that glute and tilting your pelvis backward.
Shift your weight slightly forward into the front leg while keeping your torso upright.
Hold the position once you feel a stretch along the front of the back hip and thigh.
Breathe steadily without easing off the pelvic tuck.
Release slowly, then switch your stance to stretch the other side.
formCues: Tuck the back hip, don't just lean forward.
Keep your torso upright, not hinged at the waist.
Back knee straight, heel reaching back.
Hips square to the front, no rotating open.
breathing: Breathe slowly throughout the hold; exhale as you tuck the back hip a little deeper into the stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso forward instead of tucking the back hip under.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest upright and put the motion into rotating your pelvis backward, not folding at the waist.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the back hip rotate open to the side.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep both hips square to the front, as if you were about to walk straight ahead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through the hold instead of settling into it.
commonMistakes.correction: Give the position at least 20 to 30 seconds; hip flexors relax more slowly than smaller muscle groups.

programmingNotes: This is light enough to do daily, especially if you sit for most of the day or train your lower body often.
Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds and repeat two or three times per leg.
It pairs well before squats, lunges, or running, since tight hip flexors can tilt the pelvis forward and change how those movements feel.
safetyNotes: Keep the stretch at a steady pull rather than a sharp pinch at the front of the hip joint.
Use a wall or chair for balance if your front knee or ankle feels unstable in the split stance.

faq.question: How long should I hold the standing hip flexor stretch?
faq.answer: Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds and repeat two or three times per leg, breathing steadily the whole time.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch every day?
faq.answer: Yes, it's gentle enough for daily use, especially if you sit most of the day or train your lower body often.

faq.question: Why do I feel this more in my lower back than my hip?
faq.answer: Check that you're tucking the back hip under rather than arching your lower back forward; the stretch should come from the pelvis tilting, not from bending the spine.

faq.question: What's a deeper version of this stretch once it feels easy?
faq.answer: The intermediate hip flexor and quad stretch adds a deeper combined position once the standing version stops giving you much of a pull.

alternatives.name: On Your Side Quad Stretch
alternatives.reason: Stretches the same hip flexor and quad group lying on your side, useful if balancing in a split stance is uncomfortable.

easierVariations.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor
easierVariations.reason: Uses a kneeling base instead of a standing split stance, giving you the floor for balance while you learn the same pelvic tuck.

harderVariations.name: Intermediate Hip Flexor and Quad Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Builds on the same split stance with an added quad stretch once the hip flexor pull alone feels too mild.

summary: The Pallof press has you stand sideways to a cable machine, holding a handle at chest height, and press it straight out in front of you before pulling it back in. The cable is constantly pulling you to rotate toward the machine, and your job is to press and return without letting your torso twist at all. It's a core exercise built around resisting rotation rather than creating it, which makes it a useful counterpart to the twisting and crunching movements that make up most ab training.
whyItWorks: Most core exercises either flex your spine forward, like a crunch, or actively rotate it, like a twist. The Pallof press asks for neither: the cable pulls sideways toward the machine, trying to rotate your torso, and your abdominals, along with your chest, shoulders, and triceps as you press the handle out, have to resist that pull and keep your body facing forward the entire time. This kind of anti-rotation work trains your core's ability to stabilize your spine under an off-center load, which matters just as much for everyday movement and other lifts as the ability to flex or rotate on purpose does, and it's a demand that most standard ab exercises don't train directly.
setup: Set a cable pulley to roughly chest height and attach a handle.
Stand sideways to the machine, a few steps away, so the cable has tension pulling toward it.
Hold the handle with both hands at your chest, elbows tucked in.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart and brace your core before the first rep.
execution: Press the handle straight out in front of your chest, extending your arms fully.
Hold the extended position for a moment, resisting the cable's pull to rotate you toward the machine.
Pull the handle back in to your chest with control.
Keep your torso facing forward throughout the entire rep, not twisting toward or away from the machine.
Complete all reps on one side before turning around to face the other direction.
formCues: Press straight out, not at an angle.
Keep your hips and shoulders square to the front the whole time.
Resist the twist; don't let the cable turn your torso.
Move at a controlled pace on both the press and the return.
breathing: Exhale as you press the handle out, inhale as you pull it back to your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the torso rotate slightly toward the cable machine during the press.
commonMistakes.correction: Stand further from the machine or reduce the weight until you can press straight out without any twist in your hips or shoulders.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too close to the machine, so the cable angle pulls more downward or upward than sideways.
commonMistakes.correction: Position yourself far enough away, and at the right pulley height, that the cable pulls directly sideways toward the machine at chest level.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps instead of holding the extended position briefly.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause for a beat with your arms fully extended before pulling back in; that pause is where most of the anti-rotation demand happens.

programmingNotes: This works well anywhere in a core-focused block, and it's gentle enough to include as a warm-up activator before heavier lifts that need spinal stability, like squats or overhead presses.
Two to three sets of 8 to 12 reps per side is a reasonable range, since the hold at full extension adds time under tension beyond what the rep count alone suggests.
Increase the challenge by stepping further from the machine or adding weight, rather than by moving faster; speed defeats the point of an anti-rotation exercise.
safetyNotes: Keep the resistance light enough that you can press out without any twist; using the twist to help complete a rep trains the opposite of what this exercise is for.
Keep your knees soft and your stance stable, since a wobbly base makes it harder to isolate the anti-rotation demand in your core.
If you feel any twinge in your lower back rather than tension across your abdominals, lighten the load and check that your ribs aren't flaring open as you press.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of Pallof presses should I do?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 8 to 12 reps per side works well, with a brief hold at full extension on each rep to make the most of the anti-rotation demand.

faq.question: What can I do instead if the cable machine is busy?
faq.answer: A standing cable wood chop or cable Russian twist on the same machine trains similar core stability with more active rotation, a useful swap when you want the same equipment but a different challenge.

faq.question: Why do I feel my shoulders more than my core during the Pallof press?
faq.answer: Check that you're not pressing too heavy a weight or standing too close to the machine, both of which can shift the effort into your shoulders instead of asking your core to resist the rotational pull.

faq.question: How is the Pallof press different from a regular ab exercise like a crunch?
faq.answer: A crunch trains your core to move, curling your spine forward; the Pallof press trains your core to resist movement, keeping your torso still against a rotational pull, which is a different and equally useful skill.

alternatives.name: Standing Cable Wood Chop
alternatives.reason: Uses the same cable station to train rotational core control, a useful alternative if you want to challenge the same anti-rotation muscles through movement instead of a hold.

alternatives.name: Cable Russian Twists
alternatives.reason: Trains the same cable-resisted core stability with active rotation, a good option when you want more movement in the exercise.

harderVariations.name: Pallof Press With Rotation
harderVariations.reason: Adds a controlled rotation at the end of the press, so your core has to control movement instead of only resisting it.

summary: The close-grip triceps push-up moves your hands in under your chest, almost touching, so the elbows travel close to your ribs instead of flaring out to the sides. That narrow path shifts the emphasis from chest to triceps, making it one of the more direct bodyweight moves for building pressing strength through a full elbow lockout. It suits anyone who already owns a standard push-up and wants to add a triceps-focused variation to their routine.
whyItWorks: Elbow flexion and extension is the triceps' main job, and a push-up only trains it heavily when the elbows stay tucked near the torso rather than winging out. Bringing your hands close together forces exactly that path: the upper arm stays close to your side through the whole rep, so more of the work to straighten the elbow falls on the triceps instead of getting shared with the chest. The chest and shoulders still stabilize the shoulder blades and start the press off the bottom, but the last few inches to lockout become a triceps-dominant finish.
setup: Start in a high plank with your hands under your chest, index fingers and thumbs almost touching to form a diamond or narrow triangle shape.
Set your feet hip-width apart, toes tucked, legs straight.
Brace your core so your hips stay level with your shoulders, no sagging or piking.
Point your elbows back toward your feet rather than out to the sides.
execution: From the high plank, bend your elbows and lower your chest toward your hands, keeping the elbows tracking back along your ribs.
Descend until your chest is close to your hands or the floor, whichever your shoulders allow without pain.
Pause briefly at the bottom without letting your hips drop.
Press through your palms to straighten your elbows and return to the top.
Keep your torso rigid from shoulders to ankles through the entire rep.
Repeat for the set without letting the elbows flare wider as you fatigue.
formCues: Elbows skim your ribs, not your ears.
Hands close enough to form a diamond under your chest.
One straight line from shoulders to ankles the whole rep.
Drive through the palm to finish the lockout.
breathing: Inhale as you lower your chest toward your hands, then exhale as you press back up to lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare out to the sides like a standard push-up.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively pull the elbows in toward your ribs on the way down; if they keep flaring, widen your hand position slightly until you can control the path.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing the hands so close that the wrists have to bend at an awkward angle.
commonMistakes.correction: Leave a small gap between your thumbs and index fingers instead of touching them, and turn your fingers out slightly if your wrists feel strained.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag or pike up to make the rep feel easier.
commonMistakes.correction: Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs before you lower, and stop the set once you can't hold that line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only lowering a few inches instead of reaching a full elbow bend.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower until your chest is near your hands so the triceps work through their full range, even if that means doing fewer reps.

programmingNotes: Because the narrow hand position concentrates more force through a smaller set of muscles than a standard push-up, most people fatigue faster here; 3 sets of 6 to 12 reps once or twice a week, on non-consecutive days, is plenty to build strength.
Pair it with a pulling exercise like a row in the same session so your pushing and pulling volume stay balanced.
If your wrists ache before your triceps do, that's usually a sign to build up total push-up volume with a standard grip first.
safetyNotes: Stop if you feel sharp pain in the wrists or elbows rather than muscle fatigue; the narrow hand position increases wrist demand compared to a shoulder-width push-up.
Keep the elbows tracking back rather than flaring, since a wide elbow path under load places more strain on the shoulder joint.

faq.question: How many close-grip push-ups should I do per set?
faq.answer: Six to twelve clean reps is a solid working range. If you can't keep your elbows tracking close to your ribs past a certain rep, that's your real set limit for the day, not the number you were hoping to hit.

faq.question: Is the close-grip push-up better than a regular push-up for triceps?
faq.answer: It's more triceps-dominant because the narrow hand position keeps the elbows tucked through the whole range, while a standard push-up spreads the work across chest, shoulders, and triceps more evenly. Both are worth having in a routine.

faq.question: Why do my wrists hurt during close-grip push-ups?
faq.answer: Bringing the hands directly under the chest changes the wrist angle compared to a shoulder-width push-up. Try leaving a small gap between your hands instead of touching them, or angle your fingers outward slightly to find a more comfortable line.

faq.question: Can I do this push-up variation without any equipment?
faq.answer: Yes, it's a bodyweight movement done on the floor. If it's too hard at first, do the incline version with your hands raised on a step or bench instead.

faq.question: How is this different from a diamond push-up?
faq.answer: They train the same tucked-elbow, triceps-heavy path. Many people use the names close-grip and diamond interchangeably, though some prefer to keep a small gap between the thumbs and index fingers here rather than touching them directly, which is easier on the wrists.

alternatives.name: Tríceps Push Up
alternatives.reason: Trains the same chest-and-triceps combination with a slightly different hand placement, a good swap if the tight elbow position bothers your wrists.

easierVariations.name: Incline Push-Up Close-Grip
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the same narrow hand position but raises your hands on a bench or step, cutting the load until your triceps and wrists are ready for the floor.

harderVariations.name: Close-Grip Push-Up off of a Dumbbell
harderVariations.reason: Resting your hands on a dumbbell handle adds a few extra inches of range at the bottom, asking the triceps and chest to work through a deeper stretch.

summary: The machine bench press seats you in front of a fixed handle path, pressing forward to work the chest, with the shoulders and triceps assisting. Because the machine controls the bar path, it removes the balance and stabilization demands of a free-weight bench press, letting you focus purely on pushing. It's a strong entry point for anyone new to pressing movements, and a useful lower-fatigue alternative for experienced lifters on a day when a barbell bench isn't the priority.
whyItWorks: A barbell or dumbbell bench press asks your chest and triceps to move the weight while your shoulders, core, and grip work to keep the bar stable and on a straight path. Beginners often struggle less with chest strength than with that stabilization demand, which is where a fixed machine path helps: it sets the trajectory for you, so the resistance goes almost entirely into your chest, shoulders, and triceps doing the pressing. That makes it easier to learn the pressing motion itself before adding the extra skill of balancing a free weight.
setup: Adjust the seat height so the handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Sit back fully against the pad with your feet flat on the floor.
Grip the handles with your wrists stacked directly over your elbows.
Set a resistance you can press through a full range with control.
execution: Press the handles forward and slightly together, extending your arms.
Stop just short of locking your elbows out fully at the top.
Pause briefly at full extension.
Return the handles back toward your chest under control.
Keep your shoulder blades pulled back against the pad throughout the movement.
Repeat for the full set at a steady, even pace.
formCues: Shoulder blades stay pinned to the pad.
Wrists stack over the elbows, not bent back.
Stop just short of locking the elbows out.
Control the return, don't let the handles snap back.
breathing: Exhale as you press the handles forward, inhale as you return them toward your chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders round forward off the pad as you press.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulder blades pulled back and pressed into the pad for the entire set, even if that means using less weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Locking the elbows out hard at the top of every rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop just short of full lockout so the tension stays on your chest and triceps instead of resting on the joint.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting the seat too low, so the handles line up with the shoulders instead of the chest.
commonMistakes.correction: Adjust the seat until the handles sit level with the middle of your chest before starting the set.

programmingNotes: Three to four sets of 8 to 12 reps builds solid pressing strength, and because the machine removes the stabilization demand, most lifters can train this pattern twice a week.
It works well as a first pressing exercise for someone new to the gym, or as a lower-fatigue substitute for barbell bench press on a lighter training day.
Pair it with a pulling movement like a seated cable row in the same session to keep pushing and pulling balanced.
Increase the resistance once you can complete every set with a controlled tempo and a brief pause at full extension, rather than the last rep or two looking rushed.
safetyNotes: Adjust the seat height correctly before loading the machine; a poor setup can shift strain toward the shoulders instead of the chest.
Keep the weight at a level where your shoulder blades can stay pinned to the pad through the full set.

faq.question: How much weight should I start with on the machine bench press?
faq.answer: Start light enough to complete 10 to 12 reps with your shoulder blades staying pinned to the pad the whole set. Add weight gradually once that feels controlled.

faq.question: Machine bench press vs barbell bench press, which is better for beginners?
faq.answer: The machine is the easier entry point since it removes the balance and stabilization demands of a free bar, letting you focus on the pressing motion itself. The barbell version builds more overall stability and is worth learning once pressing form feels solid on the machine.

faq.question: How many sets of machine bench press should I do per week?
faq.answer: Two sessions a week of 3 to 4 sets each works well for most lifters, since the fixed path keeps fatigue relatively low compared to a free-weight press.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders hurt on the machine bench press?
faq.answer: This usually means the seat is set too low, putting the handles in line with your shoulders instead of your chest, or your shoulder blades are rounding forward off the pad. Raise the seat and keep your shoulder blades pulled back throughout the set.

faq.question: Does the machine bench press build as much chest as a barbell bench press?
faq.answer: It builds real chest strength and size, but the fixed path trains only one plane of motion, while a barbell or dumbbells let you adjust the pressing angle slightly and add the demand of stabilizing the weight yourself. Many lifters use the machine to rack up pressing volume without taxing their stabilizers as much, saving the barbell for days when that broader stability carryover matters most.

alternatives.name: Leverage Chest Press
alternatives.reason: A different plate-loaded chest press machine with a similar fixed pressing path, useful if the bench press station is taken.

easierVariations.name: Cable Chest Press
easierVariations.reason: Keeps a seated, guided pressing pattern but with a cable's lighter starting resistance instead of a plate-loaded stack.

harderVariations.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
harderVariations.reason: Removes the fixed path entirely, requiring you to balance and control two independent weights through the whole press.

summary: The lever incline chest press seats you at an upward angle and drives a pair of weighted arms forward and up, targeting the upper portion of the chest along with the front shoulders and triceps.
