Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting hang.
Keep your forehead resting on the pad throughout, resisting the urge to lift your head and check your form.
Repeat for the set with a light, deliberate tempo.
formCues: Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
Tilt the wrists slightly forward at the top, like pouring a jug.
Head stays down on the pad the whole set.
Light weight, full control on every rep.
breathing: Exhale as you raise the dumbbells out to the sides, inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using body momentum to fling the dumbbells up instead of raising them with the shoulders.
commonMistakes.correction: Lighten the dumbbells until the lift comes purely from squeezing the shoulder blades, with no swing at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the head off the pad partway through to check form.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the forehead down and trust the form cues instead of watching yourself mid-set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the traps take over and turning the raise into a shrug.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears through the entire range.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a weight too heavy to lift through the full arc.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the weight until you can complete the full range of motion on every single rep.

programmingNotes: This is a small, isolated muscle group working with light dumbbells, so it tolerates frequent training. Fitting it in 2 to 3 times across a training week, for 3 sets of 12 to 15 reps, builds rear delt size without much recovery cost.
It works best as an accessory near the end of a push or pull session, once your shoulders are already warm from heavier pressing or rowing.
Add weight in small jumps of a pound or two per dumbbell, since this muscle responds more to consistent volume than to heavy loading.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light enough that your neck stays relaxed against the pad; straining to hoist a heavier weight shifts tension into the neck.
If your shoulders start to ache partway through a set, that's a sign the load is too heavy for strict form, not a reason to push through.

faq.question: What's the point of resting my head on the bench for this raise?
faq.answer: It blocks your torso from swinging to help lift the weight, so the raise comes purely from your rear delts instead of momentum.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for rear delt raises?
faq.answer: Start light enough to complete 12 to 15 reps with a full, controlled arc every time. This muscle group grows from volume more than from heavy loading.

faq.question: What can I do without an incline bench?
faq.answer: A cable rear delt fly trains the same muscle standing at a cable station, using constant tension from the cable instead of a bench for support.

faq.question: Why do I feel this in my traps instead of my rear delts?
faq.answer: Your shoulders are likely shrugging up as you raise the weight. Keep them pulled down away from your ears and lighten the load if you need to.

faq.question: How is this different from a regular bent-over rear delt raise?
faq.answer: A regular bent-over version relies on your own core and lower back to hold the hinge steady, which lets a tired back sneak a little swing into the lift. Resting your forehead on the bench removes that variable entirely, so the exercise is more forgiving for beginners still learning to isolate the muscle.

alternatives.name: Cable Rear Delt Fly
alternatives.reason: Trains the same rear-delt raising pattern standing at a cable station, useful when no incline bench is free.

harderVariations.name: Seated Bent-Over Rear Delt Raise
harderVariations.reason: Removes the bench support under your head, so your own trunk has to hold the bent-over position while your rear delts do the raising.

summary: Flexor Incline Dumbbell Curls put you on an incline bench with your arms hanging straight down and slightly behind your torso. That position stretches the biceps at the bottom of every rep and takes your shoulders out of the movement, so the biceps do almost all of the lifting. It suits anyone who wants more biceps size or strength without turning the exercise into a shoulder or back move.
whyItWorks: On a flat bench or a standing curl, your arms hang at your sides and the biceps only lengthen to about where your torso ends. Lean back on an incline and your arms drop behind your body instead, which pulls the biceps into a deeper stretch before you curl a single rep. That extra stretch under load is what makes incline curls feel harder than a standing curl with the same dumbbells, and it's also why they tend to build noticeable size when you do them consistently. Because your back is pinned to the pad, there's nowhere for your shoulders or torso to help, so the biceps carry the whole rep.
setup: Set an adjustable bench to a 45 to 60 degree incline.
Sit back with your shoulder blades and head against the pad, holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Allow your arms to drop straight down, palms facing forward or slightly inward.
Keep your feet flat on the floor for a stable base.
execution: Brace your upper back against the pad and keep it there for the whole set.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending your elbows, keeping your upper arms still.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face your shoulders as you near the top.
Squeeze your biceps briefly at the top of the rep.
Lower the dumbbells slowly, resisting the weight the entire way down.
Let your arms return to a full hang behind your torso before starting the next rep.
formCues: Shoulder blades pinned to the pad the whole set.
Elbows stay put, only the forearms swing.
Full stretch at the bottom, full squeeze at the top.
Slow on the way down, that's where the size comes from.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbells up, inhale as you lower them back to the stretched position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward as the weight gets heavy.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the upper arms glued to your sides; if the elbows start traveling, drop the weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutting the bottom of the rep short instead of reaching a full stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the arms hang fully behind the torso before starting the next curl; that stretch is the point of the incline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a bench angle so flat that it turns into a standard curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Set the incline to at least 45 degrees so your arms genuinely hang behind your body.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and letting the dumbbells drop.
commonMistakes.correction: Count two to three seconds on the way down; the slow negative is where most of the growth happens.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps works well since the deep stretch makes heavy loads harder to control than on a standing curl.
Place it later in an upper body or arm session, after any pressing work, since fatigued shoulders don't limit this exercise the way they can a compound pull.
Twice a week is plenty for most lifters; this is single-joint accessory work, not a lift that needs daily practice.
Increase the dumbbell weight only once you can control the full stretch and the full squeeze on every rep, not just the first few.
safetyNotes: Skip a steep incline if it causes shoulder pinching at the bottom stretch; a slightly lower angle is fine.
Choose a weight you can lower under control; letting the arms drop into the stretch position can strain the front of the shoulder.

faq.question: How many sets of incline dumbbell curls should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps, twice a week, builds solid biceps size and strength for most lifters without overtraining a small muscle group.

faq.question: Incline dumbbell curls vs standard dumbbell curls, what's the difference?
faq.answer: The incline angle pulls your arms behind your torso, giving the biceps a deeper stretch at the bottom of the rep. A standing curl keeps your arms at your sides with a shorter range. Both work the biceps, but the incline version usually feels harder at the same weight.

faq.question: Can I do incline dumbbell curls without a bench?
faq.answer: Not really; the exercise depends on the incline pinning your torso back so your arms hang behind you. A standing or seated dumbbell curl is the closest substitute if you don't have an adjustable bench.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders hurt during incline curls?
faq.answer: A steep incline combined with a heavy weight can pull on the front of the shoulder during the deep stretch. Lower the bench angle slightly or reduce the weight until the bottom position feels comfortable.

alternatives.name: EZ-Bar Curl
alternatives.reason: Works the same biceps flexion pattern with a bar instead of dumbbells, handy when an incline bench isn't free.

alternatives.name: Cable Preacher Curl
alternatives.reason: Keeps the upper arm fixed and the biceps isolated using a cable station instead of a bench.

easierVariations.name: Dumbbell Bicep Curl
easierVariations.reason: A standing curl with the same equipment but a shorter range of motion, useful while you build control of the stretched position.

harderVariations.name: Concentration Curls
harderVariations.reason: Isolates one arm at a time with an even stricter path, once you can control both arms together on the incline.

summary: The cable rope overhead triceps extension has you face away from a high pulley, hold a rope behind your head with your elbows pointed forward, and extend your forearms up and forward until your arms straighten. It stretches your triceps at the shoulder as well as the elbow, and it suits anyone who wants to target the long head of the triceps more than a standard pushdown does.
whyItWorks: Your triceps' long head crosses both the elbow and the shoulder, so it only stretches fully when your arm is overhead. A pushdown keeps your arms at your sides the whole time and barely stretches that head, but an overhead extension loads the triceps at its longest length, a lengthened position that recruits more total muscle fiber than the shorter range a pushdown allows.
setup: Attach a rope to a high pulley and face away from the machine.
Hold the rope ends with an overhand grip and step forward until your arms are stretched overhead, elbows pointed forward.
Set your feet in a comfortable split stance for balance and keep your ribs down.
execution: Extend your forearms up and slightly forward until your arms are straight, spreading the rope ends apart at the top.
Pause briefly with your arms fully extended.
Bend your elbows to lower the rope back behind your head under control.
Repeat for the set, keeping your upper arms still throughout.
formCues: Keep your elbows pointed forward and still, only your forearms should move.
Spread the rope ends apart as your arms straighten.
Avoid letting your ribs flare or your lower back arch as you extend.
Lower under control instead of letting the rope yank your arms back down.
breathing: Exhale as you extend your arms overhead, inhale as you lower the rope back behind your head.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift out to the sides or swing forward and back.
commonMistakes.correction: Pin your elbows next to your head and keep them still, letting only your forearms travel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back and flaring the ribs to help finish the extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and keep your ribs stacked over your hips through the whole set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping short of full elbow extension at the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Straighten your arms fully at the top of each rep to get the full range this exercise is meant to load.

programmingNotes: Since this stretches the triceps under load, moderate reps in the 10 to 15 range with a controlled tempo work better than chasing heavy singles.
The long-head stretch position makes this a good exercise to place early in an arm session, before the triceps are fatigued from pressing work.
Twice a week is enough for most lifters, since the triceps already gets indirect work from bench press and overhead press variations.
safetyNotes: Stop the set if you feel pinching at the front of your shoulder rather than a stretch in your triceps.
Choose a rope length and stance that let you keep your elbows still, and adjust the pulley height if your elbows drift.
Avoid locking your elbows out aggressively at full extension.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of overhead triceps extension should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps with a slow tempo works well, since the stretched position under load is the point, not maximum weight.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and a cable triceps pushdown?
faq.answer: A pushdown keeps your arms at your sides and mostly misses the long head of the triceps, while the overhead position stretches that head fully and loads it through its longest range.

faq.question: Can I do this without a cable machine?
faq.answer: A dumbbell overhead triceps extension or a one-arm version with a single dumbbell trains the same overhead stretch without a cable stack.

faq.question: Why does my lower back feel this instead of just my triceps?
faq.answer: That usually means your ribs are flaring to help finish the rep. Brace your core, keep your ribs down, and reduce the weight until your triceps do the work alone.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell One-Arm Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead stretch one arm at a time without needing a cable station.

easierVariations.name: Cable Lying Triceps Extension
easierVariations.reason: Removes the overhead shoulder position and its mobility demand while still loading the triceps through a long stretch.

harderVariations.name: Sled Overhead Triceps Extension
harderVariations.reason: Uses a plate-loaded sled for a higher load ceiling once cable resistance stops being enough.

summary: The decline crunch is a bodyweight ab exercise done on a bench angled downward at the foot end, which lets gravity add resistance to the same spinal-flexion pattern as a standard crunch. Anchoring your feet at the top also lets your torso drop back further than a floor crunch allows, extending the range under load. It suits lifters who've outgrown a standard floor crunch and want more challenge before moving to weighted or cable versions.
whyItWorks: A floor crunch is limited by how far your torso can lower before your shoulders touch the ground, which caps how much range and resistance gravity can add. Anchoring your feet on a decline bench removes that floor, letting your torso extend further back before you curl forward, which lengthens the range of motion and makes gravity pull harder on your torso through more of the rep. That's why a bodyweight decline crunch feels noticeably harder than a floor crunch even though nothing but the bench angle changed.
setup: Set a decline bench to a moderate angle and hook your feet under the ankle pads.
Lie back with your hands lightly touching the sides of your head or crossed over your chest.
Let your torso extend back toward the bench without fully relaxing your abs.
Brace your core before starting the first rep.
execution: Curl your torso up and forward by contracting your abs, leading with your ribs rather than your chin.
Rise until your torso is roughly upright, or as far as feels controlled without straining your neck.
Pause briefly with your abs fully contracted.
Lower back down under control, extending only as far back as you can control without your abs going slack.
Keep tension on your abs at the bottom rather than resting fully.
Repeat for the set, keeping the same controlled range on every rep.
formCues: Curl from your ribs, not by yanking your head and neck forward.
Keep your hands light against your head, don't pull on your neck to help the crunch.
Control the descent instead of letting gravity drop your torso fast.
Stop the lower range at a point where your abs stay engaged, not fully stretched and relaxed.
breathing: Exhale as you curl your torso up, then inhale as you lower back down under control.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling on the neck with your hands to help curl up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your hands light against your head and let your abs do the lifting instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the torso back too fast at the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower with control and stop before your abs fully relax, keeping tension on the muscle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a decline angle that's too steep before you're ready.
commonMistakes.correction: Start at a shallow decline angle and increase it only once the movement feels controlled through the full range.

programmingNotes: As a bodyweight ab movement with added range, two to three sessions a week fits most training splits without excess soreness that bleeds into other core-dependent lifts.
Two to three sets of 12 to 15 reps is a solid target once you've mastered a standard floor crunch.
Once bodyweight decline crunches feel easy for that rep range, adding a light weight held to the chest is a simple next step before moving to a cable crunch.
safetyNotes: Avoid a decline angle steep enough that you feel strain in your lower back rather than your abs.
Keep the range controlled rather than letting your torso swing back fast, that shifts stress toward the hip flexors and lower back.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for decline crunches?
faq.answer: Two to three sets of 12 to 15 reps is a solid target once a standard floor crunch feels easy.

faq.question: Decline crunch vs regular crunch, what's the difference?
faq.answer: The decline angle removes the floor as a limit, letting your torso extend further back before curling forward, which adds range and lets gravity add more resistance than a floor crunch.

faq.question: Can I do decline crunches without a decline bench?
faq.answer: A regular floor crunch trains the same movement pattern without needing any equipment, just with less range and resistance.

faq.question: Why do I feel decline crunches in my hip flexors instead of my abs?
faq.answer: That usually means the torso is dropping back too far or too fast at the bottom, letting the hip flexors take over. Control the descent and stop before your abs fully relax.

alternatives.name: Reverse Crunch
alternatives.reason: Reverse crunches pull the hips toward the ribs instead of the ribs toward the hips, a useful substitute that still targets the rectus abdominis without a decline bench.

alternatives.name: Ab Crunch Machine
alternatives.reason: A seated ab crunch machine trains the same flexion pattern with a guided, back-supported path.

easierVariations.name: Crunches
easierVariations.reason: A flat-floor crunch trains the same spinal-flexion pattern without the added range and stability demand of a decline bench.

harderVariations.name: Weighted Crunches
harderVariations.reason: Holding a weight during the crunch adds resistance once bodyweight decline crunches stop being a challenge.

harderVariations.name: Decline Oblique Crunch
harderVariations.reason: Adding a rotation to the same decline position brings the obliques into the same range you've already built.

summary: The preacher hammer dumbbell curl combines the strict, momentum-free position of a preacher bench with a neutral, palms-facing grip instead of the usual underhand curl grip. That grip shift pulls your forearms into the lift alongside your biceps, so you build grip and forearm strength at the same time as arm size. It suits anyone who wants biceps work that also carries over to grip-dependent lifts like rows and deadlifts.
whyItWorks: A standard curl grip, palms facing up, puts almost all the tension on the biceps. Turning your palms to face each other, the hammer grip, shifts some of that tension onto the brachialis and the forearm muscles that control wrist and grip strength, since they now have to help stabilize the neutral wrist position under load. Pinning your arm to the preacher pad still removes any help from your shoulders or hips, so the biceps and forearms are left to do the entire rep on their own, just split between two muscle groups instead of one. That split is also why grip endurance for pulling exercises tends to improve faster from this version than from a standard curl, even when the biceps stimulus itself feels about the same.
setup: Set the preacher bench pad height so your armpits rest just over the top edge when seated.
Grip one dumbbell per hand, palms turned to face each other and thumbs pointed up.
Rest the backs of your upper arms flat against the pad before you start.
Keep your chest against the bench and your feet flat on the floor.
execution: Start with your arms extended and the dumbbells hanging just above the bottom of the pad.
Curl both dumbbells up while keeping your palms facing each other the whole way.
Squeeze at the top without letting your upper arms lift off the pad.
Lower the dumbbells slowly back to the starting position, resisting the whole way down.
Pause briefly at the bottom before starting the next rep.
formCues: Palms stay facing each other from top to bottom.
Upper arms stay pinned to the pad the entire set.
Control the lowering phase instead of letting the weight drop.
Keep your wrists neutral, not bending forward or back.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the dumbbells up, and inhale as you lower them back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rotating the wrists toward a regular curl grip partway through the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your palms facing each other from the first inch of the curl to the last; rotating the grip shifts tension away from the forearms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the upper arms off the pad near the top of the rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your armpits pressed against the pad the whole set; if you have to lift your arms to finish, drop the weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the dumbbells swing instead of moving in a straight, controlled line.
commonMistakes.correction: Move slowly enough that the dumbbells never gain momentum; a swinging weight means the muscle has stopped doing the work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutting the bottom of the range short.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your arms extend nearly straight at the bottom before curling back up to get the full stretch out of each rep.

programmingNotes: As a single-joint isolation move, two or three times a week fits well, including alongside other arm or pulling work.
Sets of 10 to 12 reps suit the muscle-building and grip-strength goals most lifters use this for.
Use a lighter weight than you'd use for a standard preacher curl; the neutral grip changes how the load pulls on your arm, and most lifters need to drop the weight a bit to compensate.
It pairs well after a heavier pulling exercise like rows, letting you finish training grip and forearms while your arms are already warm.
safetyNotes: Keep the range of motion controlled at the bottom; letting your elbows snap into full extension under load can strain the joint over time.
Choose dumbbells you can hold securely through the full stretch; a grip that slips at the bottom of the rep is how weights end up getting dropped.

faq.question: What's the difference between a preacher curl and a preacher hammer curl?
faq.answer: A regular preacher curl uses an underhand grip that targets mostly biceps. The hammer version uses a neutral, palms-facing grip that shares the work between your biceps and forearms.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of preacher hammer dumbbell curl should I do?
faq.answer: Two to four sets of 10 to 12 reps works well for building both arm size and forearm strength.

faq.question: Can I do this exercise with a barbell instead of dumbbells?
faq.answer: Not with a true neutral grip; a barbell forces your palms into a fixed position. Dumbbells or a rope attachment let each hand rotate to hold the hammer grip.

faq.question: Why do my forearms get tired faster with this curl than a regular preacher curl?
faq.answer: The neutral grip recruits your forearm muscles to help stabilize the wrist and dumbbell, so they fatigue alongside your biceps instead of staying mostly uninvolved.

faq.question: Should I train each arm separately on the preacher bench?
faq.answer: You can curl both dumbbells together or one at a time. Training one arm at a time lets you focus more closely on keeping the upper arm pinned and the tempo controlled.

alternatives.name: Cross Body Hammer Curl
alternatives.reason: Keeps the same neutral grip and forearm involvement in a standing, cross-body path when a preacher bench isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Hammer Curls
easierVariations.reason: A standing neutral-grip curl that allows some momentum, a good starting point before the preacher position removes that help.

summary: The chair upper body stretch has you sit tall and reach both arms forward and down, using a chair for a stable base while you lengthen through your shoulders. It's a quick way to open up rounded shoulders and a tight chest after sitting at a desk or driving for a while, and it takes no equipment beyond the chair you're already sitting in.
whyItWorks: Reaching your arms forward while rounding slightly through your upper back pulls your shoulders into a stretched position, taking them out of the hunched, forward-rolled posture most desks encourage. Because your biceps and chest cross the front of your shoulder joint, they lengthen along with it, which is why you feel the pull across your chest and down the front of your arms too. Sitting keeps your hips and lower back out of the movement entirely, so the stretch stays isolated to your upper body instead of turning into a spinal stretch.
setup: Sit toward the front edge of a chair with your feet flat on the floor.
Interlace your fingers in front of you, or hold your forearms if that's more comfortable.
Sit tall to start, with your spine long.
execution: Extend your arms out in front of you at shoulder height.
Round your upper back slightly and push your hands forward, away from your chest.
Let your chin drop gently toward your chest as your shoulders round forward.
Hold the reach for several seconds, feeling the stretch across your upper back and shoulders.
Release and sit back up tall.
Repeat for the desired number of holds.
formCues: Push through your hands, not just your shoulders.
Let your upper back round, don't force it from your neck.
Keep your seat planted and your hips still.
Breathe out as you reach into the stretch.
breathing: Exhale as you round forward and reach, then breathe normally while you hold before inhaling back to sitting tall.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears while reaching.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulders sliding down away from your ears as you push your hands forward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding only from the neck instead of the upper back.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the round come from between your shoulder blades, with your chin following naturally rather than leading.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through the hold without actually pausing.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold the reached position for a few full seconds so your shoulders have time to actually lengthen.

programmingNotes: This is a gentle static stretch with essentially no fatigue cost, so it's fine to do several times a day, especially during long stretches of sitting.
Three to five holds of 15 to 20 seconds each is plenty.
It works well as a quick desk break or as part of a cool-down after upper body training.
safetyNotes: Reach only as far as feels like a comfortable pull, not a sharp or pinching sensation.
If you have a shoulder injury, keep the reach shallow and stop if you feel any joint pain rather than just a muscle stretch.

faq.question: How long should I hold the chair upper body stretch?
faq.answer: About 15 to 20 seconds per hold, repeated three to five times, is enough to feel real relief through your shoulders and upper back.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch without a chair?
faq.answer: Yes, the same reach works standing, though sitting keeps your lower back and hips completely out of it, which is useful if you want the stretch isolated to your upper body.

faq.question: Why does this stretch help my chest too, not just my shoulders?
faq.answer: Rounding your shoulders forward while you reach pulls your chest into a lengthened position along with your shoulders, since the two work together whenever your arms move forward.

alternatives.name: Round The World Shoulder Stretch
alternatives.reason: Moves the same shoulders and chest through a full circular range instead of one fixed reaching position.

alternatives.name: Shoulder Stretch
alternatives.reason: Isolates one shoulder at a time across your body, useful if you want to feel a stronger stretch on one side.

summary: This quad stretch has you lie on your back with your hips at the edge of a bench or table, letting one leg hang off while gravity pulls the thigh down and the knee stays bent. It's a passive, low-effort way to open up the front of the hip and thigh, useful as a cooldown after squats or lunges, or simply to counter a day of sitting.
whyItWorks: The quadriceps cross both the knee and the hip, so a deep stretch needs the knee bent and the hip extended at the same time. Hanging one leg off the edge of a bench does exactly that: your body weight and gravity slowly pull the thigh into extension while the bent knee keeps tension on the muscle the whole time, without you having to actively hold the position with your own strength.
setup: Lie on your back on a sturdy bench or table with your hips right at the edge.
Pull your opposite knee firmly toward your chest with both hands and hold it there to keep your lower back flat.
Let the leg you're stretching hang off the edge, knee bent, foot pointing toward the floor.
execution: Relax the hanging leg completely and let gravity pull the thigh down toward the floor.
Keep pulling the opposite knee to your chest to stop your lower back from arching as the stretch deepens.
Hold the stretch for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing normally.
If you want more stretch, gently press down on the hanging thigh with your hand instead of forcing it with muscle.
Release slowly and switch sides.
formCues: Let gravity do the work, don't force the leg down.
Keep the opposite knee pulled in the whole time to protect your lower back.
Relax the hanging foot and calf completely.
Breathe normally instead of holding your breath through the stretch.
breathing: Breathe slowly and evenly throughout the hold, since tensing your breath tends to tense the hip flexors you're trying to relax.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the lower back arch off the bench as the leg hangs down.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep pulling the opposite knee firmly to your chest to flatten your lower back against the surface.

commonMistakes.mistake: Actively pushing the hanging leg down with muscle effort.
commonMistakes.correction: Let it hang loosely and rely on gravity, adding gentle hand pressure only if you want a bit more.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the release by swinging the leg off the bench.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower the leg back down slowly and support it with your hand before sitting up.

programmingNotes: Hold for 20 to 30 seconds per side, and repeat two or three times per leg if the hip still feels tight.
It fits naturally at the end of a lower-body session, since the muscle is already warm and the passive hold needs no extra effort.
Since it's a gentle static stretch, doing it daily is fine, especially on days after squats, lunges, or long periods sitting.
safetyNotes: Use a stable, sturdy surface at a height where your hips can sit right at the edge safely.
Ease off if you feel a pinch in the front of the hip instead of a stretch through the thigh; that usually means you've gone further than your hip flexor is ready for.
Skip added hand pressure if you have a knee injury, and stick to the passive hang alone.

faq.question: How long should I hold the on-your-back quad stretch?
faq.answer: 20 to 30 seconds per side is a good target, repeated two or three times if the front of your hip still feels tight.

faq.question: What can I use instead of a bench for this stretch?
faq.answer: A sturdy table, a bed edge, or even a step platform works, as long as your hips can rest right at the edge with the other leg free to hang.

faq.question: Is this stretch good for tight hip flexors from sitting?
faq.answer: Yes, since the hanging leg combines a bent knee with hip extension, which directly targets the muscles that shorten from long periods of sitting.

faq.question: On-your-back quad stretch vs standing quad stretch: which is better?
faq.answer: The standing version needs balance and some active grip strength to hold your ankle. This lying version is more passive, letting gravity do the work, which can suit beginners or anyone with balance concerns.

alternatives.name: On Your Side Quad Stretch
alternatives.reason: Stretches the same muscle lying on your side instead, useful when you don't have a bench or table edge nearby.

harderVariations.name: Quad Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Moves to a standing hold, which needs active balance and grip instead of letting gravity do the work.

summary: The round the world shoulder stretch takes your arm through a full, slow circle from your side to overhead and back, opening the shoulder joint through a wider range than a simple arm circle. It stretches the shoulders directly, with the chest and biceps getting pulled along for the ride as your arm travels behind and above your body.
whyItWorks: Moving your arm through a large, continuous circle takes the shoulder capsule through nearly its full range of motion in one smooth pass, rather than isolating just flexion or just rotation the way a single-plane stretch does. The chest and biceps lengthen naturally as your arm swings back and overhead, since both cross the front of the shoulder joint.
setup: Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart and your arms relaxed at your sides.
Pick one arm to start, keeping the other relaxed or resting on your hip.
Move slowly enough that you can stop anywhere in the circle without losing balance.
execution: Start with your arm hanging at your side, palm facing your leg.
Sweep your arm forward and up toward the ceiling, keeping it as straight as comfortable.
Continue the circle back and down behind your body as far as your shoulder allows.
Complete the circle by bringing your arm back to the starting position at your side.
Repeat for several slow circles, then switch directions and repeat on the other arm.
formCues: Keep the circle slow enough to control at every point.
Let your shoulder blade glide naturally instead of locking it in place.
Stop and reverse direction if you feel pinching rather than a stretch.
Keep your torso still so the movement stays in the shoulder, not the spine.
breathing: Breathe slowly and continuously through the whole circle rather than holding your breath at any point.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through the circle.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down enough to feel each part of the range, especially as your arm passes behind your body.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear throughout the circle.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulder relaxed and down, letting the arm do the moving instead of the shoulder hiking up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only doing a small forward circle.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the circle travel as far behind your body as is comfortable to get the full range of the stretch.

programmingNotes: This is a gentle mobility drill, so it works well daily, especially as a warm-up before upper-body training.
2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 slow circles per direction, per arm, is enough to open the shoulders without overdoing it.
Use it before overhead pressing or throwing movements to rehearse the full range you'll need.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement pain-free. A stretch sensation is fine, but sharp or pinching pain means the range is too large for today.
Go especially slow through the part of the circle where your arm passes behind your body, since that's where shoulders are most vulnerable.

faq.question: How many reps of the round the world shoulder stretch should I do?
faq.answer: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 slow circles per direction, per arm, is plenty for a daily mobility routine.

faq.question: What's the difference between arm circles and the round the world stretch?
faq.answer: Arm circles usually stay in front of the body in a smaller loop, while round the world takes the arm through a bigger circle that includes the range behind your body.

faq.question: Can I do this stretch every day?
faq.answer: Yes. It's gentle enough for daily use, especially as part of a warm-up before upper-body training.

faq.question: Why does my shoulder click during this stretch?
faq.answer: Occasional clicking without pain is common and usually harmless. If it comes with pain or catching, shrink the range of the circle and check in with a professional if it persists.

alternatives.name: Arm Circles
alternatives.reason: Works the same shoulder mobility with a simpler, front-facing circular path.

easierVariations.name: Shoulder Circles
easierVariations.reason: A smaller, slower circle builds shoulder mobility before working up to the fuller range of round the world.

summary: This version of the calf raise loops a resistance band under your feet, or anchors it under a fixed point, so pressing up onto your toes has to work against steady band tension instead of just bodyweight. It's a practical option when you're training away from a gym, and it still trains the same toe-point motion that machine and barbell calf work builds.
whyItWorks: Your calf's job is pointing your toes and lifting your heels, whether that's climbing a step or pushing off in a sprint. A band adds resistance to that motion without needing a rack, a machine, or free weights, and because band tension increases the higher you rise, it naturally loads the top portion of the raise harder, right where a lot of bodyweight-only calf raises start to feel too easy.
setup: Loop a resistance band under the balls of both feet, or anchor one end under a stable surface if using a single band.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding the free ends or handles at your sides.
Find a wall or support nearby if you want extra balance, though it isn't required.
execution: Press through the balls of your feet, rising up onto your toes against the band's pull.
Pause briefly at the top of the raise.
Lower your heels back down slowly, letting the band stretch you back toward the floor under control.
Repeat for the set, keeping your legs straight but not locked.
formCues: Rise straight up onto your toes rather than rolling your ankles to either side.
Keep tension on the band throughout, don't let it go slack at the bottom.
Pause at the top instead of bouncing straight back down.
Keep your knees soft and stacked over your ankles the whole set.
breathing: Exhale as you press up onto your toes, inhale as your heels lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the band go slack at the bottom of each rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep steady tension on the band throughout the range instead of resetting from zero every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rolling the ankles inward or outward while rising.
commonMistakes.correction: Press straight up through the balls of your feet, keeping your weight centered.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing through reps with quick, small pulses near the top.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and use the band's full available range on every rep.

programmingNotes: Calves tolerate frequent, light training well, so daily or near-daily band work is reasonable as long as the band stays light enough to avoid true muscle soreness.
Fifteen to twenty-five reps per set fits the light, portable nature of band resistance better than chasing low reps with heavy load.
Use it as a warm-up before machine or barbell calf work, or as a standalone session when you're training on the road without equipment.
safetyNotes: Check the band for nicks or wear before each use, a worn band can snap under tension.
Anchor any fixed end securely so it can't slip loose mid-rep.
Stop if you feel sharp pain in the Achilles rather than a normal muscular burn in the calf.

faq.question: How many reps of banded calf raises should I do?
faq.answer: Fifteen to twenty-five reps per set, for two or three sets, suits the lighter, portable resistance a band provides.

faq.question: Can I do this exercise every day?
faq.answer: Yes, calves recover quickly and a light band load is gentle enough for daily or near-daily work if you're not adding heavier calf training elsewhere.

faq.question: What's a good substitute if I don't have a resistance band?
faq.answer: A seated calf raise machine trains the same rise-onto-toes motion if one is available.

faq.question: Why don't I feel much from banded calf raises?
faq.answer: A band that's too light or slack at the bottom of the rep won't challenge the calf enough. Use a heavier band, keep tension on throughout, and slow the tempo down.

alternatives.name: Seated Calf Raise
alternatives.reason: Trains the same rise-onto-toes motion on a machine, useful when you don't have a band or a stable anchor point for one.

harderVariations.name: Calf Raise On A Dumbbell
harderVariations.reason: Standing on a raised edge instead of flat ground adds a deeper stretch and a balance challenge once band tension stops feeling like enough.

summary: Reverse preacher curls take the pronated, palms-down grip of a regular reverse curl and lock your upper arm against a preacher bench, removing any chance to swing the weight up. That strictness makes it one of the more demanding forearm and brachialis builders in the catalog, since the muscles doing the work can't get help from momentum or the hips. It suits lifters with some curling experience who already handle the standing reverse curl comfortably and want a stricter, more isolated version.
whyItWorks: The preacher bench fixes your upper arm at a set angle in front of your body, which removes the small backward lean and hip drive that sneaks into standing curls once fatigue sets in. With that cheat pattern gone, the brachialis and the brachioradialis and wrist extensors of the forearm, the muscles a pronated grip favors, have to handle the entire range on their own. The bottom of the movement also stretches those muscles more than the standing version does, which is a big part of why this variation feels harder for the same weight.
setup: Set the preacher bench pad height so your armpits rest just over the top edge when seated.
Load the EZ curl bar lighter than you would for a standing reverse curl; the strict position removes any assistance from momentum.
Take a pronated, overhand grip on the bar's angled grips, hands roughly shoulder width apart.
Rest your upper arms flat against the pad before the first rep, with the bar hanging at arm's length.
execution: Curl the bar upward by bending your elbows, keeping your upper arms pressed against the pad the entire time.
Keep your wrists flat as you lift; don't let them bend backward to compensate for grip fatigue.
Raise the bar until your forearms are close to vertical, without letting your upper arms lift off the pad.
Squeeze briefly at the top, feeling the tension across your forearms and the outer upper arm.
Lower the bar slowly, letting your arms straighten fully at the bottom since the pad supports the joint.
Reset your grip if it starts to slip before starting the next rep.
formCues: Upper arms glued to the pad.
Wrists flat, never bent back.
Full stretch at the bottom, controlled.
Lighter weight than the standing version.
breathing: Exhale as you curl the bar up, inhale as you lower it back to full extension.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the upper arms off the pad to help finish a rep.
commonMistakes.correction: If you need to peel your arms off the pad to complete the rep, the set is over; reduce the weight before adding more reps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare wide apart during the curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your grip roughly shoulder width and your elbows tracking straight up and down, not splaying outward as fatigue builds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bouncing out of the fully stretched bottom position.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause briefly at the bottom before curling back up. Bouncing shifts stress onto the elbow tendons instead of the muscles you're trying to train.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a weight that only allows a partial range of motion.
commonMistakes.correction: Drop the load until you can complete the full range from a dead stretch to near-vertical without cutting the bottom short.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 reps is enough; the strict, fully stretched position is more taxing on the elbow tendons than the rep count suggests.
Twice a week is a sensible ceiling for most lifters, since the deep stretch at the bottom needs more recovery time than a standing curl does.
Put it toward the end of an arm or pull session, after any heavier compound rowing or pulling work is finished.
If your elbows feel cranky the next day, switch to the standing reverse curl for a week before coming back to this version.
safetyNotes: Never bounce out of the bottom stretch; that jerking motion is a common way to strain the elbow tendons on a preacher bench.
If you feel sharp or pinching pain at the front of the elbow rather than muscle fatigue, stop the set and reassess your load or range.

faq.question: What muscles do reverse preacher curls work?
faq.answer: Mainly the brachialis and the forearm muscles a pronated grip favors, especially the brachioradialis, with the biceps assisting in a weaker, secondary role.

faq.question: How many reverse preacher curls should I do?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 controlled reps is a solid range, since the strict position and full stretch make this harder than it looks for a given weight.

faq.question: Why do reverse preacher curls feel harder than standing reverse curls?
faq.answer: The preacher bench removes any hip drive or backward lean you'd normally use to help the bar up, so the target muscles handle the whole range alone, including a deeper stretch at the bottom.

faq.question: My elbows hurt after reverse preacher curls; what should I check?
faq.answer: Look for two things: bouncing out of the bottom stretch, or a load too heavy for a full range of motion. Both put extra strain on the elbow tendons; lighten the weight and control the bottom before continuing.

alternatives.name: Reverse Cable Curl
alternatives.reason: Cable tension stays constant through the range instead of easing off near the top, useful if the preacher bench isn't free or your elbows want a break from the fixed angle.

easierVariations.name: Reverse Barbell Curl
easierVariations.reason: Standing without a preacher bench lets you use a touch of body English near the top, which is a gentler place to start than the fully locked, strict version.

summary: This variation takes the standard reverse fly and adds an external rotation at the top of each rep, turning the palms upward as the arms reach the sides. That extra twist brings the rotator cuff, specifically the muscles behind the shoulder that rotate the arm outward, into a movement that would otherwise train the rear deltoid alone. It's a step up from the plain reverse fly, built for lifters who want more direct rotator cuff work layered onto their rear delt training rather than a separate exercise for it.
whyItWorks: A plain reverse fly raises the arms out to the sides but doesn't ask the shoulder to rotate, so the infraspinatus and teres minor, the rotator cuff muscles responsible for turning the arm outward, get only light, incidental work. Adding an external rotation at the top of the raise, where the forearm turns so the palm faces up or forward, recruits those muscles directly alongside the rear deltoid. Combining both actions in one movement trains the rear shoulder's raising strength and its rotational control together, which is closer to how the shoulder actually has to stabilize during real pulling and throwing motions.
setup: Choose dumbbells lighter than you'd use for a plain reverse fly; the added rotation is a harder coordination task.
Hinge forward from the hips until your torso is close to parallel with the floor, with a soft bend in your knees.
Let the dumbbells hang below your shoulders with your palms facing each other and your elbows slightly bent.
Keep your neck neutral and your core lightly braced before the first rep.
execution: Raise both dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with your elbows as in a standard reverse fly.
As your arms approach shoulder height, rotate your forearms so your palms turn to face forward or slightly upward.
Finish the rep with your arms roughly level with your shoulders and your palms rotated, feeling the added tension across the back of the shoulder.
Pause briefly at the top of the combined raise and rotation.
Reverse the rotation first, turning your palms back to face each other as you begin lowering the dumbbells.
Lower the dumbbells back down along the same arc under control.
formCues: Raise first, rotate at the top.
Rotate the forearm, not just the wrist.
Small, controlled range throughout.
Reverse the rotation before lowering.
breathing: Exhale as you raise and rotate, inhale as you rotate back and lower the dumbbells.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rotating only at the wrist instead of turning the whole forearm.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the rotation come from the forearm and shoulder, not a quick flick of the wrist; a wrist-only twist skips the rotator cuff muscles this exercise is meant to train.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to combine the raise and rotation into one rushed motion.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down and treat it as two connected steps: raise the arms, then rotate at the top, rather than blending them into a single fast swing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a weight heavy enough that the rotation disappears under fatigue.
commonMistakes.correction: If the rotation stops happening by the last few reps of a set, the load is too heavy; drop the weight until you can complete every rep with the full turn.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too upright instead of hinging forward at the hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the same forward hinge as a standard reverse fly; standing tall removes the rear delt emphasis this movement depends on.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps is plenty, since the coordination demand of the rotation matters more here than raw volume.
Once or twice a week is enough, since this asks more precision from the rotator cuff than a simple raise and doesn't need high frequency to be effective.
Use it after your main shoulder or pulling work, when you have the focus left to control the rotation cleanly instead of rushing through it.
If your rotator cuff already gets direct work elsewhere in your program, this can replace a plain reverse fly rather than being added on top of it.
safetyNotes: Keep the weight light enough that you never feel a pinch or catch at the front or back of the shoulder during the rotation.
Stop the exercise if the rotation causes any sharp or clicking sensation rather than normal muscle fatigue, and check your range and load before continuing.

faq.question: What does adding external rotation to a reverse fly change?
faq.answer: It brings the rotator cuff muscles, mainly the infraspinatus and teres minor, into a movement that would otherwise train the rear deltoid alone, combining raising strength with rotational control.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for this exercise?
faq.answer: Go lighter than your plain reverse fly weight. The rotation is a coordination challenge first, and a heavy load usually makes the rotation disappear under fatigue.

faq.question: Reverse fly vs reverse fly with external rotation: which should I do?
faq.answer: Start with the plain reverse fly to build the raising pattern, then add the rotation once that feels controlled, since it layers rotator cuff work on top of the same base movement.

faq.question: Why does my shoulder feel a slight pinch during the rotation?
faq.answer: That usually means the weight is too heavy or the range of motion is too large for now. Lighten the load and shorten the rotation slightly, and stop the exercise if the sensation continues.

alternatives.name: Cable Rear Delt Fly
alternatives.reason: A plain cable rear delt fly still trains the rear shoulder directly if adding a rotation feels like too much to coordinate for now.

easierVariations.name: Reverse Flyes
easierVariations.reason: Dropping the rotation at the top and just raising the arms out to the sides is simpler to learn before adding a second motion on top of it.

summary: The 3/4 sit-up curls your torso most of the way toward your knees, stopping just short of a full sit-up, using your abdominals through a longer range than a crunch while asking less of your hip flexors than the last stretch of a complete sit-up. It's a middle-ground option: more demanding than a crunch, gentler than a full sit-up, and a sensible place to build toward the complete range.
whyItWorks: As your torso rises off the floor during a sit-up, the abdominals do most of the early work, but the final quarter, where your torso approaches vertical, increasingly relies on the hip flexors to finish the job. Stopping at three quarters keeps the movement in the range where your abs are doing the heaviest lifting, which is often exactly what someone wants if they're building ab strength without wanting the hip flexors to dominate the exercise. It's a practical middle step for anyone whose full sit-up feels more like a hip flexor exercise than an ab one.
setup: Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Cross your arms over your chest or lightly support your head with your fingertips, without pulling on your neck.
Brace your core lightly before the first rep.
execution: Curl your chest up and forward toward your knees, leading with your upper abs.
Continue rising until your torso is roughly three quarters of the way toward vertical.
Pause briefly at that point, feeling the tension across your abdominals.
Lower your torso back down with control, keeping the movement smooth.
Stop just before your shoulder blades touch the floor and begin the next rep.
Keep your feet planted throughout; don't let them lift as you curl up.
formCues: Curl, don't yank the neck.
Stop at three quarters, not full sit-up height.
Feet planted the whole rep.
Smooth up, smooth down.
breathing: Exhale as you curl up, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Yanking the head and neck forward to help the torso rise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your fingertips light against your head, and let your abs lead the movement rather than your neck muscles.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the feet lift off the floor as the torso curls up.
commonMistakes.correction: Press your heels down actively throughout the rep; lifting feet is often a sign the abs are fatiguing and other muscles are compensating.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum to swing up instead of a controlled curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down; a controlled 3/4 curl trains more than a fast, momentum-driven one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing back down and letting the torso drop rather than lowering with control.
commonMistakes.correction: Control the descent just as deliberately as the rise; the lowering phase is doing real work too.

programmingNotes: Start with 2 or 3 sets of 10 to 15 reps, two or three days a week.
Use it as a stepping stone toward the full sit-up, or keep it as your regular ab movement if you prefer less hip flexor involvement.
Progress by adding a brief pause at the top of the range before moving to the full sit-up or a resisted version.
Pairs well with a lower-ab move like the reverse crunch to train the abdominal wall from both ends.
safetyNotes: If your neck strains, support your head lightly with your fingertips rather than pulling it forward with your hands.
If your lower back arches at any point, shorten the range slightly until your core control catches up.

faq.question: What's the difference between a 3/4 sit-up and a full sit-up?
faq.answer: A full sit-up brings your torso all the way to vertical, relying more on the hip flexors in that final stretch. The 3/4 version stops short of that point, keeping more of the work on the abdominals throughout the range.

faq.question: How many 3/4 sit-ups should I do?
faq.answer: Ten to fifteen controlled reps, for 2 or 3 sets, is a reasonable starting point. Prioritize a smooth, controlled curl over a high rep count.

faq.question: Why does my neck hurt during sit-ups?
faq.answer: Usually the hands are pulling the head forward to help the torso rise. Rest your fingertips lightly against your head instead, and let your abdominals do the lifting.

faq.question: Is a 3/4 sit-up better than a full sit-up for beginners?
faq.answer: For many beginners, yes: it trains the abs through a solid range while asking less of the hip flexors than the final stretch of a full sit-up, which some people find less controlled early on.

alternatives.name: Crunches
alternatives.reason: A shorter-range version that stops even earlier, useful if the 3/4 range still strains your neck or back.

alternatives.name: Janda Sit-Up
alternatives.reason: Covers the same upper-ab curling motion with a specific heel-drive technique to reduce hip flexor involvement.

easierVariations.name: Reverse Crunch
easierVariations.reason: Keeps the range small and curls the hips instead, an easier way to build ab control before a fuller sit-up.

harderVariations.name: Sit-Up
harderVariations.reason: Completes the last quarter of the range, taking your torso all the way up to your knees.

harderVariations.name: Weighted Sit-Ups - With Bands
harderVariations.reason: Adds resistance to the same curling motion once bodyweight reps stop being enough of a challenge.

summary: This is a lying triceps move where you lower a close-grip barbell in a slight arc toward your chin, rather than straight down to your forehead the way a standard skull crusher does. That small change in bar path pulls your elbows forward a few degrees as you lower, turning it into a hybrid between a triceps extension and a press. It's an intermediate isolation exercise for anyone who already owns clean skull-crusher technique and wants a variation that stresses the triceps a bit differently.
whyItWorks: A pure skull crusher keeps the upper arms fixed and hinges only at the elbow, which isolates the triceps almost completely. Aiming the bar toward your chin instead of your forehead lets your elbows travel forward slightly during the descent, adding a small pressing component to the movement. That shift changes the angle of resistance through the range, which is why lifters use it as a change of pace once the standard version stops feeling challenging.
setup: Lie flat on a bench with your feet planted on the floor and your lower back settled against the pad.
Grip an EZ-bar with hands close together, arms extended straight up over your upper chest.
Keep a spotter nearby if you're using a weight that challenges your last few reps.
Set your shoulder blades back and down before the first rep.
execution: Start with the bar locked out above your upper chest.
Bend your elbows and let them drift forward slightly as you lower the bar in an arc toward your chin.
Stop the bar a few inches from your chin, keeping tension on the triceps rather than resting the weight.
Reverse the arc, pressing the bar back up and slightly back to the starting position.
Lock out just short of your elbows snapping fully straight.
Repeat for the set, keeping the same arc on every rep.
formCues: Let the elbows drift forward on purpose, this isn't a fixed-elbow skull crusher.
Stop the bar short of touching your chin.
Press back up along the same arc you lowered on.
Keep your wrists straight, not bent back under the bar.
breathing: Inhale as you lower the bar toward your chin, exhale as you press it back to the starting position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows travel so far forward that it turns into a close-grip bench press.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the elbow drift small and deliberate, just enough to aim the bar at your chin instead of your forehead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the bar quickly toward the chin instead of controlling the descent.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the lowering phase down and use a weight you can stop at any point along the arc.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows out wide instead of tracking them forward and in.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your elbows narrow and pointed toward your chin throughout the rep.

programmingNotes: Once a week as a triceps isolation move fits well for most lifters, since it follows heavier pressing work rather than replacing it.
3 sets of 8 to 12 reps is a reasonable range once your bar path is consistent rep to rep.
Pair it with a pushing session where your shoulders and chest are already warmed up from earlier pressing.
safetyNotes: Keep a spotter within reach for working sets, since the bar travels close to your face and neck.
Use a weight you can fully control through the arc; a bar that gets away from you near your chin is a real risk.
Stop if you feel wrist strain and check that your grip isn't letting the bar roll back into your wrists.

faq.question: How many sets and reps for the lying close-grip barbell triceps press to chin?
faq.answer: Three sets of 8 to 12 reps, once a week as part of a push or arm day, works well since it's a triceps isolation move rather than a primary strength lift.

faq.question: Is this the same as a skull crusher?
faq.answer: It's closely related but not identical. A skull crusher keeps the upper arms fixed and lowers the bar to the forehead in a straight hinge, while this variation lets the elbows drift forward a bit so the bar arcs toward the chin instead.

faq.question: What can I use instead if a barbell hurts my wrists?
faq.answer: A cable lying triceps extension keeps the same lying position and steady resistance without locking your wrists into a fixed bar grip.

faq.question: Press to chin vs regular skull crusher: which should I pick?
faq.answer: Both train the triceps well. Start with the standard skull crusher to learn a clean elbow hinge, then try the press-to-chin version once that feels solid, as a way to vary the angle of resistance.

alternatives.name: Lying Triceps Press
alternatives.reason: Covers the same close-grip lying triceps pattern with an EZ-bar, useful as a near-identical swap.

alternatives.name: Cable Lying Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the triceps lying down with steady cable resistance instead of a bar, which can be easier on the wrists.

easierVariations.name: EZ-Bar Skullcrusher
easierVariations.reason: Uses a straight elbow hinge to the forehead instead of the angled path to the chin, which is a simpler motion to learn.

harderVariations.name: JM Press
harderVariations.reason: Blends the same elbow-hinge path with an actual press lockout, asking for more coordination between the two motions.

summary: The reverse band box squat combines a box squat, where you sit back to a box before standing, with bands anchored overhead that pull up on the bar. That upward pull removes weight from the bar right as you're seated on the box, then hands the full load back as you drive up to standing. It lets a lifter handle more total weight while training explosive drive off the box, both staples of powerlifting technique work.
whyItWorks: A box squat already trains you to sit back onto a fixed point and drive up from a dead stop, which builds explosive hip drive and removes any bounce out of the bottom. Reverse bands add another layer on top of that: because the bands stretch furthest when you're seated on the box, they pull hardest there, taking weight off the bar during the most demanding part of the lift. As you drive up and the bands shorten, more of the loaded weight returns to the bar, right where your quads, glutes, and lower back are in their strongest position to finish the rep. Training that top-end push against a heavier load builds the kind of drive that carries over to a bigger squat off the floor.
setup: Anchor bands to a secure point at the top of a power rack or monolift and loop the other ends around the bar, matched evenly on each side.
Set a box or bench behind you at a height that lets your hip crease reach just at or below your knee.
Load the bar so that even with the bands pulling up, you can stand up with the full weight.
Set up under the bar as you would for a normal squat, with a stable, shoulder-width stance.
execution: Unrack the bar with the bands already under tension.
Sit back toward the box, keeping your shins close to vertical and your chest up.
Touch the box lightly without relaxing your hips or bouncing off it.
Drive up hard through your heels, accelerating as the bands take less of the load.
Stand fully tall, hips and knees locked out, before resetting for the next rep.
formCues: Sit back and down rather than squatting straight down, so your hips reach the box first.
Keep your core braced through the touch on the box, not just during the standing portion.
Push the floor away through your whole foot as you drive up, not just your toes.
Keep the bar path vertical over your midfoot throughout the rep.
Use the same stance width and bar position you use in a regular squat so the pattern still carries over.
breathing: Take a full breath and brace before unracking the bar, hold it through the sit-back and the box touch, then exhale once you've stood up to lockout.

commonMistakes.mistake: Relaxing the hips or bouncing off the box between the sit-back and the drive up.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your core and hips braced through the touch, treating it as a brief pause, not a rest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting uneven band tension pull the bar off center.
commonMistakes.correction: Match the band thickness and anchor height on both sides so the load stays balanced.

commonMistakes.mistake: Squatting straight down instead of sitting back toward the box.
commonMistakes.correction: Push your hips back first, as though reaching for a chair slightly behind you.

programmingNotes: This is an advanced overload technique best used once a week, typically on a max-effort or speed squat day.
Sets of two to five reps suit the strength and drive-off-the-box focus here, rather than higher-rep volume work.
Cycle it in blocks of a few weeks at a time, since the nervous system responds fastest to this kind of new stimulus early in a training block.
Track how confident the drive off the box feels alongside the bar weight, since the goal is a faster, more decisive standing phase, not just a heavier number.
safetyNotes: Have a spotter or safety pins set at an appropriate height, since the bar can be loaded heavier than your regular squat max.
Check band anchors, hooks, and box stability before every session.
Build a solid box squat and regular squat technique first before adding band-assisted overload.

faq.question: How much weight should I load for a reverse band box squat?
faq.answer: Many lifters load somewhat more than their regular box squat max, since the bands remove weight near the box. Start conservatively and let how the bottom position feels guide the load.

faq.question: What's the difference between reverse bands and regular bands on a box squat?
faq.answer: Regular bands anchor to the floor and add resistance as you stand, making the top of the squat harder. Reverse bands anchor overhead and pull up on the bar, taking weight off near the box and returning full weight as you stand.

faq.question: Do I need a box for this exercise or can I just squat?
faq.answer: The box is part of what makes this movement work. It gives you a consistent depth and a dead stop that removes stretch reflex bounce, both of which the reverse band setup is designed to train against.

faq.question: Is reverse band box squat good for beginners?
faq.answer: No. It's meant for lifters who already have solid box squat technique. Build that foundation first before adding band overload.

alternatives.name: Box Squat with Bands
alternatives.reason: Uses straight bands instead of a reverse-band setup, adding resistance near the top of the squat rather than removing it near the box.

easierVariations.name: Box Squat
easierVariations.reason: Drops the band assistance so you learn to sit back onto the box and drive up under the bar's full, unassisted weight first.

harderVariations.name: Box Squat with Chains
harderVariations.reason: Flips to the opposite resistance curve, adding load as you stand instead of removing it near the box, for lifters ready to chase strength through both directions.

summary: The knee/hip raise on parallel bars is a supported ab exercise done on a dip station or captain's chair, where you rest your forearms on the pads and lift your knees toward your chest by curling your pelvis. Because your forearms carry your weight instead of your hands, it's often a more approachable entry point into hanging-style ab work than a fully hanging leg raise, while still training the same lower abdominal region.
whyItWorks: Lifting the knees toward the chest from a hanging or supported position requires the abdominals to curl the pelvis upward against the pull of gravity on the legs, rather than just holding a static brace. Supporting your forearms on pads removes the grip and shoulder-stabilization demand of a fully hanging variation, which lets you focus the effort more directly on that pelvic curl instead of splitting attention between your grip and your abs. The longer your legs stay extended during the lift, the longer the lever your abs have to control, which is why bending the knees on the way up, rather than raising straight legs, makes the movement more approachable for most people while still asking the abdominals to do real work.
setup: Position yourself in the parallel bar or captain's chair station, resting your forearms on the pads and gripping the handles.
Let your body hang with your back against the pad and your torso upright.
Let your legs hang straight down to start, with a slight brace through your core.
execution: Brace your core before starting the movement.
Curl your pelvis and lift your knees up toward your chest.
Continue lifting until your thighs sit level with your hips, or as high as you can control.
Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
Lower your legs back down slowly until they're straight again.
Repeat without using momentum to swing into the next rep.
formCues: Curl the pelvis, don't just swing the legs.
Keep your back pressed against the pad.
Pause briefly at the top before lowering.
Control the descent instead of dropping the legs.
breathing: Exhale as you curl your knees up, inhale as you lower your legs back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swinging the legs using momentum instead of curling the pelvis.
commonMistakes.correction: Pause and reset between reps if you notice your body swinging, and slow the tempo down until the movement comes from your abs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back and shrugging the shoulders up to compensate.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulders down away from your ears and your back flat against the pad throughout the set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only lifting the knees a small amount without curling the pelvis at all.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on tilting your hips up, not just bending your knees; the pelvic curl is what makes this an ab exercise rather than a hip flexor one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Gripping the handles so hard that the forearms fatigue before the abs do.
commonMistakes.correction: Rest your forearms into the pads and let them carry your weight, keeping your hand grip light rather than white-knuckled.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 8 to 12 controlled reps is a solid working range for most people.
Place it toward the end of a core or upper body session, since your forearms and shoulders will already be doing some stabilizing work.
Because it's a bodyweight ab isolation move rather than a heavy compound lift, training it two to three times a week fits most programs without much recovery concern.

Once 12 controlled reps feel easy, extend the legs a little straighter on each rep before adding external ankle weight; a longer lever is a simpler progression than rushing to full straight-leg raises.
safetyNotes: Stop swinging and reset your position if you feel strain building in your lower back rather than your abs.
Lower your legs with control rather than letting them drop and jerk at the bottom of the range.
If your shoulders start to ache mid-set, that's usually a sign your torso is sagging away from the pad rather than staying upright.

faq.question: What muscles does the knee/hip raise on parallel bars work?
faq.answer: It mainly targets the abdominals, especially the lower portion, by curling the pelvis up toward the ribs.

faq.question: How is this different from a hanging leg raise?
faq.answer: The parallel bar version supports your forearms so your grip doesn't fatigue as quickly, letting you focus more directly on the ab curl. A hanging leg raise demands grip and shoulder stability on top of that same abdominal work.

faq.question: How many reps should I do?
faq.answer: Eight to twelve controlled reps for two or three sets is a reasonable starting point.

faq.question: What can I do if I don't have access to a parallel bar station?
faq.answer: A reverse crunch on the floor trains a similar pelvis-curling motion without needing any equipment.

faq.question: Should my knees stay bent or straight during this exercise?
faq.answer: Bent knees are the standard, more approachable version. Straightening your legs increases the demand on your abs significantly, so save that for once bent-knee reps feel controlled and easy.

alternatives.name: Flat Bench Lying Leg Raise
alternatives.reason: Works the lower abdominals through a similar pelvis-curl pattern using just a bench, no parallel bar station required.

easierVariations.name: Reverse Crunch
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same pelvis-curling motion lying on the floor, with no need to support your bodyweight on your arms.

harderVariations.name: Hanging Leg Raise
harderVariations.reason: Removes the forearm pads, so your grip and shoulders now have to stabilize your whole bodyweight while your abs do the same lift.

summary: The chest push from a 3 point stance has you kneel on one leg, hold a medicine ball at your chest, and throw it explosively forward against a wall or to a partner. Taking your legs out of the equation forces your chest, shoulders, and triceps to generate the throw on their own, which makes it a useful first step into explosive medicine ball training before you add a standing base or a run. It suits anyone building upper body push power for sports, or just wanting a fast, satisfying way to train chest strength.
whyItWorks: Kneeling on one leg removes your legs from the movement, so the throw comes almost entirely from your chest, shoulders, and triceps extending forcefully at the same time, the same muscles that drive a bench press or push up but trained here for speed instead of load. Your abdominals brace hard through your torso to keep you upright and stop your hips from swaying as you throw, since there is no wide standing base to anchor you. Because the ball leaves your hands, the exercise trains how fast you can produce force, not just how much force you can produce, which is a different quality than a slow, controlled chest press builds. Your triceps specifically handle the final part of the extension, straightening your elbows through the last few inches of the throw, which is why they tend to feel this drill even more directly than a standard push up.
setup: Kneel on one knee with your other foot planted in front, like a lunge position, facing a solid wall or a partner a few steps away.
Hold a medicine ball at chest height with both hands, elbows out to the sides.
Brace your core so your torso stays upright and still.
execution: Pull the ball in slightly toward your chest to load the throw.
Extend your arms explosively, pushing the ball forward and away from your chest.
Release the ball at full arm extension.
Catch the rebound off the wall, or receive the pass back from your partner.
Absorb the catch by letting your elbows bend, then reset the ball at your chest.
Repeat for the desired number of reps before switching your kneeling leg.
formCues: Keep your torso upright, the throw shouldn't rock you backward.
Push through full arm extension on every rep.
Brace your abs before each throw, not after.
Land the catch soft, let your elbows absorb the ball.
breathing: Exhale sharply as you extend and release the ball, then inhale as you catch and reset.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning back to try to generate more throwing force.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your torso stacked and upright, let your chest and arms do the work instead of using body lean for momentum.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the ball with stiff, locked elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your elbows bend as the ball arrives so you absorb the catch instead of jarring your joints.

commonMistakes.mistake: Kneeling too close to the wall to get a real extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Kneel far enough back that your arms fully extend before the ball reaches the wall.

commonMistakes.mistake: Switching kneeling legs mid-set instead of finishing one side first.
commonMistakes.correction: Complete all reps on one kneeling leg before switching, alternating mid-set makes it hard to tell whether one side is genuinely weaker.

programmingNotes: Three sets of 5 to 6 explosive throws per side is plenty. This is a power drill, not a conditioning one, so extra reps just teach you to throw slower.
Twice a week is enough, since what limits how often you should do this is your ability to stay genuinely explosive, not muscle soreness from the light implement.
Do it early in a session while you're fresh, and rest fully between throws rather than rushing into the next one.
If one kneeling side throws noticeably weaker or less controlled than the other, spend an extra set on that side rather than automatically matching volume between them.
safetyNotes: Use a medicine ball with some bounce, not a hard slam ball, so it rebounds predictably off the wall.
Pad your kneeling knee on a hard floor, and keep enough distance from the wall that a mistimed throw doesn't bounce straight back into your face.

faq.question: How many chest push reps from a 3 point stance should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of 5 to 6 explosive throws per side is a solid amount. End a set once the throws start feeling slower, since the point is speed, not fatigue.

faq.question: Can I do this chest push without a wall?
faq.answer: Yes, a partner standing a few steps away can catch and return the ball instead of a wall, which also lets you both work on catching and absorbing force.

faq.question: What's the difference between the 3 point stance chest push and the standing version?
