It trains the same pressing muscles as a bench press, but asks them to produce force fast enough to send a ball flying instead of just moving a bar. Because you need a partner or a wall to catch the ball, this is best done as a conditioning or power drill rather than a solo strength exercise, and it shows up most often in athletic warm-ups and sport-specific conditioning circuits.
whyItWorks: Throwing a medicine ball straight up from your chest trains the same triceps, chest, and shoulder muscles as a bench press, but the ball leaving your hands means you cannot slow down at the top the way you naturally would with a barbell. That forces your pressing muscles to produce their peak force as fast as possible, which builds explosive pressing power that a controlled lift does not train on its own.
setup: Lie on your back on the floor or a bench with your feet planted and knees bent.
Hold a medicine ball with both hands against your chest, elbows bent and pointing out to the sides.
Have a partner stand nearby to catch and return the ball, or set up so you can catch it safely on the way back down.
Choose a ball weight you can press with real speed, not the heaviest one you can lift slowly and carefully.
execution: Press the ball straight up off your chest as explosively as you can.
Let go of the ball at full extension so it leaves your hands and travels upward.
Track the ball with your eyes and get your hands back up to catch it as it comes down.
Absorb the catch by letting your elbows bend back toward your chest before resetting for the next throw.
formCues: Throw straight up, not toward your face or off to one side.
Fully extend your arms at release instead of pushing from a partial bend.
Catch softly by bending your elbows on impact rather than catching with stiff arms.
breathing: Exhale sharply as you throw the ball, and take a full, relaxed breath while you reset before the next rep, so you start each new throw from a calm, controlled state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pushing the ball instead of throwing it, so it barely leaves your hands.
commonMistakes.correction: Commit to a full release at the top of the press so the ball actually travels upward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching the ball with locked elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your elbows bend on the catch to absorb the impact instead of taking the full force through straight arms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing from a position where the shoulder blades are not in contact with the floor or bench.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper back pinned to the surface beneath you so the throw comes from your arms and chest, not from your shoulders lifting off the pad.

programmingNotes: This is a power drill, so keep sets short, 5 to 8 throws, with full recovery between sets rather than grinding through high reps.
It fits well early in a session as part of a power or plyometric warm-up, before your muscles are fatigued from heavier pressing work.
Two to three sessions a week is fine, since the load is light and the main demand is on speed and coordination rather than heavy mechanical tension.
Increase the ball weight only once your current one flies up with real speed and control, rather than chasing a heavier ball before your throwing mechanics are consistent.
safetyNotes: Use a medicine ball with some give to it, not a hard rubber ball that could injure your hands or face on a bad catch.
Make sure you have clear space above and around you before throwing, especially if you are indoors.
Warm up your shoulders and chest with a few lighter presses before loading your first explosive set of throws.

faq.question: How many reps should I do for supine chest throws?
faq.answer: Five to eight explosive throws per set is plenty, since the goal is speed and power, not endurance.

faq.question: Do I need a partner for this exercise?
faq.answer: A partner makes it easier and safer to catch the ball, but you can also do it solo if you can reliably get your hands back up in time to catch it yourself.

faq.question: What muscles does the supine chest throw work?
faq.answer: It mainly trains your triceps, with your chest and shoulders assisting the same way they do in a bench press.

faq.question: What can I use instead of a medicine ball?
faq.answer: A standing medicine ball chest pass against a wall trains similar pressing power if lying down is not practical, though it loses the overhead catch element.

faq.question: Is the supine chest throw the same as a plyometric bench press?
faq.answer: They train the same explosive pressing quality, but the supine chest throw uses a ball you actually release into the air, while a plyometric bench press keeps the bar in your hands and claps or resets quickly after a brief loss of contact.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Floor Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same lying pressing muscles without needing a ball or a catching partner, though without the explosive release.

easierVariations.name: Medicine Ball Chest Pass
easierVariations.reason: A standing, controlled pass is an easier way to learn the explosive pressing pattern before adding the lying position and catch.

harderVariations.name: Plyo Push-up
harderVariations.reason: Trains the same explosive pressing power but through your full bodyweight instead of a ball, raising the demand once the throw feels easy.

summary: This stretch has you sit on one chair with one leg propped straight out on another surface in front of you, then lean forward from your hips to stretch the back of that leg. It's an easy option for anyone who spends a lot of time sitting, since it only needs two chairs or a chair and a low surface, and it targets the hamstring without needing to get down on the floor.
whyItWorks: Straightening your knee and propping your heel up puts your hamstring on stretch right away, since that muscle crosses both your hip and your knee and lengthens most when both joints extend at once. Leaning forward from your hips adds more length on top of that by increasing the angle at your hip joint, while your adductors get a light stretch too since your leg sits slightly rotated as you reach forward. Because you're supported by a chair the whole time, your lower back and standing leg don't have to work to hold you up, which lets you focus the stretch on your hamstring instead of on balance.
setup: Sit toward the front edge of a chair with good posture.
Extend one leg straight out, resting your heel on another chair or a low, stable surface in front of you.
Keep your other foot flat on the floor for support.
execution: Flex your extended foot so your toes point up toward the ceiling.
Hinge forward from your hips, keeping your back relatively straight rather than rounding it.
Lean forward until you feel a stretch along the back of your extended leg.
Hold the position, breathing steadily, without bouncing.
Return to upright slowly, then switch legs and repeat.
formCues: Hinge from your hips, don't just round your upper back forward.
Keep the extended knee straight but not locked hard.
Flex your foot to add a bit more stretch through your calf and hamstring.
Ease into the stretch slowly instead of dropping into it.
breathing: Breathe slowly and evenly while you hold the stretch, letting each exhale help you settle a little further into the position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding your upper back forward instead of hinging from your hips.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and fold from your hip joint, the stretch should come from leg and hip position, not a slumped spine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bouncing to try to reach further into the stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Hold the position still and let the muscle relax over a few breaths instead of pulsing into it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Locking the extended knee hard to feel more of a pull.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a soft, straight knee. Locking it doesn't deepen the stretch and adds unnecessary strain on the joint.

programmingNotes: This is a gentle static stretch, so it's suitable daily, especially if you sit for long stretches during the day.
Hold each side for 20 to 30 seconds, two or three times, rather than one long forced hold.
It fits well after a workout when your muscles are warm, or as a break during a desk-heavy day.
safetyNotes: Use a stable chair or surface that won't slide or tip while your leg rests on it.
Stretch to a point of mild tension, not sharp pain.
Skip or ease off this stretch if you have a recent hamstring injury until it's healed.

faq.question: How long should I hold the chair leg extended stretch?
faq.answer: 20 to 30 seconds per leg, repeated two or three times, is a good target. Gentle and repeated works better than one long, forced hold.

faq.question: What if I only have one chair?
faq.answer: The hamstring stretch done standing, or the seated floor hamstring stretch, target the same muscle without needing a second surface to prop your leg on.

faq.question: Why do I feel this stretch in my calf too?
faq.answer: Flexing your foot toward your shin adds tension through your calf along with your hamstring, since both muscles cross the back of your leg. That's expected and not a sign of doing it wrong.

faq.question: Can this stretch help lower back tightness?
faq.answer: Tight hamstrings can pull on your pelvis and contribute to a stiff-feeling lower back, so loosening them may help indirectly. It isn't a treatment for back pain, so see a professional if the discomfort is sharp or ongoing.

alternatives.name: Hamstring Stretch
alternatives.reason: Targets the same hamstring lengthening from a standing position, useful when you only have one chair or none at all.

alternatives.name: Seated Floor Hamstring Stretch
alternatives.reason: Delivers a similar forward-reach hamstring stretch from the floor instead of a chair, handy if you'd rather sit down for it.

harderVariations.name: Leg-Up Hamstring Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Raises the working leg higher than a chair allows, deepening the same forward-reach hamstring stretch once the chair version feels easy.

summary: The wide-grip lat pulldown has you pull a cable attachment down from overhead to roughly chest height using a grip wider than shoulder width. It's one of the most accessible ways to train the lats, since the cable controls the resistance path and lets you work the same overhead pulling pattern as a pull-up without needing to lift your full bodyweight. It suits anyone building toward a pull-up, or anyone who wants to train back width on a cable machine.
whyItWorks: Pulling a bar down from overhead to your chest mirrors the same joint action as a pull-up: your shoulder extends and your elbow bends as the lats, the body's widest back muscle, drag your arm down and back. A grip wider than shoulder width puts your shoulders into a position closer to full abduction at the top of the movement, which lengthens the lats more at the start of the pull and asks them to do more of the work rather than letting the biceps take over early. Because a cable machine sets the resistance direction for you, it's a more forgiving way to build that same pulling strength than a free-hanging pull-up, where your whole bodyweight has to move through the same range. That makes it a natural stepping stone for anyone still working toward their first strict pull-up, and a useful volume tool even after they get there.
setup: Sit at the lat pulldown machine with your thighs secured under the pads.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder width, with your palms facing away from you.
Lean back very slightly from vertical and pull your shoulder blades down and back before the first rep.
Keep your chest lifted and your core braced through the set.
execution: Pull the bar down by driving your elbows toward your hips, not by curling with your arms.
Bring the bar down to roughly chest or upper chest height.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the bottom of the pull.
Let the bar rise back up under control, following the same path back to the start.
Stop the ascent once your arms are fully extended but before your shoulders shrug up toward your ears.
Reset your shoulder position before the next rep.
formCues: Drive your elbows down and back, don't curl with your arms.
Keep your chest up, don't lean back excessively to cheat the pull.
Pull the bar to your chest, not past it toward your stomach.
Control the ascent instead of letting the weight yank your arms up.
breathing: Exhale as you pull the bar down to your chest, inhale as you let it rise back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso back dramatically to use body weight instead of the lats to move the bar.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your lean minimal and let your back muscles do the pulling, not your body swinging backward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pulling the bar down to the stomach instead of the chest.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the pull once the bar reaches roughly chest height, which keeps the shoulder in a safer position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulders shrug up toward the ears at the top of the movement.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your shoulder blades pulled down and set before each rep, rather than letting the weight pull your shoulders up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the weight snap the arms straight at the top instead of controlling the stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Let the bar rise at a controlled pace, keeping light tension in the lats even at full arm extension.

programmingNotes: Because a cable guides the resistance path, this is gentler on the joints than a loaded barbell pull, so two sessions a week fits comfortably into most back-training splits.
Three or four sets of 10 to 12 reps builds a solid foundation of pulling strength and back width.
Use it earlier in a back session if pull-ups aren't available yet, or later as a volume builder after rows and pull-ups.
Increase the weight only once you can complete every rep by driving the elbows down rather than leaning back further to move the bar.
safetyNotes: Keep the movement controlled on the way up. Letting the bar yank your arms overhead at speed puts unnecessary stress on the shoulder joint.
If a wide grip bothers your shoulders, a slightly narrower grip trains the same muscles with less joint stress.
Set the thigh pads snugly before the first rep, since sliding off the seat mid-set can pull you into an awkward pulling angle.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for wide-grip lat pulldowns?
faq.answer: Three or four sets of 10 to 12 reps is a solid range for building back width and pulling strength.

faq.question: Wide-grip lat pulldown vs close-grip, what's the difference?
faq.answer: A wide grip stretches the lats more at the top and emphasizes back width. A close grip shortens that stretch and tends to bring the biceps and middle back into the pull more.

faq.question: What can I do at home without a lat pulldown machine?
faq.answer: A resistance band anchored overhead lets you train the same wide, overhead pulling pattern without a cable machine.

faq.question: Why can't I feel my lats working on lat pulldowns?
faq.answer: That's usually a sign the arms are doing most of the pulling. Focus on driving the elbows down and back before the hands even start moving, which shifts the work onto the lats.

alternatives.name: Resistance Band Lat Pulldown
alternatives.reason: Trains the same wide overhead pull without needing a cable machine, useful for a home setup.

easierVariations.name: Close-Grip Front Lat Pulldown
easierVariations.reason: A narrower grip that's generally easier to control and puts less strain on the shoulders while you learn the pulling pattern.

harderVariations.name: Full Range-Of-Motion Lat Pulldown
harderVariations.reason: Extends the top and bottom of the pull further, demanding more control through a longer range than the standard version.

summary: The barbell shoulder press asks you to drive a loaded bar straight overhead from your shoulders, using your deltoids as the prime mover with your chest and triceps finishing the lockout. Done standing, it also demands real core and glute bracing to keep the bar path straight without arching your lower back. It's a foundational overhead push for anyone building real pressing strength, not just shoulder size.
whyItWorks: Pressing a loaded bar overhead is one of the few common lifts that trains the shoulder through a full range against gravity in the vertical plane, rather than the horizontal plane a bench press works. Because the bar has to travel in a straight line from your shoulders to overhead, your core and glutes have to brace hard to stop your lower back from arching to help the bar up, which is why a strict barbell press builds real trunk stability alongside shoulder strength.
setup: Set the bar in a rack at roughly collarbone height and take a grip just outside shoulder width.
Unrack the bar onto your front shoulders, elbows slightly in front of the bar.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, glutes and abs braced before the first press.
execution: Press the bar straight up, moving your head back slightly to let it pass your face.
Push your head through once the bar clears your forehead, so it finishes directly over your ears.
Lock your elbows out fully at the top without shrugging to finish the lockout.
Lower the bar back to your shoulders under control, following the same straight path.
Keep your ribs down and glutes squeezed the entire rep to avoid arching.
Reset your brace before each rep rather than resetting only between sets.
formCues: Bar travels in a straight line, head moves out of the way and back through.
Glutes and abs braced hard, no arching the lower back to help the press.
Lockout finishes with the bar over your ears, not out in front.
Elbows track slightly forward at the bottom, not flared straight out to the sides.
breathing: Take a breath and brace before you press, exhale as you lock out overhead, then reset your breath before lowering.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to help drive the bar overhead.
commonMistakes.correction: Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs before every rep so the press comes from your shoulders, not a lower back arch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing the bar out in front of your face instead of straight up, ending with it too far forward at lockout.
commonMistakes.correction: Move your head back just enough to let the bar pass, then push your head through so the bar finishes over your ears.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the traps to finish the last few inches of the lockout.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on locking the elbows straight rather than shrugging the shoulders upward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flaring the elbows straight out to the sides at the bottom.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the elbows tracking slightly in front of the bar for a stronger starting position.

programmingNotes: This is a heavy, demanding overhead press, so once a week as your main shoulder lift is a sensible default unless it's carrying your only pressing volume that week.
Three or four sets of 5 to 8 reps builds strength well; higher reps in the 8 to 12 range works better once you're pressing for size.
Because it demands full-body bracing, program it early in a session rather than after a fatiguing lower body lift.
A lighter seated or dumbbell press on a second day can round out shoulder volume without adding another heavy bar session.
safetyNotes: Warm up your shoulders and thoracic spine before loading the bar; a stiff upper back often shows up as an arched lower back under the press.
Use a rack you can bail out of, or press from the floor of a rack, rather than pressing a weight you can't safely lower if a rep fails.

faq.question: How many sets of barbell shoulder press should I do?
faq.answer: Three or four sets of 5 to 8 reps for strength, or 8 to 12 reps if you're training more for size, covers most goals well.

faq.question: Barbell shoulder press vs dumbbell shoulder press, which is better?
faq.answer: The barbell lets you load more total weight and gives a fixed bar path to groove, which is useful for building raw pressing strength. Dumbbells let each shoulder move independently and demand more stabilization. Many lifters use the barbell as their main strength lift and dumbbells as accessory volume.

faq.question: How often should I do barbell shoulder presses?
faq.answer: Once a week as a dedicated, heavy session is usually enough recovery time, since it's a demanding compound lift. If it's your only overhead pressing that week, you can add a lighter second session.

faq.question: Why does my lower back hurt during barbell shoulder presses?
faq.answer: That's almost always an arch forming to help drive the bar up. Lower the weight, squeeze your glutes, and brace your abs hard before every rep until the arch disappears.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Shoulder Press
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead push with independent arm movement, useful on days a barbell rack isn't free.

easierVariations.name: Seated Dumbbell Press
easierVariations.reason: Removes the standing balance and full-body bracing demand, letting you focus on the pressing pattern with a lighter, more forgiving load.

harderVariations.name: Push Press
harderVariations.reason: Adds a leg drive to move heavier loads overhead once the strict press feels solid, building explosive power on top of raw strength.

summary: The front leg raise swings a straight leg forward and up, stretching the hamstrings on the way as the leg rises against gravity. It's a dynamic stretch rather than a strength move, useful for waking up tight hamstrings before a run, a leg session, or any activity that needs a long, free stride. It suits anyone, from complete beginners to trained athletes, since the only real requirement is enough balance to stand on one leg briefly.
whyItWorks: Raising a straight leg to the front lengthens the hamstrings, the muscle group running down the back of the thigh, right as your hip flexes. Doing that lengthening with motion, rather than holding a static stretch, warms the tissue and takes it through a range closer to what walking, running, or kicking actually demand. Repeating the raise for several reps also builds a small amount of control and balance in the standing leg, since it has to hold you steady while the other leg swings.
setup: Stand next to a wall or sturdy chair if you want light support for balance.
Wear shoes or bare feet on a surface with good grip.
Stand tall with your weight on one leg before starting the swing.
execution: Stand with feet together, holding a wall or chair lightly if needed.
Keeping your leg straight, raise one leg forward and up as high as comfortable.
Feel the stretch build through the back of the raised leg's thigh.
Lower the leg back down with control rather than letting it drop.
Repeat for the set, then switch to the other leg.
formCues: Keep the raised leg straight the whole time, don't bend the knee to cheat the height.
Rise only as high as you can without rounding your lower back.
Move with control, not a fast kick.
breathing: Exhale as the leg rises, inhale as it lowers back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the knee to fake a higher raise.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep the leg straight and accept a lower range; a straight leg at hip height stretches more than a bent leg swung to the chest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to gain a few extra inches.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the raise the moment your lower back starts to round; the stretch belongs in the hamstring, not the spine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Kicking the leg up fast like a strike.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down; a controlled raise stretches the muscle safely, a fast kick just tests your balance.

programmingNotes: Ten to fifteen slow reps per leg works well as part of a warm-up before running, squatting, or any leg-dominant session.
As a gentle mobility drill, doing it daily is fine, especially before activity, since it costs the body almost nothing to recover from.
It also works as a cooldown, done slower and held a beat longer at the top, once muscles are already warm.
safetyNotes: Hold a wall or chair if your balance feels shaky; a fall risk isn't worth skipping the support.
Stop well short of pain; a stretch should feel like tension building, never like a sharp pull.

faq.question: How long should I hold a front leg raise?
faq.answer: You don't need to hold it at all, this is a dynamic stretch. Raise and lower for 10 to 15 reps per leg instead of pausing at the top.

faq.question: Is front leg raise a warm-up or a cool-down move?
faq.answer: Both work. Faster, lighter reps before a workout wake the hamstrings up; slower reps with a longer pause at the top after a workout help them relax.

faq.question: Can I do front leg raises without a wall or chair?
faq.answer: Yes, if your balance is steady. Standing near support just gives you a safety net while you find your rhythm.

faq.question: Why do my hamstrings feel tight during front leg raises?
faq.answer: Tight hamstrings are extremely common, especially with a lot of sitting. That tightness is exactly what this stretch is meant to ease over repeated sessions, not fix in one go.

alternatives.name: Seated Floor Hamstring Stretch
alternatives.reason: Reaches the same hamstring stretch from a seated position, useful when standing balance isn't an option.

easierVariations.name: Hamstring Stretch
easierVariations.reason: Trades the standing balance challenge for a simpler static stretch you can hold while seated or lying down.

harderVariations.name: Leg-Up Hamstring Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Rests the leg on an elevated surface for a longer, held stretch once the dynamic swing feels easy.

summary: The cable incline triceps extension isolates your triceps by locking your upper arm in place on an incline bench while your forearm swings through an overhead arc against cable resistance. Lying on an incline changes the angle of pull compared to a flat or standing version, keeping tension on your triceps even when your arm is fully bent behind your head. It's a solid pick for anyone chasing arm size or lockout strength who wants a joint-friendly way to load the triceps through a longer stretch than a pushdown allows.
whyItWorks: Your triceps' only job is straightening your elbow, and the incline bench pins your upper arm against the pad so your shoulder can't help swing the weight, leaving your triceps to do all the work. Because the cable pulls from behind and above you rather than straight down like a dumbbell would, tension stays on the muscle even at the bottom of the movement, where your elbow is bent the most and a free weight would normally go slack. That extended time under tension at the lengthened position is where a lot of triceps growth work happens, since the long head of the triceps crosses your shoulder joint and gets a deeper stretch overhead than it does during a pushdown. The incline angle also takes some of the shoulder strain out of the overhead position compared to doing the same extension standing straight up.
setup: Set an incline bench in front of a low cable pulley fitted with a rope or single handle.
Lie back on the bench and grip the attachment with both hands overhead, elbows bent and pointing toward the ceiling.
Pin your upper arms close to your ears so only your forearms will move.
Take the slack out of the cable before your first rep.
execution: Keeping your upper arms still, straighten your elbows and extend the attachment up and slightly forward.
Squeeze your triceps hard at full extension without locking out violently.
Lower the attachment back behind your head under control, letting your elbows bend fully.
Stop the descent once you feel a full stretch, without letting your upper arms drift away from your ears.
Repeat for the full set without resting at the bottom.
formCues: Elbows stay pinned by your ears the whole set.
Extend until straight, then squeeze.
Lower slow enough to feel the stretch, not to drop.
Let your forearms do the moving, not your shoulders.
breathing: Exhale as you straighten your elbows and extend the weight overhead, and inhale as you lower it back into the stretch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows flare out or drift forward away from the ears during the extension.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms pinned in place and isolate the movement to your forearms swinging around a fixed elbow.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using momentum from the shoulders to help push through a heavy rep.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and use a lighter weight until your triceps alone can complete the full range.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutting the bottom of the range short to avoid the deeper stretch.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower under control until your elbows are fully bent, since that stretched position is where much of the benefit comes from.

programmingNotes: As an isolation move with a long stretch, three sets of ten to twelve reps placed after your main pressing work lets you load the triceps without pre-fatiguing your lockout strength.
It pairs well with a chest or shoulder day, since those sessions already warm up the triceps through pressing before this move finishes them off directly.
Twice a week is a reasonable ceiling for most lifters, since the deep stretch position can leave the triceps sorer than a standard pushdown, especially early on.
safetyNotes: Start with a light weight until you know how your elbows respond to the deep overhead stretch.
Keep the incline angle moderate rather than fully upright if you feel strain in your shoulders at the bottom of the range.
Stop short of a hard, painful stretch at the bottom, a comfortable deep stretch is the goal, not the limit of your range.

faq.question: How many sets and reps of cable incline triceps extensions should I do?
faq.answer: Three sets of ten to twelve reps works well for most lifters, done after your main pressing exercise so your triceps are already warm but not yet exhausted.

faq.question: Can I train triceps overhead without a cable machine?
faq.answer: A resistance band anchored low or a single dumbbell held overhead can recreate the same stretch, and a standing towel triceps extension needs no equipment at all.

faq.question: How is this different from a regular triceps pushdown?
faq.answer: A pushdown loads your triceps mostly with your elbow at your side, while this incline version pulls from overhead, giving your triceps a longer stretch at the bottom that a pushdown can't reach.

faq.question: Why do my shoulders feel this more than my triceps?
faq.answer: If your elbows drift forward or your upper arms move during the set, your shoulders start sharing the load. Pin your upper arms against the bench and keep them still through the whole rep.

alternatives.name: Standing Overhead Barbell Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead triceps extension pattern with a barbell instead of a cable, useful in a free-weight area with no pulley available.

easierVariations.name: Standing Towel Triceps Extension
easierVariations.reason: Replaces the cable with a towel pulled overhead, letting you groove the same overhead elbow extension without any equipment at all.

harderVariations.name: Kneeling Cable Triceps Extension
harderVariations.reason: Removes the stable incline bench and puts you kneeling upright, adding a core-control demand on top of the same triceps extension pattern.

summary: Ankle circles have you lifting one foot slightly off the floor and rotating it in slow, controlled circles, first one direction and then the other. It's a simple mobility drill for the ankle joint and surrounding calf muscles, not a strength exercise, and it works well as a quick warm-up before running, jumping, or any lower-body training session.
whyItWorks: The ankle is a joint that moves in several directions at once, and most daily movement only uses a narrow slice of that available range. Rotating it deliberately through a full circle takes the joint through flexion, extension, and rotation together, which helps lubricate the joint and wake up the surrounding muscles before they're asked to work harder. Because the movement is slow and controlled rather than ballistic, it's a low-risk way to prepare the ankle for the sudden direction changes and impact that come later in a workout.
setup: Sit in a chair or stand holding onto something stable for balance.
Lift one foot slightly off the floor.
Keep your leg relatively still, letting the movement happen at the ankle joint.
execution: Rotate your foot in a slow, controlled circle, moving through the full available range.
Complete several circles in one direction.
Reverse direction and complete the same number of circles the other way.
Keep the movement smooth and unhurried throughout.
Switch to the other foot and repeat.
Avoid forcing the range beyond what feels comfortable.
formCues: Slow, controlled circles.
Full range, not a small wiggle.
Both directions, equal reps.
Leg stays still, only the ankle moves.
breathing: Breathe naturally and steadily throughout; there's no need to coordinate breath with this gentle movement.

commonMistakes.mistake: Moving too fast to actually cover the full range of motion.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow down significantly; the value of this drill comes from a deliberate, full circle, not from speed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only rotating in one direction and skipping the reverse.
commonMistakes.correction: Complete equal circles in both directions so the joint gets balanced mobility work.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the whole leg swing instead of isolating the movement at the ankle.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your knee and hip still, focusing the rotation entirely at the ankle joint itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forcing the range when the joint feels stiff or uncomfortable.
commonMistakes.correction: Work within a comfortable range and let it expand gradually over sessions rather than pushing through resistance.

programmingNotes: Do 10 to 15 circles in each direction per foot, as part of a warm-up before running, jumping, or lower-body training.
It also works well as a quick mobility break during a long day of sitting.
There's no need for dedicated sets beyond a warm-up context; this is a preparation drill, not a training stimulus on its own.
safetyNotes: The movement should feel like gentle mobility work, never pain; stop and reduce the range if anything feels sharp.
If you have a specific ankle injury or instability, check with a professional before adding new ankle mobility work.

faq.question: How many ankle circles should I do?
faq.answer: Ten to fifteen circles in each direction per foot is a reasonable amount, typically as part of a warm-up rather than a standalone workout.

faq.question: When should I do ankle circles?
faq.answer: Before activities that demand ankle mobility and stability, like running, jumping, or lower-body training. They also work well as a quick break during long periods of sitting.

faq.question: Do ankle circles help with ankle stiffness?
faq.answer: They can help the joint feel looser and more mobile in the short term by moving it through its available range. Persistent stiffness or pain is worth having checked by a professional rather than managed with mobility drills alone.

faq.question: Are ankle circles a warm-up or a stretch?
faq.answer: They're closer to a mobility drill than a static stretch. The joint moves continuously through a circle rather than holding one lengthened position, which is why they fit well as a warm-up rather than a post-workout cooldown.

alternatives.name: Calf Stretch Hands Against Wall
alternatives.reason: Targets the same lower leg with a static stretch instead of a mobility drill.

alternatives.name: Anterior Tibialis-SMR
alternatives.reason: Covers the front of the same lower leg with rolling pressure instead of joint rotation.

harderVariations.name: Standing Gastrocnemius Calf Stretch
harderVariations.reason: Moves from gentle rotation to a real weight-bearing stretch once the ankle joint feels warmed up.

summary: A plyo push-up is an explosive push-up where you push hard enough that your hands leave the floor at the top. It takes the strength you already have from a regular push-up and asks your chest, shoulders, and triceps to produce that force fast instead of slowly, building upper-body power instead of just upper-body strength.
whyItWorks: A regular push-up trains how much force your chest and arms can produce. A plyo push-up trains how fast you can produce it, since you have to accelerate your whole body upward hard enough to briefly leave the ground. That rate of force development carries over to anything that needs a quick, explosive push: a shove in a contact sport, catching yourself from a fall, or throwing a punch. It's also a landing drill: catching your body weight on bent elbows teaches your shoulders and core to absorb impact safely.
setup: Set up in a standard push-up position, hands under your shoulders and body in a straight line from head to heels.
Make sure you have clear space around your hands to land, and a firm, non-slip surface.
Brace your core so your hips don't sag before you move.
Start with a regular push-up or two to warm your shoulders up before going explosive.
execution: Lower into a push-up with control, same as a normal rep.
Push explosively off the floor, driving hard enough that your hands leave the ground at the top.
Let your elbows bend slightly to absorb the landing as your hands touch back down.
Immediately sink back into the next push-up rather than resetting between reps.
Keep your body in a straight line from your shoulders to your ankles on every rep.
Stop the set once your reps start slowing down or your hands stop leaving the floor cleanly.
formCues: Push like you're trying to launch off the floor, not just complete a rep.
Land soft with bent elbows, never locked out or flat-palmed.
Keep your hips level with your shoulders throughout, no sagging or piking.
Reset your brace for a split second between reps rather than chaining them sloppily.
breathing: Exhale sharply as you push explosively off the floor and inhale as you lower back down into the next rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing with straight, locked elbows.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your elbows bend slightly the instant your hands touch down, so your arms absorb the landing instead of your joints taking the full shock.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips sag or pike up during the explosive push.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep bracing your core through the jump portion, not just the lowering phase, so your body stays one straight line in the air.

commonMistakes.mistake: Grinding out extra reps once the hands stop leaving the floor.
commonMistakes.correction: End the set the moment the explosiveness fades; the whole point is power output, and slow, grinding reps at that point train something else entirely.

programmingNotes: Because this trains explosive power, low reps done fresh work better than high reps done tired; three to five sets of three to six reps with full rest between sets is a solid starting range.
Do plyo push-ups early in a session, right after your warm-up, while your nervous system is fresh enough to move fast.
Master 15 to 20 clean, controlled regular push-ups before adding the explosive version, since the landing demands real shoulder and core stability.
safetyNotes: Train on a surface with some give, like a mat or a gym floor, rather than concrete, since you're absorbing real impact through your wrists and elbows on every landing.
Stop immediately if you feel any sharp pain in your wrists on landing; a slightly bent-elbow, soft landing should feel like control, not a jolt.

faq.question: How many plyo push-ups should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five sets of three to six explosive reps, resting fully between sets, builds power better than high-rep sets. Once the explosiveness fades, stop that set rather than pushing through tired reps.

faq.question: Do I need to be strong to do plyo push-ups?
faq.answer: You need a solid base first. Being able to do 15 to 20 clean regular push-ups is a reasonable benchmark before adding the explosive, hands-off-the-floor version, since you'll be landing that same body weight through bent arms.

faq.question: Plyo push-up vs clap push-up, what's the difference?
faq.answer: They're the same movement at heart. A clap push-up simply adds a clap during the airborne moment as a way to check that your hands genuinely left the ground and had time to do something extra.

faq.question: Why do my wrists hurt after plyo push-ups?
faq.answer: That's usually a landing problem, not a strength problem: locking your elbows or landing flat-palmed sends the impact straight into your wrist joints. Focus on bending your elbows slightly the instant you touch down to let your arms absorb the shock instead.

easierVariations.name: Incline Push-Up
easierVariations.reason: Lowers the amount of body weight your arms have to move, a safer place to build pushing power before adding a full explosive floor push-up.

easierVariations.name: Push Up
easierVariations.reason: Builds the base strength and control this move assumes you already have, without the explosive, hands-off-the-floor landing.

harderVariations.name: Single-Arm Push-Up
harderVariations.reason: Trades explosive power for unilateral control, a much harder strength challenge once regular push-up patterns feel easy on both fronts.

summary: The one-arm medicine ball slam raises a medicine ball overhead to one side and drives it down into the floor with force, using your core and hip to generate the power rather than your arm alone. Because the ball starts and finishes off to one side, your obliques do real anti-rotation work holding your torso together through the whole motion. It suits anyone who wants an explosive, stress-releasing movement that doubles as rotational core training.
whyItWorks: A slam is a whole-body power movement disguised as an arm exercise. The real force comes from extending your hip and torso as you raise the ball, then reversing that extension hard as you drive the ball down, similar to the mechanics behind a swing or a throw. Because the ball travels up and down on one side of your body instead of straight overhead with two hands, your obliques and deep core muscles have to control the sideways pull on your spine through the whole rep, which is what makes the one-arm version a genuine core exercise and not just a shoulder movement.
setup: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, medicine ball on the floor to one side of you.
Pick up the ball with one hand and hold it near your hip.
Brace your core and pick a clear patch of floor in front of you for the slam.
execution: Raise the ball up and across your body toward the opposite shoulder, extending through your hip and torso as it rises.
At the top, reverse direction hard, driving the ball down toward the floor in front of you.
Let your hip and core lead the downward drive, with your arm following through rather than muscling the ball down alone.
Slam the ball into the floor with force, bending your knees slightly to absorb the motion as you finish.
Pick the ball back up and reset before the next rep.
formCues: Hip and core drive the slam.
Ball travels in one clean arc.
Knees soften as you finish.
Reset fully between reps.
breathing: Inhale as you raise the ball, exhale sharply as you drive it down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Slamming the ball mostly with the shoulder and arm instead of the hip and core.
commonMistakes.correction: Start the downward drive by snapping your hips and torso forward first, letting the arm follow that motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back sharply on the way down to add force.
commonMistakes.correction: Let your hips and knees bend to absorb the finish instead of folding through your lower back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a ball that's too light to slam with real intent, so the movement turns into a soft toss.
commonMistakes.correction: Pick a weight heavy enough that you feel real resistance on the way up, so the slam down has something to work against.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing too close to the slam spot and getting hit by the bounce.
commonMistakes.correction: Use a ball designed not to bounce, or leave enough space that a bounce won't reach your shins.

programmingNotes: Medicine ball slams use a light to moderate ball and short, explosive reps, so they fit well as a power or conditioning finisher rather than a heavy strength lift.
3 or 4 sets of 6 to 10 reps per arm is enough to train power without the reps turning sloppy.
Because the load is light, 2 or 3 sessions a week works well if you're using it for conditioning; keep it to once or twice if you're pairing it with heavier rotational core work.
Do it early in a session when you can still generate real power, since fatigued slams lose most of their point.
safetyNotes: Use a slam ball or dead-bounce medicine ball rather than a bouncy one, so it doesn't rebound back at your face or shins.
Keep the range and force moderate until you're confident in your footing and floor space.

faq.question: How many one-arm medicine ball slams should I do?
faq.answer: 6 to 10 reps per arm for 3 or 4 sets is a good range, since the movement is about power and intent rather than high volume.

faq.question: What size medicine ball should I use for slams?
faq.answer: Something light enough to raise overhead with control but heavy enough to feel real resistance, often lighter than the ball you'd use for a squat or press.

faq.question: Can I do medicine ball slams at home?
faq.answer: Yes, as long as you have a hard floor that won't be damaged and enough overhead and side clearance to raise and slam the ball safely.

faq.question: Why do slams help with stress, not just fitness?
faq.answer: The explosive, full-body effort and the loud finish give you a physical outlet for tension that a slower lift doesn't, which is part of why people often reach for slams on a rough day.

faq.question: Should I alternate arms on every rep or finish one side first?
faq.answer: Either works, but finishing one arm's full set before switching makes it easier to notice if one side is generating less power or losing control of the ball late in the set.

alternatives.name: Medicine Ball Full Twist
alternatives.reason: Trains rotational core power with the same ball when you don't have the ceiling height or floor space to slam overhead.

alternatives.name: Russian Twist
alternatives.reason: Trains a similar rotational core pattern with no equipment at all, useful if a medicine ball isn't available.

easierVariations.name: Overhead Slam
easierVariations.reason: Uses both hands to raise and slam the ball, cutting the anti-rotation demand on your core while you learn the overhead-to-slam timing.

summary: The scissors jump is a plyometric exercise where you jump from a lunge position and switch your legs in the air, landing in the opposite lunge, like the blades of a pair of scissors crossing. It trains your quads, glutes, and hamstrings to produce and absorb force quickly, building explosive lower-body power and coordination. It suits lifters who already move comfortably through a bodyweight lunge and want to add impact and speed to that pattern.
whyItWorks: A regular lunge trains your legs to produce force slowly and under control, but the scissors jump asks the same muscles to do it explosively, driving you off the ground and switching legs mid-air before landing in a fresh lunge. That combination of a powerful jump and a controlled landing trains your quads, glutes, and hamstrings to absorb force just as much as produce it, which is the demand that carries over to sprinting, cutting, and jumping in most sports. The alternating pattern also forces each leg to work independently, so it exposes and corrects side-to-side strength differences that a two-legged jump can hide. Your core also has to work overtime here, bracing against the rotation and shift in balance that happens every time you swap legs mid-flight, which is part of why this exercise tires you out faster than its short duration would suggest.
setup: Stand in a split stance with one foot forward and one foot back, both knees slightly bent.
Keep your chest up and your core braced.
Find a clear, flat landing space with enough room to jump without hitting anything.
execution: Dip down slightly by bending both knees, then drive explosively off the ground.
While airborne, switch your legs so your back leg comes forward and your front leg goes back.
Land softly in the opposite lunge position, absorbing the impact through your bent knees.
Immediately dip and jump again, continuing to alternate legs each rep.
formCues: Land softly and under control to confirm you're absorbing the impact through your legs.
Keep your front knee tracking over your foot, not caving inward, on every landing.
Keep your torso upright rather than leaning forward during the jump.
Use your arms to help drive the jump, swinging them the opposite direction of your legs.
breathing: Exhale as you drive up into the jump, and inhale as you land and reset for the next rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing stiff-legged instead of bending the knees.
commonMistakes.correction: Focus on landing softly with bent knees to absorb the impact, rather than letting your joints take the full shock.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the front knee collapse inward on landing.
commonMistakes.correction: Actively keep your knee tracking in line with your toes as you land in each lunge.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaning the torso too far forward during the jump.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your chest lifted and your core braced so the jump comes from your legs, not a forward lean.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the reps without resetting balance between jumps.
commonMistakes.correction: Take a brief moment to stabilize in each landing before driving into the next jump, especially early on.

programmingNotes: As a high-impact plyometric move, 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 10 reps per leg, with full recovery between sets, gets the power benefit without accumulating excess fatigue.
Program it early in a workout, right after your warm-up, when your legs are fresh enough to jump with good landing mechanics.
Because of the repeated jumping impact, 1 to 2 times a week is plenty; more frequent plyometric work raises the risk of overuse without added benefit.
safetyNotes: Master the bodyweight walking lunge with good knee tracking before adding the jump.
Land on a surface with some give, like a gym floor or grass, rather than bare concrete.
Stop the set if your landings start feeling unstable or your knees start caving inward from fatigue.
Wear supportive footwear that grips the floor, since a slip mid-jump is far riskier than during a standard lunge.

faq.question: How many reps of scissors jumps should I do?
faq.answer: 6 to 10 reps per leg for 3 to 4 sets is a solid starting point, since the explosive effort tires your legs faster than a slow lunge would.

faq.question: What's the difference between a scissors jump and a split jump?
faq.answer: They're essentially the same alternating jumping lunge pattern; both switch your legs in the air and land in the opposite lunge, just under slightly different names.

faq.question: Do I need to jump high?
faq.answer: No. Focus on switching your legs cleanly and landing softly rather than jumping for height; a controlled, moderate jump trains the pattern just as well and is easier on your joints.

faq.question: Can beginners do scissors jumps?
faq.answer: Only once you can perform a bodyweight walking lunge with good knee alignment. If that still feels unstable, build strength there first before adding the jump and landing impact.

alternatives.name: Split Jump
alternatives.reason: Trains the same alternating jumping lunge pattern.

easierVariations.name: Bodyweight Walking Lunge
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same alternating lunge stance without the jump and landing impact.

harderVariations.name: Knee Tuck Jump
harderVariations.reason: Adds a more explosive vertical jump that demands more power and coordination than switching legs in a lunge jump.

summary: The kettlebell one-legged deadlift has you hinging at the hips while standing on a single leg, holding a kettlebell in the opposite hand as your free leg extends behind you for balance. It trains the same hip hinge as a standard deadlift, but on one leg at a time, adding a real balance and hip stability demand on top of the hamstring work. It suits lifters who already move well through a two-legged hip hinge and want to build single-leg strength and stability.
whyItWorks: Standing on one leg removes the stable base a two-legged stance provides, so your hamstrings and glutes have to control the hip hinge while also managing balance through the standing leg and hip. Your lower back stays engaged isometrically to keep your spine in a neutral line as your torso tips forward, working harder to resist rotation than it would with two feet planted evenly. Because each side works independently, this movement also exposes and helps correct any strength or stability difference between your left and right hip.
setup: Stand on one leg holding a kettlebell in the opposite hand, with a slight bend in your standing knee.
Set your shoulders level and your core braced before you start hinging.
Pick a fixed point ahead of you to focus on for balance.
execution: Hinge forward at the hips, letting your free leg extend straight back behind you.
Lower the kettlebell toward the floor as your torso tips forward, keeping your back flat.
Keep your hips square to the ground rather than letting them rotate open.
Reverse the motion once you reach a range you can control, driving your hips forward to stand back up.
Return to a tall standing position with your free leg back under you before the next rep.
formCues: Hips stay square to the floor, don't let them rotate open.
Keep the kettlebell close to your standing leg on the way down.
Reach your free leg straight back, not out to the side.
Only go as deep as you can control without wobbling.
breathing: Inhale as you hinge forward and lower the kettlebell, exhale as you drive your hips forward to stand back up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the hips rotate open toward the kettlebell side.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep both hip points facing the floor throughout the hinge; think of your hips as headlights that stay pointed straight down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rounding the lower back to reach further down.
commonMistakes.correction: Stop the descent at the point where your back starts to round, even if that means a shorter range of motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending the standing knee too much, turning the hinge into a squat.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep a soft, mostly fixed bend in your standing knee and let the movement happen at the hip instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the rep and sacrificing balance for speed.
commonMistakes.correction: Slow the tempo down and treat each rep as a balance drill first, a strength exercise second.

programmingNotes: Three sets of six to eight reps per leg is a solid starting point, since balance tends to break down before the muscles fully fatigue.
Because this challenges coordination as much as strength, place it earlier in a lower-body session while you're not yet fatigued.
Build range of motion and control before adding weight; a wobbly heavy rep teaches your body less than a controlled light one.
safetyNotes: Practice near a wall or sturdy surface you can touch for balance while you're still learning the pattern.
Stop if your standing knee or hip feels unstable rather than pushing through a wobble; reset your stance and try again.

faq.question: What muscles does the kettlebell one-legged deadlift work?
faq.answer: Mainly your hamstrings, with your glutes and lower back working hard to control the hip hinge and stabilize your standing leg.

faq.question: How do I stay balanced during a single-leg deadlift?
faq.answer: Focus your eyes on a fixed point ahead of you, keep a slight bend in your standing knee, and move slowly. Balance improves with practice more than with any single cue.

faq.question: Should I hold the kettlebell in the same hand as my standing leg or the opposite hand?
faq.answer: Most people find holding it in the hand opposite your standing leg easier to balance, since the weight naturally counterbalances your extended free leg.

faq.question: How much weight should I use for a kettlebell one-legged deadlift?
faq.answer: Start light, sometimes even bodyweight only, until your balance and hip control are solid. This exercise rewards control far more than heavy loading.

alternatives.name: Stiff-Legged Dumbbell Deadlift
alternatives.reason: Covers the same hamstring-dominant hinge pattern on both legs, useful when single-leg balance isn't the focus of the day.

easierVariations.name: Romanian Deadlift
easierVariations.reason: Trains the same hamstring hip hinge on two stable legs, removing the balance demand while the pattern is still new.

summary: The low cable triceps extension has you stand with your back to a low pulley, hands overhead holding a rope or bar attachment, and extend your elbows to straighten your arms toward the ceiling. Routing the cable from behind and below keeps constant tension on your triceps through the entire range, including the fully stretched position at the bottom, which a dumbbell can't match once gravity stops pulling on it. It's a beginner-friendly way to isolate the triceps without needing a bench or a heavy bar.
whyItWorks: The triceps' main job is straightening the elbow, and it does that hardest when the arm starts in a deeply bent, overhead position, which is exactly where a low cable places the resistance. Because the cable pulls down and back rather than straight down like gravity does, your triceps stay under load even as your arms pass overhead, where a dumbbell extension would otherwise go slack. Your shoulders hold a static overhead position throughout, which is why this move also demands some shoulder mobility and control, not just triceps strength.
setup: Set a pulley to its lowest position and attach a rope or straight bar.
Face away from the machine, grab the attachment with both hands, and raise it overhead with your elbows bent.
Take a small step forward so the cable stays taut, and brace your torso so it doesn't sway with the pull.
execution: Start with your elbows bent, hands behind your head, upper arms close to your ears.
Extend your elbows to press the attachment up and slightly forward until your arms are straight.
Pause briefly at full extension, keeping your upper arms still.
Bend your elbows and lower the attachment back behind your head with control.
Stop the descent once you feel a full stretch across the triceps, without letting your upper arms drift forward.
Repeat without letting your torso rock to help the lift.
formCues: Pin your elbows next to your ears and leave them there.
Only your forearms should move.
Straighten fully at the top, don't stop short.
Keep your ribs down instead of arching to help the pull.
breathing: Exhale as you straighten your elbows, inhale as you lower back down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the elbows drift forward and down during the extension, turning it into a shoulder press.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your upper arms pinned next to your ears for the whole set, so only your forearms travel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back to add momentum to the lift.
commonMistakes.correction: Brace your core and keep your ribs stacked over your hips, using your triceps alone to move the weight.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping the extension short of straight arms, which trims off the hardest part of the range.
commonMistakes.correction: Push all the way to a full, straight-arm lockout every rep, then control the return.

programmingNotes: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps is plenty, since this is a single-joint isolation move rather than a heavy strength lift.
Program it after your main pressing work, once your triceps are already warm from compound pushing movements.
Because the load stays light to moderate and the joint involved is small, twice a week works for most people without extra recovery cost.
safetyNotes: If you feel sharp pain at the elbow rather than muscle fatigue, stop and lower the weight; a small, well-controlled range is safer than chasing a heavier stack.
Keep your shoulders down and away from your ears throughout; shrugging under the overhead position adds unnecessary strain to the neck and traps.

faq.question: How many sets and reps should I do for the low cable triceps extension?
faq.answer: Two or three sets of 10 to 15 reps is a sensible range, since this move is meant to isolate the triceps after your heavier pressing work rather than replace it.

faq.question: What can I do at home without a cable machine?
faq.answer: An overhead extension with a single dumbbell or a resistance band anchored under your foot copies the same overhead elbow-extension pattern without a cable station.

faq.question: Low cable triceps extension vs triceps pushdown, which is better?
faq.answer: Neither replaces the other; the overhead position loads the long head of the triceps harder through the stretch, while the pushdown loads the triceps more evenly with less shoulder demand. Many lifters use both across a week.

faq.question: Why do my elbows hurt during this exercise?
faq.answer: Elbow discomfort here is usually a sign the weight is too heavy for you to keep your elbows pinned still, or that you're locking out too forcefully at the top. Lighten the load and stop the lockout just short of hyperextending.

alternatives.name: Cable Rope Overhead Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Delivers the same overhead stretch on the triceps with a rope attachment that lets your hands split apart at the bottom of the movement.

alternatives.name: Standing Overhead Barbell Triceps Extension
alternatives.reason: Trains the same overhead extension pattern with a barbell when no cable station is free.

easierVariations.name: Triceps Pushdown
easierVariations.reason: Uses a high pulley pushing down in front of you instead of a low pulley overhead, a more stable path that's easier to control while you learn to keep your elbows still.

harderVariations.name: Standing Low-Pulley One-Arm Triceps Extension
harderVariations.reason: Trains one arm at a time from the same low pulley angle, demanding more shoulder stability and exposing any strength gap between arms.

summary: The dumbbell seated box jump starts you sitting on a low box or bench, dumbbells held at your sides, and asks you to jump straight up onto a taller box without any preparatory dip or swing. Starting from a dead stop removes the stretch and rebound your legs normally get from a quick countermovement, so this version is a pure test of how much force your quads and hips can produce from a standstill. It's an advanced plyometric exercise suited to lifters who already jump comfortably onto a box from standing and want to build raw starting power for sports like sprinting or jumping.
whyItWorks: A standing jump gets a real assist from the stretch-shortening cycle, the quick dip and rebound that lets your legs store and release elastic energy before you leave the ground. Starting seated eliminates that assist entirely, so your quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings have to generate force from a completely still position, which is a closer test of raw concentric strength than a countermovement jump. Adding dumbbells increases the total mass your legs have to accelerate off the box, so the exercise also builds strength through the same explosive pattern rather than just training jump height on its own.
setup: Sit on a low, stable box or bench with your feet flat on the floor and knees bent to about 90 degrees.
Hold a light dumbbell in each hand down at your sides.
Set a taller landing box directly in front of you, close enough to reach with a controlled jump.
Sit tall with your chest up and your weight balanced over your feet before jumping.
execution: From a completely still seated position, drive through your feet and jump straight up and forward onto the taller box.
Swing your arms forward as you jump to help drive the movement, keeping the dumbbells light enough to control.
Land softly on the box with bent knees, absorbing the impact rather than landing stiff-legged.
Stand up fully on the box to complete the rep before stepping back down.
Reset completely, letting your heart rate settle, before sitting back down for the next rep.
formCues: No dip or swing before jumping, start dead still.
Land soft, with bent knees, not stiff-legged.
Full stand on the box before stepping down.
Reset fully between reps, don't rush the next one.
breathing: Take a full breath before each jump, then exhale sharply as you drive up off the box.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rocking or leaning forward before the jump to build momentum from a seated dip.
commonMistakes.correction: Start each rep from a fully still seated position; if you need momentum to get off the box, the dumbbells are too heavy for this variation.

commonMistakes.mistake: Landing on the box with locked or nearly straight knees.
commonMistakes.correction: Bend the knees deeply on landing to absorb the impact, treating every landing like the most important part of the rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing a landing box that's too tall, forcing a scraped shin or a rushed, incomplete jump.
commonMistakes.correction: Pick a box height you can clear with room to spare; the goal is explosive power, not testing your maximum jump height.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stacking reps back to back without resetting, letting fatigue creep into the landings.
commonMistakes.correction: Rest fully between each jump. This is a power exercise, not a conditioning one, and tired legs land poorly.

programmingNotes: Three to five reps for two or three sets is plenty; this exercise trains explosiveness, not endurance, so more reps just add fatigue without adding power.
Once or twice a week is enough given how demanding this is on the joints and nervous system, with a full day of rest around it.
Do this early in a session while your legs are completely fresh, since tired legs both jump lower and land worse.
Rest close to a full minute or more between reps so each jump is close to your best effort, not a fatigued one.
safetyNotes: This is an advanced, loaded plyometric movement. Only attempt it once you can comfortably and confidently box jump from standing without dumbbells first.
Choose a landing box you can clear with margin to spare, and always step back down rather than jumping backward off the box.

faq.question: How many reps of seated box jumps should I do?
faq.answer: Three to five reps for two or three sets, with a full rest between each jump. This is a power exercise, so quality reps matter far more than a high total count.

faq.question: What box height should I use for a seated box jump?
faq.answer: Pick a height you can clear comfortably with room to spare, usually lower than the box you'd use for a standing box jump since you're starting without a dip. It's better to start too low than too high.

faq.question: Do I need dumbbells for this exercise?
faq.answer: No. A bodyweight seated box jump trains the same starting-strength pattern and is the right place to build confidence before adding any load.

faq.question: Why does this feel so much harder than a regular box jump?
faq.answer: Starting seated removes the small dip and swing your legs normally use to store energy before a jump, so all the force has to come from a dead stop. That makes it a tougher, more specific test of raw leg power.

alternatives.name: Freehand Jump Squat
alternatives.reason: Trains the same explosive concentric jump without needing a box or dumbbells.

easierVariations.name: Box Jump (Multiple Response)
easierVariations.reason: Starts from standing instead of seated and drops the dumbbells, letting you use a natural dip before jumping.

harderVariations.name: Weighted Jump Squat
harderVariations.reason: Removes the box, asking you to absorb your own landing under load instead of landing softly on an elevated platform.

summary: Back flyes with bands train the rear of your shoulders and the muscles between your shoulder blades, the exact areas that pressing and desk hours leave behind. Holding a band anchored in front of you, you sweep your arms wide like opening a pair of curtains against resistance. All you need is one band and a door or post, which makes it the easiest rear-delt work to do anywhere.
whyItWorks: The rear delts and mid back are pulling muscles, and this movement gives them a pull with nothing else in the way: arms nearly straight, band resisting, shoulder blades squeezing together at the end of every rep. Bands also pull hardest exactly where these muscles are strongest, at the widest point of the sweep, so the squeeze lands right where you want to feel it. Training this area balances all the pressing and sitting your week already contains, and shoulders that pull as well as they push tend to be shoulders that last.
setup: Anchor the band at chest height around a post, railing, or a door anchor, and check it's secure.
Hold one end in each hand and step back until the band is taut with your arms extended forward.
Stand tall, feet hip-width, knees soft, shoulders down away from your ears.
execution: Start with arms extended in front of you at chest height, palms facing each other.
Keep a slight, fixed bend in your elbows for the whole movement.
Sweep both arms out and back in a wide arc, like opening curtains.
Finish with your arms out to your sides and your shoulder blades squeezed together.
Hold that squeeze for a full second.
Return your arms forward with control, resisting the band the whole way back.
formCues: Open like curtains, wide and unhurried.
Elbows locked in a soft bend; no biceps curling.
Finish each rep by pinching a coin between your shoulder blades.
Shoulders stay down; ears and shoulders are not friends here.
breathing: Exhale as you sweep the band open, inhale as your arms return forward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears as the arms open.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your shoulder blades down before the first rep and pick a lighter band if they keep creeping up.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bending and straightening the elbows so the movement becomes a row-curl hybrid.
commonMistakes.correction: Freeze the elbow angle and move only at the shoulders; the arc should look identical every rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the band snap the arms back together between reps.
commonMistakes.correction: Take two slow seconds on the return; the resisted way back is half the exercise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Grabbing so much band tension that the torso twists and leans to help.
commonMistakes.correction: Step closer or use a lighter band; this movement rewards strict reps at modest tension, not heaving.

programmingNotes: Rear delts love volume: 3 sets of 15 to 20 reps with a one-second squeeze, two or three days a week.
Adjust difficulty by stepping further from the anchor or doubling the band, not by loosening your form.
It slots anywhere: warm-up before pressing, superset partner between bench sets, or finisher on an upper day.
A simple weekly balance check: for every pressing session, make sure something pulls, and this counts.
safetyNotes: Inspect the band for nicks and the anchor for slippage before each session; a snapping band at face height is this exercise's only real hazard.
Work in a smooth, pain-free arc; if the shoulder complains at the widest point, shorten the sweep.

faq.question: What do band back flyes work?
faq.answer: The rear deltoids on the back of your shoulders, plus the muscles between your shoulder blades in the middle back, with the triceps helping keep the arms extended. The band's pull is what your shoulder blades squeeze against.

faq.question: How many reps of band flyes should I do?
faq.answer: These muscles respond to higher reps: 15 to 20 per set, for 3 sets, with a deliberate one-second squeeze at the end of each rep. If 20 feels easy, add distance from the anchor before adding sets.

faq.question: Band back flyes vs face pulls: which is better?
faq.answer: They cover very similar ground. Face pulls add more rotation work and suit a cable station; band flyes need only a band and travel anywhere. Pick the one you'll actually do consistently, or alternate them week to week.

faq.question: Can band flyes fix rounded shoulders?
faq.answer: No exercise fixes posture by itself, but strengthening the rear shoulders and mid back gives you the muscle to hold a taller position comfortably. Pair the reps with breaks from long sitting and the effect adds up over months.

alternatives.name: Dumbbell Reverse Fly
alternatives.reason: The identical fly motion with dumbbells and a hinge, when you have weights instead of a band.

alternatives.name: Face Pull
alternatives.reason: Pulls toward the face on a cable to train the same rear delts and upper back with steady tension.

easierVariations.name: Band Pull Apart
easierVariations.reason: The same band and the same rear shoulders with a simpler setup: just stretch the band across your chest.

harderVariations.name: Barbell Rear Delt Row
harderVariations.reason: Rows the load into the same rear delts and mid back with a barbell, once band tension stops challenging you.

summary: The chin-up is a bodyweight pulling exercise where you grip an overhead bar with your palms facing you and pull your chin above it. It builds your lats, biceps, and forearms at the same time, and it suits anyone who wants a demanding upper-body pull that needs no equipment beyond a bar to hang from.
whyItWorks: Gripping the bar with your palms facing you puts your forearms and biceps in a stronger mechanical position than an overhand grip does, which is why most people can do more chin-ups than pull-ups with the same training background. That doesn't make it an easier exercise overall, since your entire bodyweight is still the resistance. Your lats do the bulk of the pulling work, dragging your elbows down and back, while your biceps and forearms handle the elbow flexion and grip, and your middle back helps stabilize your shoulder blades through the whole range.
setup: Grip the bar with your palms facing you, hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Hang with your arms fully extended and your shoulder blades set, not shrugged up around your ears.
Cross your ankles behind you and brace your core lightly before the first rep.
If you're using a step or box to reach the bar, remove it once you're hanging.
execution: Pull your elbows down and back, driving them toward your hips.
Keep your chest lifted and your body from swinging as you rise.
Continue pulling until your chin clears the bar.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower yourself under control until your arms are fully straight again.
Reset your shoulder blades at the bottom before starting the next rep.
formCues: Elbows drive down and back, toward your hips.
Chin clears the bar, not just your nose.
Full arm extension at the bottom, every rep.
Control the lowering phase, don't just drop.
breathing: Inhale at the bottom of the hang, then exhale as you pull yourself up toward the bar.

commonMistakes.mistake: Kipping or swinging the legs to build momentum instead of pulling with the upper body.
commonMistakes.correction: Keep your ankles crossed and your core braced so your body stays in a straight line; if you need momentum to finish a rep, that rep counts as assisted, not full.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping short with only the nose or forehead reaching the bar.
commonMistakes.correction: Aim for your chin to clear the bar. If you can't get there yet, use a band-assisted pull-up until the range is available.

commonMistakes.mistake: Letting the shoulder blades stay shrugged at the bottom of the hang.
commonMistakes.correction: Set your shoulder blades down and back before each pull; a shrugged bottom position skips the muscles that should be starting the rep.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rushing the lowering phase and dropping straight down.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower yourself over 2 to 3 seconds instead of releasing all at once; the descent builds strength just as much as the pull.

programmingNotes: Two sessions a week, with a day or two between them, is enough to build pulling strength without your grip and elbows staying sore into the next session.
If you can't yet do a full rep, spend those two sessions on band-assisted pull-ups and scapular pull-ups instead, and test a strict rep every few weeks.
Once sets of 8 clean reps feel manageable, add weight in small increments rather than chasing more reps at bodyweight.
Pair it with a pushing exercise like a bench or overhead press on the same day to keep your upper body balanced.
safetyNotes: Skip kipping or swinging versions if you're new to the movement; strict form protects your shoulders far better than momentum-driven reps.
If your elbows or wrists ache rather than your muscles feeling worked, check your grip width and drop the volume for that session.

faq.question: How many chin-ups should a beginner do?
faq.answer: If you can do any strict reps at all, start with 3 or 4 sets of as many clean reps as you can manage, twice a week. If you can't yet do one, band-assisted pull-ups and scapular pull-ups build the strength you need first.

faq.question: What's the difference between a chin-up and a pull-up?
faq.answer: A chin-up uses an underhand grip, palms facing you, which involves the biceps more and is usually easier to do more reps of. A pull-up uses an overhand grip and leans slightly more on the lats and upper back.

faq.question: Can I do chin-ups at home without a gym?
faq.answer: Yes, a doorway pull-up bar or a sturdy beam is all you need. If you don't have anywhere to hang from, a close-grip lat pulldown at a gym or a resistance band pulldown at home trains the same muscles.

faq.question: Why do my elbows hurt during chin-ups?
faq.answer: Elbow discomfort is often a sign of too much volume too soon, or a grip width that stresses the joint. Cut back your sets for a session or two and make sure you're getting full arm extension at the bottom of each rep.

faq.question: Do chin-ups build biceps as well as curls do?
faq.answer: Chin-ups load the biceps hard, especially through the bottom half of the pull, but a curl isolates the muscle through a longer, more controlled range without your lats and grip fatiguing first. Most lifters get the best of both by using chin-ups for pulling strength and adding curls when biceps size specifically is the goal.

alternatives.name: Close-Grip Front Lat Pulldown
alternatives.reason: Trains the same pulling muscles on a cable stack with adjustable weight, useful if a pull-up bar isn't available or full bodyweight reps aren't there yet.

easierVariations.name: Band Assisted Pull-Up
easierVariations.reason: A resistance band under your feet or knees takes over part of your bodyweight, letting you practice the same pulling path before you can do a full rep unassisted.

easierVariations.name: Scapular Pull-Up
easierVariations.reason: Builds the shoulder blade control the chin-up needs, using only a small range of motion so you can practice it even if a full rep is still out of reach.

harderVariations.name: Weighted Pull Ups
